pages.title: AD Penalty Clause in Nepal's PPA — Research Compilation
headings: AD Penalty Clause in Nepal's Standard PPA — Research Compilation
pages.excerpt: Research compilation on the Available Declaration (AD) penalty mechanism in Nepal's standard hydropower PPA. Based on direct PPA text analysis by Parajuli (2023) and ERC regulatory commentary.
pages.body_text: AD Penalty Clause in Nepal's Standard PPA — Research Compilation # Summary Research compilation on the Available Declaration (AD) penalty mechanism in Nepal's standard hydropower PPA. Based on direct PPA text analysis by Parajuli (2023) and ERC regulatory commentary. # Key data extracted Article 10.2 formula: Penalty = [0.80 × min(Contract Energy, AD) - (Actual + Scheduled Outage + Forced Outage + Force Majeure)] × Purchase Rate No curtailment exemption: Off-taker curtailment is not listed as excusable cause. NEA can order reduced output and simultaneously penalise for the resulting shortfall. Article 10.1(Ka) reserve margin: NEA can withhold up to 10% of peak-period Contract Energy as system reserve with zero compensation — and then still penalise for shortfall below 80%. No "deemed generation" provision: Unlike IFC model PPAs, Nepal's standard PPA does not treat off-taker curtailment as compensable deemed generation. # Limitations Research compilation, not the contract corpus itself. The page summarizes PPA-clause analysis and regulatory commentary; it is not a complete archive of signed PPAs. Clause-level focus. The source isolates Article 10.1/10.2 AD-penalty mechanics and does not quantify how often NEA actually applies penalties in practice. Curtailment interaction unresolved. The no-deemed-generation finding identifies a contractual exposure, but the source does not provide case-by-case adjudication history. Legal interpretation boundary. The analysis describes contract structure and regulatory implications; it is not a formal legal opinion. # Used By barahi-hydropower

Gaps we would like to close
pages.excerpt: Primary source for Nepal's off-grid and distributed solar story. AEPC ("Alternative Energy Promotion Centre") is the government institution responsible for rural electrification through renewables, standing alongside (not inside) NEA. It is the operator and financier of the solar
pages.body_text: AEPC Renewable Framework and Progress Reports Primary source for Nepal's off-grid and distributed solar story. AEPC ("Alternative Energy Promotion Centre") is the government institution responsible for rural electrification through renewables, standing alongside (not inside) NEA. It is the operator and financier of the solar-home-system (SHS) programme, community mini-grids, institutional rooftop systems, and the subsidy / concessional-finance channel that rural solar rides on. # What the source covers Periodic AEPC "Progress Report" / "Renewable Energy Framework" / annual yearbook documents cover: Cumulative SHS installations by district, province, and year Village-scale mini-grid portfolio (locations, capacity, operator) Institutional solar (schools, clinics, govt offices) Improved cookstove and biogas programmes (context, not solar) Subsidy structure and donor-financing channels Policy and regulatory framework for rural renewables # Key data points (approximate, 2021–2024 window) Cumulative SHS installed: ~1.1 million systems (as of ~2021, with additions through 2024) Cumulative SHS capacity: ~80–100 MWp Community mini-grids (operational): ~30 sites, ~1.1 MWp aggregate Institutional solar: ~25,000 sites (rural clinics, schools, telecom, govt offices), ~15 MWp aggregate Geography: Karnali, Sudurpaschim, and remote hill districts of Koshi / Gandaki / Bagmati dominate installations (see data-rooftop-shs-deployment) Subsidy structure: Tiered, with higher subsidies for remote/difficult districts; typical residential SHS subsidy ~30–50% of capex Annual new installations: declining as grid reach expands (grid displaces SHS on economic grounds above ~30 HH/km²), replacement/upgrade cycle becoming dominant # Why AEPC matters strategically AEPC's relationship with NEA is the most under-discussed institutional story in Nepal solar: 1. AEPC reaches households NEA cannot. Remote hill and Karnali districts are uneconomic for grid extension at current tariffs; AEPC's subsidized SHS is the only electrification pathway that fits those geographies. 2. AEPC is the operational home of community-level solar. No mini-grid, no micro-grid, no community solar cooperative in Nepal exists without AEPC technical backstop or finance. 3. AEPC is the natural host for the agrivoltaic programme. If agrivoltaics-and-land implies a lease-template law and a tariff adder, AEPC's rural footprint and cooperative linkages make it the natural programme administrator — not NEA. 4. AEPC integrates into the political coalition for solar. The rural-electrification constituency that has sustained AEPC for three decades is the same constituency that would vote for Terai agrivoltaics and Karnali off-grid scale-up. # Documents and subsources The "AEPC renewable framework" source is a composite of: AEPC Yearbook / Annual Progress Report (annual, typically one-year lag in publication) National Renewable Energy Framework (NREF) 2017 and revisions Renewable Energy Subsidy Policy 2016 and updates AEPC-published feasibility studies for specific mini-grid and institutional projects Donor project completion reports (ADB, WB, EIB, UNDP) that flow through AEPC programmes # Relevance to project This is the anchor source for: aepc — the institution entity rooftop-minigrid-offgrid — the off-grid / mini-grid track data-rooftop-shs-deployment — district-level SHS counts agrivoltaics-and-land — AEPC as natural programme host claim-solar-political-coalition-is-rural — the rural-electrification politics And it is the first place to look when the question is "how much solar is actually deployed in Nepal total — utility + rooftop + off-grid?", because NEA's 141.74 MWp DoED operating-plant total captures only the first track. # Data-quality notes AEPC yearbooks lag by ~1–2 years in publication. District-level data fidelity is high (AEPC subsidizes per-system; each install has a record) but aggregation into the public yearbook is lagged and sometimes incomplete. The 1.1 M cumulative SHS count includes decommissioned and replaced systems; the operational fleet is likely 700,000–900,000 at any time. Mini-grid reliability / continuous-operation data is uneven; some grids have been dormant between donor-project cycles. # Gaps we would like to close A proper 2024 district-level registry — ideal source for the map layer in data-rooftop-shs-deployment. Operational-status snapshot of the ~30 mini-grids (how many are actually running as of 2024?). AEPC–NEA integration agreement — the grid-edge protocol for when grid reaches an off-grid site. # Related aepc rooftop-minigrid-offgrid data-rooftop-shs-deployment eib-rural-solar-phase2 — donor channel running through AEPC wb-grid-solar-ee-project — adjacent donor channel (NEA-side) nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 — the complementary utility-side primary source

pages.title: Arun-3 Project Status & PDA Summary (2025)
pages.excerpt: Reference compilation for the 900 MW Arun-3 Hydroelectric Project — combining the 2014 Project Development Agreement (PDA) between Nepal and SJVN with 2024–2025 construction progress reports.
pages.body_text: Arun-3 Project Status & PDA Summary (2025) # Summary Reference compilation for the 900 MW Arun-3 Hydroelectric Project — combining the 2014 Project Development Agreement (PDA) between Nepal and SJVN with 2024–2025 construction progress reports. # Key Data Points Project basics Installed capacity: 900 MW (4 × 225 MW Francis turbines) Location: Phaksinda (dam) to Pukhuwa (powerhouse), Sankhuwasabha District Design: peaking run-of-river, 3.4 hours/day at full rated output Estimated cost: USD 1.6+ billion Annual energy: 3,924–4,019 GWh (design) Concession: 30-year Build-Own-Operate-Transfer (BOOT) Commercial structure (PDA, 2014) Developer: SJVN (Satluj Jal Vidyut Nigam), via subsidiary SAPDC Nepal's free-power share: 21.9% (~197 MW equivalent, royalty-free) Additional 10% offered to Nepal on commercial terms Remaining electricity exported to India via a new 400 kV DC line to Sitamarhi, Bihar Schedule and progress (December 2025) Construction start: 2018/19 Original COD target: March 2025 — not met SJVN applied for COD extension to September 2026; Project Review Panel formed to decide Physical progress: 74.61% (power generation side) Financial progress: 74.6% 400 kV cross-border transmission line: 58.3% physical progress # Relevance to Project Primary source for Arun-3's capacity, schedule, cost, and the Nepal–India free-power / export structure that makes Arun-3 a flagship example of India-developed, India-dispatched hydropower inside Nepal. # Limitations Self-reported data: SJVN cost and progress figures are self-reported; no independent audit is cited. Social impact gap: Social, resettlement, and environmental impact data is sourced from SAPDC's own materials, not independent assessment. Seasonal profile incomplete: The 3.4-hour/day peaking design is noted but the full seasonal generation shape is not provided. Grid absorption unknown: India-side grid absorption constraints for the exported power are not addressed. Schedule fluidity: COD target has already been missed; the September 2026 extension is under review and not assured. # Used By arun-3 # See also arun-3 hydro-geopolitics stranded-generation

pages.title: CARE Ratings Nepal — Sanima Mai Hydropower Credit Assessments
headings: CARE Ratings Nepal — Sanima Mai Hydropower Credit Assessments
pages.excerpt: CARE Ratings Nepal surveillance reports and rating rationales for Sanima Mai Hydropower Limited, a 22 MW private IPP on the Mai Khola (eastern Nepal). The Sanima Mai generation data provides one of the most complete multi-year time series for tracking Q-design discharge performan
pages.body_text: CARE Ratings Nepal — Sanima Mai Hydropower Credit Assessments # Summary CARE Ratings Nepal surveillance reports and rating rationales for Sanima Mai Hydropower Limited, a 22 MW private IPP on the Mai Khola (eastern Nepal). The Sanima Mai generation data provides one of the most complete multi-year time series for tracking Q-design discharge performance against contracted energy. # Key data extracted ## Generation vs contracted energy (Q40 design) Fiscal Year | Contracted (GWh/yr) | Actual (GWh/yr) | % of Contracted | ---|---|---|---| FY 2076/77 | 121.7 | 116.8 | 96.0% | FY 2077/78 | 121.7 | 107.1 | 88.0% | FY 2078/79 | 121.7 | 88.8 | 73.0% | FY 2079/80 | 121.7 | 103.4 | 85.0% | The declining trajectory from 96% to 73%, followed by partial recovery to 85%, exemplifies the hydrological volatility facing Q40-designed RoR plants on monsoon-dominated tributaries. Unlike Chilime's glacially-buffered Q65+ design, Sanima Mai's Q40 parameter produces higher variability and lower average delivery relative to contract. ## PPA structure Wet season: NPR 4.80/kWh (promotional, escalated to NPR 5.08 after 5 years) Dry season: NPR 8.40/kWh (escalated to NPR 8.89) 3% annual escalation for 5 years PPA year: 2010 # Limitations Single-project scope: Sanima Mai is one 22 MW RoR IPP on the Mai Khola; its generation and financial patterns are not representative of all RoR projects across Nepal's diverse river basins. Data recency: Generation data covers through FY 2079/80 only; more recent fiscal years are not included. The partial recovery to 85% may have continued or reversed. Q40 design context: The Q40 exceedance design is less conservative than the Q65+ designs common on glacially-fed rivers; hydrological variability observations apply to Q40-configured projects specifically. PPA vintage: The PPA terms described (2010, 3% escalation, NPR 4.80/8.40 wet/dry) are specific to this project's 2010-vintage PPA and do not represent current NEA PPA terms. Credit rating source: CARE Ratings surveillance reports prioritize creditworthiness metrics; they may not capture all technical or hydrological operating conditions in detail. # Used By No pages currently reference this source.

pages.excerpt: The Chilime Hydropower Company Limited (CHCL) annual report for fiscal year 2078/79 provides the verified primary-source data for Chilime's dual-tier PPA billing architecture and generation performance. Chilime is an NEA subsidiary (NEA retains 51% controlling stake), and its PPA
pages.body_text: Chilime Hydropower Company Limited Annual Report FY 2078/79 # Summary The Chilime Hydropower Company Limited (CHCL) annual report for fiscal year 2078/79 provides the verified primary-source data for Chilime's dual-tier PPA billing architecture and generation performance. Chilime is an NEA subsidiary (NEA retains 51% controlling stake), and its PPA (signed June 25, 1997) uses a categorically different billing architecture from modern IPPs. # Key data extracted ## Dual-tier billing architecture Category | Tariff (NPR/kWh) | FY2078/79 Volume (GWh) | FY2078/79 Revenue (NPR) | ---|---|---|---| Regular Energy | 8.17 | 133.24 | 1,088,000,000 | Excess Energy | 4.08 | 22.82 | 93,110,000 | Total | 7.57 (blended) | 156.06 | 1,181,740,179 | In FY2078/79, 85.4% of total generation (133.24 of 156.06 GWh) was classified as Regular Energy and billed at NPR 8.17 year-round — regardless of season. For comparison with modern private IPP tariff structures, see ppa-pricing. ## Generation overperformance Fiscal Year | Contracted (GWh/yr) | Actual (GWh/yr) | % of Contracted | ---|---|---|---| FY 2075/76 | 132.9 | 153.7 | 115.6% | FY 2076/77 | 132.9 | 146.3 | 110.1% | # Limitations Date gap: FY 2078/79 corresponds to 2021/22; more recent annual reports may show different generation or tariff treatment. Subsidiary scope: CHCL is an NEA subsidiary with a 1997 PPA; its billing architecture is not representative of post-2010 private IPP contracts. Single-plant view: Does not cover other NEA subsidiaries (e.g., Rasuwagadhi) or the broader IPP tariff matrix. No audited financial statements: Revenue and volume figures are as reported by CHCL, not independently audited in this document. # Used By No pages currently reference this source.

pages.title: DoED Licensing Directive 2075 — Hydropower Project Licensing
pages.excerpt: "विद्युत आयोजनाको अनुमतिपत्र सम्बन्धी निर्देशिका, २०७५" (Directive on Licensing of Electricity Projects, 2075 BS), issued by the Department of Electricity Development (DoED) in 2075 BS and now published by DoED as the fifth-amendment version.
pages.body_text: DoED Licensing Directive 2075 # Summary "विद्युत आयोजनाको अनुमतिपत्र सम्बन्धी निर्देशिका, २०७५" (Directive on Licensing of Electricity Projects, 2075 BS), issued by the Department of Electricity Development (DoED) in 2075 BS and now published by DoED as the fifth-amendment version. # Key provisions Q45 design discharge mandate: Projects must size their design discharge on Q45 exceedance ("Probability of Accident Q45 of Hydrological Time Series Data"). Earlier practices used Q40 or even Q25. Q80 exemption: Projects ≤1 MW for rural electrification may use Q80. Licence fee basis: DoED charges licence fees on Q45 basis but has allowed Q40 if a PPA is ultimately signed. Amended directive record: DoED's current public page identifies the directive as the fifth-amendment version, with fifth amendment date 2081/08/18. No climate adjustment requirement: DoED has not mandated climate-adjusted hydrological decrement factors in feasibility studies, despite draft ICIMOD guidelines. # Limitations Legal directive, not implementation record. The directive establishes licensing requirements; it does not show how consistently DoED applies them across individual projects. Hydrology rule specificity. The Q45 rule is explicit, but the source does not provide the hydrological datasets or statistical methods used by applicants. Climate-adjustment absence. The directive does not mandate climate-adjusted hydrology; that absence is a regulatory gap, not a quantified estimate of project risk. Amended text boundary. This source page now points to the current DoED publication page for the fifth-amendment version. Any claim about the original 2075 wording should be checked against the specific version cited. # Used By figure-index trishuli-galchhi

pages.body_text: Dudhkoshi Storage — NEA Proposal & Feasibility Record # Summary Reference compilation for the Dudhkoshi Storage Hydroelectric Project, covering the original 1980s ADB-supported feasibility, the 2021 restart with land acquisition, the 2024 NEA construction proposal to government, and the 2024–2025 financing conversations with AIIB. # Key Data Points Capacity: 635 MW (NEA / Investopaper) or 670 MW (ELC / Power Technology) — design basis varies between the two references Main powerhouse: 600 MW underground + 70 MW dam-toe ecological flow unit Annual energy (design): 3,377–3,444 GWh/year Dam: 200–220 m height at Lamidanda / Rabhuwaghat Headrace tunnel: 13.3 km, reservoir to Dhitung powerhouse Active reservoir volume: 1.581 MCM (per Power Technology) Estimated total cost: ~USD 2.2 billion (~NPR 308 billion) Districts: Okhaldhunga, Khotang, Solukhumbu Developer: Nepal Electricity Authority Financing track: AIIB sovereign funding proposed Schedule: construction from ~2027, commercial operation ~2031 (ELC / Power Technology estimate) Land: ~20,000 ropani private, ~162 households fully displaced, ~988 partially affected # Relevance to Project Primary source for Dudhkoshi's technical envelope, financing posture, social footprint and timeline — the three axes on which its buildability will actually be judged. Note: two self-consistent but divergent capacity numbers (635 MW vs 670 MW) are present in respected secondary sources; this page records both. # Limitations Capacity ambiguity: Two self-consistent but divergent capacity figures (635 MW vs 670 MW) exist across respected secondary sources; the design basis for each is not fully reconciled. Seismic gaps: Detailed seismic design basis is not covered despite the project's proximity to Everest-region fault systems. Reservoir-induced seismicity modelling is absent. GLOF integration unverified: The 2024 Thame GLOF in the same river system is directly relevant, but GLOF integration into the dam's design flood is not addressed. Self-reported data: Cost, schedule, and social impact figures are drawn from secondary compilations of NEA/AIIB materials, not independent audit. Pre-financing status: The AIIB sovereign funding is proposed, not committed; financing is not closed. # Used By dudhkoshi-storage # See also dudhkoshi-storage glof-risk storage-deficit

pages.title: EIB Promotion of Solar Energy in Rural and Semi-Urban Regions II
headings: EIB Promotion of Solar Energy in Rural and Semi-Urban Regions II (Phase II)
pages.excerpt: European Investment Bank line of up to EUR 8 million for the development of ground-mounted, grid-connected solar PV installations at four locations in Nepal. Implemented through the Government of Nepal with AEPC-facilitated site selection and NEA-grid interconnection.
pages.body_text: EIB Promotion of Solar Energy in Rural and Semi-Urban Regions II (Phase II) European Investment Bank line of up to EUR 8 million for the development of ground-mounted, grid-connected solar PV installations at four locations in Nepal. Implemented through the Government of Nepal with AEPC-facilitated site selection and NEA-grid interconnection. The second phase of a two-phase EIB solar programme; Phase I (earlier in the decade) financed smaller distributed and rural installations. Phase II is notable for being among the first EU-financing instruments for utility-scale grid-connected solar in Nepal, parallel to the World Bank Grid Solar & EE Project. # What the programme covers Credit size: up to EUR 8 million Instrument: EIB concessional loan to Government of Nepal Implementation partners: AEPC (site selection, community engagement), NEA (grid interconnection, off-take), Ministry of Energy (oversight) Target: four ground-mounted grid-connected solar PV sites Geographic focus: rural and semi-urban locations, likely in the Middle Hills region (site names to be verified from EIB project documentation and AEPC implementation reports) Time horizon: implementation expected 2023–2027 window # Key data points Specific figures require verification from the EIB project portal and AEPC implementation progress reports; the public-domain anchor facts: EUR 8 million credit ceiling Four ground-mounted sites Grid-connected (distinguishing it from Phase I distributed installations) Rural / semi-urban focus AEPC-implemented — this is critical: the programme runs on AEPC's cooperative-facilitation model rather than a pure-NEA tender, which makes it a test case for the AEPC-anchored solar-scaling thesis argued in rooftop-minigrid-offgrid and agrivoltaics-and-land # Why this source matters Three institutional-frame reasons: 1. It is a bridge between off-grid AEPC and utility-scale NEA tracks. Most financing either funds SHS/mini-grids via AEPC (track 3) or funds utility-IPP solar via NEA (track 1). EIB Phase II finances utility-scale grid-connected PV through AEPC — a rare institutional bridge. If it works well, it is a template for future donor programming. 2. Scale matches the agrivoltaic test case. EUR 8M / ~4 sites is ~EUR 2M per site ≈ NPR 280M per site ≈ 3–5 MWp. This is exactly the right size for early agrivoltaic pilot projects — big enough to matter, small enough that community co-operation can be worked out site-by-site. 3. Geographic focus on rural / semi-urban Middle Hills tests Zone C of the solar-resource-geography-nepal classification, where most Nepali household solar investment actually lives. # Parallel / adjacent programmes Programme | Donor | Channel | Track | ---|---|---|---| Grid Solar & EE Project (wb-grid-solar-ee-project) | World Bank | NEA | Utility | EIB Phase II (this page) | EIB | AEPC → NEA interconnect | Utility, AEPC-delivered | 960 MW Tender (nea-960mw-solar-tender) | Private IPP + debt | NEA | Utility | SREP Nepal | CIF / ADB / WB | AEPC | Off-grid | Karnali Off-grid Solar + BESS | WB | AEPC / NEA hybrid | Off-grid + grid edge | Biogas / improved cookstove programmes | Multi-donor | AEPC | Non-solar, non-electricity | # Documents and subsources EIB Project Page — eib.org/en/projects (search: Promotion of Solar Energy in Rural and Semi-Urban Regions II, Nepal) AEPC implementation monitoring reports — annual, AEPC internal with public summaries NEA Annual Report — references the programme in solar-projects rollup Ministry of Energy press releases — at site identification / inauguration milestones # Data-quality notes Site-specific details (exact locations, MWp per site, operator selection) have limited public-domain disclosure until AEPC / NEA implementation progress reports are published. The EUR 8M / four-site summary in the NEA FY 2024/25 annual report is the cleanest public reference anchor. Timeline ambitions and actual delivery pace may diverge — worth re-checking in FY 2025/26 NEA annual report. # Relevance to project Supporting source for: rooftop-minigrid-offgrid — AEPC as an institutional anchor beyond off-grid agrivoltaics-and-land — test-scale candidate for template pilots hybrid-siting-logic — mid-hill zone siting experiment aepc — institutional expansion of AEPC mandate claim-solar-political-coalition-is-rural — the rural-cooperative politics this programme rides on # Gaps we would like Publication of the four specific site locations and their MWp, district, developer, and COD target. AEPC implementation status reports at project-mid-point (likely 2026). Cross-reference with any agrivoltaic pilot element — if the EIB-AEPC line funds an agrivoltaic demonstration, it is the single most important test for the agrivoltaics-and-land thesis. # Related wb-grid-solar-ee-project — parallel donor programme (NEA-track) aepc-renewable-framework — institutional home nea-960mw-solar-tender — private-finance counterpart rooftop-minigrid-offgrid — the track this programme belongs to nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 — the public-disclosure anchor

pages.title: Global Solar Atlas (Nepal coverage)
headings: Why this source is the map-layer anchor
pages.excerpt: The primary satellite-derived solar resource dataset for Nepal's explorer map layer and the reference cross-check for every GHI / DNI number used elsewhere in the wiki. Provided as a free-to-use web-tile and downloadable-data service by Solargis under the World Bank Group ESMAP p
pages.body_text: Global Solar Atlas (Nepal Coverage) The primary satellite-derived solar resource dataset for Nepal's explorer map layer and the reference cross-check for every GHI / DNI number used elsewhere in the wiki. Provided as a free-to-use web-tile and downloadable-data service by Solargis under the World Bank Group ESMAP programme. Cross-validated against the in-situ wb-esmap-solar-resource-assessment pyranometer network (14 stations, 2015–2019), so the derived spatial maps carry ~±5% accuracy at station locations and somewhat wider error bands in untested high-mountain terrain. # What the source provides Global Horizontal Irradiance (GHI) — annual and monthly means at ~9 arc-second (~250 m) spatial resolution Direct Normal Irradiance (DNI) — same spatial detail Diffuse Horizontal Irradiance (DIF) — for tilted-array optimization Photovoltaic Electricity Output (PVOUT) — modelled output for a reference PV system at each location Optimal tilt angle maps Air temperature 2-m height climatology Tile-ready map service (XYZ / WMS endpoints for integration into web maps) # Nepal-specific findings GHI range across Nepal: ~3.8 to ~6.5 kWh/m²/day Highest GHI zones: trans-Himalayan rain-shadow (Mustang, Dolpa, upper Humla, upper Manang) — 5.8–6.5 kWh/m²/day Lowest GHI zones: Kathmandu Valley and east-facing mid-hill slopes — 4.2–4.6 kWh/m²/day Terai plains: 4.8–5.3 kWh/m²/day — broadly uniform with the north Indian plains PVOUT (specific yield): 1,500–1,800 kWh/kWp/year in trans-Himalayan, 1,350–1,500 in Terai, 1,150–1,350 in mid-hill — the yield hierarchy that translates GHI into MWh/MWp # Why this source is the map-layer anchor The wiki explorer's proposed layer (see data-map-inventory, data-nepal-solar-resource-zones) is built from Global Solar Atlas classifications, specifically: 1. Raw satellite GHI grid is classified into five zone bands (A, B, C, D, E) by threshold 2. Zone polygons are intersected with district boundaries for display 3. Map tiles are served directly from the Global Solar Atlas XYZ endpoint as an overlay basemap option in the explorer The attribution required by the Global Solar Atlas licence (CC BY 4.0) is included in the layer legend and the map credits. # Licence and data access Licence: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 (CC BY 4.0) Attribution: "Solargis, The World Bank Group" in any derived product Tile service: XYZ / WMS endpoints (see Global Solar Atlas documentation) Data download: National-level GeoTIFF layers available directly from the Global Solar Atlas download section (annual GHI, DNI, PVOUT) API: Solargis commercial API for higher-resolution or bespoke time-series (not needed for map display) # Cross-validation against ESMAP station data Global Solar Atlas vs measured (from wb-esmap-solar-resource-assessment): Station | GSA GHI | Measured GHI | Bias | ---|---:|---:|---:| Kathmandu | 4.4 | 4.3 | +2% | Pokhara | 4.5 | 4.5 | 0% | Nepalgunj | 5.2 | 5.1 | +2% | Simara | 4.9 | 4.9 | 0% | Biratnagar | 5.0 | 4.9 | +2% | Dhankuta | 4.5 | 4.4 | +2% | Jumla | 5.3 | 5.2 | +2% | Surkhet | 4.9 | 4.8 | +2% | Jomsom | 5.5 | 6.0 | −8% | Trans-Himalayan is the one zone where satellite systematically under-estimates GHI (Jomsom 8% bias). This is the most important caveat: for Mustang / Dolpa / upper Manang planning, field measurement should be used where available, and the "Zone A 5.8–6.5" range cited in the wiki is calibrated to measurement rather than to the satellite layer. # Related wb-esmap-solar-resource-assessment — the calibration source solar-resource-geography-nepal — the concept-page interpretation data-nepal-solar-resource-zones — the classification used in the map layer data-map-inventory — where this appears in the explorer irena-remap-nepal — independent scenario use of the same data

pages.title: Green Hydrogen Roadmap for Nepal
pages.excerpt: Strategic roadmap for producing green hydrogen from Nepal's surplus monsoon hydropower via electrolysis. Envisions an entirely new domestic industrial ecosystem absorbing stranded wet-season power.
pages.body_text: Green Hydrogen Roadmap for Nepal # Summary Strategic roadmap for producing green hydrogen from Nepal's surplus monsoon hydropower via electrolysis. Envisions an entirely new domestic industrial ecosystem absorbing stranded wet-season power. # Key Data Points Primary target: domestic green ammonia/fertilizer production (Nepal imports 100% of chemical fertilizers) A domestic green fertilizer plant could absorb up to 500 MW of continuous baseload power Replacing coal in Nepal's cement clinker production would require 227,743 tonnes of green hydrogen annually, needing 2,002 MW of dedicated hydropower Projected viable production cost: $2.15/kg by 2035 Government adopted Green Hydrogen Policy in 2024 with tax exemptions and regulatory framework Commercial pilots targeted for 2025–2027, industrial scale by 2035 # Relevance to Project Central to green-hydrogen-nepal and the demand-creation argument in domestic-led-hydro-strategy. Addresses stranded-generation by creating domestic demand for surplus monsoon power. # Limitations Roadmap, not committed project pipeline. The ammonia, fertilizer, and cement-substitution figures are planning scenarios rather than financed projects. Demand-creation assumptions. The roadmap assumes industrial offtake, electrolysis deployment, water availability, and fertilizer-market integration that are not yet demonstrated in Nepal. Cost trajectory uncertainty. The projected $2.15/kg production cost by 2035 depends on equipment-cost declines, power-price assumptions, and utilization rates. Policy still early-stage. The 2024 Green Hydrogen Policy creates a framework, but pilot delivery, permitting, and industrial procurement models remain unsettled. # Used By green-hydrogen-nepal

pages.title: ICIMOD HKH Glacier Change Summary
pages.excerpt: Regional glacier change assessment for the Hindu Kush Himalaya. Documents the scale and pace of glacier retreat affecting Nepal's river systems and long-term hydropower viability.
pages.body_text: ICIMOD HKH Glacier Change Summary # Summary Regional glacier change assessment for the Hindu Kush Himalaya. Documents the scale and pace of glacier retreat affecting Nepal's river systems and long-term hydropower viability. # Key Data Points Glacier area across HKH fell by ~12% between 1990 and 2020, with faster recent ice loss Nepal-specific inventories show substantial long-run glacier retreat Glacier retreat rate: ~0.4–0.5m water equivalent per year Under high-emission scenarios, 65% glacier volume reduction projected by 2100 # Relevance to Project Underpins peak-water concept and glof-risk. Relevant to koshi-basin (278 glaciers, 51 km³ ice). The 12% area loss and 65% volume projection are key numbers for the climate dimension of the public energy-system story, including the peak-water framing for the 2040–2070 build window. # Limitations Regional aggregate, not Nepal-disaggregated. The 12% area loss and 65% volume projection are HKH-wide figures; Nepal-specific glacier inventories may show different retreat rates and volume trajectories. 2023 publication window. Does not capture the most recent acceleration in glacier mass loss reported in subsequent ICIMOD and WMO assessments. Scenario-dependent projections. The 65% volume reduction figure is under a high-emission scenario; lower-emission pathways produce different outcomes. The source page does not differentiate between scenario bands. Glacier retreat rate is a regional average. The ~0.4–0.5m water equivalent per year varies significantly by sub-basin and elevation band. # Used By claim-climate-harder-not-easier peak-water

pages.body_text: ICIMOD Koshi Basin Programme # Summary ICIMOD's research programme on the koshi-basin, covering downstream impacts, agricultural dependency, and flood dynamics. Supports the geopolitical significance of Nepal's eastern river system. # Key Data Points Koshi basin supports >40 million people Contributes disproportionately high sediment loads to the Ganges system Koshi irrigates ~500,000–600,000 ha in Bihar The Koshi is known as the "River of Sorrow" in Bihar due to shifting course and catastrophic flooding # Relevance to Project Central to hydro-geopolitics and ganges-contribution. Also relevant to sediment-as-design-constraint given extreme sediment loads. . # Limitations Programme page, not a single technical report. The source summarizes ICIMOD's Koshi Basin Programme rather than providing one citable methods document. Directional sediment framing. The page supports high-level sediment and flood-risk context but does not provide design-grade suspended-sediment parameters. Downstream aggregate scale. Population and irrigation figures are basin-scale context; they do not allocate impacts by project, district, or season. Programme date ambiguity. The page uses a 2023 source date, but the programme spans multiple outputs with different publication dates. # Used By intervention-q-design-climate-adjustment

pages.title: ICIMOD Threats to the Koshi River Basin
headings: ICIMOD Threats to the Koshi River Basin
pages.excerpt: ICIMOD's 2018 outreach publication Understanding Sediment Management, focused on sediment dynamics, erosion, and environmental threats in the koshi-basin. Provides the evidence base for treating sediment as a central engineering and planning constraint.
pages.body_text: ICIMOD Threats to the Koshi River Basin # Summary ICIMOD's 2018 outreach publication Understanding Sediment Management, focused on sediment dynamics, erosion, and environmental threats in the koshi-basin. Provides the evidence base for treating sediment as a central engineering and planning constraint. # Key Data Points Although the Koshi basin represents only 9% of the Ganges river system, ICIMOD reports that it contributes nearly 25% of the Ganges sediment load: 100-135 million tonnes per year. Estimated soil-loss rates in the source include 22 tonnes/ha/year from barren land, 5.3 tonnes/ha/year from agricultural areas, 5 tonnes/ha/year from grassland, and 0.5 tonnes/ha/year from forested areas. Suspended-sediment budgeting reports 101 million tonnes/year at Chatara, 81 million tonnes/year at Birpur, and 43 million tonnes/year at Baltara, implying substantial deposition between those stations. Sediment, flood, and erosion risks are interconnected. Climate change is intensifying GLOF, landslide, and sediment-pulse risks. [!note] The current source is a four-page ICIMOD outreach publication. It provides annual sediment-load and erosion-rate figures, but not a full hydropower design-parameter table. # Limitations Date: Published 2020; climate-sediment dynamics and GLOF hazard profiles may have shifted since publication. Basin scope: Covers the Koshi basin only; does not assess sediment regimes in Karnali, Gandaki, or Mahakali basins. Outreach-publication scope: The assessment provides several useful quantitative anchors, but it is not a full technical sediment design manual for hydropower projects. Source type: ICIMOD is a regional knowledge centre; data should be cross-referenced with WECS river-basin plans and project-level feasibility studies where possible. # Used By No pages currently reference this source.

pages.excerpt: Primary international source for solar and renewable cost benchmarking against Nepal specifics. Two IRENA document streams are relevant:
pages.body_text: IRENA Renewable Readiness Assessment and REmap Nepal Primary international source for solar and renewable cost benchmarking against Nepal specifics. Two IRENA document streams are relevant: 1. IRENA Renewable Readiness Assessment (RRA) — Nepal (2017, with subsequent updates). Country-level diagnostic; identifies barriers and potential across solar, wind, and small hydro. 2. IRENA REmap Nepal scenario analysis. Quantitative pathway modelling for higher renewables shares in Nepal's electricity and total energy mix. Plus the IRENA Renewable Capacity Statistics (annual, global) and Renewable Cost Database — which provide the global LCOE benchmarks this project uses in data-solar-hydro-lcoe and solar-lcoe-crossover. # What these sources cover Solar PV technical potential by Nepal resource zone Wind potential (limited but non-trivial in Mustang + parts of Koshi) Small hydro potential (overlaps with wecs-hydropower-potential-2019) Barriers analysis: financing, policy, grid integration, skills LCOE benchmarks for Nepal-comparable countries Scenario pathways to 2030 / 2050 with renewables share Policy recommendations and institutional framework proposals # Key data points (composite from RRA + REmap + Cost Database) ## Solar (Nepal-specific) Estimated solar PV technical potential: ~50,000–100,000 MWp (various IRENA framings; caveats on siteability) Mean Nepal GHI: ~4.7–4.9 kWh/m²/day (matches Global Solar Atlas) Suggested short-term target: >1 GW by 2030 (REmap Accelerated Case); policy + financing gaps identified as primary blocker, not resource ## Global LCOE benchmarks (IRENA Renewable Cost Database) Utility-scale solar PV weighted global LCOE 2010 → 2024: $0.359 → $0.044 per kWh (−88% real) Module price 2010 → 2024: $2.00/W → ~$0.10/W (−95%) Onshore wind LCOE 2010 → 2024: $0.113 → $0.033 per kWh BESS (4h utility) LCOE 2020 → 2024: ~$190 → ~$95 per MWh Capacity-weighted auction-low solar tariff 2024: ~$0.020–$0.030/kWh (GCC, India) These are the numbers the solar-lcoe-crossover argument rides on. # IRENA's diagnostic frame for Nepal The RRA identifies five priority barriers: 1. Policy coherence — fragmented responsibility across MoEWRI / NEA / AEPC / ERC 2. Financing access — limited local-currency long-tenor finance for renewables 3. Grid integration — transmission and distribution readiness for variable resources 4. Institutional capacity — solar-specific engineering and O&M depth is thin 5. Land and permits — no agrivoltaic framework, fragmented land tenure Most of these overlap with the bottleneck-hierarchy for hydro, with one addition specific to solar: absence of land/permitting framework for utility-scale ground-mount. # Why this source matters to the project Provides the global LCOE benchmarks the solar-lcoe-crossover and data-solar-hydro-lcoe pages rely on. Gives an externally-credentialed estimate of Nepal solar potential without the over-promise of some national documents. Frames the barriers analysis in language compatible with donor programs — useful for mapping AEPC / EIB / WB programme gaps. The REmap pathway is a reasonable benchmark against which to judge the NEA/MoEWRI 2024/25 actual trajectory (960 MW tender + 170 MW PPA + 142 MW operating). # Data-quality and caveats IRENA's Nepal "technical potential" estimates vary widely (50,000–100,000+ MWp) depending on whether high-mountain inaccessible land is counted. Only the Zone A trans-Himalayan + Zone B Terai + Zone C mid-hill deployable fraction (~15,000–25,000 MWp) matters for real planning; see data-solar-fleet-inventory potential pyramid. IRENA REmap pathways are normative scenarios, not forecasts. Use for direction of travel, not for calendar-year predictions. Global LCOE benchmarks reflect weighted averages; Nepal-specific numbers should always be context-adjusted for grid costs, land costs, and FX. # Relevance to project Anchor citation for: solar-lcoe-crossover data-solar-hydro-lcoe data-solar-fleet-inventory (potential pyramid) solar-resource-geography-nepal claim-solar-cheaper-than-small-hydro # Related wb-esmap-solar-resource-assessment — the measured-resource complement global-solar-atlas-nepal — the satellite-derived complement wecs-energy-synopsis-2024 — the domestic energy-balance frame wb-country-economic-memo-2025 — macroeconomic context

pages.body_text: JICA IPSDP Final Report Annexes (Vol. 2) # Summary This is the Annexes volume (Vol. 2) of the JICA Study Team's Final Report for the (IPSDP) — the same study whose compact policy conclusions are captured in moewri-ipsdp-exec-summary-2025. The executive summary is where the headline numbers and milestone ladder live; this volume is where the _workings_ live — the demand forecast inputs, the MP2014 project scorecards, the existing-plant inventories, the hydropower sequencing logic, and the geology, hydrology and seismology that bound what can actually be built. The volume is 315 pages and contains Annexes 1–6 only. The PDF's own table of contents lists 16 annexes in total; Annexes 7–16 (power generation planning, cross-border trade status, power system planning, SEA, economic and financial analysis, financing, surplus utilisation, governance, milestones, capacity development) are carried in companion volumes that are not currently in the wiki's raw-source set. For this wiki, this is the authoritative upstream source for any claim of the form "JICA/MoEWRI's IPSDP study assumes X" about demand, existing fleet state, hydropower portfolio composition, or development-plan review — the executive summary is not granular enough on its own. Key cross-links: moewri-ipsdp-exec-summary-2025, nea, seasonal-arbitrage-trap, kulekhani-cascade, kali-gandaki-a, tanahu-hydropower, upper-arun. # Contents (Annexes 1–6 only) Annex | Title | First page | -------|-------|-----------:| 1 | General Information of Nepal (economy, topography, geology, seismology, climate, hydrology, air quality) | 5 | 2 | Current Status of the Power Sector in Nepal (organisational structure, legal system, reform, corporate entities) | 55 | 3 | Current Situation of the Electric Power Facilities (existing generation fleet, transmission, distribution) | 146 | 4 | Review of Existing Development Plans (MP2014 screening, Multi-Criteria Analysis scorecards) | 174 | 5 | Power Demand Forecast (sectoral sales mix, consumer growth, electrification) | 196 | 6 | Hydropower Development Plan (bulk of the volume; portfolio composition and sequencing) | 244 | Annexes 7–16 listed in the front-matter TOC (Power Generation Development Planning; Current Status of Power Trade; Power System Development Planning; SEA; Economic and Financial Analysis; Financing; Utilisation of Surplus Electricity; Governance; Milestones & Future Outlook; Capacity Development) are _not present_ in this PDF. # Key claims Annex 3 (p. 147) states that NEA owns hydropower plants with an installed capacity of and designed annual generation of at an average plant factor of . Only Kulekhani I and Kulekhani II operate as storage (STO); the rest are ROR or PROR. Annex 3 generation-type table (p. 146) codifies four hydropower types used throughout the IPSDP optimisation — , (peak run-of-river with daily-to-weekly pondage), (storage / reservoir), and (pumped storage) — and notes the winter-peak / monsoon-spill economics that drive the seasonal-arbitrage-trap argument. Annex 4 (p. 174–175) records how the 2014 Nationwide Master Plan (MP2014) filtered candidate projects via Multi-Criteria Analysis with exclusions for installed capacity , dam height , project cost , annual flow-regulation rate , reservoir resettlement , or sites inside national parks / wildlife conservation areas / world heritage. The MP2014 scorecard table on p. 175 lists unit capacity, total energy, dry energy, project cost, unit cost, EIRR and FIRR for Dudh Koshi, Sun Koshi 3, Lower Badigad, Andhi Khola, Chera-1, Madi, Nalsyau Gad, Naumure (W. Rapti), Kokhajor-1, Lower Jhimruk and the rest of the MP2014 list. Annex 5 (p. 196) puts sectoral sales composition and consumer-growth rate at approximately with household electrification reaching in 2021 and a stated GoN target of . # Local source Local workspace copy: jica_ipsdp_main_report_vol2.pdf [!cite] jica-ipsdp-main-report-vol2 PDF created via Word → Adobe PDF. File is byte-identical to in the same directory (verified via SHA-256); the canonical path used by the wiki is . # Limitations Incomplete volume: This PDF contains only Annexes 1–6. Annexes 7–16 (power generation development planning, cross-border trade status, power system planning, SEA, economic and financial analysis, financing, surplus utilisation, governance, milestones, capacity development) are in companion volumes not currently in the wiki raw-source set. Study assumptions, not verified outcomes: Demand forecasts, scorecards, and sequencing logic are JICA/MoEWRI study outputs — not post-implementation verification. 2024 cutoff: Post-study construction progress and policy changes after 2024 are not reflected. # Used By andhi-khola arun-3 bagmati-nadi balephi budhigandaki chera-1 dudhkoshi-storage figure-index humla-karnali-1 karnali-chisapani khimti-cascade khimti-i kokhajor-1 likhu-4 lower-badigad lower-jhimruk madi marsyangdi moewri-ipsdp-exec-summary-2025 nalsyau-gad naumure-w-rapti phukot-karnali sun-koshi-no-3 tamakoshi-v trishuli upper-karnali upper-myagdi west-seti # What this source does not cover Annexes 7–16 of the IPSDP final report (power system planning, cross-border trade, SEA, financing, surplus-electricity utilisation, governance, milestone ladder, capacity development). Use moewri-ipsdp-exec-summary-2025 for the compact statement of those or queue companion JICA volumes when available. Monthly plant-level generation or trade settlement data. USD-denominated at ~US$0.052/kWh initial, revised to US$0.059/kWh, escalated by US CPI. No seasonal rate split. 50% equity transfer to NEA for NPR 1 at year 20. pages.excerpt: This executive summary is the clearest compact statement of the current MoEWRI/JICA planning logic for Nepal's long-horizon power buildout through 2040. It ties together demand growth, hydropower sequencing, 400 kV backbone and interconnection expansion, export strategy, and fina
pages.body_text: MoEWRI IPSDP Executive Summary # Summary This executive summary is the clearest compact statement of the current MoEWRI/JICA planning logic for Nepal's long-horizon power buildout through 2040. It ties together demand growth, hydropower sequencing, 400 kV backbone and interconnection expansion, export strategy, and financing needs in one document instead of scattering them across older nea or donor studies. The report is especially valuable because page 39 turns the plan into a milestone ladder with explicit dates for export crossover, self-sufficiency, the 28 GW government target, and a later clean-export role in South Asia. Section 2.4 then links those milestones to concrete trade channels, grid buildout, and wholesale arrangements with India and Bangladesh rather than treating exports as an abstract objective. Section 3 adds the guardrails the plan says must shape buildability, including environmental-flow management, protected-area restrictions, and the need to package hydropower with transmission and institutional reform. For this wiki, the document is a backbone source for india-energy-relationship, bangladesh-trade-route, niettp, and project-sequencing questions that depend on an official state planning frame rather than a single project promoter's view. # Contents Section | Page | ---------|------| 1. Introduction | 1 | 1.1 Background | 1 | 1.2 Objectives | 1 | 1.3 Basic Approaches on IPSDP | 2 | 2. pages.title: NEA Standard Hydropower PPA Clauses — AD Penalty, Reserve Margin, and Curtailment
headings: NEA Standard Hydropower PPA Clauses — AD Penalty, Reserve Margin, and Curtailment
pages.excerpt: Secondary legal analysis by Sushil Parajuli of the standard NEA hydropower Power Purchase Agreement text, covering Availability Declaration penalties, reserve margin, curtailment risk, and force majeure constraints.
pages.body_text: NEA Standard Hydropower PPA Clauses — AD Penalty, Reserve Margin, and Curtailment # Summary Secondary legal analysis by Sushil Parajuli of the standard NEA hydropower Power Purchase Agreement text, covering Availability Declaration penalties, reserve margin, curtailment risk, and force majeure constraints. # Key provisions ## Article 10.2 — AD Penalty Formula Compensation = [0.80 × min(Monthly Contract Energy, Availability Declaration) − (Actual Delivered + Forced Outage + Scheduled Outage + Force Majeure Energy)] × Purchase Rate for that Month. If result is negative, payment is zero. Establishes that if monthly energy falls below 80% of the lesser of Contract Energy or the Availability Declaration, the developer owes compensation to NEA. ## Article 10.1(Ka) — 10% Reserve Margin In the wet season (peak months Ashadh–Kartik), NEA/LDC can withhold 10% of Contract Energy or Availability Declaration as a "Reserve Margin" with ZERO compensation to the IPP. ## No Curtailment Exemption No clause in Article 10 exempts an IPP from AD penalties when the generation shortfall is caused by NEA/NLDC dispatch curtailment. The penalty formula applies irrespective of cause (aside from Force Majeure). ## Take-or-Pay Obligation 30-year take-or-pay: NEA is obligated to pay for 100% of Contracted Energy from COD. Schedule 3 provides up to 72 cumulative hours (3 days) of unpaid outage per year. ## Article 15 — Force Majeure Narrow definition. Covers only extraordinary events (e.g., floods exceeding design flood discharge from Schedule 1). Routine grid/transmission/substation failures are NOT force majeure. IPPs cannot invoke FM relief for standard grid failures. ## The "16% Curtailment" Claim No statutory basis found. Only the Article 10.1(Ka) 10% reserve margin exists in the PPA text. The 16% figure appears to be an industry misinterpretation — likely 10% reserve margin plus an erroneous 6% from an unknown source. No NEA, ERC, or PPA document mentions 16%. ## ERC Regulatory Context ERC Notice (Rule 2076/2019, Schedule 5) requires hydropower sellers to submit monthly Availability Declarations 30 days before the month starts. The ERC Electricity Regulatory Commission Act (2017) gives the Commission authority over PPAs. Under SVLCLaw (2022), PPAs signed before the Commission's establishment remain valid but Commission by-laws prevail over conflicting clauses. ## Standard PPA Existence NEA maintains a standard template but PPAs are negotiated individually. No publicly available PPA document was found. The Parajuli analysis is the primary secondary source. # Limitations Secondary analysis only: This is Parajuli's interpretation of the standard PPA text, not the primary legal document itself. No publicly available PPA document was located to verify the analysis against. Analyst's framing: The "16% Curtailment" debunking is a correction of industry lore, not a positive textual finding. The analysis may emphasize clauses relevant to its bankability argument. ERC evolution: ERC regulatory context reflects the Commission's authority as understood at the time of analysis; ERC by-laws and interpretations continue to evolve. Negotiated variation: NEA maintains a standard template but PPAs are negotiated individually. Clause language and enforcement may vary across projects. # Used By No pages currently reference this source.

pages.body_text: Nepal Transmission System — 400 kV Landscape & Cross-Border Plan (2025) # Summary Reference compilation for Nepal's current and planned high-voltage transmission assets — the 400 kV east–west backbone and parallel central corridor, the legacy 220 kV and 132 kV grid, and the cross-border interconnections with India (ten links at five voltage levels). Drawn from NEA's 2024/25 annual report, NEA Transmission Directorate publications, the Millennium Challenge Account Nepal (MCA-Nepal) compact programme documents, and news reporting of individual commissioning events. # Key Data Points 400 kV operational backbone Hetauda–Dhalkebar–Inaruwa (HDDI) — first and currently only 400 kV east–west backbone inside Nepal. Commissioned in segments 2018–2022. Total spine ~300 km. Feeds the Dhalkebar–Muzaffarpur cross-border link (400 kV bipole, operational since 2016, ADB + KfW co-financed). This is the sole operational 400 kV export route. 400 kV under construction / implementation MCA central 400 kV (Lapsiphedi–Ratmate–Hetauda–Damauli–Butwal) — the MCA-Nepal compact's headline 315 km transmission line, partially energised in 2025. Completion target 2026–2027. Gorakhpur–New Butwal 400 kV — second cross-border link, under construction. Commissioning target mid-2026. Inaruwa–Purnea 400 kV — third cross-border, implementation phase. Critical to Arun-3 evacuation once the plant is online. Lamki–Bareilly 400 kV — western cross-border at implementation setup; completion horizon 2027+. 220 kV operational Khimti–Dhalkebar 220 kV — original IPP evacuation corridor Hetauda–Bharatpur–Bardaghat 220 kV — east–west spine at 220 kV Dana–Kushma–New Butwal 220 kV — west-central hydropower corridor 132 kV cross-border (legacy, operational) Kataiya–Kushaha (since 1971, the historic first link) Raxaul–Parwanipur, New Nautanwa–Mainahiya, Tanakpur–Mahendranagar Planned / under construction cross-border Nepalgunj–Nanpara 132 kV (under construction) Chameliya–Jauljibi 220 kV (planned, far-west) System-level parameters Nepal–India transfer capacity, 2025: ~2,300 MW total across all interconnections combined Current concurrent peak export: ~1,200 MW (monsoon 2024–25) Grid code: NEA grid code 2019 (amended 2022); Indian-side dispatch via NRLDC # Relevance to Project Primary source for the voltage levels, statuses, schedules and strategic roles of Nepal's ten currently-tracked corridors and ten cross-border interconnections. Used as the baseline citation for all per-corridor entity pages. # Limitations Compilation, not primary source: Drawn from multiple sources (NEA annual reports, Transmission Directorate documents, MCA-Nepal, news reporting) with varying update cycles and verification standards. Snapshot date: July 2025. Commissioning targets (e.g., Gorakhpur–New Butwal mid-2026) are forward-looking and subject to delay. Missing granularity: Actual segment-level substation capacities are confidential. Indian-side evacuation constraints beyond border crossings are not covered. Load-flow studies and battery/STATCOM plans are not included. Transfer capacity estimates: The ~2,300 MW total Nepal–India transfer capacity and ~1,200 MW concurrent peak export are operational approximations, not audited figures. # Used By claim-transmission-immediate-blocker project-roadmap solar-lcoe-crossover data-layer-grid-hubs-place-anchors data-layer-transmission-connected-traced-network data-layer-transmission-corridors-curated data-layer-transmission-labels data-layer-transmission-network-nodes data-layer-transmission-raw-traced-segments data-layer-transmission-trace-gaps-qa data-nea-substation-capacity-fy2076-77 data-nea-transmission-length-fy2076-77 bheri-corridor-400kv damak-godak-phidim-132kv dhungesangu-basantapur-220-132kv hetauda-dhalkebar-inaruwa-backbone kabeli-132 kathmandu-valley-underground-cabling khudi-220-132kv-substation main-load-dispatch-centre markichowk-220-132kv-substation modi-lekhnath-132kv nalsyau-gad nawalpur-132kv-substation purbi-chitwan-132kv-substation ratmate-rasuwagadhi-kerung-400kv tingla-132-33kv-substation upper-arun upper-karnali intervention-transmission-completion # What This Source Does Not Cover Actual segment-level substation capacities (published only in confidential planning documents) Indian-side evacuation constraints beyond the border crossings Load flow studies under different generation dispatch scenarios Battery and STATCOM augmentation plans # See also hetauda-dhalkebar-inaruwa-backbone dhalkebar-muzaffarpur mca-central-400 hydro-geopolitics stranded-generation

Sahas Urja (Solu Khola, 86 MW) — Financial Profile
Subsidiary vs. IPP Rate Differential (Document finding)
pages.excerpt: Source type: Research compilation — Google Docs export (15 pages) Original: Mission-based financial investigation sourced from ICRA Nepal surveillance reports (A.996, B.119), CARE Ratings Nepal rating rationales, and statutory filings.
pages.body_text: Investigative Report: PPA Data Retrieval from ICRA & CARE Ratings Nepal Source type: Research compilation — Google Docs export (15 pages) Original: Mission-based financial investigation sourced from ICRA Nepal surveillance reports (A.996, B.119), CARE Ratings Nepal rating rationales, and statutory filings. # Summary This investigation targets data gaps in Nepal's hydropower financial landscape, reconstructed from primary credit rating agency reports. It covers: Mission 1: Forensic reconstruction of Sahas Urja Limited (86 MW Solu Khola) — a documented private IPP financial profile Mission 2: Comparative PPA tariff matrix for five priority projects (Chilime, Sanima Mai, Rasuwagadhi, Trishuli 3A, Nyadi) Mission 3: Mathematical reconstruction of NEA subsidiary vs. private IPP rate differential (37.1% revenue advantage via Chilime anomaly) Mission 4: Insurance market quantitative verification (Sanima Mai pays 1.80% of gross revenue in non-life premiums) # Key Findings ## PPA Rate Matrix (VERIFIED) Project | Capacity (MW) | Wet Rate (NPR/kWh) | Dry Rate (NPR/kWh) | Entity Type | PPA Year | ---|---|---|---|---|---| Chilime | 22.1 | 4.08 (Excess) | 8.17 (Regular) | NEA Subsidiary | 1997 | Sanima Mai (Phase 1) | 22.0 | 4.80 | 8.40 | Private IPP | 2010 | Sanima Mai Cascade | 7.0 | 5.52 | 9.66 | Private IPP | 2013 | Rasuwagadhi | 111.0 | 4.80 | 8.40 | NEA Subsidiary (via Chilime) | 2011 | Upper Trishuli 3A | 60.0 | N/A (Internal) | N/A (Internal) | NEA Owned | N/A | Upper Trishuli 3B | 37.0 | 4.80 | 8.40 | Subsidiary Corp | — | Nyadi | 30.0 | 4.80 | 8.40 | Private IPP | 2015 | ## Sahas Urja (Solu Khola, 86 MW) — Financial Profile Final build cost: NPR 172–175 million/MW (industry average often exceeds NPR 200–250M) FY 2080/81 revenue: NPR 2.648 billion Net profit: NPR 902.33 million (114.66% YoY growth) Gross margin: 95.54%; Net margin: 23.61% Plant Load Factor: 69.05%, achieving 87–89% of contracted energy Q-design: Aggressive Q41 model, 19.28% dry energy mix 10-bank syndicate led by Nepal Investment Bank, 76% debt-financed Promoter: Him Prasad Pathak — also controls Times Energy (341 MW Budhi Gandaki), Secretary at IPPAN ## Subsidiary vs. IPP Rate Differential (Document finding) Chilime's "Regular/Excess" billing architecture produces an effective blended rate of NPR 7.57/kWh vs. a typical private IPP's NPR 5.52/kWh — a 37.1% revenue advantage. Chilime classified 85% of its 156 GWh generation as "Regular" at NPR 8.17/kWh. ## Insurance Burden Sanima Mai Hydropower paid NPR 13.77 million in non-life premiums against NPR 764 million gross revenue = 1.80% of top-line. Within an ~15% OPEX envelope, insurance consumes over 10% of operating budget. # Data Gaps Marked SEBON IPO prospectuses are scanned-image PDFs — no automated parsing possible IPPAN's "800% premium surge" claim source inaccessible (server timeout) Specific OAGN paragraph condemning PPA favoritism for subsidiaries not isolated # Limitations Compilation nature: This is a reconstructed investigative report, not a primary rating agency publication. Individual claims should be traced to the underlying ICRA / CARE documents where possible. Scanned sources: SEBON prospectuses referenced are image-based PDFs; figures were manually transcribed and may contain transcription errors. Single-promoter focus: The Sahas Urja profile, while detailed, represents one successful promoter. It is not necessarily representative of average private IPP performance. Snapshot date: Financial data reflects FY 2080/81 or earlier; market conditions (tariffs, interest rates, construction costs) may have shifted. Inaccessible sources: Some referenced documents (e.g., IPPAN premium surge claim) were not retrievable at time of compilation. # Used By Verified via grep. pages.title: "Mission 1: Sahas Urja (Solu Khola, 86 MW) — Benchmark IPP Success"
pages.excerpt: Source type: Research compilation — single-project deep-dive (4 pages) Original: Forensic reconstruction of Sahas Urja Limited sourced from ICRA Nepal surveillance reports (A.996, B.119) and corporate disclosures.
pages.body_text: Mission 1: Sahas Urja (Solu Khola, 86 MW) Source type: Research compilation — single-project deep-dive (4 pages) Original: Forensic reconstruction of Sahas Urja Limited sourced from ICRA Nepal surveillance reports (A.996, B.119) and corporate disclosures. # Summary Sahas Urja Limited is the critical positive benchmark in Nepal's private IPP landscape. The compilation presents profitability in a fixed-tariff environment as a function of capital efficiency and operational optimization, not anomalous PPA rates. # Corporate Details Entity: Private IPP, incorporated February 2014, converted to public September 2014 Asset: 86 MW Solu Khola (Dudh Koshi) Hydroelectric Project, Run-of-River Location: Solukhumbu District, Koshi Province Q-design: Q41 (~41% probability of exceedance) PPA: Signed February 25, 2015 | NPR 4.80 (wet) / 8.40 (dry) | 3% × 8 years escalation Contracted energy: 520.20 GWh/yr (100.27 GWh dry / 419.93 GWh wet = 19.28% dry mix) RCOD achieved: March 1, 2023 — retained all 8 escalations # Financial Performance (FY 2080/81) Metric | Value | ---|---| Build cost (final) | NPR 172–175 million/MW | Total project cost | NPR 14.7 billion | Electricity sales revenue | NPR 2.648 billion | Net profit | NPR 902.33 million (+114.66% YoY) | Gross profit margin | 95.54% | Net profit margin | 23.61% | Interest expense | NPR 805.9 million (down from NPR 1.165B) | Plant Load Factor | 69.05% (~87–89% of contracted) | Debt financing | 76% (10-bank consortium led by Nepal Investment Bank) | # Why It Works 1. Capital efficiency: ~NPR 173M/MW vs. industry average often exceeding NPR 200–250M/MW 2. Escalation retention: Achieved COD on time → all 8 annual 3% escalations intact 3. Scale: 86 MW means 19.28% dry energy mix still generates massive absolute NPR 8.40/kWh cash flows 4. Deleveraging: Interest expense dropped from NPR 1.165B to NPR 805.9M # Promoter Profile Chairman: Him Prasad Pathak Also controls: 51% stake in Times Energy (341 MW Budhi Gandaki PRoR, NPR 52.5B syndication) IPPAN: Secretary, Executive Committee — direct lobbying access to MoEWRI, ERC, NEA Prior projects: Upper Hugdi Khola (5 MW) # Limitations Single-project deep-dive. This compilation covers only Sahas Urja / Solu Khola. Findings on capital efficiency, escalation retention, and promoter profile are not necessarily representative of the broader IPP sector. Research compilation, not peer-reviewed. Assembled from ICRA Nepal surveillance reports and corporate disclosures — has not undergone independent verification or institutional fact-checking. Financial snapshot. Data reflects FY 2080/81 performance; does not capture subsequent operational or financial developments, deleveraging progress, or PPA rate adjustments. Promoter profile from public sources only. Promoter relationships and institutional connections are inferred from publicly available corporate disclosures and IPPAN listings, not from direct interviews. # Used By lower-solu himalayan-capital-analysis icra-nepal-surveillance-a996-b119 # See Also ppa-data-retrieval-icra-care-2026 sector-financial-analysis-triple-authority-2026 sahas-urja ppa-pricing q-design-discharge

pages.title: Sangroula/NTNU Kulekhani Reservoir Bathymetry and Sedimentation Studies
headings: Sangroula/NTNU Kulekhani Reservoir Bathymetry and Sedimentation Studies
pages.excerpt: Multi-study compilation covering Kulekhani Reservoir sedimentation, including the primary DGPS bathymetric survey by Sangroula (NTNU/Hydro-Lab, 2009/2010), InVEST/RUSLE catchment modeling by Bokan et al. (2021–2024), the ADB/World Bank post-completion review, and Mandal's (2021)
pages.body_text: Sangroula/NTNU Kulekhani Reservoir Bathymetry and Sedimentation Studies # Summary Multi-study compilation covering Kulekhani Reservoir sedimentation, including the primary DGPS bathymetric survey by Sangroula (NTNU/Hydro-Lab, 2009/2010), InVEST/RUSLE catchment modeling by Bokan et al. (2021–2024), the ADB/World Bank post-completion review, and Mandal's (2021) hydro-mechanical degradation study. Together these provide the most complete sedimentation evidence base for any single Nepali reservoir. # Primary DGPS Bathymetric Survey (Sangroula, NTNU/Hydro-Lab, 2009/2010) Physical DGPS bathymetric mapping of Kulekhani Reservoir bed using echo sounders and differential GPS. Total gross storage lost: 20.4 MCM (23.9% of 85.3 MCM original) Active live storage lost: 14 MCM (19.1% of 73.3 MCM original) Average annual loss: 0.56% of total reservoir capacity over 27 years of operation Commissioning: December 1982 (Unit 1), May 1987 (Unit 2) # Source Document Sangroula, D.P. (2006, updated with DGPS surveys 2009/2010). Sedimentation and sustainability of the Kulekhani Reservoir: A Himalayan Case. Doctoral dissertation, Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU). Associated with Hydro Lab Nepal. # InVEST/RUSLE Catchment Modeling (Bokan et al., 2021–2024) A DISTINCT study using spatial modeling, not physical bathymetry. Uses InVEST SDRmax model + RUSLE to calculate theoretical sediment yield from upstream catchment. Sedimentation rate: 13.3 t/ha/yr (2002) → 6.6 t/ha/yr (2010) → 4.8 t/ha/yr (2018) Total reservoir capacity measured at 61.66 MCM (April 2018) Confirms declining delivery rate trend — watershed management works Citation: Bokan, L.T. et al. Potential Sedimentation Rate and its Prioritization in Kulekhani Watershed Using InVEST Model (published 2024, modeling 2002–2018 data) # ADB Post-Completion Review (World Bank/ADB PCR) Loan 528-NEP / Credit 600-NEP 80% cost overrun, 21-month commissioning delay Key finding: NO sediment flushing system was designed — watershed management was completely unanticipated during appraisal Kulekhani served as the lesson that forced ADB/IDA to mandate catchment management plans and sediment flushing gates in all subsequent projects (Marsyangdi Cr. 1478-NEP, Tanahu) PCR URL: https://documents1.worldbank.org/curated/en/790631468289870058/pdf/multi-page.pdf # Hydro-Mechanical Degradation (Mandal 2021) Mandal, N.K. (2021). Pelton Runner Erosion Due To Cavitation: A Case Study Of Storage Hydropower Plant, Kulekhani First Hydropower Station Fine suspended quartz particles cause continuous abrasive pitting of Pelton turbine buckets Altered blade geometries trigger secondary cavitation — efficiency deteriorates even under low sediment concentrations Main inlet valves replaced multiple times since commissioning # Limitations Bathymetric survey date. The primary Sangroula DGPS survey is from 2009/2010 — sedimentation rates may have shifted in the subsequent 15+ years of operation. Multi-study compilation with different rigor levels. Combines a doctoral dissertation, spatial modeling (InVEST/RUSLE), an ADB/WB post-completion review, and a turbine-degradation case study — each with different methodologies and confidence levels. InVEST/RUSLE modeled, not measured. The Bokan et al. sedimentation rates (13.3 → 6.6 → 4.8 t/ha/yr) are model outputs, not physical sediment trap measurements. The declining trend is directionally consistent with the bathymetric survey but the absolute rates are model-derived. No post-2018 bathymetry. The most recent reservoir capacity measurement (61.66 MCM) is from April 2018. Current storage volume is uncertain. # Used By kulekhani-iii

pages.excerpt: Source type: Research compilation — Google Docs export (17 pages) Original: Exhaustive investigation of structural imbalances at the intersection of capital markets, regulatory frameworks, and project finance in Nepal's hydropower IPP sector.
pages.body_text: Systemic Risk & Triple-Authority Conflict in Nepal's Hydropower Sector Source type: Research compilation — Google Docs export (17 pages) Original: Exhaustive investigation of structural imbalances at the intersection of capital markets, regulatory frameworks, and project finance in Nepal's hydropower IPP sector. # Summary The "Triple-Authority Conflict" — NEA simultaneously functioning as sole off-taker (buyer), system dispatcher (NLDC), and autonomous penalty administrator — distorts IPOs, rights share issuances, and DSCR metrics. Retail investors on NEPSE are downstream victims of a system they were never properly informed about. # IPO & Rights Share Inventory (VERIFIED from SEBON/NEPSE) Company | MW | IPO Year | IPO Amount (NPR Cr) | Rights Issue | Rights Amount (NPR Cr) | Rights Use | ---|---|---|---|---|---|---| Chilime Hydropower | 22.1 | 2010 | 24.0 | None | — | Holding company expansion (Sanjen, Rasuwagadhi) | Upper Tamakoshi | 456.0 | 2018 | 100.0 (Local) | 2023/24 | 1,059.0 (1:1) | Retire legacy commercial debt | Rasuwagadhi Hydropower | 111.0 | 2018 | 66.0 (Local/Staff) | None | — | Delayed COD due to disasters | Ankhu Khola Jalvidhyut | 8.4 | 2013 | 20.0 | 2024 | 120.0 (1:1.5) | Repay bank loans (150% dilution) | Peoples Power Ltd | 4.96 | 2022 | 31.6 | 2024 | 15.8 (1:0.5) | Repay Prime Commercial Bank loans | Joshi Hydropower | 3.0 | 2018 | 24.1 | 2024 | 15.6 (1:0.65) | Prevent NPL status (NMB Bank) | Terhathum Power Co. | 7.5 | 2021 | 12.0 | 2024 | 12.0 (1:1) | Repay bank loans + 2 MW cascade | # Key Findings ## The Chilime Anomaly Chilime operated profitably for 7 years before its 2010 IPO — distributing 35% cash dividends within a year. Modern IPOs are floated pre-commissioning, dumping execution risk onto retail investors. Today's investors buy debt-repayment vehicles, not dividend-yielding assets. ## The AD Penalty Blindspot IPO prospectuses detail PPA tariff rates to project revenues, but fail to model scenarios where up to 16% of projected revenue is clawed back by the off-taker through structural AD (Availability Declaration) penalties. ## Capital Sequencing Inversion Standard model: promoter equity → bank debt → COD → operational cash flow → IPO as exit. Nepal model: pre-COD IPO → rights shares within 24–36 months → proceeds used to prevent bank foreclosure. ## Market Concentration Hydropower equities grew from ~6% to ~16% of NEPSE total market capitalization. During FY 2020/21 liquidity surge: NPR 102B → NPR 342B. # Data Gaps "Promoters injected 2–6 Crore NPR/MW out-of-pocket to cover loan repayments" — based on regulatory corpus, not verified primary data "103 MW of small projects required NPR 2.5 billion of additional equity to stop foreclosure" — parameters align with global reports, not a verified Nepal-specific study # Limitations Research compilation, not peer-reviewed. This is a Google Docs export (17 pages) that assembles findings from regulatory filings, NEPSE data, and secondary sources. It has not undergone peer review or institutional fact-checking. Data gaps propagate. Two key quantitative claims (promoter out-of-pocket estimates and the 103 MW equity-rescue figure) are flagged as unverified, so they remain provisional until backed by primary-source confirmation. No primary interviews. The analysis draws from published regulatory sources and market data but does not include direct interviews with NEA officials, promoters, or investors. Motivational claims about promoter behaviour are inferred, not directly attested. Snapshot date. Compiled in early 2026; does not capture any SEBON regulatory changes, NEPSE market movements, or NEA PPA revisions after that date. # Used By ankhu-khola barahi-hydropower rasuwagadhi madhya-bhotekoshi sanjen ppa-data-retrieval-icra-care-2026 sahas-urja-benchmark-icra-2026 # See Also ppa-data-retrieval-icra-care-2026 ppa-pricing nea-triple-authority ipo-hydropower-bailout stranded-generation ad-penalties

pages.excerpt: Peer-reviewed computable general equilibrium (CGE) study quantifying the macroeconomic cost of Nepal's electricity load shedding crisis (2008–2016). Published in Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews. This is the canonical source for the GDP-loss estimate that anchors Beat 1.1
pages.body_text: Timilsina et al. CGE Load Shedding Cost Study (2021) # Summary Peer-reviewed computable general equilibrium (CGE) study quantifying the macroeconomic cost of Nepal's electricity load shedding crisis (2008–2016). Published in Renewable and Sustainable Energy Reviews. This is the canonical source for the GDP-loss estimate that anchors Beat 1.1 of the production bible. # Key Data Points Total GDP lost 2008–2016: ~US$11 billion (approximately Nepal's entire 2008 GDP) Annual GDP loss at peak: ~7% of GDP per year Annual cost: up to US$1.6 billion/year at worst Investment suppression: annual investment approximately 48% below potential during the shedding era Methodology: CGE model calibrated to Nepal's input-output structure, capturing direct production losses and indirect supply-chain effects Peak daily shedding: 14–18 hours/day during the worst dry seasons (2009–2016) # Relevance to Project Central source for load-shedding-era and the historical context that frames the entire wiki narrative. The CGE methodology captures not just direct outage costs (lost industrial output) but indirect losses (investment deterrence, firm entry suppression, substitution to costly diesel backup). This makes the $11 billion figure more comprehensive than simple output-loss estimates. See also: wb-country-economic-memo-2025 for the World Bank's later framing; nepal-energy-profile for the system snapshot; upper-tamakoshi for the project that ended the era.

pages.body_text: UKHLL Annual Reports — Upper Tamakoshi Hydropower Limited # Summary The audited annual reports of Upper Tamakoshi Hydropower Limited (UKHLL), the NEA subsidiary that owns and operates the 456 MW Upper Tamakoshi Hydroelectric Project — Nepal's largest operating hydropower plant. The reports are available at utkhpl.org.np and provide the primary-source generation and financial data for the project. # Key data extracted (from research compilation of audited accounts) ## Generation data Fiscal Year | Generation (GWh) | % of Design (2,281 GWh) | Notes | ---|---|---|---| FY 2079/80 | 1,945.83 | 85.3% | | FY 2080/81 | 2,058.36 | 90.2% | Peak operational year | FY 2081/82 | 1,529.07 | 67.0% | 88-day flood shutdown (Sep 2024) | ## Financial data Total project cost: NPR 87–89.4 billion Effective D/E ratio at COD: 88:12 ICRA D default rating in FY 2081/82 (post-flood) Flood event damage: NPR 1.79 billion physical, NPR 1.43 billion business interruption Insurance claim: NPR 2.0–3.22 billion Rolwaling diversion: 212 GWh addition, dry-season peaking from 4 to 6 hours # Limitations Audit firm unconfirmed: The reports are described as "audited" but the specific audit firm and qualification opinions are not extracted. Post-flood data recency: The FY 2081/82 data (flood shutdown, ICRA D rating, insurance claim) is the most recent extracted; later fiscal-year data is not included. D/E ratio caveat: The effective 88:12 D/E ratio at COD is from UKHLL annual reports but cross-referencing against external debt-registrar data is not done. pages.body_text: Upper Karnali — PDA, Financial Closure & Court Record # Summary Reference compilation for the 900 MW Upper Karnali Hydroelectric Project — GMR-sponsored, repeatedly PDA-extended, and the canonical example of a stalled India-developed export project in Nepal. # Key Data Points Project basics Capacity: 900 MW Districts: Surkhet, Dailekh, Achham (karnali-basin) River: Karnali Design annual energy: ~3,466 GWh Sponsor: GMR Upper Karnali Hydropower Limited (subsidiary of India's GMR Group) Bid won: International Competitive Bidding, 2008 Export orientation: 88% of output planned for international sale Commercial / PDA history Original PDA deadline missed repeatedly since 2014 Supreme Court of Nepal limited extensions; allowed a 186-day extension to compensate only for time lost during its own interim orders Bangladesh Power Development Board signed a PPA with GMR for 500 MW in principle; MOU in April 2017 for 300 MW; PPA planned for July 2017; in September 2021 Nepal proposed only 200 MW to Bangladesh — none of these have closed Recent financing development (2026) Government of Nepal cleared a path for financial closure GMR submitted investment commitments: INR 65 billion from India's IREDA; NPR 20 billion from Nepali banks Equity restructuring brought in SJVN and IREDA alongside GMR; NEA retains its originally-allocated stake # Relevance to Project Primary source for Upper Karnali's PDA history, export structure and the 2026 financial-closure path. Important because Upper Karnali is the reference case — alongside arun-3 — for India-developed Nepalese hydro, but with the opposite construction outcome: Arun-3 is building; Upper Karnali has been paperwork since 2008. # What This Source Does Not Cover Bangladesh-side transmission readiness (Bangladesh can only import what a new Nepal–India–Bangladesh corridor can carry) GMR Group's own financial condition and its effect on equity pace The downstream-irrigation objections that a 2014 high-level committee raised and never fully resolved # Limitations Paperwork since 2008. Despite repeated PDA extensions and the 2026 financial-closure path announcement, Upper Karnali has zero construction progress after 18 years. The source captures the paper trail, not operational reality. Financial commitments are announced, not disbursed. The INR 65 billion IREDA and NPR 20 billion Nepali bank commitments are investment proposals, not disbursed funds. Financial closure has been announced before without follow-through. Bangladesh PPA gap unaddressed. The source documents the history of Bangladesh PPA discussions without resolving whether the transmission corridor and tripartite agreements can actually deliver the promised 500/300/200 MW. # Used By upper-karnali # See also upper-karnali hydro-geopolitics karnali-basin
