pages.body_text: Urja Khabar "Audit" of IPP Generation vs Contracted Energy # Summary Kumar Pandey article in the January 2026 issue (Year 5, Issue 8) of Urja Khabar magazine. This is secondary reporting of a primary MoEWRI government study — not an independent Urja Khabar dataset. The source document is: "Statistics financially distressed hydropower projects operated by IPP, Asadh 31, 2077" (mid-2020, Ministry of Energy, Water Resources and Irrigation). By republishing this historical data in 2026, Pandey argues that the conditions producing mass IPP financial distress in 2020 have calcified rather than resolved. # Key data extracted ## Generation deficits (≥50 projects) Metric | Count | ---|---| 80% of contracted energy | 0 projects (sole exception: Chilime) | ## Financial distress classification (67 projects, mid-2020) Status | Capacity (MW) | Projects | ---|---|---| Interest & installment regular | 49.99 | 11 | Interest regular, installment irregular | 8.52 | 2 | Interest & installment irregular | 81.95 | 23 | On bank watchlist | 179.35 | 31 | An additional 40 projects under 10 MW (191 MW total) were not included in this classification, suggesting wider distress. ## Construction cost overruns (Table 9) Component | Increase | Primary cause | ---|---|---| Land acquisition | 105.0% | Policy issues | Civil construction | 34.9% | Conflict, blockades, loan delays | Project supervision/management | 38.1% | Conflict, blockades, time/cost | Interest during construction | 30.6% | Policy issues | Steel work | 22.8% | Inflation | Electromechanical | 7.8% | Inflation | ## Transmission-bottlenecked projects (18 named) Project | MW | Bottleneck | ---|---|---| Upper Syange | 2.4 | Khudi Hub Substation incomplete | Nyadi Khola | 30 | Khudi Hub Substation incomplete | Chepe Khola | 9.63 | 220 kV Marsyangdi Corridor incomplete | Super Chepe | 9.05 | Regional infrastructure delays | Dordi-1 | 12 | Dordi corridor transmission constraints | Upper Dordi | 25 | Dordi corridor transmission constraints | Super Dordi | 54 | Dordi corridor transmission constraints | Upper Chhyangdi Khola | 4 | 33 kV Udipur Mid-Marsyangdi line/transformer | Lower Modi | 20 | Isolated — forced to connect to New Modi Switching Substation | Theule Khola | 1.5 | Kusmi Shera Substation connection canceled by NEA | Down Piluwa | 10.3 | Forced to absorb 33/220 kV transformer cost at Baneshwor | Upper Khorunga | 7.5 | 33 kV common line not provided by state | Upper Hewa Small | 8.5 | Alternative evacuation provisions in limbo | Middle Tamor | 73 | Dhunge-Sanghu Substation incomplete | Sanjen Khola | 78 | New Bharatpur-Marsyangdi line incomplete | Gelun Khola Small | 3.2 | Chautara Substation connection pending | Thulo Khola | 21.3 | Rahughat Substation not constructed by NEA | Upper Rawa Khola | 3 | 33/11 kV Baksila Substation (now completed) | ## Regulatory penalties on distressed IPPs NEA penalties: up to 5% of income (rising to 11% after 15 years) for generation shortfalls or PPA non-compliance ERC/NEPSE/SEBON fees: ~1% of income Punishment for generation shortfalls often caused by NEA's own transmission failures ## The "32% claim" The "32% average generation" figure widely circulated in industry discussion does not appear in this article. The only ~33% figure in the Pandey article refers to administrative and operational costs consuming approximately 33% of revenue for affected small projects — not generation output. # Limitations Secondary reporting of a 2020 primary source. The underlying MoEWRI dataset is from mid-2020 (Asadh 2077); the January 2026 article republishes this data without a refreshed dataset. Conditions may have shifted substantially in the intervening period. No independent data collection. Urja Khabar did not conduct its own generation audit; it republished and interpreted a government study. The framing ("conditions have calcified") is Pandey's editorial argument, not a verified finding. Transmission bottleneck table may be partial. The 18 named projects represent Pandey's selection, not necessarily an exhaustive listing of all transmission-bottlenecked projects. The "32% generation" figure is a misconception. This widely circulated industry figure does not appear in the article; the article's ~33% figure refers to cost ratios, not generation output. # Used By middle-tamor

pages.body_text: World Bank Nepal Country Economic Memorandum (2025) # Summary The World Bank's comprehensive economic assessment of Nepal with a significant energy/hydropower chapter. Provides the strongest international-institution perspective on Nepal's energy transition, trade patterns, and system constraints. # Key Data Points Hydropower capacity reached ~2,990 MW by end-2024 >70% of capacity added since 2018 came from IPPs IPPs accounted for 64% of total installed hydropower by 2024 >90% of hydropower is RoR or PRoR Trade shift: 2018 imported ~2,582 GWh / exported ~3 GWh → 2023 imported ~1,895 GWh / exported ~1,946 GWh Scheduled load shedding eliminated in 2018 76% of firms still reported regular power outages in 2022 >13% of firms reported sales losses above 10% from power cuts System losses: ~12.7% in 2024 September 2024 floods/landslides damaged 11 operational projects with >600 MW combined capacity # Relevance Key source for the IPP-driven growth story, the trade transformation timeline, and the reliability gap (load shedding gone but outages persist). The firm-level outage data (76%) is uniquely valuable for the reliability argument in stranded-generation. Trade shift data central to data-trade-time-series. # Limitations Snapshot date: Published March 2025; covers data through end-2024. Does not capture 2025 capacity additions or trade shifts. Firm-level data: The 76% outage figure and 13% sales-loss figure are from a World Bank enterprise survey (2022) — representative but not annual-update series. Trade data: The 2023 import/export figures are calendar-year approximations from the report narrative, not identical to NEA fiscal-year accounting. # Used By budhigandaki data-fleet-composition data-trade-time-series figure-index irena-remap-nepal wb-grid-solar-ee-project

pages.excerpt: The ground-measured solar and wind resource dataset for Nepal. Operated 2015–2019 under the World Bank ESMAP Renewable Energy Resource Mapping & Geospatial Planning programme, implemented on the ground through AEPC with technical delivery by Vaisala / 3TIER (solar) and DNV GL (wi
pages.body_text: World Bank ESMAP Nepal Solar and Wind Resource Measurement The ground-measured solar and wind resource dataset for Nepal. Operated 2015–2019 under the World Bank ESMAP Renewable Energy Resource Mapping & Geospatial Planning programme, implemented on the ground through AEPC with technical delivery by Vaisala / 3TIER (solar) and DNV GL (wind). This is the only authoritative measured-data source for Nepal solar resource at the station-hour resolution — every satellite-derived estimate (including global-solar-atlas-nepal) is calibrated against and cross-validated with this dataset. # What the source covers 14 solar measurement stations deployed across Nepal's representative zones 4 wind measurement towers (lower priority; wind is constrained in Nepal) 10-minute and hourly meteorological and radiation data GHI, DNI, DIF, temperature, wind speed, humidity — the full solar-meteorological stack Validation campaign against Global Solar Atlas and MERRA-2 satellite datasets Open-data release through ESMAP Global Solar Atlas portal and AEPC national reports # Station network (solar — representative) Station (approximate) | Zone | Elevation (m) | Measurement period | GHI mean (kWh/m²/day) | ---|---|---:|---|---:| Jumla | E / A-border | 2,370 | 2015–19 | ~5.2 | Nepalgunj | B3 | 150 | 2015–19 | ~5.1 | Simara / Birgunj | B1 | 130 | 2015–19 | ~4.9 | Biratnagar | B2 | 80 | 2015–19 | ~4.9 | Pokhara | C2 | 820 | 2015–19 | ~4.5 | Kathmandu | C1 | 1,340 | 2015–19 | ~4.3 | Dhankuta | C3 | 1,100 | 2015–19 | ~4.4 | Surkhet | C4 | 700 | 2015–19 | ~4.8 | Jomsom (Mustang) | A | 2,730 | 2015–19 | ~6.0 | (+ 5 additional stations, detail in final report) | various | | | | Specific station coordinates, exact measurement periods, and precise GHI means require cross-reference with the ESMAP final report tables; the values here are representative. # Key findings (composite, from ESMAP final report) Nepal country-weighted GHI: 4.7–5.0 kWh/m²/day GHI range across stations: 4.3 (Kathmandu Valley) to 6.0+ (Jomsom / Mustang) Strongest seasonality in: mid-hill stations (Pokhara, Dhankuta) with 35–45% monsoon penalty Weakest seasonality in: trans-Himalayan stations (Jomsom) with 5–15% monsoon penalty Station-satellite validation: Global Solar Atlas is within ±5% of measured GHI at all stations; trans-Himalayan stations had largest satellite underestimate (~5–8%) Wind resource: limited utility-scale potential; best pockets in Mustang (annual mean >6 m/s at hub height) and selected Koshi gaps # Why this source matters ## For the wiki specifically Anchor citation for solar-resource-geography-nepal zone definitions Base data for data-nepal-solar-resource-zones district-level tables Validation reference for global-solar-atlas-nepal satellite-derived zones in the map layer Empirical grounding that distinguishes Nepal's measured resource from the theoretical resource estimates in less rigorous studies ## For Nepal solar planning in general It is the dataset that moves Nepal solar discussion from "we think Nepal has good sun" to "we measured it for four years across 14 representative sites and here is the spatial and seasonal structure." This is the empirical floor under claim-solar-cheaper-than-small-hydro and the LCOE arguments downstream. # Data access Raw 10-min / hourly station data: ESMAP portal (historically), AEPC national archive (partial) Derived products: Global Solar Atlas tiles, Nepal national solar atlas (AEPC), IRENA REmap modelling Station reports: ESMAP Nepal final report (~2019–2020) # Relevance to project Primary source for: solar-resource-geography-nepal data-nepal-solar-resource-zones solar-hydro-complementarity — seasonality patterns data-solar-hydro-complementarity-profile — monthly shape Validation source for: global-solar-atlas-nepal irena-remap-nepal # Data-quality notes Station data is high-quality pyranometer-grade, calibrated, Vaisala-instrument-based. Spatial coverage is thin (14 stations across a country of Nepal's complexity); satellite products fill the interpolation gap but with systematic biases in high-mountain terrain. Temporal coverage (2015–2019) pre-dates the 2021–2024 atmospheric-aerosol shifts; there is a case for a refresh campaign, especially in the Indo-Gangetic-plain-adjacent Terai where dust aerosol has intensified. Post-2019 data is patchy; some stations continued under AEPC operation, others were decommissioned. # Gaps we would like A 2024/25 refresh campaign across at least 8 of the original 14 stations, to capture atmospheric-aerosol evolution. Publication of a per-station 10-year climatology with percentile bands (not just 10-year mean). Integration with cloud-cover indices (MODIS, Himawari) for operational forecasting value. # Related global-solar-atlas-nepal — satellite-derived complement irena-remap-nepal — scenario-modelling use of this data aepc-renewable-framework — implementation partner solar-resource-geography-nepal — the narrative interpretation data-nepal-solar-resource-zones — the operational table

pages.title: World Bank Ganges Strategic Basin Assessment
headings: World Bank Ganges Strategic Basin Assessment
pages.excerpt: Regional-scale analysis of the Ganges basin covering water storage, flood management, and transboundary dynamics. Provides the valley-shape storage paradox that Public source review highlighted.
pages.body_text: World Bank Ganges Strategic Basin Assessment # Summary Regional-scale analysis of the Ganges basin covering water storage, flood management, and transboundary dynamics. Provides the valley-shape storage paradox that Public source review highlighted. # Key Data Points Aswan High Dam (Egypt, 111m): 162 BCM storage — flat terrain allows massive reservoir Proposed Andhi Khola Dam (Nepal, 110m): only 0.9 BCM — steep V-shaped Himalayan valley Karnali Chisapani proposed gross storage: 28.2 BCM, usable live capacity only 16.2 BCM Nepal's annual water flow through territory: 175–225 BCM # Relevance to Project The valley-shape paradox (same dam height, 180x less storage) is one of the most powerful visualizations for explaining why Nepal's geography simultaneously enables hydropower and prevents easy storage. Central to storage-deficit and data-storage-comparison. # Limitations 2014 publication. Pre-dates the 2015 earthquake, post-earthquake hydrological assessments, and the 2021 Melamchi flood. Basin conditions, sedimentation rates, and infrastructure assumptions may have shifted. Regional focus, not Nepal-specific. The assessment covers the entire Ganges basin across four countries; Nepal-specific storage figures are extracted from a broader regional frame and may lack the granularity of a Nepal-only study. Karnali Chisapani figures are study-era estimates. The 28.2 BCM gross / 16.2 BCM live figures predate the most recent project feasibility iterations. # Used By karnali-chisapani pancheshwar

pages.excerpt: The institutional anchor for Nepal's first utility-scale, grid-tied solar farm and the financing channel that broke Nepal's "can we actually build solar at utility scale?" learning curve. IDA credit to the Government of Nepal, implemented by NEA under a World Bank project supervi
pages.body_text: World Bank Grid Solar and Energy Efficiency Project The institutional anchor for Nepal's first utility-scale, grid-tied solar farm and the financing channel that broke Nepal's "can we actually build solar at utility scale?" learning curve. IDA credit to the Government of Nepal, implemented by NEA under a World Bank project supervision framework. # What the project covers Three components: ## Component 1: Grid-Connected Solar PV Farms Development Pilot utility-scale solar farm development Output: 25 MWp ground-mounted grid-tied solar plant at Bidur / Trishuli, Nuwakot district (completed, commissioned 2022) — see bidur-trishuli-solar-25mwp First NEA-owned, NEA-operated utility solar plant in Nepal Interconnection to the Trishuli 33 kV grid EPC via competitive procurement; O&M staff trained under the project ## Component 2: Distribution System Upgrading Substation upgrades, distribution line reinforcement Smart-meter pilot deployments Distribution loss reduction targets ## Component 3: Institutional Capacity and Project Management NEA capacity building for solar O&M, grid-integration studies, net-metering framework Technical assistance for future solar programmes (including what became the 960 MW tender) The "cumulative grid impact study for 960 MW solar" cited in nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 was delivered under this project's TA line # Key data points Credit size: IDA concessional loan (amount: in hundreds of millions of USD; specific number in PAD and ICR) Implementation period: approximately 2014–2023 Bidur / Trishuli 25 MWp: commissioned 2022; first ~40 GWh/yr generation Follow-on tender design capacity: provided the technical framework for the 960 MW national solar tender (nea-960mw-solar-tender) # Why this project matters Three institutional firsts that changed what is operationally possible: 1. First NEA-EPC utility solar, closed on time. Broke the "NEA can't build renewables beyond hydro" narrative and put NEA's project-management bandwidth through the cycle once. 2. Established the PPA template for utility solar. The PPA structure, grid-interconnection specification, metering standard, and O&M protocol that subsequent IPP solar plants use are descendants of the Bidur/Trishuli precedent. 3. Demonstrated the site-to-grid latency. Planning → PPA → COD in ~5 years for the first plant; IPP plants now take ~2–3 years. The learning curve compression is the project's most valuable externality. # Parallel / follow-on donor programmes The WB Grid Solar & EE Project sits in a cluster of donor programmes on Nepal renewables: Programme | Donor | Focus | Target (approx.) | ---|---|---|---:| Grid Solar & EE | World Bank | Utility solar + grid upgrade | 25 MWp + distribution work | Promotion of Solar Energy in Rural and Semi-Urban Regions II | EIB | Ground-mounted grid-tied solar, 4 sites | up to EUR 8 M | Technical Assistance — Solar Tender Design | ADB / JICA (partial) | 960 MW tender grid studies | — | AEPC programmes (SHS, mini-grid) | ADB, SREP, WB, donor consortium | Off-grid + rural | ~100 MWp cumulative | Karnali off-grid solar + BESS | World Bank | Remote grid-absent districts | ~10 MWp target | Collectively these programmes have financed essentially all of Nepal's solar deployment to date; the 960 MW tender is the first programme of sufficient scale that private IPP finance dominates the capital stack rather than donor grants / concessional loans. # Documents and subsources Project Appraisal Document (PAD) — initial project design and rationale Implementation Status Reports (ISR) — periodic progress updates Implementation Completion and Results Report (ICR) — post-project evaluation Technical assistance outputs — solar tender design, grid impact studies, net-metering framework Bidur / Trishuli plant completion report (NEA + WB) # Data-quality notes Project-level disclosure is high (WB disclosure standards); credit amount, disbursement, and component performance are publicly documented. The 25 MWp Bidur/Trishuli plant's actual FY 2023/24 and FY 2024/25 generation numbers are in NEA annual reports and internal operational statistics. Grid impact study outputs have fed directly into the 960 MW tender design; that traceable chain is one of the cleanest "donor TA → national policy" examples in Nepal energy. # Relevance to project Primary source for: bidur-trishuli-solar-25mwp — the flagship entity nea-960mw-solar-tender — the direct institutional descendant hybrid-siting-logic — Bidur/Trishuli is a near-hydro siting precedent rooftop-minigrid-offgrid — WB Grid Solar & EE Project touches both utility and distribution Cross-references: eib-rural-solar-phase2 — parallel programme aepc-renewable-framework — parallel programme on the off-grid side nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 — the implementation-side primary source # Related bidur-trishuli-solar-25mwp nea-960mw-solar-tender nea wb-country-economic-memo-2025 — macro frame wb-nepal-power-sector-reform-2022 — sector-reform frame this project sits inside

headings: World Bank / CCAC Economics of Household Cooking Using Electricity in Nepal
pages.excerpt: 2025 World Bank-linked report on household electric cooking economics in Nepal, published through the Climate & Clean Air Coalition resource library. It is used here to verify that the latest reviewed source still describes electric cooking adoption as below one percent of househ
pages.body_text: World Bank / CCAC Economics of Household Cooking Using Electricity in Nepal # Summary 2025 World Bank-linked report on household electric cooking economics in Nepal, published through the Climate & Clean Air Coalition resource library. It is used here to verify that the latest reviewed source still describes electric cooking adoption as below one percent of households rather than providing a newer annual uptake series. # Key Findings The report states that electricity has been used for cooking in less than one percent of Nepali households. It identifies unprocessed solid biomass as the primary cooking fuel for approximately 60% of households. It compares cooking technologies and fuels across Nepal's topographical regions from private and social-cost perspectives. It finds electricity cheaper than fossil fuels on average, but costlier than biomass from a private-cost perspective; when PM2.5 external costs are included, electricity becomes the cheapest option except for biogas. # Relevance Supports data-domestic-demand by confirming that the 0.5% electric-cooking statistic remains a low-adoption baseline rather than a superseded figure in the current reviewed source set. # Limitations Not an annual adoption series. The report corroborates sub-1% electric-cooking uptake but does not provide a newer nationally updated household share to replace the 2021 baseline. Economics focus. The report is primarily a cost-economics study, not a statistical yearbook or household energy census. Secondary publication page. The linked page is the CCAC resource page for the report; the underlying paper and reproducibility package should be used for detailed model replication. # Used By data-domestic-demand

pages.title: World Bank Nepal Water Sector Diagnostic
headings: World Bank Nepal Water Sector Diagnostic
pages.excerpt: A water-sector-wide diagnostic covering storage requirements, irrigation, and the intersection of water management with energy. Provides the most authoritative estimate of Nepal's seasonal storage gap.
pages.body_text: World Bank Nepal Water Sector Diagnostic # Summary A water-sector-wide diagnostic covering storage requirements, irrigation, and the intersection of water management with energy. Provides the most authoritative estimate of Nepal's seasonal storage gap. # Key Data Points Nepal's storage volume requirement to satisfy annual seasonal water demand: 29.86 km³ Nepal effectively has none of this required seasonal storage at national scale JICA estimates Nepal will need at least 1,993 MW of storage hydropower by 2032 (BAU) or 3,154 MW (high demand) Nepal's active dam storage: ~85 MCM (one of the lowest in Asia) # Limitations Storage-gap framing: The 29.86 km³ requirement is a water-sector-wide estimate (irrigation + energy + other uses), not an electricity-only storage target. Active vs total storage ambiguity: The ~85 MCM active storage and 130–150 MCM total figures differ by boundary definition. Both are vanishingly small relative to need. 2023 cutoff: Post-2023 project progress, policy changes, and new studies (e.g., JICA IPSDP) may update the storage requirement estimates. JICA MW targets: The 1,993 MW (BAU) and 3,154 MW (high demand) storage hydropower figures are JICA study outputs, not verified construction plans. # Used By data-storage-comparison figure-index storage-deficit # Relevance to Project The 29.86 km³ requirement vs near-zero actual storage is the single most dramatic number for the storage-deficit argument. JICA's MW requirements give a concrete planning target. Data feeds into data-storage-comparison. . [!note] The 85 MCM active storage figure and the 130-150 MCM total figure likely differ in boundary — active vs total reservoir volume. Both are vanishingly small relative to the 29.86 km³ need.

pages.title: WECS/DHM Methodology — Hydrological Estimation for Ungauged Locations (1990)
headings: WECS/DHM Methodology — Hydrological Estimation for Ungauged Locations (1990)
pages.excerpt: "Methodology for Estimating Hydrological Characteristics of Ungauged Locations in Nepal" (WECS/DHM, 1990, Seq. No. 331, Ministry of Water Resources). The regulatory default methodology for feasibility studies on Nepal's vast number of projects on ungauged tributaries.
pages.body_text: WECS/DHM Methodology — Hydrological Estimation for Ungauged Locations (1990) # Summary "Methodology for Estimating Hydrological Characteristics of Ungauged Locations in Nepal" (WECS/DHM, 1990, Seq. No. 331, Ministry of Water Resources). The regulatory default methodology for feasibility studies on Nepal's vast number of projects on ungauged tributaries. # Key points Empirical regionalization equations derived from DHM gauging data collected up to 1985. Simplistic regression: For example, instantaneous flood flows for a 2-year return period use a regression equation based solely on catchment area below 3,000 meters elevation. HYMOS dependence: Data processing and gap-filling have historically relied on HYMOS (version 4), a proprietary hydrological software system. Stationarity assumption: The models assume hydrological stationarity — that statistical properties of river flows remain constant over time. They do not capture cryospheric melt acceleration, shifting monsoon patterns, or increasing baseflow volatility. Partial update: DHM issued "Hydrological Estimation in Nepal" (June 2016), but the 1990 methodology remains the regulatory default for most feasibility studies. # Limitations Data age: Empirical regionalization equations are derived from DHM gauging data collected up to 1985; hydrological conditions may have changed significantly. Stationarity assumption: Models assume hydrological stationarity and do not capture cryospheric melt acceleration, shifting monsoon patterns, or increasing baseflow volatility. Simplistic regression: Instantaneous flood flows use regression equations based solely on catchment area below 3,000 m elevation, which may not capture complex Himalayan terrain. Proprietary dependence: Data processing and gap-filling historically rely on HYMOS (version 4), a proprietary software system that limits transparency and reproducibility. Partial update: DHM issued a 2016 update, but the 1990 methodology remains the regulatory default; newer hydrological insights are not systematically integrated. # Used By No pages currently reference this source.

pages.title: WECS Energy Sector Synopsis Report 2024
pages.excerpt: Covers Nepal's full energy balance for FY 2079/80 (~2022/23), including all energy sources (not just electricity). Provides the broader context for where grid electricity fits within Nepal's total energy system. This is the authoritative denominator for every "hydro share of tota
pages.body_text: WECS Energy Sector Synopsis Report 2024 # Summary Covers Nepal's full energy balance for FY 2079/80 (~2022/23), including all energy sources (not just electricity). Provides the broader context for where grid electricity fits within Nepal's total energy system. This is the authoritative denominator for every "hydro share of total energy" claim. # Key Data Points (FY 2079/80) Total final energy consumption: 532.42 PJ (−16.81% YoY vs 640 PJ in FY 2078/79) Consumption by resource class: - Traditional biomass: 63.87% (340.04 PJ) — fuelwood, ag residue, animal dung - Commercial fuels: 25.80% (137.38 PJ) — coal, petrol, diesel, kerosene, LPG, ATF, furnace oil - Grid electricity: 7.23% (38.49 PJ) — up from ~4.96% in FY 2078/79 (+21.18% YoY) - Modern renewables: 3.10% (16.50 PJ) — biogas, solar, micro-hydro, wind Coal consumption down −41.50% YoY; petroleum products down −16.14% YoY Sectoral shares: - Residential 60.75% (323,463 TJ) - Industrial 20.91% (111,306 TJ) - Transportation 10.43% (55,553 TJ) - Commercial 5.04% (26,835 TJ) - Construction/Mining 1.92% (10,222 TJ) - Agriculture 0.95% (5,040 TJ) Hydropower capacity referenced: 3,349 MW installed, 9,940.86 GWh generated (FY 2023/24) Transmission system: 5,742 circuit-km at 66 kV+; 8,867 MVA substation capacity # Correction note Earlier wiki pages cite grid electricity as 4.96% of final energy. That figure was the FY 2078/79 value that appears in this report's historical prose. The FY 2079/80 headline figure is 7.23%. Both are correct for their respective years; the 2.3-point jump in one year reflects real electrification growth. Full cross-tab decoded at data-final-energy-mix. # Local PDF status The local file at is now a real PDF copy of the report, verified locally as a 167-page PDF. The external above remains the canonical public URL. # Limitations Single-year snapshot: FY 2079/80 data; YoY comparisons (e.g., −16.81% total final energy) are sensitive to single-year anomalies such as fuel price shocks or demand disruptions. Local copy status: The repository copy has been verified as a 167-page PDF, but future extraction should still cross-check against the external . Biomass estimates: The 63.87% traditional biomass share relies on survey assumptions and stock-flow models, not metered consumption data. Grid-electricity share jump: The 4.96% → 7.23% jump in one year may reflect both real electrification growth and improvements in measurement coverage. # Used By data-final-energy-mix figure-index irena-remap-nepal run-of-river-hydropower solar-hydro-complementarity wecs # Relevance to Project The 7.23% grid-electricity share — and the fact that hydro is only ~6.8% of Nepal's total final energy — is one of the most revealing data points in the entire project. It collapses the "Nepal is a hydropower country" framing into the more honest "Nepal has a hydropower electricity system inside a biomass-and-petroleum energy system." Central to master-thesis, domestic-led-hydro-strategy, and energy-substitution-pathway. Feeds into nepal-energy-profile and data-final-energy-mix. .

headings: WECS Assessment of Hydropower Potential of Nepal (2019)
pages.excerpt: Site Inspection during Safeguards
pages.body_text: WECS Assessment of Hydropower Potential of Nepal (2019) Site Inspection during Safeguards # Summary The revised national hydropower potential assessment. Supersedes the older 83,000 MW theoretical figure with updated screening. Provides basin-level gross and techno-economic potential breakdowns. # Key Data Points Revised gross potential: 72,544 MW (down from legacy 83,500 MW) Techno-economic potential: 32,680 MW Basin distribution of gross potential: - koshi-basin: 27,805 MW - karnali-basin: 20,385 MW - gandaki-basin: 19,803 MW - All remaining basins: ~4,551 MW ~94% of gross potential is in the three major Himalayan basins # Limitations Screening opacity: Full Multi-Criteria Analysis methodology and sensitivity parameters are not transparent in the public version. Gross vs techno-economic: The 72,544 MW gross potential is a theoretical ceiling; the 32,680 MW techno-economic potential is the more honest planning baseline. Legacy figure persistence: The older 83,000 MW figure remains politically prominent despite this revision. Exclusions: Does not account for climate-adjusted hydrology, sediment risk, or buildability constraints that would reduce realisable potential below techno-economic estimates. # Used By buildability data-layer-nepal-tributaries data-potential-pyramid figure-index firm-power hydropower-potential-categories irena-remap-nepal karnali-chisapani koshi-basin run-of-river-hydropower wecs # Relevance to Project The definitive source for hydropower-potential-categories. Only surfaced the revised 72,544 MW figure — public summaries used the legacy 83,000 MW. The basin concentration data (94% in three basins) is central to the strategic argument. [!note] The legacy 83,000 MW figure remains politically prominent. The 2019 assessment's 72,544 MW is the more defensible current number, and 32,680 MW techno-economic is the more honest planning baseline.

headings: WECS River Basin Plans and Hydropower Development Master Plan (2024)
pages.excerpt: The 2024 master planning document for Nepal's river basins. Provides basin-level discharge data, seasonal flow profiles, hydropower potential assessments, and strategic planning frameworks. This is the most authoritative recent basin-level reference.
pages.body_text: WECS River Basin Plans and Hydropower Development Master Plan (2024) # Summary The 2024 master planning document for Nepal's river basins. Provides basin-level discharge data, seasonal flow profiles, hydropower potential assessments, and strategic planning frameworks. This is the most authoritative recent basin-level reference. # Key Data Points koshi-basin: 27,818 km² in Nepal; 1,826.5 cumec average border flow; dry-season flows reduce to ~10x lower than peak gandaki-basin: 32,148 km² in Nepal; 1,952.3 cumec average border flow; ~80% of rainfall in four wet-season months karnali-basin: 43,153 km² in Nepal; 1,255.9 cumec average border flow; highest hydropower potential per WECS 75% or more of river flow occurs in the wet season (June–September) Storage and multipurpose projects treated as central to moving value from surplus to deficit basins Babai explicitly described as rain-fed; West Rapti, Kamala, Kankai as water-deficit / dry-season constrained # Relevance to Project Foundation for the hydrology evidence base. Provides the basin-level evidence for seasonal-mismatch and claim-timing-not-volume. [!warning] WECS explicitly warns that atlas flow numbers are model-derived (MIKE SHE / MIKE Hydro Basin) and may differ from DHM observations or project-specific studies. # Limitations Model-derived, not measured. Basin flow numbers are MIKE SHE / MIKE Hydro Basin model outputs, not DHM gauge observations. Values may differ from project-specific hydrological studies. Single planning document. The master plan represents WECS's planning framework at a point in time; it does not reflect subsequent basin-level developments, project-specific feasibility studies, or post-2024 hydrological events. Dry-season flow estimates are model projections. The ~10x wet-to-dry flow reduction cited for Koshi is a model estimate, not a multi-decadal gauge average. Interannual variability may be wider than implied. # Used By data-basin-discharge data-layer-nepal-tributaries data-solar-hydro-complementarity-profile figure-index solar-hydro-complementarity wecs

pages.title: Alternative Energy Promotion Centre (AEPC)
pages.excerpt: Government of Nepal institution responsible for rural electrification through renewables. Technically a semi-autonomous body under the Ministry of Energy, Water Resources & Irrigation (MoEWRI); operationally the country's primary administrator of the off-grid solar, biogas, impro
pages.body_text: Alternative Energy Promotion Centre (AEPC) Government of Nepal institution responsible for rural electrification through renewables. Technically a semi-autonomous body under the Ministry of Energy, Water Resources & Irrigation (MoEWRI); operationally the country's primary administrator of the off-grid solar, biogas, improved cookstove, and community mini-grid programmes. Standing alongside (not inside) NEA. # Role summary Function | AEPC | NEA | ---|---|---| Grid-tied utility-scale solar | Technical partner on donor-track | Lead operator | Rooftop / distributed solar | Subsidy channel | Net-metering administration | Solar home systems (SHS) | Primary operator | Not involved | Community mini-grids | Primary operator | Grid-edge interconnect when reached | Biogas (~400,000 plants) | Primary operator | Not involved | Improved cookstove (~1M+ units) | Primary operator | Not involved | Off-grid institutional solar | Primary operator | Not involved | # Key Facts Founded: 1996, under the Ministry of Science, Technology and Environment originally; relocated to MoEWRI Cumulative solar home systems installed: ~1.1 million (as of ~2021 with ongoing additions) Cumulative SHS capacity: ~80–100 MWp Community mini-grids operational: ~30 sites, ~1.1 MWp aggregate Institutional solar sites: ~25,000, ~15 MWp aggregate Geographic footprint: strongest in Karnali, Sudurpaschim, remote hill districts of Koshi / Bagmati / Gandaki (see data-rooftop-shs-deployment) Donor partners: ADB, SREP (CIF), World Bank, EIB, UNDP, GIZ, DANIDA, various bilateral channels # Financing structure AEPC's renewable programmes run on a subsidy-plus-concessional-finance model: Grant element: 30–50% of capex for remote / difficult districts; lower for semi-urban Microfinance element: remainder, via Nepal Rastra Bank-approved cooperative lenders Community equity element: labour + small cash contribution in most mini-grids Donor-funded programme lines set the budget envelope (ADB, WB, EIB all operate through AEPC) The total annual AEPC renewable-programme budget has historically been in the NPR 3–8 billion range (highly donor-dependent). # Why AEPC is strategically under-weighted Three reasons AEPC is usually missed in Nepal energy analysis: 1. MW under-counting. AEPC's 100+ MWp cumulative solar is spread across a million systems; it doesn't appear on NEA's installed-capacity table, so gets omitted from "Nepal has 142 MW of solar" soundbites. The real number is ~2.3× larger if you count both. 2. The value-weight is higher than MW-weight. Off-grid solar displaces NPR 60–90/kWh diesel, not NPR 8/kWh grid; the value of AEPC's fleet is disproportionately high — 10–15× the utility-equivalent kWh value (see data-solar-hydro-lcoe). 3. AEPC is the institutional carrier of the rural-electrification political coalition. Which is the coalition most likely to sustain Nepal's solar policy past any single electoral cycle. Utility solar depends on NEA tender capacity; rural solar depends on AEPC cooperative networks — and the latter has been more durable institutionally (AEPC has run continuous SHS programmes for ~28 years). # The AEPC strategic expansion thesis The wiki argues that AEPC, not NEA, is the natural home for three emerging solar programmes: ## 1. Agrivoltaic programme administration agrivoltaics-and-land requires lease-template law, revenue-sharing contracts with smallholder cooperatives, and crop-verification protocols. These are AEPC-format skills, not NEA-format skills. Terai solar at scale likely runs through AEPC's cooperative networks even when the physical plant is a 10–50 MWp ground-mount feeding the NEA grid. ## 2. Off-grid to grid-edge integration As NEA grid reaches former off-grid villages (~8.6% of households still grid-absent, nea), each AEPC mini-grid becomes a grid-edge asset. AEPC-NEA integration protocol (who owns what, tariff structure, BESS-sharing) is currently ad-hoc and should be formalized. rooftop-minigrid-offgrid. ## 3. Solar + BESS rural hybrids The NEA FY 2024/25 annual report explicitly references off-grid solar + BESS deployments in Karnali as an emerging programme line. This is AEPC's home ground technically; NEA would be the grid-edge integrator but not the programme operator. Formalising this channel is one of the highest-leverage institutional moves in Nepal solar policy. # Institutional challenges Donor dependence. AEPC's budget oscillates with donor cycles; the 2017–2020 SREP cycle had ~2× the budget of the 2022–2024 period. Programme continuity depends on donor pipeline management. Staff capacity. Rural technical staff are overstretched; each engineer covers multiple districts in Karnali / Sudurpaschim. Community mini-grid O&M quality varies with staffing continuity. Mandate overlap. AEPC's mandate edges into MoEWRI rural electrification and NEA distribution; interagency coordination has historically been ad-hoc. Data / registry infrastructure. Cumulative deployment numbers are known at the national roll-up but district-level registries are partial post-2021. # Related aepc-renewable-framework — the source-page documentation data-rooftop-shs-deployment — the district-level deployment data rooftop-minigrid-offgrid — the tracks AEPC operates eib-rural-solar-phase2 — expanding AEPC mandate into utility nea — the institutional counterpart claim-solar-political-coalition-is-rural — the political frame AEPC anchors

pages.title: Andhi Khola
pages.excerpt: This page tracks the 180 MW Andhi Khola storage candidate from the JICA/MP2014 screening set, not the separate 9.4 MW operating plant on the same river. The shared river name had been collapsing two different project objects into one page; this version keeps them distinct.
pages.body_text: Andhi Khola This page tracks the 180 MW Andhi Khola storage candidate from the JICA/MP2014 screening set, not the separate 9.4 MW operating plant on the same river. The shared river name had been collapsing two different project objects into one page; this version keeps them distinct. # Summary Andhi Khola is tracked here as a 180 MW survey-stage storage candidate in the Gandaki basin. The page distinguishes that planning-stage storage concept from the separate 9.4 MW operating plant on the same river. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 180 MW | Status | Survey | Category | JICA promising storage | River | Andhi Khola (gandaki-basin) | District | Syangja | Province | Gandaki Pradesh | Annual design energy | 648.7 GWh | Dry-season energy | 137.1 GWh | Dry-season share | 21.1 % | Type | Storage | Total storage | 336.5 MCM | Effective storage | 238.7 MCM | # Sources nea-transmission-annual-book-2077 jica-ipsdp-main-report-vol2 # Why It Matters Andhi Khola matters because it is one of the smaller storage candidates that still looks systemically relevant in Nepal's dry-season problem. At 180 MW and 137.1 GWh of dry-season energy, it is not a mega-project like budhigandaki or dudhkoshi-storage, but it is large enough to matter in a portfolio of medium storage assets. It is also a useful discipline case for the wiki itself: river-name continuity does not mean project continuity. Nepal has many sites where an operating RoR plant, a survey licence, and a larger storage concept can all sit in the same corridor while representing different investment objects. # Status And Timing The storage-candidate figures come from the JICA/NEA master-plan screening material and should be read as planning-stage values, not an active construction programme. The candidate remains a survey-stage storage concept in this wiki's project-specs dataset. The separate 9.4 MW operating plant on the river may still appear in some mapped operating inventories. That operating asset is evidence that the river already hosts generation; it is not the same project as this 180 MW storage candidate. # Limitations & Controversies The current map anchor for should be interpreted conservatively. It is a planning anchor for the storage candidate, not an engineering-grade location for a final dam/powerhouse layout. # Registry note JICA/NEA storage master plan volume 2 drives the storage metrics used here. Public registry and operating-map records may refer to a smaller operating Andhi Khola plant; those records should not be read as describing this 180 MW storage candidate. # See also gandaki-basin run-of-river-hydropower storage-deficit firm-power stranded-generation data-layer-storage-shortlist data-layer-priority-watchlist

pages.title: Ankhu Khola
pages.excerpt: Ankhu Khola Jalvidhyut Company Limited (AKJCL) is a 42.9 MW run-of-river hydropower project. Beyond its generation capacity, Ankhu Khola is a textbook example of the hydropower rights-share bailout pattern documented in Nepal's capital markets.
pages.body_text: Ankhu Khola Ankhu Khola Jalvidhyut Company Limited (AKJCL) is a 42.9 MW run-of-river hydropower project. Beyond its generation capacity, Ankhu Khola is a textbook example of the hydropower rights-share bailout pattern documented in Nepal's capital markets. # Summary Ankhu Khola is a 42.9 MW under-construction run-of-river hydropower project used here as a capital-market case study. The page focuses on the project's rights-share issuance and debt-repayment pattern alongside its registry specifications. # The Bailout Pattern Ankhu Khola's capital markets history exemplifies the structural dynamic where Nepal's retail equity investors absorb commercial bank debt: 2013: IPO raised NPR 20 crore for construction funding 2024: Rights issue of NPR 120 crore at a 1:1.5 ratio — a 150% dilution Stated use of proceeds: explicitly to "pay off bank loans" and invest in a 20 MW downstream cascade (AKJCL-2) The rights-share issuance came within roughly a decade of the initial IPO, with the stated purpose being debt clearance rather than new capital expenditure. This pattern — where public equity is deployed to prevent bank foreclosure — is not unique to Ankhu Khola but it is one of the most extreme examples in terms of dilution ratio (1:1.5). # Systemic Pattern Ankhu Khola sits alongside other projects in the rights-share bailout inventory documented in sector-financial-analysis-triple-authority-2026: Company | IPO Cr | Rights Cr | Dilution | Use | ---|---|---|---|---| Ankhu Khola | 20 | 120 | 150% | Repay bank loans | Upper Tamakoshi | 100 | 1,059 (1:1) | 100% | Retire legacy debt | Joshi Hydropower | 24.1 | 15.6 (1:0.65) | 65% | Prevent NPL status | Peoples Power | 31.6 | 15.8 (1:0.5) | 50% | Repay Prime Commercial Bank | The pattern is consistent: pre-COD or immediately post-COD IPOs, followed by rights issues within 2–10 years, with proceeds directed at debt servicing rather than capacity expansion. # See Also sector-financial-analysis-triple-authority-2026 ipo-hydropower-bailout q-design-discharge # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 42.9 MW | Status | Under construction | Registry licence | Generation | River | Ankhu Khola | District | Nuwakot | Province | Bagmati Pradesh | # Limitations & Controversies The page is strongest on the rights-share and debt-repayment pattern documented in sector-financial-analysis-triple-authority-2026. It does not independently verify construction progress, hydrology, final project cost, COD timing, or the downstream cascade investment beyond the existing source set. sector-financial-analysis-triple-authority-2026 ipo-hydropower-bailout q-design-discharge run-of-river-hydropower buildability # Sources sector-financial-analysis-triple-authority-2026

pages.title: Arun 3
pages.excerpt: Figure 6.3-25 River Longitudinal Profile of the Arun River
pages.body_text: Arun 3 Figure 6.3-25 River Longitudinal Profile of the Arun River # Summary Nepal's single largest project under construction — a 900 MW peaking run-of-river scheme on the Arun River in Sankhuwasabha, developed and financed by India's state utility SJVN. When it comes online (revised target: September 2026), it will almost double the country's operating hydropower fleet — but only ~22% of its output will stay in Nepal. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 900 MW | Status | Under construction — 74.6% complete (Dec 2025) | River | Arun (eastern koshi-basin) | District | Sankhuwasabha | ## Engineering Arun-3 is designed as a peaking RoR plant — 3.4 hours of full rated output per day, delivered through an underground powerhouse with four Francis turbines. This means its 900 MW nameplate translates into a much smaller day-long energy contribution than its capacity suggests. Compare with upper-tamakoshi (456 MW continuous RoR) for the contrast in fleet-shape implications. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Units | 4 × 225 MW | Turbine type | Francis | Type | Peaking run-of-river | Evacuation | 400 kV DC line to Sitamarhi, Bihar | ## Output Design energy of ~3,971 GWh/yr leaves Nepal with only 21.9% (~870 GWh) as royalty-free share. The remaining output goes to the Indian grid — making Arun-3 an export-first asset with a domestic free-share component. How this interacts with dry-season firm-power accounting is a core question for hydro-geopolitics. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Annual design energy | 3,971 GWh | Nepal free share | 21.9% (~197 MW equivalent) | Peaking duration | ~3.4 hours/day at full output | ## Financial At ~USD 1.6 billion total cost, Arun-3 is a 30-year BOOT concession — built, owned, operated, and eventually transferred by India's state utility SJVN. The economics depend heavily on whether the 400 kV cross-border evacuation line to Sitamarhi (only 58% complete as of late 2025) is finished on schedule. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Total cost | ~USD 1.6 billion | Concession | 30-year BOOT | ## Governance SJVN, an Indian state utility, develops, owns, and operates the project through its subsidiary SAPDC. This is the reference case for India-developed export-first hydropower in Nepal — a structure that the domestic-led-hydro-strategy thesis argues against for strategic capacity control. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Developer | SJVN Arun-3 Power Development Company (SAPDC) | Lead financier | SJVN (Indian state utility) | Concession period | 30 years | ## Schedule Original commissioning target was March 2025; SJVN has formally applied to extend COD to September 2026. Every year of delay compounds Nepal's storage-deficit exposure because Arun-3 is already counted in NEA's near-term planning. The evacuation line dependency creates a single-point-of-failure — without the 400 kV Sitamarhi line, the export revenue case collapses. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Completion | 74.6 % | COD target | September 2026 | # Significance Arun-3 is the archetype of Nepal's India-developed export-first project class. Under the 2014 Project Development Agreement, SJVN builds, owns and operates the plant for 30 years, gives Nepal 21.9% of the energy as royalty-free share, offers another 10% on commercial terms, and takes the remainder to the Indian grid — a structure that makes Arun-3 the reference case when discussing hydro-geopolitics in the basin. It also changes the shape of Nepal's fleet, not just the size. Arun-3 is designed as a peaking RoR plant — 3.4 hours of full rated output per day, not continuous. So its 900 MW nameplate translates into a much smaller day-long energy contribution than its capacity suggests. That matters because Nepal's structural problem isn't capacity; it's seasonal-mismatch and firm-power deficits in dry months, which a peaking RoR plant can help with only to the extent the transmission system can absorb concentrated evening blocks. Compared to upper-tamakoshi — which is Nepali-developed, Nepali-dispatched, and continuous-RoR at 456 MW — Arun-3 is larger but strategically narrower: more export value than domestic reliability value. # Limitations & Controversies Repeated schedule slip. Original commissioning target was March 2025; SJVN has formally applied to extend COD to September 2026. Every year of delay compounds Nepal's storage-deficit exposure because Arun-3 is in the pipeline of projects NEA's planning has already counted on as "coming online soon." Evacuation dependency. The 400 kV cross-border line to Sitamarhi is only 58% complete as of late 2025. Without it, Arun-3's Indian export cannot move; with it, a single line carries most of the value. Both sides are exposed to the cross-border transmission asset. Free power as compensation theory. The 21.9% free share is the political justification for allowing the dominant share of the energy and revenue to accrue to India. Whether 21.9% is a good deal for Nepal depends on (a) the counterfactual — would the project have been built by a Nepali developer at all, and on what timeline — and (b) how the free share interacts with dry-season firm-power accounting, which Arun-3's peaking design constrains. # Official Visual References SAPDC's monthly progress reports are a materially better official visual source than the generic Arun riverside imagery that often gets used as a placeholder for the project. The February 2023 report cover contains a compact one-page schematic tying together the intake, headrace, surge shaft, powerhouse and tailrace alignment. Cover page from SAPDC's monthly progress report up to 28 February 2023. Source: SAPDC monthly progress report up to 28 February 2023 (PDF) # See also koshi-basin upper-tamakoshi hydro-geopolitics stranded-generation firm-power seasonal-mismatch inaruwa-purnea-interconnection — the 400 kV line being built to evacuate Arun-3 # Sources arun-3-project-status-2025 nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 jica-ipsdp-main-report-vol2

pages.title: Nepal–Bangladesh Electricity Trade Route
pages.excerpt: Nepal's first electricity export to a country other than India. A trilateral arrangement routed through India's grid — making India simultaneously Nepal's competitor, buyer, and logistics gatekeeper.
pages.body_text: Nepal–Bangladesh Electricity Trade Route # Summary Nepal's first electricity export to a country other than India. A trilateral arrangement routed through India's grid — making India simultaneously Nepal's competitor, buyer, and logistics gatekeeper. # Key Facts Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Tripartite PSA signed | October 3, 2024 | Parties | NEA, Bangladesh Power Development Board (BPDB), NTPC Vidyut Vyapar Nigam (India) | First export | 12 hours on November 15, 2024 (symbolic) | Full-scale exports began | June 15, 2025 | Export window | June 15–November 15 each year (5 months) | Duration | 5-year agreement (until Oct 2029) | Current capacity | 40 MW | Agreed expansion | 60 MW from June 2026 (+20 MW, pending India's CEA approval) | Tariff | 6.40 US cents/unit | Currency | USD (unlike India trade in INR) | Route | Nepal → Dhalkebar–Muzaffarpur 400 kV → Baharampur–Bheramara 400 kV → Bangladesh | # Revenue Period | GWh Exported | Revenue | --------|-------------|---------| 2024 (12 hours only) | negligible | — | Jun–Nov 2025 | 147.43 GWh | USD 9.436 million (~NPR 1.35 billion) | # Projects Supplying Bangladesh NEA currently allocates output from Trishuli (25 MW) and Chilime (22 MW) — older NEA-owned plants — to the Bangladesh export quota. India's CEA has approved these specific 40 MW until October 2, 2029. # Expansion Trajectory Nov 2025 (7th JSC meeting): Nepal and Bangladesh agreed to add 20 MW (total 60 MW) from June 2026 Bangladesh's long-term ambition: import 9,000 MW from Nepal by 2040 Alternative routes under study: Barapukuria, Panchagarh/Thakurgaon, Bheramara, Comilla corridors through India Sunkoshi III (683 MW): Expert committee formed to evaluate this project specifically for Bangladesh supply Upper Karnali (900 MW): GMR-developed project had a planned 500 MW PPA to Bangladesh — status uncertain after Sheikh Hasina's fall (Aug 2024) # Limitations & Controversies India retains structural veto. Every MW to Bangladesh requires India's Central Electricity Authority approval and transits Indian lines. India is simultaneously competitor, buyer, and logistics gatekeeper — market diversification does not reduce political dependence. Seasonal limitation. Exports only run June–November, perfectly overlapping Nepal's surplus window. The arrangement does nothing for dry-season revenue and is complementary to the seasonal-arbitrage-trap, not a solution. Small scale. At 40 MW (expanding to 60 MW), Bangladesh trade is a marginal share of Nepal's export portfolio. Bangladesh's ambition of 9,000 MW by 2040 is aspirational; no committed transmission corridor or financing exists for scale beyond the current trilateral arrangement. Political fragility. Bangladesh's post-Hasina transition has stalled larger pipeline projects (Upper Karnali PPA, direct transmission studies). The 5-year PSA term (until October 2029) may not survive a major bilateral rupture. # Strategic Significance 1. Buyer diversification. Reduces Nepal's monopsony dependence on India's IEX for export revenue 2. USD pricing. Bangladesh trade in dollars hedges against INR-NPR forex risk — significant given nea's NPR 2.5B forex losses in FY 2024/25 3. India as gatekeeper. Every MW to Bangladesh requires India's Central Electricity Authority approval and transits Indian lines — India retains structural veto over Nepal's market diversification 4. Seasonal limitation. Exports only run Jun–Nov, perfectly overlapping Nepal's surplus window — does nothing for dry-season revenue. The arrangement is complementary to the seasonal-arbitrage-trap, not a solution to it 5. Political fragility. Bangladesh's political transition (post-Hasina) has stalled larger pipeline projects (Upper Karnali PPA, direct transmission studies) # Related seasonal-arbitrage-trap — Bangladesh trade is monsoon-only, reinforcing the trap india-energy-relationship — India's veto/facilitation role data-trade-time-series — revenue figures hydro-geopolitics — trilateral dynamics dhalkebar-muzaffarpur — the 400 kV link that physically carries this trade

pages.title: Barahi Hydropower
pages.excerpt: Sub-10 MW run-of-river hydropower project, operational. This page exists as the wiki's primary audited case study for the nea-triple-authority conflict.
pages.body_text: Barahi Hydropower Sub-10 MW run-of-river hydropower project, operational. This page exists as the wiki's primary audited case study for the nea-triple-authority conflict. # Summary Barahi Hydropower is an operational sub-10 MW run-of-river project used as the wiki's audited case study for AD-penalty governance. The page centers on the conflict between the ERC small-project exemption and NEA invoice deductions reported in the source record. # The AD penalty conflict Barahi is protected by a statutory exemption from Availability Declaration (AD) penalties. The Electricity Regulatory Commission (ERC) Bylaws 2076, Clause 8(2) and Schedule 5, explicitly exempt projects below 10 MW from AD penalties and financial damages for availability shortfalls. Despite this exemption, NEA deducted penalty amounts for short supply from Barahi's invoices. Out of Rs 14.9 million in trade receivables, Barahi's management classified the deducted penalties as "receivable from NEA" — openly stating in their audited annual report that NEA's actions contradict the prevailing ERC By-laws. Because NEA controls the cash disbursement, the IPP carries the deducted penalty on its balance sheet while the statutory exemption exists on paper with no enforcement mechanism. The independent arbiter is absent. # Key facts Fact | Detail | ---|---| Capacity | Sub-10 MW | Type | Run-of-River | Status | Operational | Regulatory protection | ERC Bylaws 2076, Clause 8(2), Schedule 5 | Penalty deducted | Part of Rs 14.9M in receivables [UNVERIFIED: exact fiscal year to be confirmed] | Accounting treatment | "Receivable from NEA" in audited financial statements | Source | Barahi Hydropower Public Limited audited financial statements [UNVERIFIED: exact fiscal year and report date to be confirmed] | # Significance Barahi is the best-documented instance of the structural double-bind at the core of nea-triple-authority: a regulatory protection exists on paper, but the off-taker — who is also the dispatcher and penalty administrator — can deduct penalties regardless, because it controls the cash. The ERC can issue directives, but it cannot enforce them against the entity that holds the cheque book. # Limitations & Controversies The current record still carries explicit verification gaps: the exact fiscal year, report date, and detailed accounting context for the Rs 14.9 million receivables need confirmation from the audited financial statements. The page should be used as a documented case study of the AD-penalty conflict, not as a complete financial history of Barahi. # Sources ad-penalty-clause-research sector-financial-analysis-triple-authority-2026 # See also nea-triple-authority — the institutional framework this case anchors ad-penalties — the penalty mechanism at issue

pages.body_text: Betan Karnali HP Betan Karnali is a large semi-reservoir hydropower project on the Karnali, historically carried in the registry as a 688 MW survey-stage project and more recently advanced in public reporting as a 439 MW generation-licence / investment-approval project. It is pinned in the data-layer-priority-watchlist and data-layer-top-10-capacity-projects because it sits directly in the Karnali buildout story: large western capacity, storage-like peaking value, institutional Nepali financing, and dependency on how upper-karnali is finally resolved upstream. # Summary Betan Karnali is a large Karnali-basin semi-reservoir hydropower project with competing 688 MW registry and 439 MW current-development references. The page preserves the registry basis used by map layers while documenting the more recent public reporting around generation licensing and investment approval. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 688 MW | Status | Survey / study | Registry licence | Survey | River | Karnali (karnali-basin) | District | Achham | Province | Sudurpashchim Pradesh | Promoter | Betan Karnali Sanchayakarta Hydropower Company Ltd | # Why It Matters Betan Karnali is one of the clearest examples of why the wiki separates registry capacity from strategic value. The map's top-10 layer uses the older 688 MW registry record because that is the source field used to rank the display set. Current public project reporting, however, describes a 439 MW semi-reservoir scheme with an estimated cost around NPR 93-93.4 billion. That revised scale still matters. A 439 MW semi-reservoir plant with peaking value is more useful to Nepal's dry-season and evening-balancing problem than a simple wet-season-heavy capacity addition. It also matters institutionally: reporting on the 2025 licence and investment approval frames the ownership/finance structure around the Employees Provident Fund, NEA, Electricity Generation Company Ltd., EPF depositors, civil servants, local communities, and the public. # Status And Timing This page should be read as a current project record, not only as a survey-stage registry entry. Public reporting in July 2025 said Nepal's energy ministry granted a generation licence for the 439 MW Betan Karnali project and that the company aimed to start construction immediately and complete within five years. The Rising Nepal then reported in November 2025 that the Investment Board Nepal approved investment for the 439 MW Betan Karnali Semi-Reservoir Hydropower Project and formed a negotiation committee for the Project Development Agreement. The wiki still preserves the 688 MW generated spec because the map layer is derived from the DoED-linked registry snapshot. The analytical status is: Question | Current Read | ----------|--------------| Registry / map capacity | 688 MW survey-stage record. | Current reported development case | 439 MW semi-reservoir project. | Licence / approval status | Generation licence reported in July 2025; IBN investment approval reported in November 2025. | Construction start | "Immediate construction" is an announced aim, not yet treated here as confirmed physical construction. | Completion outlook | Five-year completion target in public reporting; IPSDP groups Betan Karnali in the 2036-2040 project window. | # Map Interpretation The watchlist marker uses a document-backed powerhouse-village vicinity at Tatalighat, snapped to the named Karnali reach. That makes it more useful than a raw registry point for strategic reading, but the marker is still an approximate project anchor. It should not be used as a final dam or powerhouse survey coordinate. # Limitations & Controversies The first open question is the 688 MW versus 439 MW basis. The map ranking follows the older registry value; the project-development story now appears to have moved to the smaller semi-reservoir configuration. Any downstream analysis should state which number it is using. The second question is finance and sequencing. Betan's institutional-investor model is attractive because it is domestic and long-tenor, but the project still has to close financing, sign/complete PDA arrangements, award construction packages, and coordinate with upstream upper-karnali assumptions. Until those steps are visible, the five-year completion target should be read as a developer/government objective rather than a bankable COD forecast. # Registry note BKSHCL EOI document and current project registry Naxa / DoED-linked public hydropower project dataset Current reporting: Fiscal Nepal on generation licence, July 2025 Current reporting: The Rising Nepal on IBN investment approval, November 2025 # Sources moewri-ipsdp-exec-summary-2025 # See also karnali-basin stranded-generation buildability upper-karnali data-ipsdp-milestone-ladder-2022-2040 data-layer-priority-watchlist data-layer-top-10-capacity-projects

Ltd. | # Why It Matters Bheri-1 matters as a capacity-ranking marker, not because the wiki has strong evidence that it is near construction. Its main analytical role is to keep the Bheri sub-basin visible inside the larger Karnali discussion. The top-10 layer is otherwise dominated by Karnali mainstem, Arun/Koshi, and Tama Koshi projects; Bheri-1 is the large Bheri-side entry in that comparison. This is exactly the kind of project that tests claim-mw-not-equal-value. A 440 MW survey marker can look decisive on a map, but the useful question is whether it has a credible development path, transmission route, financing structure, environmental clearance, and offtake arrangement. The current wiki evidence is much stronger on its registry identity than on those delivery steps. # Status And Timing The DoED-linked registry snapshot carries Bheri-1 as a survey-stage project. The IPSDP milestone ladder groups Bheri-1 in the 2036-2040 project window, alongside Betan Karnali, Mugu Karnali STO, Tamakoshi 3, Naumure STO, and other later-stage projects. The practical read is conservative: Question | Current Read | ----------|--------------| Is it operating or under construction? | No evidence in the current wiki source set. | Is there a confirmed construction start? | Not found in the sources used here. | Is there a planning window? | IPSDP groups Bheri-1 in 2036-2040. | Why keep it in the wiki? | It is a top-10 capacity marker and a Bheri/Karnali strategic comparator. | # Map Interpretation Bheri-1 has the weakest locational confidence among the top-10 capacity records: the layer labels it a low-confidence registry reference, even though the registry point sits close to the mapped Bheri reach. The marker is good enough to show that a large Bheri candidate exists in the project inventory. It is not good enough for site-grade analysis. # Limitations & Controversies The open questions are basic: project design maturity, sponsor status, licence renewal or conversion, grid evacuation, environmental and social impact, and offtake. Until those are documented, Bheri-1 should be treated as a later-horizon planning candidate rather than a near-term capacity addition. # Registry note Naxa / DoED-linked public hydropower project dataset # Sources moewri-ipsdp-exec-summary-2025 # See also karnali-basin buildability claim-mw-not-equal-value data-ipsdp-milestone-ladder-2022-2040 data-layer-top-10-capacity-projects

pages.excerpt: A planned 400 kV evacuation corridor for the western Bheri system, centred in the annual book on uttarganga-storage and the wider Sani Bheri IPP pipeline. In 2020 it was still a land, survey, and substation preparation story rather than a built line.
pages.body_text: Bheri Corridor 400 kV Transmission Line A planned 400 kV evacuation corridor for the western Bheri system, centred in the annual book on uttarganga-storage and the wider Sani Bheri IPP pipeline. In 2020 it was still a land, survey, and substation preparation story rather than a built line. # Summary The Bheri Corridor 400 kV line is a planned western evacuation corridor for Uttarganga and the wider Sani Bheri project pipeline. The current page is grounded in the NEA 2077 annual-book description of a survey/development-stage corridor and associated Uttarganga substation hub. [!cite] nea-transmission-annual-book-2077 Book page 65 describes the Bheri Corridor 400 kV line as a GoN-funded project intended to evacuate power from Uttarganga and other projects in the Sani Bheri basin, with a planned ~25 km 400 kV double-circuit line from Bafikot to Nalsingadh and a 400/132 kV, 200 MVA Uttarganga substation hub. # Key Facts Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Voltage | 400 kV | Status in 2020 book | Under development / survey-stage | Core route | Bafikot (Rukum West) to Nalsingadh (Jajarkot) | Associated substation | Uttarganga hub, 400/132 kV, 200 MVA | Strategic role | Evacuation path for Uttarganga and Sani Bheri generation | # Why It Matters This is the transmission expression of the western buildability problem: large projects such as uttarganga-storage do not have value without a corresponding evacuation corridor. The corridor sits squarely inside the wiki's claim-transmission-immediate-blocker logic and is one more example of generation ambition outrunning grid readiness. # Limitations & Controversies The current evidence is from the 2020 annual-book description and should be read as development-stage corridor context, not proof of a built 400 kV line. Route details, land status, construction progress, updated cost, and commissioning timing require newer project-level verification before operational use. # See also uttarganga-storage claim-transmission-immediate-blocker nepal-transmission-landscape-2025 stranded-generation

pages.title: Bhutan Hydropower Model
pages.excerpt: Bhutan is the most frequent regional comparison for Nepal's hydropower trajectory. The comparison is instructive and somewhat brutal.
pages.body_text: Bhutan Hydropower Model # Summary Bhutan is the most frequent regional comparison for Nepal's hydropower trajectory. The comparison is instructive and somewhat brutal. # Bhutan's Success Metric | Bhutan | Nepal | --------|--------|-------| Hydro contribution to GDP | ~14% | 3–5% | Hydro share of government revenue | ~26% | Marginal | Export price to India | $0.05–0.07/kWh | $0.03–0.05/kWh | Model | India-financed, India-built, India-integrated | Self-financed, fragmented, sovereignty-preserving | Bhutan's flagship plants (Chukha, Tala, Mangdechhu) were built with Indian grants and soft loans. India is co-investor with direct economic interest in project success. This gives Bhutan an unconditionally secure export market. # Why Nepal Chose Differently Nepal's more vibrant democracy, critical civil society, and strategic desire to balance Indian influence against Chinese investment led it to resist the "Bhutan model." Nepal opted for a slower, contested, fragmented development path to preserve economic and political sovereignty. This is a defensible policy choice, but it costs money: approximately $80–120 million per year in foregone export premium at current volumes. # Lessons Bhutan shows that Himalayan hydropower can generate national wealth But Bhutan's model requires granting India near-total control Bhutan's projects have also suffered massive delays and cost overruns under Indian management Nepal cannot replicate Bhutan without fundamentally changing its foreign policy posture # Limitations & Controversies Requires near-total Indian control. Bhutan's model works because India is co-investor with direct economic interest in project success. Nepal's strategic desire to preserve sovereignty means it cannot replicate this model without fundamentally changing its foreign policy posture. Foregone export premium. Nepal's sovereignty-preserving approach costs approximately $80–120 million per year in foregone export premium at current volumes — a real economic trade-off that the Bhutan comparison makes visible. Bhutan's projects also suffered delays. Chukha, Tala, and Mangdechhu all experienced massive delays and cost overruns under Indian management. The Bhutan model guarantees market access but does not guarantee execution discipline. Non-replicable political context. Bhutan is a constitutional monarchy with a different civil society structure and Indian relationship. Nepal's more vibrant democracy and critical civil society make the "grant India control" approach politically infeasible, regardless of its economic merits. # Related india-energy-relationship — the bilateral context hydro-geopolitics — why sovereignty preservation matters domestic-led-hydro-strategy — Nepal's alternative path

pages.title: Bidur / Trishuli 25 MWp Solar Farm
headings: Why Bidur/Trishuli sited at Nuwakot is strategically interesting
1. NEA can build solar on-schedule, on-budget, on-spec.
3. Mid-hill solar is workable but sub-optimal.
pages.excerpt: Nepal's first utility-scale NEA-EPC, NEA-owned, NEA-operated solar plant. 25 MWp ground-mounted grid-tied PV at Bidur, Nuwakot district, commissioned 2022 under the World Bank Grid Solar and Energy Efficiency Project. Interconnected to the Trishuli 33 kV grid.
pages.body_text: Bidur / Trishuli 25 MWp Solar Farm Nepal's first utility-scale NEA-EPC, NEA-owned, NEA-operated solar plant. 25 MWp ground-mounted grid-tied PV at Bidur, Nuwakot district, commissioned 2022 under the World Bank Grid Solar and Energy Efficiency Project. Interconnected to the Trishuli 33 kV grid. The plant that moved Nepal from "solar demonstration" to "utility solar." Every subsequent NEA solar programme decision rides on the engineering, procurement, operational, and commercial precedents this project established. # Specifications Item | Value | ---|---| Capacity | 25 MWp (DC) / ~22 MWac | Location | Bidur Municipality, Nuwakot District, Bagmati Province | Site elevation | ~600 m | Land area | ~25 ha (approx. 1 ha/MWp) | Technology | Crystalline silicon, fixed-tilt ground-mount | Inverters | String inverters (typical Phase II Nepal configuration) | Interconnection | Trishuli 33 kV substation, adjacent to existing NEA infrastructure | Owner | NEA | EPC | Selected through competitive procurement under WB Grid Solar & EE Project | Commissioning | 2022 | Expected annual generation | ~40 GWh/yr (CF ~18%) | Actual FY 2023/24 generation | ~38–42 GWh (NEA internal records; published aggregate) | Financing | IDA concessional credit via wb-grid-solar-ee-project | # Institutional firsts 1. First NEA-EPC utility solar. Broke the "NEA can't build anything beyond hydro" narrative. 2. First use of the now-standard NEA utility-solar PPA / O&M template. Subsequent IPP plants use descendant documentation. 3. First integration of a utility solar plant into NEA's operational dispatch / Load Dispatch Center. The forecasting and integration protocols piloted here. 4. First competitive solar EPC tender at utility scale. Established the procurement reference for Phase IV. # Why Bidur/Trishuli sited at Nuwakot is strategically interesting The site choice is a near-hydro co-location precedent without the explicit "hybrid" label. Trishuli hydropower station is ~5 km upstream; the Trishuli 33 kV substation into which Bidur/Trishuli feeds is the same substation used by multiple Trishuli-corridor hydropower projects. This is an early example of hybrid-siting-logic's Archetype 1 — shared interconnection between solar and hydro — even though Bidur/Trishuli was not tendered or designed as an explicit hybrid. The economics worked because the land was available, the grid was already there, and the terrain was workable. # Site characteristics Parameter | Value | ---|---| GHI (measured, nearest station class) | ~4.5 kWh/m²/day | Specific yield (actual) | ~1,600 kWh/kWp/yr | Zone (solar-resource-geography-nepal) | Zone C2 — Pokhara / Gandaki mid-hills edge | Monsoon cloud penalty | ~30% (mid-hill location, moderate) | Winter GHI | ~4.0 kWh/m²/day | Nuwakot's mid-hill location is not Nepal's best solar zone — Zone B Terai would produce ~10–15% more per MWp. The site choice reflects transmission-adjacency priority (Trishuli 33 kV proximity) over pure GHI optimisation. The decision is instructive: for Nepal, grid-adjacency beats resource-optimisation in siting priority, which aligns with the hybrid-siting-logic general rule. # Operational performance (FY 2023/24 + FY 2024/25) Expected specific yield: 1,600 kWh/kWp/yr (design) Actual specific yield: ~1,520–1,680 kWh/kWp/yr (within ±5% of design) Availability: high; no recorded extended outages in FY 2023/24 O&M: NEA in-house, with WB Grid Solar & EE Project technical assistance during initial years Monsoon degradation risk: moderate; 2023 monsoon cycle included no damage events # What this project teaches Three lessons forward: ## 1. NEA can build solar on-schedule, on-budget, on-spec. Bidur/Trishuli was delivered within the planned window and within the WB-project cost envelope. The "NEA procurement takes forever" critique (accurate for large hydro) was not validated here. Utility solar is fundamentally easier to deliver than hydropower; lead times of 3–5 years for NEA-EPC and 2–3 years for IPP are achievable. ## 2. Near-hydro siting works operationally. Shared substation utilisation, shared access road, shared O&M community, no measurable operational interference between hydro and PV. Validates the hybrid-siting-logic Archetype 1 thesis at 25 MWp scale; should be replicated at every operating hydropower site with ≥1 ha of adjacent buildable land. ## 3. Mid-hill solar is workable but sub-optimal. The ~30% monsoon penalty means a Zone C plant like Bidur/Trishuli produces ~10% less annual energy per MWp than a Zone B Terai plant of the same design. For new-build, Terai should be first priority. Bidur/Trishuli's site choice is defensible in hindsight because of the grid-adjacency benefit, but the default for the 960 MW tender is correctly Terai. # Related nea-solar — programme context wb-grid-solar-ee-project — financing source hybrid-siting-logic — the Archetype 1 precedent trishuli — the hydropower that shares the substation nea-960mw-solar-tender — the successor programme data-solar-fleet-inventory — the fleet this plant anchors

pages.body_text: Bishnu Priya Solar Farm (Surya Power, ~1 MWp) Small demonstration-scale IPP solar plant developed by Surya Power Company Pvt. Ltd., commissioned ~2018 in Nawalparasi district, Lumbini Province. The earliest Phase I IPP plant to reach COD and historically significant as Nepal's first grid-tied commercial IPP solar plant. # Specifications Item | Value | ---|---| Capacity | ~0.96 MWp | Location | Nawalparasi District, Lumbini Province | Owner / Developer | Surya Power Company Pvt. Ltd. | Zone (solar-resource-geography-nepal) | B1 — Central Terai | Interconnection | Nawalparasi 11 kV | Commissioning | ~2018 | Site elevation | ~130 m | Expected annual generation | ~1.5 GWh/yr | Status | Operating | # Why it matters Bishnu Priya is the proof-of-concept scale — <1 MWp, nominally demonstration but commissioned on commercial terms via a PPA with NEA. It pre-dated the larger Phase I plants (butwal-solar-ridi-8-5mwp, mithila-solar-dhanusha-10mwp) and was the first grid-tied IPP PV plant Nepal's interconnection and PPA machinery processed end-to-end. Its specific contribution to the learning curve: Validated the 11 kV interconnection template for sub-MW IPP solar. First PPA processed through NEA for IPP solar — the document formed part of the baseline for later rounds. Demonstrated the Central Terai GHI numbers at operational scale, confirming satellite estimates from global-solar-atlas-nepal. Bishnu Priya's <1 MWp scale limits its current significance operationally — it contributes <0.1% of the solar fleet — but its place in the institutional timeline is the reason it appears in the NEA FY 2024/25 annual report inventory tables. # Related nea-solar butwal-solar-ridi-8-5mwp, mithila-solar-dhanusha-10mwp — Phase I cohort data-solar-fleet-inventory
