pages.title: Karnali Basin
pages.excerpt: The Karnali basin is Nepal's western major river system and the largest by area at ~43,153 km² within Nepal. Its tributaries include Bheri, West Seti, Humla Karnali, Mugu Karnali, and Tila. The Karnali feeds the Ghaghara, which contributes ~40% of the Ganges' baseflow at Varanasi
pages.body_text: Karnali Basin # Summary The Karnali basin is Nepal's western major river system and the largest by area at ~43,153 km² within Nepal. Its tributaries include Bheri, West Seti, Humla Karnali, Mugu Karnali, and Tila. The Karnali feeds the Ghaghara, which contributes ~40% of the Ganges' baseflow at Varanasi. This is Nepal's most dramatically underused basin — essentially zero large-scale hydropower despite having the best sites. # Key Facts Fact | Value | ------|-------| Area in Nepal | 43,153 km² | Average discharge (border) | 1,256 m³/s (~39.6 BCM/yr) | Monsoon share | 65–72% | Peak-to-dry ratio | 15–20:1 (best stability) | Gross hydropower potential | 20,385 MW (28.1% of national total) | # Why It Matters Most The Karnali has the best dry-season flow stability of any major Nepali system (lowest peak-to-dry ratio at 15–20:1 vs 25–50:1 for Koshi). WECS calls it the basin with the highest hydropower potential. It is the most obvious strategic priority for future development. # Why It Remains Undeveloped Remoteness — western Nepal has historically had fewer roads, less political attention, and less financing reach Transmission gap — the grid west of Butwal relies on legacy 132 kV lines incapable of handling large generation Political neglect — eastern-centric development patterns systematically disadvantaged the west The proposed karnali-chisapani (10,800 MW) alone would transform Nepal's energy posture, but it remains conceptual # Climate Projections CMIP6 modeling projects the Karnali will experience 3–23% decrease in winter/spring discharge by end of century, alongside 18–51% increase in monsoon/post-monsoon discharge. Temporal concentration of water will become even more extreme. See peak-water. A useful basin-specific warning from ICIMOD: over 1981–2012, average precipitation in the Karnali study basin trended downward by 4.91 mm/year, yet discharge stayed broadly constant over the observed record. That is exactly the kind of rainfall-flow decoupling that makes annual averages misleading for energy planning. # Limitations & Controversies Remoteness and infrastructure gap. Western Nepal has historically had fewer roads, less political attention, and less financing reach than the central and eastern corridors. The grid west of Butwal relies on legacy 132 kV lines incapable of handling large generation, creating a chicken-and-egg problem: no transmission, no projects; no projects, no transmission justification. Political neglect. Eastern-centric development patterns have systematically disadvantaged the west. Every national hydropower master plan since the 1960s has identified Karnali as a priority; none has funded the pre-feasibility or transmission backbone to make it actionable. Climate uncertainty. CMIP6 projects a 3–23% decrease in winter/spring discharge by end of century, alongside 18–51% increase in monsoon/post-monsoon discharge. The basin's current advantage — the best dry-season stability in Nepal — may erode, making long-lead-time investments riskier. Karnali Chisapani remains conceptual. At 10,800 MW, the basin's signature project has no DPR, no timeline, and no institutional champion. Four decades of appearing in master plans without advancing is a credibility tax on the entire basin. # Downstream Significance The Karnali/Ghaghara system serves ~2–3 million ha in UP and connects to Bangladesh's Ganges flow. See ganges-contribution. # Map Assets Nepal Tributary Explorer Nepal River Geopolitics Explorer data-map-inventory

pages.title: Karnali Chisapani Project
pages.excerpt: The largest single hydropower project ever proposed for Nepal at 10,800 MW — an order of magnitude beyond anything operating or under construction. Located on the karnali-basin main stem near the Chisapani gorge in the western Terai, this is the project that would transform Nepal
pages.body_text: Karnali Chisapani Project # Summary The largest single hydropower project ever proposed for Nepal at 10,800 MW — an order of magnitude beyond anything operating or under construction. Located on the karnali-basin main stem near the Chisapani gorge in the western Terai, this is the project that would transform Nepal into one of Asia's major power producers. It is also the most purely conceptual project in the wiki: no DPR, no timeline, and no single institution driving it forward. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 10,800 MW | Status | Conceptual | River | Karnali main stem (karnali-basin) | ## Engineering A proposed ~270 m dam on the Karnali main stem — the largest single hydropower project ever proposed for Nepal. The design concept envisions a storage dam that would impound the Karnali's monsoon flow and release it through the dry season, providing both power generation and downstream regulation. But no detailed engineering design exists; the 10,800 MW figure is a planning estimate from basin potential studies, not a turbine-by-turbine layout. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Dam height | ~270 m | Dam type | Conceptual (likely rockfill or RCC) | Type | Storage | ## Storage The wb-ganges-strategic-basin-assessment describes a valley-shape paradox that constrains Karnali Chisapani's effective storage: despite the enormous dam height, the steep Karnali valley walls mean that only 16.2 of the total 28.2 BCM can be actively regulated. The remaining 12 BCM is dead storage — water sitting below the lowest outlet level, trapped by topography. This is a geological constraint, not a design choice, and it means the project's flood-control and irrigation-regulation value is structurally capped regardless of dam height. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Total storage | 28,200 MCM | Effective storage | 16,200 MCM | Dead storage (valley-shape constraint) | ~12,000 MCM | ## Output At 10,800 MW, Karnali Chisapani would be one of the world's largest single hydropower installations — comparable to Brazil's Belo Monte (11,233 MW) and exceeding China's Xiluodu (13,860 MW, though that is a cascade). But the project has no design energy estimate — a sign of just how conceptual it remains. For comparison: Belo Monte generates ~39,500 GWh/yr; a 10,800 MW storage plant on the Karnali could theoretically produce 35,000–50,000 GWh/yr depending on head and flow regime. The output benefits (flood control for downstream India, irrigation regulation for the Ghaghara system, and massive storage-deficit relief) are strategic promises, not bankable numbers. ## Financial No cost estimate exists at the conceptual stage, but a back-of-envelope calculation is sobering. At a conservative USD 1.2 million/MW for a storage dam of this scale (Three Gorges came in at ~USD 1,000/kW in 1990s dollars; large Himalayan storage runs higher), the total construction cost could reach USD 13 billion — roughly one-third of Nepal's annual GDP. Even a fraction of that would require co-investment at a scale Nepal has never attempted. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Estimated cost (rough) | USD 10–15 billion | Nepal's annual GDP (FY 2024/25) | ~USD 45 billion | Financing requirement | Bilateral / multilateral consortium essential | Primary buyer | India (no other market can absorb 10,800 MW) | ## Schedule No timeline exists. The project has never progressed beyond basin-level reconnaissance studies. See buildability and hydro-geopolitics. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Current stage | Reconnaissance / basin study only | DPR | Not initiated | Treaty framework | None | Earliest conceivable COD | 2040s (optimistic) | # Limitations & Controversies Scale far exceeds Nepal's fiscal capacity. At an estimated USD 10–15 billion (roughly one-third of annual GDP), the project requires co-investment at a scale Nepal has never attempted. Even a fractional commitment would strain sovereign balance sheets. No institutional champion. Unlike Budhigandaki (Budhigandaki Company Limited), Dudhkoshi (NEA/AIIB), or Arun-3 (SJVN India), Karnali Chisapani has no developer, no lead financier, and no project office. It exists only in basin-scale assessments. Valley-shape dead-storage constraint. Despite a ~270 m dam height, steep Karnali valley walls mean ~12,000 MCM of the 28,200 MCM total is dead storage below the lowest outlet level. This caps flood-control and irrigation-regulation value regardless of dam height. Bilateral dependency with no treaty framework. The project requires India as co-investor and primary buyer (no other market can absorb 10,800 MW), but no bilateral treaty or joint project entity exists. The Pancheshwar precedent — 30 years, zero output — does not inspire confidence. Displacement at unprecedented scale. A 270 m dam on the Karnali main stem would displace tens of thousands across multiple districts. Nepal's largest displacement to date (Budhigandaki, ~8,117 households) is domestic; a binational resettlement plan has no precedent. # Historical Context Karnali Chisapani has been a fixture of Nepal's hydropower imagination since at least the 1960s, when early basin surveys identified the Chisapani gorge as a potential mega-dam site. The project appears in every generation of Nepal's hydropower master planning — from Hari Man Shrestha's seminal 1966 PhD thesis through the 1990s basin studies to the World Bank's Ganges Strategic Basin Assessment. But it has never moved beyond the conceptual stage because the question has never been whether it can be built — the question is who builds it and who buys the power. The pattern is instructive: every time Nepal's hydropower ambition resets (post-1990 democracy, post-Maoist conflict, post-2015 constitution), Karnali Chisapani reappears as the aspirational endpoint. The gap between recurring aspiration and zero progress is itself a data point for buildability — a reminder that megaprojects require more than good topography. # Regional Comparison Project | Country | Capacity | Dam height | Status | ---------|---------|----------|-----------|--------| Karnali Chisapani | Nepal | 10,800 MW | ~270 m | Conceptual | Belo Monte | Brazil | 11,233 MW | Run-of-river | Operating (2019) | Three Gorges | China | 22,500 MW | 181 m | Operating (2012) | Itaipu | Brazil/Paraguay | 14,000 MW | 196 m | Operating (1984) | Grand Inga | DRC | 40,000+ MW | Various | Stalled (conceptual) | Xiluodu | China | 13,860 MW | 285.5 m | Operating (2014) | pancheshwar | Nepal/India | 6,480 MW | 315 m | Stalled (30 yrs) | Karnali Chisapani belongs in the same conversation as Grand Inga: a technically viable mega-site that cannot advance without a governance and financing architecture that does not yet exist. Itaipu required a bilateral treaty between Brazil and Paraguay in 1973; construction started in 1975 and took 9 years. The comparison suggests that the engineering timeline is the easy part — the political timeline is the constraint. # Downstream Bilateral Context The Karnali River becomes the Ghaghara River in India, joining the Ganges system in Uttar Pradesh. The Ghaghara is the largest tributary of the Ganges by discharge, and its monsoon floods are a recurring disaster in eastern UP and Bihar. A 16 BCM effective storage reservoir at Chisapani could regulate approximately 15–20% of Ghaghara wet-season flow, converting destructive flood peaks into dry-season irrigation releases. The bilateral calculus is asymmetric in ways that have blocked progress: Nepal's benefit: 10,800 MW of generation, massive export revenue, domestic dry-season firming, national prestige India's benefit: flood control (valued in billions of avoided damages), irrigation regulation for the Ghaghara command area, a large block of clean energy at the border The valuation problem: India can get flood-control benefits from domestic dams on the Ghaghara downstream without a treaty; Nepal cannot capture those benefits unilaterally without India as co-investor and offtaker. This is the same asymmetric valuation that has stalled pancheshwar. # Why It Remains Conceptual 1. Scale of investment far exceeds Nepal's fiscal capacity. Total cost could reach USD 10–15 billion — at minimum 4–6x the cost of Nepal's most expensive project to date (Budhigandaki at ~USD 2.77 billion). 2. Requires India as co-investor and primary buyer. No other market can absorb 10,800 MW. India's domestic hydropower ambitions (Arunachal Pradesh, Bhutan joint ventures) compete for the same political and financial bandwidth. 3. Downstream bilateral politics. Water sharing, flood-control valuation, and irrigation benefit allocation are unresolved at the conceptual level. The Pancheshwar precedent (30 years, zero output) does not inspire confidence. 4. Environmental and social displacement at unprecedented scale. A 270 m dam on the Karnali main stem would displace tens of thousands of people across multiple districts (Kailali, Bardiya, Surkhet, Achham). The reservoir would flood significant agricultural land in the Terai. 5. No institutional champion. Unlike Budhigandaki (Budhigandaki Company Limited), Dudhkoshi (NEA/AIIB), or Arun-3 (SJVN India), Karnali Chisapani has no developer, no lead financier, and no project office. 6. Pre-feasibility has never been funded. The project has never received the USD 10–20 million that a serious pre-feasibility study would require. It exists only in basin-scale assessments. # What Pre-Feasibility Would Require To move from concept to credible candidate, Karnali Chisapani would need: A bilateral agreement-in-principle with India establishing a joint project structure (treaty, not MOU — the Pancheshwar lesson) A pre-feasibility study funded by a multilateral institution (World Bank, ADB, or AIIB) covering geotechnical investigation, hydrological modelling, environmental and social baseline, and preliminary economic analysis A displacement and resettlement framework that accounts for the project's unprecedented footprint A power purchase framework with India that covers export from a plant of this scale — the existing cross-border PPAs (Arun-3, Upper Karnali) are for projects under 1,000 MW; 10,800 MW is a different order of commercial commitment A transmission corridor plan — the existing Dhalkebar-Muzaffarpur 400 kV cross-border line is rated for ~1,000 MW; Karnali Chisapani would need a dedicated high-capacity interconnector, possibly HVDC # Significance If ever realized, Karnali Chisapani would transform Nepal's energy position from regional exporter to Asian power producer. It would provide massive storage-deficit relief, flood control for downstream India, and irrigation regulation for the Ghaghara system. But the project also illustrates the valley-shape paradox from the wb-ganges-strategic-basin-assessment: despite the enormous dam, steep valley walls constrain effective storage to roughly half the total volume. The dead storage is a permanent reminder that topography, not ambition, sets the ceiling. More broadly, Karnali Chisapani is the limiting case for Nepal's hydropower strategy. If pancheshwar tests whether bilateral governance can deliver a 6,480 MW project, Karnali Chisapani tests whether the governance architecture at all can reach an order of magnitude beyond that. The answer, so far, is no. # Related karnali-basin — the river system pancheshwar — the only project in a comparable bilateral/governance class budhigandaki — the largest domestically-controlled storage advancing hydro-geopolitics — the analytical frame buildability — why megaprojects stall storage-deficit — what this project would address at scale Nepal River Geopolitics Explorer data-map-inventory # Sources wecs-hydropower-potential-2019 wb-ganges-strategic-basin-assessment jica-ipsdp-main-report-vol2

pages.title: Karnali Solar Energy Project
headings: 1. It is the first formal NEA–AEPC co-delivery structure at scale.
2. It validates solar + BESS economics at the remote site
3. It prepares the grid-edge integration question
pages.excerpt: A programme line referenced in the NEA Annual Report FY 2024/25 (Distribution / Customer Service Directorate) covering off-grid solar plants with Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) in Karnali, with operation and maintenance support from NEA. The programme is emerging as Nepal'
pages.body_text: Karnali Solar Energy Project A programme line referenced in the NEA Annual Report FY 2024/25 (Distribution / Customer Service Directorate) covering off-grid solar plants with Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) in Karnali, with operation and maintenance support from NEA. The programme is emerging as Nepal's institutional template for off-grid solar + BESS hybrid delivery in grid-absent districts. # What the project is Location: Karnali Province — the grid-weakest and resource-strongest off-grid zone in Nepal (Dolpa, Humla, Mugu, Jumla, Kalikot, Jajarkot, Rukum, Surkhet, Salyan, Dailekh). Configuration: Multi-site, each site ~50 kWp – 1 MWp solar + BESS (4–8 hour). Operational model: NEA + AEPC joint delivery with community co-operative O&M. Scale indication: approximate aggregate ~5–15 MWp across multiple sites (scope continuing to evolve; project documentation is preliminary). Status: In-development / early implementation as of FY 2024/25; firm aggregate MW to be verified from AEPC progress reports. # Why this programme matters Three things that make Karnali Solar the institutional template rather than just another remote project: ## 1. It is the first formal NEA–AEPC co-delivery structure at scale. Historically AEPC delivered off-grid solar through community cooperatives; NEA delivered grid-tied solar through tenders. Karnali Solar Energy Project is the first programme where NEA provides O&M support and technical backstop to AEPC-delivered off-grid systems, pre-structured for eventual grid-edge integration when the NEA radial feeder eventually reaches each site. ## 2. It validates solar + BESS economics at the remote site Diesel generation in remote Karnali sites costs NPR 60–90/kWh (delivered fuel + logistics + wear). Solar + 8-hour BESS at ~NPR 25–35/kWh (grant-supported) is 2–3× cheaper than the incumbent — the value gap is enormous. This is the highest-leverage per-kWh solar in Nepal, by far. ## 3. It prepares the grid-edge integration question As NEA's grid finally reaches former off-grid villages (~8.6% of households still grid-absent), what happens to the community solar + BESS asset? Karnali Solar Energy Project pre-formalises this: the asset continues to operate, is tariff-integrated with the NEA grid, and the BESS provides local reactive-power / voltage-stability service at the grid edge. Without this pre-formalisation, each off-grid system becomes stranded on grid arrival (the historical pattern). # Site-by-site data Preliminary publication from NEA FY 2024/25 references the programme at aggregate level; per-site details (exact location, MWp, BESS hours, developer, community partner) require cross-reference with AEPC monitoring reports. # Relevance to project Anchors the rooftop-minigrid-offgrid track for Karnali specifically Evidence for claim-solar-political-coalition-is-rural — the rural-coalition politics in action Operational template for solar + BESS economics beyond data-solar-hydro-lcoe's utility frame Institutional precedent for the AEPC–NEA integration protocol argued in aepc # Gaps / next data Exact site list, MWp per site, BESS specification, developer / community partner Cumulative CAPEX / CAPEX per kWp FY 2024/25 generation + diesel-displacement data AEPC monitoring report for the programme # Related aepc nea-solar rooftop-minigrid-offgrid karnali-basin — geographic context data-rooftop-shs-deployment — the Karnali SHS deployment footprint this programme builds on

pages.title: Kataiya–Kushaha 132 kV Cross-Border Interconnection
pages.excerpt: The oldest Nepal–India interconnection still in operation — the historic first link that defined the Nepal–India power trade template. Originally energised in 1971 at 33 kV, upgraded to 132 kV, it has been through five decades of bilateral tariff and exchange-rate politics.
pages.body_text: Kataiya–Kushaha 132 kV Interconnection The oldest Nepal–India interconnection still in operation — the historic first link that defined the Nepal–India power trade template. Originally energised in 1971 at 33 kV, upgraded to 132 kV, it has been through five decades of bilateral tariff and exchange-rate politics. # Summary The Kataiya-Kushaha 132 kV interconnection is the oldest operating Nepal-India grid link. The page tracks its historic role as the first Nepal-India interconnection and its continued eastern Terai import function. # Key Facts Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Voltage | 132 kV (originally 33 kV) | Status | Operational (since 1971) | Nepal terminal | Kushaha (Sunsari) | India terminal | Kataiya (Bihar) | Historic role | First Nepal–India grid tie | Direction | Predominantly imports into eastern Nepal | Interconnection ID | | # Significance Origin point of the Nepal–India grid relationship. Every later interconnection inherits contractual and technical conventions established here. Eastern Terai import backbone. Still the principal import route for dry-season supply to Saptari–Siraha–Sunsari, where domestic eastern generation is thin. Legacy accounting reference. Many of the bilateral power trade arrangements (e.g. the Radhika energy exchange protocol) were framed around this single link. # Limitations & Controversies Legacy voltage. 132 kV thermal capacity is small relative to the region's modern load. During load growth spikes it has required load shedding or emergency procurement. Planned upgrade path unclear. Discussions to convert or parallel with a 220 kV link have not progressed beyond feasibility notes. # See also india-energy-relationship dhalkebar-muzaffarpur — the successor 400 kV era hydro-geopolitics

The page records the programme as presented in the FY 2019/20 annual book, including ceremonial and cable-laying evidence. [!cite] nea-transmission-annual-book-2077 The annual book shows the program both as a ceremonial milestone on the opening pages and again in the project-management chapter, where cable-laying works in Chabahil are presented as part of the Kathmandu Valley distribution enhancement package. # Why It Matters It is one of the clearest examples of NEA trying to modernize the urban grid, not just add generation or long-distance transmission. It links directly to nea's distribution-reliability mandate and to the broader network-upgrade frame captured in nepal-transmission-landscape-2025. # Limitations & Controversies The current page is based on annual-book evidence of the programme and does not provide a full package-by-package implementation record. Coverage area, completion status, outage impact, cost, contractor performance, and current operational benefits need newer distribution-project records before detailed evaluation. # See also nea nepal-transmission-landscape-2025 data-domestic-demand

pages.title: Khimti Cascade
pages.excerpt: The Khimti Khola in Dolakha district is one of Nepal's earlier IPP-developed hydropower corridors. The cascade includes multiple projects at different stages, with the original Khimti-I plant serving as one of the country's first large private hydropower investments.
pages.body_text: Khimti Cascade The Khimti Khola in Dolakha district is one of Nepal's earlier IPP-developed hydropower corridors. The cascade includes multiple projects at different stages, with the original Khimti-I plant serving as one of the country's first large private hydropower investments. # Summary Khimti Cascade is a Dolakha hydropower corridor centered on Khimti Khola projects at operating, construction, and survey stages. The page groups the corridor so Khimti-I, Khimti-II, and smaller upstream/downstream projects can be read as a shared evacuation and development context. # Plants in the Cascade Plant | Capacity (MW) | Status | Developer | -------|--------------|--------|-----------| khimti-i | 60 | Operating | Himal Power Limited | khimti-ii | 48.8 | Under construction | — | Upper Khimti | 12.0 | Under construction | — | Upper Khimti II | 7.0 | Under construction | — | Khimti Ghwang Khola | 9.8 | Survey | — | Total | ~137.6 | | | # Significance Khimti-I (commissioned 2000) was one of Nepal's first major private hydropower projects and helped establish the BOOT (Build-Own-Operate-Transfer) model that subsequent IPPs followed. The Khimti corridor became a test case for whether private developers could execute large hydropower projects in Nepal's challenging Himalayan geology. # Transmission The khimti-dhalkebar-corridor (220 kV) was purpose-built to evacuate power from the Khimti Khola plants into the national grid backbone, connecting the Dolakha valley to the Dhalkebar substation on the east-west corridor. # Context The Khimti Khola is a tributary of the Tamakoshi River in the koshi-basin. The broader Khimti-Tamakoshi corridor in Dolakha includes multiple significant projects including upper-tamakoshi (456 MW), tamakoshi-v (99.8 MW), and tamakoshi-3 (287 MW). # Limitations & Controversies The page is a corridor overview rather than a complete project-by-project due-diligence record. Developer details, commissioning status, cost, hydrology, and evacuation risk vary across the individual projects and should be checked on the linked entity pages before analytical use. # Sources jica-ipsdp-main-report-vol2 # See also khimti-i khimti-ii khimti-dhalkebar-corridor koshi-basin upper-tamakoshi

pages.title: Khimti–Dhalkebar 220 kV Hydropower Corridor
pages.excerpt: The original "IPP-to-grid" line in Nepal. Built to evacuate khimti-i — the country's first large IPP (1996 PPA, 2000 commissioning) — toward the central grid at Dhalkebar. Its history mirrors the birth of private hydropower in Nepal and the long legal and political battles that s
pages.body_text: Khimti–Dhalkebar 220 kV Corridor # Summary The original "IPP-to-grid" line in Nepal. Built to evacuate khimti-i — the country's first large IPP (1996 PPA, 2000 commissioning) — toward the central grid at Dhalkebar. Its history mirrors the birth of private hydropower in Nepal and the long legal and political battles that surround it. # Key Facts Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Voltage | 220 kV (double circuit) | Status | Operational | Length | ~75 km | Owner | nea | Terminals | Khimti substation (Dolakha) · Dhalkebar substation (Dhanusha) | Commissioned | 2016 | Financing | World Bank (IDA) — Nepal India Regional Trade and Transportation Project | Corridor ID | | # Significance First line built for an IPP. Before khimti-i, Nepal had no practice of building high-voltage lines specifically to evacuate independent power producers — the Khimti–Dhalkebar project was the template. Legal precedent. The project's land-acquisition lawsuits (2011–15) set Nepali case law on the public-interest use of private land for transmission. Feeds the export funnel. Terminates at Dhalkebar, which is also the origin of hetauda-dhalkebar-inaruwa-backbone and dhalkebar-muzaffarpur. Roughly half of Nepal's exportable hydropower still routes through it. # Limitations & Controversies Capacity is effectively full. Contracted flow from Khimti-I + downstream IPPs exceeds 300 MW in peak monsoon; a second 220 kV or 400 kV reinforcement from the Tamakoshi–Khimti cluster has been studied but not funded. Sediment disruption risk. The corridor crosses steep Sindhupalchok and Dolakha terrain; landslide damage to tower foundations was flagged in the 2023 monsoon assessment. # See also khimti-i — the project it was built for khimti-ii — the sister plant that shares the corridor hetauda-dhalkebar-inaruwa-backbone — the 400 kV it hands off to

pages.title: Khimti -I
headings: The PPA That Broke the Template
pages.excerpt: 60 MW · operating · on the Khimti Khola · in Dolakha and Ramechhap districts. Nepal's first large private IPP. Commissioned July 2000 under a January 15, 1996 BOOT PPA.
pages.body_text: Khimti -I # Summary 60 MW · operating · on the Khimti Khola · in Dolakha and Ramechhap districts. Nepal's first large private IPP. Commissioned July 2000 under a January 15, 1996 BOOT PPA. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 60 MW | Status | Operating | Registry licence | Operation | River | Khimti Khola | District | Dolakha | Province | Bagmati Pradesh | # Sources jica-ipsdp-main-report-vol2 # Specifications (HPL project data) Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Type | Run-of-river | Commissioning | July 2000 | PPA signed | January 15, 1996 | PPA term | 20-year BOOT (expired July 11, 2020) | Developer | Himal Power Limited (HPL) | Original ownership | Butwal Power Company (17%), Statkraft SF (57%), Eviny AS (~26%) | Current owner (post-Sept 2025) | Butwal Power Company (100%) | Contracted energy | ~350 GWh/yr | Average actual generation (2000–2025) | ~360 GWh/yr (~103%) | Lifetime generation | ~9,000 GWh | Evacuation | Khimti–Dhalkebar 220 kV line | # The PPA That Broke the Template Khimti-I was built under a Power Purchase Agreement signed on January 15, 1996 — before Nepal had a standardised PPA regime, before the Electricity Regulation Commission existed, and before the NPR 4.80/8.40 wet/dry tariff structure that now governs every new private IPP. Himal Power Limited (HPL) negotiated on a blank slate. The result was structurally different from anything signed since: Parameter | Khimti-I (1996 PPA) | Standard IPP PPA (post-2010) | ---|---|---| Tariff | Initially US$0.052/kWh → US$0.059/kWh | NPR 4.80/kWh wet, NPR 8.40/kWh dry | Currency | USD-denominated | NPR | Escalation | US CPI index | ~3% annual (first 8 years only) | Seasonal split | None (flat take-or-pay demand charge) | Yes (wet/dry differential) | PPA structure | BOOT — 50% equity to NEA for NPR 1 at year 20 | Standard PPA, no equity transfer | Term | 20 years | 25–30 years | The USD denomination was the critical difference. As the NPR depreciated over two decades against the dollar, Khimti-I's effective rupee tariff rose passively — without any renegotiation. During the same period, projects signed under the NPR regime watched their real tariffs erode with inflation. Khimti-I's developers were protected from exactly the currency risk that makes Nepal's standard PPA regime structurally inadequate for long-tenor debt. See ppa-pricing. # Generation — 103% of Contracted Over 25 Years HPL's contracted energy is approximately 350 GWh/year. Over the 25 years from commissioning (2000) to 2025, total generation reached approximately 9,000 GWh — an average of ~360 GWh/year, or ~103% of contracted energy. Metric | Value | ---|---| Design (contracted) annual energy | ~350 GWh/yr | Actual total (2000–2025) | ~9,000 GWh | Average annual actual | ~360 GWh/yr | Average % of contracted | ~103% | Source: HPL official project data; Statkraft press release (2025). This places Khimti-I in a category occupied by very few Nepali private IPPs: a plant that has met or exceeded contracted energy over a multi-decade operating life. The Urja Khabar/MoEWRI audit finding — that zero of 100+ small IPPs exceeded 80% of design energy — does not apply to Khimti-I, a larger plant on a more reliable river system in a different generation era. The Khimti Khola, a Sun Koshi tributary in Dolakha, appears to have been accurately hydrologically characterized for the 1996 design study. See q-design-discharge. # Ownership — Repatriation in September 2025 HPL was founded in 1993 by Butwal Power Company (Nepal) alongside Norwegian partners. Until September 2025, the ownership structure was: Shareholder | Stake (pre-2025) | Stake (post-2025) | ---|---|---| Statkraft SF (Norway) | ~57% | 0% | Eviny AS (Norway) | ~26% | 0% | Butwal Power Company (Nepal) | ~17% | 100% | In September 2025, Statkraft and Eviny sold all shares to BPC. Himal Power Limited is now fully owned by Butwal Power Company — a Nepali state-adjacent entity. The repatriation has a structural implication: the original high-tariff USD PPA that made the project commercially viable for Norwegian investors expired in July 2020. BPC acquired a 25-year-old, debt-free, cash-generating asset at whatever price Statkraft and Eviny accepted to exit. Whether BPC is now operating under the original PPA terms, a renegotiated successor PPA, or a new standard-form agreement is not confirmed in public sources. Given that the BOOT period ended in 2020 with NEA acquiring 50% equity for NPR 1, and BPC subsequently acquired the Norwegian stakes, the current commercial structure of HPL is materially different from the 1996 BOOT arrangement. # The Khimti–Dhalkebar Line — Corridor Consequences Khimti-I's output is evacuated via the Khimti–Dhalkebar 220 kV double-circuit line (~75 km), financed by the World Bank and commissioned in 2016. This line was built specifically to evacuate Khimti's 60 MW (and Bhote Koshi's 36 MW) to eastern Nepal's load centres and the Dhalkebar interconnect with India. By 2023, this corridor had become critically congested. The rapid commissioning of the Likhu cascade (Likhu-1, Likhu-2, Likhu-4, Likhu Khola A — combined ~213 MW), all routing through the New Khimti substation at the head of the Khimti–Dhalkebar line, saturated the corridor. Likhu-2 alone lost ~40% of its contracted generation in FY 2023/24 to stranded generation because the substation transformer was undersized. The line that was built for Khimti-I's 60 MW was trying to carry over 300 MW. See buildability for the broader grid-planning failure pattern. # Historical Significance Khimti-I is the origin point of Nepal's private hydropower sector. Every subsequent IPP PPA — every take-or-pay clause, every AD penalty formula, every wet/dry tariff differential — was written in the shadow of the 1996 Khimti PPA and the political controversy it generated. Critics argued that the USD-denominated take-or-pay structure was too favourable to foreign developers; supporters argued it was the only way to attract capital into a country with no IPP track record. Both arguments were partially correct. Khimti-I delivered: 9,000 GWh over 25 years, 103% of contracted energy, zero recorded AD penalty disputes in public sources. What the post-Khimti standard PPA regime corrected — USD denomination, take-or-pay across the full contract, no seasonal rate differential — it may have over-corrected. The current NPR flat-rate structure with 3% escalation for eight years leaves projects exposed to exactly the long-tenor financial risks that Khimti's currency indexing and demand-charge structure protected against. See ppa-pricing. # Limitations & Controversies PPA expired — post-2020 commercial structure unclear. The 20-year BOOT PPA expired in July 2020. NEA acquired 50% equity for NPR 1. BPC then bought out Norwegian partners in September 2025. Whether BPC now operates under the original terms, a renegotiated PPA, or a new standard-form agreement is not confirmed in public sources. Corridor congestion. The Khimti–Dhalkebar 220 kV line that was built for Khimti-I's 60 MW is now trying to carry over 300 MW from the Likhu cascade. Likhu-2 lost ~40% of its generation in FY 2023/24 to this bottleneck. The line built for one plant has become a shared chokepoint. Non-replicable PPA terms. The USD-denominated, CPI-indexed 1996 PPA was a product of a specific era — before standardized tariffs, before the ERC, before the current NPR regime. No modern IPP can replicate these terms, making Khimti-I a historical outlier rather than a sector benchmark. Post-BOOT governance ambiguity. With NEA holding 50% equity and BPC holding the remaining 50%, the plant's governance straddles the public-private boundary. How NEA's triple-authority role interacts with BPC's private ownership of a strategic corridor asset is not documented in public sources. # See also ppa-pricing — the tariff evolution from Khimti's 1996 USD PPA to the current NPR regime q-design-discharge — why Khimti's 103% matters against the sector baseline ad-penalties — the penalty regime Khimti's PPA predates nea-triple-authority — NEA as regulator, shareholder (post-2020), and off-taker buildability — the Khimti–Dhalkebar corridor congestion as grid planning failure khimti-dhalkebar-corridor — the 220 kV line built to evacuate this plant koshi-basin — basin context for the Khimti Khola / Sun Koshi system

pages.title: Khimti II
headings: The Khimti Numbering — One River, Two Eras
pages.excerpt: 48.8 MW · under construction (generation licence) · on the Khimti Khola · in Dolakha district. A Peoples Energy Limited (PEL) project — part of the RM Group — sharing the Khimti Khola river with khimti-i but following an entirely different developer lineage and era.
pages.body_text: Khimti II 48.8 MW · under construction (generation licence) · on the Khimti Khola · in Dolakha district. A Peoples Energy Limited (PEL) project — part of the RM Group — sharing the Khimti Khola river with khimti-i but following an entirely different developer lineage and era. # Summary Khimti II is a 48.8 MW under-construction run-of-river project on the Khimti Khola in Dolakha. The page distinguishes it from Khimti-I, documents its PEL/RM Group ownership, and tracks its construction, PPA, financing, credit, and corridor-dependency risks. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 48.8 MW | Status | Under construction | Registry licence | Generation | River | Khimti Khola | District | Dolakha | Province | Bagmati Pradesh | # Sources nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 icra-nepal-surveillance-a996-b119 # Specifications (DOED / PEL data) Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Type | Run-of-river | Developer | Peoples Energy Limited (PEL, part of RM Group) | Gross head | 353.7 m | Design discharge | 16.11 m³/s | Headrace tunnel | 6.293 km | Turbines | 3 × 16.267 MW vertical-axis Pelton | Project cost | NPR 8.65 billion (~NPR 177M/MW) | Debt / equity | 75:25 | Financing consortium | Sanima Bank (lead), Siddhartha Bank, Nabil Bank, Janata Bank, NIC Asia, NMB Bank, Bank of Kathmandu, Civil Bank, Global IME, NCC Bank (10-bank consortium) | CARE Nepal rating | CARE-NP BB (June 2023) | ICRA rating | ICRA IR BB- (July 2024) | PPA signed | October 1, 2015 | PPA term | 30 years | PPA structure | NPR 4.80/kWh (wet), NPR 8.40/kWh (dry), 80% take-or-pay, 3% × 8-year escalation | RCOD (original) | July 2023 | RCOD (extended) | July 2024 | Target COD | Mid-2024 (2081 BS) | Construction progress | ~50% at April 2023; ~80% at mid-2024 | Evacuation | Khimti–Dhalkebar 220 kV corridor | # Not a BPC Project Peoples Energy Limited is independent of Butwal Power Company. A common handoff assumption collapses the two Khimti projects into a single developer narrative, but the ownership is entirely separate: Khimti-I (60 MW, operating since July 2000) — owned by Himal Power Limited, now 100% Butwal Power Company (BPC) following Statkraft and Eviny's exit in September 2025. See khimti-i. Khimti-II (48.8 MW, under construction) — developed by Peoples Energy Limited, an RM Group company. BPC holds no equity. BPC's relevance to Khimti-II is limited to its presence as the Khimti-I owner on the same corridor. The RM Group is a diversified Nepali industrial conglomerate with interests extending beyond hydropower. PEL was established as a dedicated generation SPV for the Khimti-II project. This ownership separation — one river, two projects, two developers, different eras — exemplifies the fragmented IPP landscape in Nepal's private generation sector. # The Khimti Numbering — One River, Two Eras The Khimti Khola hosts two distinct projects separated by a generation gap: | Khimti-I | Khimti-II | ---|---|---| Capacity | 60 MW | 48.8 MW | Developer | Himal Power Limited (now BPC) | Peoples Energy Limited (RM Group) | PPA signed | January 15, 1996 | October 1, 2015 | PPA type | USD-denominated BOOT (20 yr) | NPR-denominated standard (30 yr) | Commissioning | July 2000 | Under construction (target mid-2024) | Full ownership | BPC (Nepali, post-2025) | RM Group (Nepali) | Historical significance | Nepal's first large private IPP | Pre-revenue IPO candidate (see below) | The 1996 Khimti-I PPA was written on a blank slate — USD-denominated, with no seasonal tariff split and no capacity fee structure. By the time Khimti-II's PPA was signed in October 2015, the standard-form NPR PPA template was fully entrenched: wet/dry differential, flat 3% × 8-year escalation, 80% take-or-pay. Two projects on the same river, built under entirely different commercial regimes — Khimti-I's developers were currency-hedged; Khimti-II's are not. See ppa-pricing. # The PPA — Standard Post-2015 Structure Khimti-II's 30-year PPA, signed October 1, 2015, is the standard post-2010 NEA template: NPR 4.80/kWh in the wet season, NPR 8.40/kWh in the dry season, with 80% take-or-pay coverage and 3% annual escalation for the first eight years only. The PPA provides neither currency indexation nor a demand-charge component — exactly the structural weaknesses that the Khimti-I 1996 PPA's USD denomination was designed to avoid. At 75:25 debt-to-equity, Khimti-II's leverage sits on the lower end of the Nepal IPP range (most private projects since 2015 have been at 78:22 or higher). The 10-bank consortium led by Sanima Bank reflects both the project's scale (NPR 8.65 billion total cost, ~NPR 177M/MW) and the fragmented domestic lending landscape: no single Nepali bank can underwrite a project above NPR ~2 billion on its own books. # Construction — Late-Stage but Delayed Construction reached ~50% completion by April 2023 and ~80% by mid-2024, with the required commercial operation date (RCOD) originally set for July 2023 and subsequently extended by one year to July 2024. The target COD is mid-2024 (2081 BS). Khimti-II's 6.293 km headrace tunnel — the longest single underground structure in the project — is the critical-path item typical of Nepali RoR construction. Three 16.267 MW vertical-axis Pelton turbines (total 48.8 MW installed) operate under a 353.7 m gross head with 16.11 m³/s design discharge. The Pelton selection reflects the high-head, relatively low-flow profile of the upper Khimti Khola. # The Khimti–Dhalkebar Corridor — Shared Risk Khimti-II evacuates through the Khimti–Dhalkebar 220 kV double-circuit line, the same ~75 km corridor that carries Khimti-I (60 MW), the entire Likhu cascade (likhu-1, likhu-2, likhu-4, likhu-khola-a — combined ~213 MW), and Upper Tamakoshi (456 MW). The line was originally financed by the World Bank to evacuate Khimti-I's 60 MW and Bhote Koshi's 36 MW. By 2023 it was carrying over 300 MW of connected capacity through the New Khimti substation. The congestion that stranded ~40% of likhu-2's contracted generation in FY 2023/24 — caused by an undersized 100 MVA substation transformer — is the defining transmission risk for every project on this corridor. The late-2023 transformer upgrade to 300 MVA relieved the immediate bottleneck, but a single substation failure returns all Khimti–Dhalkebar projects to stranded-generation status. For Khimti-II, a project still under construction, commissioning into a corridor that has already demonstrated congestion failure is a structural risk that no PPA provision addresses. See buildability and stranded-generation. # IPO Connection — Pre-Revenue Fundraising Peoples Energy Limited sought approval from the Securities Board of Nepal (SEBON) to issue an initial public offering (IPO) during the construction phase — before a single kilowatt-hour had been generated. This follows the pre-revenue IPO pattern that has become a defining feature of Nepal's post-2015 hydropower development: promoters seek public equity to meet the 25% equity component of 75:25 debt-equity structures, issuing shares while the project is still a hole in the ground. The rationale is promoter-side: IPO proceeds reduce the equity burden on the RM Group's balance sheet and provide a secondary-market exit path before commissioning risk has been resolved. For public investors, the trade is buying into a project with zero operational track record, no revenue, and incomplete construction — at a valuation set by the promoter's cost projections. The Urja Khabar/MoEWRI audit finding that zero of 100+ small IPPs exceeded 80% of design energy is the relevant baseline for what public shareholders are actually buying. See ipo-hydropower-bailout. # Credit Profile CARE Ratings Nepal assigned CARE-NP BB to Khimti-II's bank facilities in June 2023, and ICRA assigned ICRA IR BB- in July 2024. Both ratings sit in the speculative grade — one notch below the BBB- assigned to likhu-khola-a and likhu-2 (both operational), and above the B+ assigned to likhu-4 (under construction). The ratings reflect: Construction execution risk — the project was at ~80% completion at the time of the ICRA rating, with the tunnel remaining the critical path item Single-corridor dependency — the Khimti–Dhalkebar line is shared with substantially larger generators that can crowd out smaller IPPs during congestion events Standard PPA weaknesses — no currency hedge, 3% escalation for 8 years only, 80% take-or-pay leaving 20% exposed to NEA dispatch discretion Mitigants — the 75:25 gearing is conservative by Nepal standards, the 10-bank consortium diversifies refinancing risk, and the Pelton turbine configuration on a high-head site implies strong operating margins once commissioned # Limitations & Controversies Several fields depend on rating reports and source snapshots rather than post-COD operating evidence. RCOD, target COD, construction progress, final cost, IPO status, and corridor congestion exposure should be refreshed against current project disclosures before financial or delivery conclusions are treated as settled. # See also khimti-i — the 60 MW predecessor on the same river (different developer, different era) khimti-dhalkebar-corridor — the 220 kV backbone shared with the Likhu cascade likhu-2 — stranded generation case study on the same corridor likhu-khola-a — another IPP on the same corridor (MV Dugar Group) buildability — transmission planning failure as structural IPP risk stranded-generation — the grid evacuation bottleneck problem ppa-pricing — the tariff evolution from Khimti-I's USD PPA to the current NPR regime ipo-hydropower-bailout — the pre-revenue IPO pattern koshi-basin — basin context

pages.excerpt: Planned 50 MW solar project at Khungri, Pyuthan district, designed to integrate into the Khungri substation adjacent to Madi Khola and Lungri Khola hydropower. The first at-scale solar-hydro hybrid (Archetype 1) configuration in Nepal, referenced in the NEA Annual Report FY 2024/
pages.body_text: Khungri Solar Hybrid (50 MW, Pyuthan) Planned 50 MW solar project at Khungri, Pyuthan district, designed to integrate into the Khungri substation adjacent to Madi Khola and Lungri Khola hydropower. The first at-scale solar-hydro hybrid (Archetype 1) configuration in Nepal, referenced in the NEA Annual Report FY 2024/25 as part of the Madhesh-Lumbini corridor reinforcement. # Specifications Item | Value | ---|---| Capacity (solar) | 50 MW | Location | Khungri village, Pyuthan District, Lumbini Province | Interconnection | Khungri 33/132 kV substation (shared with Madi Khola and Lungri Khola hydropower) | Zone (solar-resource-geography-nepal) | C4 — Western mid-hills (elevation ~1,300–1,800 m) | Configuration | Ground-mount PV integrated with existing hydro evacuation | Status | Planned / early implementation (FY 2024/25 report) | Expected COD | 2026 (subject to PPA and financial close) | Owner | NEA + IPP (structure to be finalised) | # Why this project matters Khungri is the first operational implementation of the hybrid siting logic encoded in hybrid-siting-logic, at a meaningful scale: ## 1. It is the template for Archetype 1 scale-up. Bidur/Trishuli (bidur-trishuli-solar-25mwp) was near-hydro co-location by accident; Khungri is designed as hybrid from the start. If the project delivers on schedule, it validates: Shared substation loading between solar mid-day and hydro evening-peak. Anti-phased transformer utilisation (solar loads midday, hydro loads evening-peak). Reduced grid-reinforcement capex compared to greenfield 50 MW. ## 2. Mid-hill siting with evacuation advantage. Pyuthan is Zone C4 (western mid-hills, GHI ~4.4–4.8). This is not top-tier Nepal solar resource — Terai would produce ~10–15% more MWh per MWp. But the shared substation with two hydropower plants means the project's all-in LCOE (including grid costs) is likely lower than a Terai greenfield. The economics here are being driven by grid cost, not GHI, exactly as hybrid-siting-logic argues. ## 3. It is geographically near the Dana–Kushma–Butwal corridor. The site sits on the dana-kushma-butwal-corridor interconnection axis, so the plant's output is naturally evacuated to the NEA backbone via the Butwal hub. This gives Khungri an evacuation headroom that purely rural Zone C mid-hill solar sites do not have. # Operational questions to watch Question | Why it matters | ---|---| Does the shared substation handle simultaneous hydro + solar peak days? | Validates (or breaks) the hybrid thesis at 50 MW scale | What is the actual monsoon-day solar output relative to hydro output? | Tests whether Pyuthan zone solar is a net winter complement or a monsoon cannibaliser | How is the PPA structured: joint for hydro + solar, or separate? | Precedent for future hybrid deals | What is the specific GHI at Khungri vs the Pokhara reference station? | Tests the Zone C4 GHI assumption used in the resource map | # Lessons the project can teach If Khungri delivers successfully, it provides the precedent for rolling hybrid into the next NEA tender — mandating that any new hydropower project above ~20 MW include a co-located solar feasibility study, with capex sharing for the substation upgrade. This is the lowest-friction way to scale Archetype 1 from 50 MW (Khungri) to ~500–800 MW across the hydro fleet by 2030. # Related hybrid-siting-logic — the concept this project operationalises nea-solar — programme parent dana-kushma-butwal-corridor — transmission axis bidur-trishuli-solar-25mwp — precedent, if unintentional naumure-w-rapti — nearby hydro developments that could inform future hybrid design data-solar-fleet-inventory

It is pinned in data-layer-top-10-capacity-projects because it is the eighth-largest marker in the display set and part of the same Arun corridor that makes arun-3 nationally important. # Summary Kimathanka Arun HEP is a 450 MW survey-stage project in the upper Arun/Koshi corridor. The page tracks it as a later-horizon top-10 capacity marker linked to the same eastern basin logic as Arun-3. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 450 MW | Status | Survey / study | Registry licence | Survey | River | Arun (eastern koshi-basin) | District | Sankhuwasabha | Province | Province No 1 | Promoter | Vidhyut Utpadan Company Limited | # Why It Matters Kimathanka Arun matters because it extends the Arun corridor story upstream. arun-3 is the near-term, India-developed 900 MW anchor; Kimathanka Arun is a later-horizon state-promoted project that would add another large block in the same eastern basin. That makes it important for transmission and sequencing. A 450 MW project in upper Arun geography is not just a generation question; it depends on road access, evacuation planning, environmental constraints, and how the broader Arun cascade is prioritized. # Status And Timing The current layer treats Kimathanka Arun as survey-stage. The IPSDP milestone ladder groups Kimathanka Arun in the 2036-2040 project window. There is no confirmed construction start in the current wiki evidence set. # Limitations & Controversies The marker is a river-aligned project reference derived from a registry point. Use it for corridor and top-10 comparison, not final site analysis. The current wiki evidence does not confirm construction start, final design, financing, environmental and social approvals, evacuation arrangements, or COD timing. IPSDP places the project in a later 2036-2040 window, so it should not be treated as near-term supply. # Registry note Naxa / DoED-linked public hydropower project dataset # Sources moewri-ipsdp-exec-summary-2025 # See also koshi-basin buildability arun-3 data-ipsdp-milestone-ladder-2022-2040 data-layer-top-10-capacity-projects
