pages.body_text: Kokhajor-1 Kokhajor-1 is a 111.5 MW JICA promising-storage candidate in the Koshi basin. It is pinned in data-layer-storage-shortlist because it has a high dry-energy share for a relatively small project. # Summary Kokhajor-1 is a 111.5 MW JICA promising-storage candidate in the Koshi basin. The page records its high dry-season share and storage metrics as part of the storage-shortlist portfolio. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 111.5 MW | Status | Survey / study | Category | jica promising storage | Basin | Koshi (koshi-basin) | Annual energy | 278.9 GWh | Dry-season energy | 94.1 GWh | Dry share | 33.7% | Total storage | 218.7 MCM | Effective storage | 166.1 MCM | ## Storage Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Total storage | 218.7 MCM | Effective storage | 166.1 MCM | ## Output Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Annual design energy | 278.9 GWh | Dry-season energy | 94.1 GWh | Dry-season share | 33.7 % | Type | Storage | # Sources jica-ipsdp-main-report-vol2 # Why It Matters Kokhajor-1 contributes 94.1 GWh of dry-season energy from 278.9 GWh annual energy, a 33.7% dry share. That is the point of the project in the wiki: it is not a top-capacity candidate, but it helps show that smaller storage sites can have strong seasonal value. Its analytical role is portfolio logic. Nepal's storage deficit will not be solved only by one large dam; distributed storage candidates can matter if they provide dependable dry-season energy near usable grid corridors. # Status And Timing Kokhajor-1 is a planning candidate from the JICA/NEA storage material. The current wiki evidence set does not carry a confirmed construction start, developer award, or COD target. The next useful evidence would be an updated feasibility package, project sponsor, environmental review, grid-interconnection plan, and whether it remains in the preferred storage portfolio after newer screening. # Limitations & Controversies The marker uses a Kokhajor Khola river anchor from Nominatim. It is suitable for orientation, not final engineering geography. The current record is planning-stage. It does not verify a developer award, active licence conversion, feasibility update, environmental review, grid-interconnection plan, final dam location, or COD target beyond the JICA/NEA storage-screening context. # Registry note JICA/NEA storage master plan volume 2 # See also koshi-basin storage-deficit firm-power data-layer-storage-shortlist

pages.title: Koshi Basin
pages.excerpt: The Koshi (Sapta Koshi) basin is Nepal's eastern major river system. It drains ~27,818 km² within Nepal through seven major tributaries, including the Arun, Tamor, and Sunkoshi. The Arun is one of Nepal's oldest rivers — older than the Himalayas themselves, predating the mountain
pages.body_text: Koshi Basin # Summary The Koshi (Sapta Koshi) basin is Nepal's eastern major river system. It drains ~27,818 km² within Nepal through seven major tributaries, including the Arun, Tamor, and Sunkoshi. The Arun is one of Nepal's oldest rivers — older than the Himalayas themselves, predating the mountain uplift. The basin is the largest glacierized in Nepal (278 glaciers, 51 km³ ice volume) and carries the largest gross hydropower potential of any single basin. # Key Facts Fact | Value | ------|-------| Area in Nepal | 27,818 km² | Average discharge (border) | 1,827 m³/s (~57.6 BCM/yr) | Monsoon share | 67–78% | Peak-to-dry ratio | 25–50:1 | Gross hydropower potential | 27,805 MW (38.3% of national total) | Glaciers | 278 (51 km³ ice) | Sediment significance | ~120 Mt/yr, nearly 25% of Ganges sediment load | # Hydropower Significance Largest gross potential of any basin in Nepal per wecs-hydropower-potential-2019. Contains the dudhkoshi-storage project (670 MW) and upper-tamakoshi (456 MW, largest operating plant). The Arun corridor hosts Upper Arun (900 MW, under construction). # Constraints Extreme sediment loads — ICIMOD framing puts the basin near 120 million tonnes/year into the Ganges system, or nearly 25% of the total sediment load. See sediment-as-design-constraint. Flood hazard — known as the "River of Sorrow" in Bihar due to catastrophic flooding and course shifts. The 2008 Koshi breach displaced 2+ million people. glof-risk — the 2024 Thame Valley GLOF traveled >80 km down the Dudh Koshi, destroying hydropower facilities. High hazard does not eliminate the basin's value, but it demands buildability filters on every project. # Downstream Significance Koshi irrigates ~500,000–600,000 ha in Bihar. Supports >40 million people downstream. Contributes disproportionate sediment to the Ganges system. Central to hydro-geopolitics and ganges-contribution. # Limitations & Controversies Extreme sediment loads. The basin carries ~120 Mt/yr into the Ganges system — nearly 25% of the total sediment load. This makes every project in the basin a sediment-as-design-constraint case study, with turbine erosion and reservoir siltation as permanent operating risks. Flood hazard. Known as the "River of Sorrow" in Bihar due to catastrophic flooding and course shifts. The 2008 Koshi breach displaced 2+ million people. A dam or barrage failure in this basin would have cross-border consequences an order of magnitude beyond any single project. GLOF exposure. The 2024 Thame Valley GLOF traveled >80 km down the Dudh Koshi, destroying hydropower facilities. With 278 glaciers and 51 km³ of ice volume, the basin has the highest GLOF frequency risk in Nepal. Peak-to-dry ratio of 25–50:1. The most extreme seasonal flow variation of any major basin, making run-of-river projects structurally winter-poor and concentrating value in the monsoon months when prices are lowest. # Map Assets Nepal Tributary Explorer Nepal River Geopolitics Explorer data-map-inventory

pages.title: Kulekhani Cascade
pages.excerpt: Repair works on draft tube during overhauling
pages.body_text: Kulekhani Cascade Repair works on draft tube during overhauling 6.6 kV Bus conductor maintenance Machine floor of KL1 Energy generation pattern of PROR/ROR and storage (GWh) # Summary Nepal's only operating reservoir hydropower system. A cascade of three plants on the Kulekhani River, approximately 50 km south of Kathmandu in Makwanpur district. Built with World Bank support in the 1970s–1980s, it remains — 40+ years later — the single operational counterexample to Nepal's otherwise entirely run-of-river fleet. # Specifications Plant | Capacity (MW) | Type | Page | -------|--------------|------|------| Kulekhani I | 60 | Reservoir | kulekhani-i | Kulekhani II | 32 | Cascade | kulekhani-ii | Kulekhani III | 14 | Cascade | kulekhani-iii | Total | 106 | | | Combined generation in FY 2081/82: 279.8 GWh (KL-I: 170.56 + KL-II: 74.9 + KL-III: 34.3) Storage volume: ~85–150 MCM (see data-storage-comparison) The Kulekhani I dam (Indra Sarobar) is a 114 m rockfill dam impounding the Kulekhani River ## Engineering Kulekhani I is a seasonal-storage reservoir: a 114 m rockfill dam creates a headpond that captures monsoon inflow (~June–September) and releases it through the dry season (~November–May) to Kulekhani II and III downstream. This is the only facility in Nepal where water can be stored in one season and released in another for power generation. Every other plant is run-of-river-hydropower. The cascade operation means KL-I releases become KL-II inflow, and KL-II releases become KL-III inflow — a true cascade, not three independent plants. This operational interdependence means Kulekhani's value is in the system, not any individual turbine. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Kulekhani I dam height | 114 m | Kulekhani I dam type | Rockfill | Storage type | Seasonal-storage reservoir | Cascade operation | KL-I → KL-II → KL-III | ## Output Kulekhani's seasonal generation pattern is what distinguishes it from RoR. While RoR plants generate ~70–80% of their annual energy in the four monsoon months, Kulekhani shifts a substantial portion into the dry season. The combined 279.8 GWh in FY 2081/82 is modest by total-hydro standards (~3% of national generation), but its timing — concentrated in the dry months and peak evening hours — provides firm-power that no RoR plant can match. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Annual generation (FY 2081/82) | 279.8 GWh | KL-I generation | 170.56 GWh | KL-II generation | 74.9 GWh | KL-III generation | 34.3 GWh | ## Grid Services Beyond energy, Kulekhani provides services that RoR plants cannot: Black start capability — KL-I can restart the Kathmandu valley grid without external power, a critical grid-resilience function Peak-hour dispatch — the reservoir can ramp generation to match evening peak demand (~6–10 PM), when RoR plants are output-limited by declining diurnal flows Frequency regulation — turbine response to load changes supports grid frequency stability in a system with growing variable solar These services are not priced in the PPA, which pays the same NPR/kWh as any RoR plant. The value of storage is captured in grid reliability, not in Kulekhani's revenue line. This is part of the broader ppa-pricing challenge: Nepal's tariff structure does not compensate storage for the services it uniquely provides. ## Schedule Kulekhani I was commissioned in 1982, making it Nepal's first major storage hydropower project — and, 40+ years later, still its only one. The cascade additions (KL-II in 1986, KL-III in 2019) extended the system but did not add new reservoir capacity. Compare with the pipeline: tanahu-hydropower (140 MW storage, ~67% complete) and dudhkoshi-storage (635 MW, pre-construction) are the next storage projects that would break this four-decade monopoly. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Kulekhani I commissioned | 1982 | Kulekhani II commissioned | 1986 | Kulekhani III commissioned | 2019 | Age of Nepal's only storage anchor | 40+ years | # Historical Context Kulekhani was built with World Bank financing in the late 1970s as part of Nepal's first generation of utility-scale hydropower. At the time, Nepal had fewer than 100 MW of installed capacity, nearly all run-of-river. The choice to build a storage reservoir 50 km from Kathmandu — rather than another RoR plant on a larger river — reflected a specific calculation: the capital city needed reliable dry-season power, and proximity to load mattered more than scale. The project was completed on time and on budget, and has operated continuously for over 40 years. But the model was never replicated. Every subsequent NEA project — kali-gandaki-a (144 MW, 2002), upper-tamakoshi (456 MW, 2021) — chose the RoR engineering model. The reasons are instructive: storage dams require larger upfront capital, longer construction timelines, resettlement programs, and environmental approvals that RoR diversion schemes avoid. In a system where NEA's capital budget was always constrained and political cycles are short, the RoR model won every time after Kulekhani. The result: 106 MW of storage in 1982, 106 MW of storage in 2026. Four decades of hydropower expansion added ~3,300 MW of RoR capacity with zero additional reservoir storage. Kulekhani is not simply an exception to Nepal's RoR-heavy pattern; it is the exception that became the rule, a data point that could have become the first of many and instead became the only one. # The Storage Paradox The storage-deficit page describes the arithmetic: Nepal's ~3,400+ MW of installed hydro is over 95% run-of-river, generating ~70–80% of annual energy in the four monsoon months. Kulekhani — 106 MW, ~3% of installed capacity — is the only plant that can time-shift water across seasons. This ratio (106:3,400) is the number behind every argument in this wiki about seasonal-mismatch and firm-power. It means that in the driest months (February–April), when national demand peaks and river flows bottom, the entire storage-dependent portion of the grid is 106 MW. Everything else depends on whatever the rivers are carrying that day. The pipeline projects that would change this ratio — tanahu-hydropower (140 MW), dudhkoshi-storage (635 MW), budhigandaki (1,200 MW) — would bring the storage-to-RoR ratio from 1:32 to roughly 1:3 if all are completed. But Kulekhani has been carrying this burden alone since 1982. # Sedimentation As Nepal's oldest operating reservoir, Kulekhani is also the best data point for sediment-as-design-constraint. The Kulekhani catchment drains the Mahabharat range, and monsoon sediment inflow has been gradually reducing the reservoir's active storage volume. The original design assumed a 50-year sediment life, meaning the reservoir would lose roughly 1–2% of active storage per year to silt accumulation. If this assumption holds, Kulekhani I's active storage has declined from ~85 MCM at commissioning to approximately 50–60 MCM today — a loss of roughly one-third of its original regulation capacity. This is not a crisis (the reservoir still functions), but it is a warning for every planned storage project with a 50–100 year design life: Himalayan sediment loads make "dead storage" a dynamic quantity, not a design-time constant. # Significance Kulekhani is the outlier in Nepal's generation fleet. It is the only facility in Nepal that can shift water from wet to dry season for power generation. Everything else is run-of-river-hydropower. The fact that 106 MW of storage represents Nepal's entire reservoir base — against 3,400+ MW of total hydro — encapsulates the storage-deficit. Kulekhani is also evidence that storage can operate in Nepal. A 40-year operating history with World Bank financing, on-time construction, and continuous dry-season service shows that the model has a domestic precedent. The question is not whether Nepal has built storage — it already did. The question is why it stopped. # Limitations & Controversies Sedimentation. As Nepal's oldest operating reservoir, Kulekhani I has gradually lost active storage volume to monsoon sediment inflow from the Mahabharat range catchment. If the original 50-year sediment-life assumption holds, active storage has declined from ~85 MCM at commissioning to approximately 50–60 MCM today — a loss of roughly one-third of its original regulation capacity. Single-point-of-failure risk. At 106 MW and 40+ years of operation, Kulekhani is the only facility in Nepal providing seasonal water storage for power generation. Equipment aging and the absence of any backup reservoir create concentrated grid-reliance risk. Scale ceiling. Even at full original capacity, Kulekhani's storage volume is insufficient to close the national dry-season gap on its own. It provides roughly 3% of national generation but must carry the entire seasonal time-shifting burden for the grid. # Related kulekhani-i — the upper reservoir plant (60 MW) kulekhani-ii — the second cascade plant (32 MW) kulekhani-iii — the third cascade plant (14 MW) data-storage-comparison — Nepal's storage in international context storage-deficit — why this matters firm-power — what Kulekhani can provide that RoR cannot sediment-as-design-constraint — the silent erosion of reservoir value tanahu-hydropower — the next storage project (140 MW, under construction) dudhkoshi-storage — the next major storage candidate (635 MW) ppa-pricing — why storage services are not compensated # Map Assets Nepal Tributary Explorer Cross-Border View With Projects data-map-inventory # Sources nea-annual-report-fy2024-25

pages.title: Kulekhani I
headings: Why 106 MW of Storage Is Not Enough
A declining rate — but irreversible accumulation
pages.excerpt: 60 MW · operating · on the Kulekhani · in Makawanpur district.
pages.body_text: Kulekhani I 60 MW · operating · on the Kulekhani · in Makawanpur district. [!note] Cascade context Kulekhani I is the upper reservoir plant in Nepal's only operational reservoir hydropower system. See kulekhani-cascade for the full three-plant system overview including kulekhani-ii (32 MW) and kulekhani-iii (14 MW). Combined generation in FY 2081/82: 279.8 GWh across all three plants. # Summary Kulekhani I is Nepal's 60 MW upper reservoir hydropower plant and the anchor of the country's only operating storage cascade. The page documents its seasonal-shifting role, FY 2081/82 operating data, and sedimentation evidence. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 60 MW | Status | Operating | Registry licence | Operation | River | Kulekhani | District | Makawanpur | Province | Bagmati Pradesh | # Sources nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 # Specifications (NEA FY 2081/82) Kulekhani I is Nepal's only reservoir-type hydropower station — a dam-and-reservoir facility that stores monsoon runoff and releases it for generation during the dry months when the RoR fleet collapses. Two 30 MW Francis units operate as a peaking plant, also supporting voltage and system stability for the central grid. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Type | Reservoir (seasonal storage) | Units | 2 × 30 MW Francis | Location | Dhorsing, Makwanpur District | Design generation (primary) | 165 GWh/yr | Design generation (secondary) | 46 GWh/yr | Design generation (total) | 211 GWh/yr | FY 2081/82 generation | 170.56 GWh | Year-over-year change | +64.5% | Cumulative lifetime generation | 5,785.9 GWh | Reservoir max level (FY 2081/82) | 1,531.5 masl | Reservoir min level (FY 2081/82) | 1,486.28 masl | Drawdown range | ~45.2 m | Spillway | 65 m uncontrolled + 2 radial gates | The reservoir has a 65 m uncontrolled spillway and two radial gates designed for operation at EL. 1530 masl. On 12 Ashoj 2081, heavy rainfall caused the water level to rise beyond the spillway's capacity — both radial gates were opened at 1,530.20 masl to stabilize the reservoir, a reminder that even Nepal's only reservoir must handle extreme inflow events that RoR headworks simply pass through. # The Seasonal Shift in Practice Kulekhani I takes the water that RoR plants must spill during monsoon surplus and converts it into dry-season generation from Mangsir through Baisakh (November–May). The NEA report states the plant "stores monsoon water and operates mainly during the dry season to meet peak demand." The reservoir level data confirms this cycle: a 45.2 m drawdown between the post-monsoon peak (1,531.5 masl in Ashoj) and the dry-season trough (1,486.28 masl in Baisakh/Chaitra). This seasonal shifting is categorically different from the 4–6 hours of "peaking" pondage that PRoR plants like Marsyangdi and Kali Gandaki A use for daily load-smoothing. Those plants cannot store water across months — when the river drops in January, so does their output. Kulekhani I can. The 64.5% year-over-year increase in generation (FY 2080/81 to 2081/82) tells the other half of the story. A reservoir plant is still governed by the monsoon that fills it. In a good monsoon year, the reservoir fills early and generation rises; in a drought year, the drawdown deepens and dry-season output collapses. The 279.8 GWh combined cascade generation in FY 2081/82 was a function of heavy monsoon filling, not a guaranteed floor. # Why 106 MW of Storage Is Not Enough The cascade page notes that 106 MW across Kulekhani I + II + III is Nepal's entire reservoir hydropower base against a fleet of 3,400+ MW — a ratio of roughly 3%. Kulekhani I's operational data makes this concrete. The NEA's own Large Generation O&M Department data (page 21 of the FY 2024/25 report) shows that seven plants totaling 465 MW generated 2,487 GWh in FY 2081/82 — about 86% of NEA's total annual generation. Kulekhani I's 170.56 GWh represents only 6.9% of that large-plant subtotal. In dry-season months, when the RoR fleet output collapses to 25–40% of monsoon peak, Kulekhani I is the only facility that can meaningfully offset the shortfall. At 60 MW, it cannot close the gap alone. The reservoir can shift water across months, but the plant's capacity puts a hard ceiling on what shifting can accomplish. See storage-deficit for the system-level arithmetic. # Sedimentation — Quantified Kulekhani I was commissioned in December 1982 (Unit 1) and May 1987 (Unit 2), with a reservoir storage volume of 85.3 MCM. Sediment monitoring began in June 1989 and has been conducted continuously since. Multiple post-2010 Differential GPS bathymetric surveys and RUSLE modelling studies provide updated capacity loss figures. ## Capacity loss trajectory Metric | Value | -----------|-------| Original reservoir capacity | 85.3 MCM | Reservoir area | 2.2 km² | Catchment area | 126 km² | Cumulative sediment by 2010 | 25.3 MCM (~30% loss) | Total gross storage lost (post-2010 DGPS) | 20.4 million m³ (23.9%) | Active live storage lost | 14 million m³ (19.1%) | Estimated total capacity loss (DGPS bathymetry, 2009/2010) | ~24% | Commissioning | December 1982 (Unit 1), May 1987 (Unit 2) | Dam type | Inclined core rockfill, 114 m height | ## A declining rate — but irreversible accumulation While the absolute capacity loss has deepened, the rate of sedimentation entering the reservoir has steadily declined due to improved watershed management, afforestation, and land-use changes in the upstream catchment: Year | Sedimentation rate (t/ha/yr) | ---|---| 2002 | 13.3 | 2010 | 6.6 | 2018 | 4.8 | This is evidence that watershed-level sediment control works — the rate has dropped by nearly two-thirds over 16 years. But because sedimentation is cumulative and largely irreversible without economically paralyzing dredging operations, the total volumetric loss has continued to deepen even as the inflow rate slowed. Physical DGPS bathymetric surveys (Sangroula, NTNU/Hydro-Lab, 2009/2010) measured cumulative total storage loss at 20.4 MCM out of 85.3 MCM original — 23.9% gross loss, 19.1% active live storage loss. Separate InVEST/RUSLE spatial catchment modeling (Bokan et al., 2021–2024) tracked the declining watershed sediment delivery rate (13.3→4.8 t/ha/yr) but does not directly measure reservoir volume. Source: JICA Nationwide Master Plan Study on Storage-type Hydroelectric Power Development in Nepal, Vol. 1 (2014), pp. 72–73, citing Sangroula (2007); Sangroula, D.P., Sedimentation and sustainability of the Kulekhani Reservoir: A Himalayan Case, NTNU doctoral dissertation (2006, DGPS surveys 2009/2010); Bokan, L.T. et al., Potential Sedimentation Rate and its Prioritization in Kulekhani Watershed Using InVEST Model (2024, modeling 2002–2018 data). ## What this means A ~24% gross capacity loss over ~30 years (20.4 MCM of 85.3 MCM original, per DGPS bathymetry) means current total storage is approximately ~65 MCM. However, the critical metric for generation is active live storage: with 14 MCM of live storage lost (19.1%), effective seasonal-shifting capability is reduced to roughly ~59 MCM. The "106 MW of storage" claim in planning documents remains misleading — not because the absolute loss is higher, but because even a 19% active storage loss materially reduces the system's dry-season peaking capacity. This has two structural implications: 1. Kulekhani's own future. Every year of continued sedimentation — even at the declining rate — further reduces capacity. The reservoir will eventually reach dead storage (capacity below which intake gates cannot function) unless dredging or flushing interventions are deployed at scale. The sloping intake structure and sediment control dam (see Countermeasures below) have slowed but not stopped this trajectory. 2. Template for future storage. Tanahu (140 MW), Dudhkoshi (635 MW), and Budhigandaki (1,200 MW) are all proposed reservoir projects in catchments with comparable or higher sediment yields. The ERC's 2026 reservoir directive mandates a 50-year design life for new storage projects. Kulekhani's ~19% live storage loss over 30 years — in a catchment with aggressive afforestation and sediment control dams — suggests that without aggressive watershed management and sediment bypass systems from day one, a 50-year reservoir will lose more than half its capacity before its design life expires — and the cost-plus tariff written at commissioning will not cover the mid-life capacity that no longer exists. See sediment-as-design-constraint and storage-deficit. ## Countermeasures deployed Following the flood damage, Japan-supported disaster prevention projects implemented three sediment management measures at Kulekhani: Sediment control dam constructed upstream on the Kulekhani River and at the river mouth in the reservoir to trap sediment before it reaches the main reservoir body. Sloping intake structure to prevent clogging of the intake by sediment and enable water withdrawal even as sedimentation levels rise. Hydrosuction Sediment Removal System (HSRS) under examination — uses the water head between upstream and downstream to suck sediment from the reservoir bottom and discharge it downstream through a pipeline. These measures, combined with watershed afforestation, have reduced the annual sedimentation rate from 13.3 t/ha/yr (2002) to 4.8 t/ha/yr (2018). But the cumulative capacity loss continues — and no intervention deployed to date has reversed it. # Limitations & Controversies Kulekhani I is well documented relative to many entity pages, but its storage-loss figures come from multiple measurement and modeling frames that should not be casually merged. Current live storage, sedimentation rate, operating rule curves, dredging feasibility, and climate-era inflow reliability require updated technical verification before using the page for project-design benchmarking. # See also kulekhani-cascade — full three-plant system overview (106 MW combined) kulekhani-ii — downstream cascade plant (32 MW, commissioned 1986) storage-deficit — why 106 MW against 3,400 MW defines Nepal's energy problem firm-power — what reservoir generation provides that RoR cannot seasonal-mismatch — the monsoon-to-drought cycle Kulekhani partially offsets sediment-as-design-constraint — reservoir sedimentation dynamics tanahu-hydropower — next proposed reservoir (140 MW, under construction) dudhkoshi-storage — long-term storage development (635 MW)

pages.title: Kulekhani II
headings: Aging Infrastructure in a Critical Role
pages.excerpt: 32 MW · operating · on the Kulekhani · in Makawanpur district.
pages.body_text: Kulekhani II 32 MW · operating · on the Kulekhani · in Makawanpur district. [!note] Cascade context Kulekhani II is the second plant in Nepal's only operational reservoir hydropower system. It operates as a cascade plant using discharge from kulekhani-i (60 MW, reservoir). See kulekhani-cascade for the full three-plant system overview including kulekhani-iii (14 MW). Combined generation in FY 2081/82: 279.8 GWh. # Summary Kulekhani II is the 32 MW middle plant in Nepal's only operating reservoir-fed hydropower cascade. The page tracks its dependence on Kulekhani I releases, supplementary inflows, FY 2081/82 performance, and aging-infrastructure role. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 32 MW | Status | Operating | Registry licence | Operation | River | Kulekhani | District | Makawanpur | Province | Bagmati Pradesh | # Sources nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 # Specifications (NEA FY 2081/82) Kulekhani II is a 32 MW cascade plant commissioned in 1986 — the second link in Nepal's only operating reservoir hydropower system. It uses tailrace discharge from kulekhani-i (60 MW, reservoir), supplemented by flow from the Mandu River and the Rapti Pumping Station, to generate peaking power when the central grid needs it most. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Type | Cascade (reservoir-fed) | Commissioning | 1986 | Design generation | 104.6 GWh/yr | FY 2081/82 generation | 74.9 GWh | FY 2081/82 vs target | 89% | Year-over-year change | +56% | Cumulative lifetime generation | 2,436.5 GWh | Supplementary sources | Mandu River intake, Rapti Pumping Station | Location | Makwanpur District | Each year, the Mandu intake is cleaned post-monsoon and the Rapti Pumping Station is maintained — operated as needed during the dry season to augment generation. In FY 2081/82, KL2 completed 7.2 kV VCB switchgear work, transformer oil filtration, replacement of a damaged 600 mm² conductor, and civil works at both intakes. # The Cascade's Middle Link The Kulekhani system operates as a sequential cascade: KL1 releases from the reservoir, KL2 generates from the tailrace plus supplementary sources, and KL3 (14 MW) uses the regulated flow from KL2 combined with Khani Khola natural flow. The system is coherent — KL1's dispatch decisions determine what KL2 and KL3 receive. KL2's 56% year-over-year increase mirrors KL1's 64.5% rise — both driven by the same monsoon-filling event. This coordination makes the cascade efficient when water is abundant but also concentrated: in a drought year, the entire cascade contracts together, since the bottleneck is reservoir fill, not turbine capacity at any single plant. The combined cascade design is 356.5 GWh/yr (KL1: 211 + KL2: 104.6 + KL3: 40.85). FY 2081/82 combined actual: 279.8 GWh — 78.5% of design. This is the hydrology-dependence in practice. The reservoir allows seasonal shifting but cannot create water; when the monsoon underperforms, the cascade underperforms as a unit. # Aging Infrastructure in a Critical Role At 39 years old (commissioned 1986), Kulekhani II is among the oldest NEA plants still in regular service. The FY 2081/82 maintenance scope — VCB switchgear replacement, conductor repair, transformer oil filtration — reflects a plant in its fourth decade where electrical infrastructure becomes the primary maintenance driver. The cascade's strategic importance magnifies the aging concern. If KL1 requires a major dam or turbine overhaul, KL2's generation suspends automatically — it has no independent water source. Both plants are vintage, both have NEA as sole owner/operator, and both are essential to the dry-season grid. There is no redundancy. See storage-deficit. # Limitations & Controversies Kulekhani II's performance cannot be evaluated independently of Kulekhani I reservoir operation. The page relies on NEA annual-report operating data and does not separately verify plant-level outage history, remaining equipment life, Rapti/Mandu supplementary-flow reliability, or rehabilitation needs. # See also kulekhani-cascade — full three-plant system overview (106 MW combined) kulekhani-i — upstream reservoir plant (60 MW, anchor of the cascade) storage-deficit — why 106 MW against 3,400 MW is the system problem firm-power — what stored-water generation provides that RoR cannot seasonal-mismatch — the cycle the cascade partially addresses sediment-as-design-constraint — what decades of sedimentation mean for reservoir life

pages.title: Kulekhani III
headings: 117% of Target, 79% of Design — No Contradiction
pages.excerpt: 14 MW · operating · on the Kulekhani · in Makwanpur district.
pages.body_text: Kulekhani III 14 MW · operating · on the Kulekhani · in Makwanpur district. [!note] Cascade context Kulekhani III is the tail-end plant in Nepal's only operating reservoir hydropower system. It uses regulated flow from Kulekhani II and the natural flow of the Khani Khola. See kulekhani-cascade for the full three-plant system overview. Combined generation in FY 2081/82: 279.8 GWh across all three plants. # Summary Kulekhani III is the 14 MW tail-end plant in Nepal's only operating reservoir-fed cascade. The page tracks its role as the downstream efficiency link that depends on Kulekhani I and II dispatch as well as Khani Khola natural flow. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 14 MW | Status | Operating | River | Kulekhani | District | Makawanpur | Province | Bagmati Pradesh | # Specifications (NEA FY 2081/82) Kulekhani III is the smallest and most downstream plant in Nepal's only operating reservoir cascade. At 14 MW, it sits below kulekhani-ii (32 MW), which sits below kulekhani-i (60 MW) and its reservoir. The water Kulekhani III generates from has already been stored in the Kulekhani Reservoir, shifted from monsoon inflow to dry-season dispatch, passed through Kulekhani I's turbines, collected in a forebay, passed through Kulekhani II, and collected again before reaching the third plant's intake. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Type | Cascade (reservoir-fed, tail-end) | Design generation | 40.85 GWh/yr | FY 2081/82 generation | 34.3 GWh | FY 2081/82 vs target | 117% | FY 2081/82 vs design | 79% | Year-over-year change | +54% | Cumulative lifetime generation | 176.3 GWh | Supplementary source | Khani Khola (natural flow) | Location | Makwanpur District | The 54% year-over-year increase mirrors the surge at kulekhani-i (+64.5%) and kulekhani-ii (+56%) — all three cascade plants rose together because a strong monsoon filled the reservoir. Recent upgrades included shaft alignment and generator bearing replacement in Unit 2, plus 7.2 kV vacuum circuit breaker installations in both units. # The Cascade Tail-End — Efficiency Argument Kulekhani III's position makes it the cascade's efficiency argument: the value of storage is not just in the first turbine — dispatchable water can generate at every stage of the cascade before returning to the natural river system. At 14 MW, the absolute contribution is small. But the principle matters: reservoir storage is a multiplier on cascade economics, not just a single-plant advantage. # 117% of Target, 79% of Design — No Contradiction In FY 2081/82, Kulekhani III generated at 117% of its internal target — one of the highest target-achievement ratios in the documented NEA fleet. Against design energy, performance was approximately 79%. The gap between these two figures reflects deliberate conservatism in target-setting for a tail-end cascade plant. The target accounts for the fact that Kulekhani III's inflow is not the river directly — it is whatever water the two upstream plants have dispatched. If Kulekhani I draws down the reservoir deeply (as it does in dry years), Kulekhani III gets less water. The internal target is set to reflect this dependency; the design energy reflects what the plant could do if upstream conditions were optimal year-round. This distinguishes Kulekhani III from the chilime pattern. Chilime overperforms because its design assumptions were conservative relative to actual hydrology. Kulekhani III overperforms against its internal target because that target builds in the upstream dependency — not because its design energy was set too high. The two mechanisms are different. # Second-Order Hydrology Dependence Kulekhani III's generation is twice removed from monsoon quality: 1. Good monsoon → Kulekhani Reservoir fills → KL1 dispatches freely in dry season → KL2 gets consistent inflow → KL3 runs at high utilisation 2. Poor monsoon → Reservoir partially fills → KL1 conserves releases → KL2 gets less → KL3 runs below capacity The 64% year-on-year swing at KL1 (FY 2080/81 to 2081/82) is amplified at the cascade tail-end. A good inflow year lifts all three plants; a poor year may prompt KL1 to reserve water for dry-season dispatch rather than let it flow through all three plants at full rate. The cascade operator must balance immediate generation against storage preservation — a real-time decision that has no equivalent in RoR operation. Kulekhani III is simultaneously the cascade's most efficient (% of target) and most dependent generator. # Significance for the Storage Thesis The three-plant cascade — 60 + 32 + 14 = 106 MW — generated 279.8 GWh in FY 2081/82 from a single reservoir system. Compare with marsyangdi (69 MW, pure RoR), which generates in a similar GWh range from direct river flow. The comparison is not about total energy — it is about timing. The cascade can choose when to generate; a RoR plant cannot. At 14 MW, Kulekhani III's contribution to that dispatchability is small but the architecture it demonstrates — reservoir → cascade → grid — is the template every future storage proposal depends on. The storage-deficit page frames the broader argument. Kulekhani III is the concrete endpoint: the last turbine in Nepal's only storage system, proving that reservoir-to-cascade generation works at every stage — and that Nepal has built exactly one such system. # Limitations & Controversies Kulekhani III's output is second-order dependent on upstream reservoir and cascade dispatch, so target achievement should not be read as standalone hydrological strength. The page does not independently verify unit availability, rehabilitation needs, Khani Khola contribution, or future performance under lower reservoir-fill years. # Sources nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 sangroula-ntnu-kulekhani-bathymetry # See also kulekhani-cascade — full cascade overview (106 MW total) kulekhani-i — the reservoir plant that determines everything downstream kulekhani-ii — the middle cascade link storage-deficit — the storage gap this cascade represents firm-power — what dispatchable reservoir generation provides seasonal-mismatch — the system problem this cascade partially addresses

pages.title: Likhu -1
headings: Transmission Dependency — The Single Corridor Risk
pages.excerpt: 77 MW · operating · on the Likhu Khola · in Solukhumbu, Okhaldhunga, and Ramechhap districts. The largest plant in the Likhu Cascade (213 MW combined across 4 plants).
pages.body_text: Likhu -1 77 MW · operating · on the Likhu Khola · in Solukhumbu, Okhaldhunga, and Ramechhap districts. The largest plant in the Likhu Cascade (213 MW combined across 4 plants). # Summary Likhu-1 is a 77 MW operating run-of-river hydropower project on the Likhu Khola in Solukhumbu, Okhaldhunga, and Ramechhap districts. It is the largest plant in the 213 MW Likhu Cascade and the first MV Dugar–Mogha Energy project to reach operational scale in this basin. The page tracks it as a cascade leader with an 80/20 take-or-pay PPA structure, using the current CARE Nepal credit-rating source set. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 77 MW | Status | Under construction | Registry licence | Generation | River | Likhu Khola (eastern koshi-basin) | District | Solukhumbu | Province | Province No 1 | # Sources likhu-cascade-research-compilation # Specifications (CARE Nepal / DoED data) Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Type | Run-of-river | COD | April 2024 | Developer | Pan Himalaya Energy Ltd (PHEL) | Primary equity | MV Dugar Group + Mogha Energy DMCC (UAE) | Design discharge | 26.4 m³/s | Headrace tunnel | 6.57 km (low-pressure) | Intake structure | 5.25 m weir | Turbines | Horizontal Francis (Andritz Hydro) | PPA structure | 80% take-or-pay, 20% take-and-pay | CARE Nepal rating | CARE-NP BB+ (March 2025, upgraded from BB) | Evacuation | New Khimti substation → Khimti–Dhalkebar 220 kV | [!warning] Registry status correction. The Ministry of Energy registry and the auto-generated spec table list Likhu-1 as "Under construction." The plant commissioned in April 2024. The narrative follows CARE Nepal credit rating data and developer operational disclosures. # The Cascade Leader Likhu-1 is the largest plant in the 213 MW Likhu cascade, and the only one with a better-than-standard PPA structure: 80% of contracted energy on take-or-pay terms (versus 75% at likhu-2). This means the developer carries less revenue risk from NEA curtailment — a meaningful protection in a cascade where the New Khimti substation bottleneck stranded 40% of Likhu-2's generation in FY 2023/24. The plant diverts 26.4 m³/s through a 5.25 m weir and a 6.57 km headrace tunnel to a surface powerhouse equipped with horizontal Francis turbines from Andritz Hydro. At 77 MW, it is the largest plant in the cascade and the second-largest private RoR IPP in the Likhu basin after the MV Dugar Group's 77 MW completed this project while simultaneously developing Likhu-2 and Likhu Khola A — a cluster investment model that concentrated three SPVs under shared equity and shared construction management. # Financial Recovery Likhu-1's credit trajectory tells the same transmission-bottleneck story as likhu-2, but from a better starting position: FY 2023/24 (commissioning year): constrained by the same New Khimti substation bottleneck that limited the entire cascade. CARE Nepal assigned a BB rating. FY 2024/25: following the 200 MVA transformer upgrade, the corridor unblocked. Operating income reached NPR 1,060 million. CARE upgraded the rating to BB+ in March 2025. The BB+ rating is below Likhu-2's BBB- — reflecting higher leverage or lower debt service coverage. But the upward trajectory mirrors the cascade pattern: the asset performs when the grid permits. # The MV Dugar FDI Model Likhu-1, Likhu-2, and Likhu Khola A share a common equity architecture: the MV Dugar Group (a Nepali conglomerate) paired with Mogha Energy DMCC, a UAE-based investment firm. This FDI structure — a domestic group clustering multiple projects under shared foreign capital — is a departure from Nepal's traditional single-project domestic bank consortium model. Butwal Power Company (BPC) holds no equity in any cascade plant. The market misattribution (BPC as cascade developer) persists because BPC's subsidiary HCEL provided engineering consultancy during construction. The actual equity is MV Dugar + UAE FDI. For the UAE investors, the Likhu cluster offers a risk-diversified entry: three projects (77 + 55 + 29 = 161 MW cumulative under Dugar control) share the same river basin, the same transmission corridor, and the same regulatory regime — but operate as separate SPVs with separate PPAs and separate debt. If one underperforms, the other two are not legally affected. This structuring is standard for the Dugar approach and represents a model other Nepali conglomerates could replicate. # Transmission Dependency — The Single Corridor Risk All four cascade plants share one evacuation route: the New Khimti substation into the Khimti–Dhalkebar 220 kV line. When the substation had only a 100 MVA transformer, the entire 213 MW cascade competed for approximately half its rated corridor capacity. The 200 MVA upgrade (late 2023) resolved the immediate bottleneck — but the structural vulnerability remains: a single substation fire, 220 kV line fault, or transformer failure returns the entire cascade to stranded-generation status. Following the upgrade, NEA secured Central Electricity Authority (CEA) approval to wheel power from Likhu-2 and Likhu-4 across the Dhalkebar– Muzaffarpur 400 kV interconnector into the Indian day-ahead market. This transformed the same corridor that caused stranded generation in 2023 into a dual-market export pathway — domestic dispatch in dry season, Indian export in monsoon surplus. See buildability. # Limitations & Controversies The current page is strongest on credit-rating and cascade-level context from CARE Nepal disclosures. It does not independently verify final design parameters, construction-phase quality records, current operating performance month-by-month, or environmental/social compliance status beyond the existing source set. The single-corridor evacuation risk is documented at the cascade level but not quantified against real-time grid capacity. # See also likhu-2 — downstream 55 MW plant, stranded generation case study buildability — transmission planning failure as structural IPP risk q-design-discharge — cascade performance vs design energy stranded-generation — the grid evacuation bottleneck problem ppa-pricing — the take-and-pay revenue risk at the cascade level koshi-basin — basin context for the Likhu Khola system khimti-dhalkebar-corridor — the 220 kV backbone the cascade depends on

pages.title: Likhu -2
headings: The Recovery — Grid Fixed, Plant Proved
Likhu-4 — A Different Story in the Same Cascade
pages.excerpt: 55 MW · operating · on the Likhu Khola · in Ramechhap and Okhaldhunga districts. Part of the Likhu Cascade (213 MW combined across 4 plants).
pages.body_text: Likhu -2 # Summary 55 MW · operating · on the Likhu Khola · in Ramechhap and Okhaldhunga districts. Part of the Likhu Cascade (213 MW combined across 4 plants). # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 55 MW | Status | Under construction | Registry licence | Generation | River | Likhu Khola (eastern koshi-basin) | District | Solukhumbu | Province | Province No 1 | # Sources likhu-cascade-research-compilation # Specifications (CARE Nepal data) Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Type | Run-of-river | COD | July 31, 2023 | Developer | Global Hydropower Associate Limited (GHAL) | Primary equity | MV Dugar Group + Mogha Energy DMCC (UAE) | Contracted energy | 242.37 GWh/yr | PPA tariff (wet / dry) | NPR 4.80 / NPR 8.40/kWh | Project cost | ~NPR 10,968–11,246 million (~NPR 204M/MW) | Debt / equity | ~78:22 | Lead financier | Machhapuchchhre Bank (MBL) — consortium of 6 banks | CARE Nepal rating | CARE-NP BBB- (Is) (March 2026) | [!warning] Registry status correction. The Ministry of Energy registry and the auto-generated spec table list Likhu-2 as "Under construction." The plant commissioned on July 31, 2023 and has two full operating years of generation data. The narrative follows the CARE Nepal rating and developer operational data. # The Stranded Generation Case Study Likhu-2 generated only ~146 GWh (60% of contracted energy) in its first full operating year (FY 2023/24). The COD was July 31, 2023 — two weeks into the fiscal year — making FY 2023/24 a full operating year. At 60% of contracted energy, Likhu-2 would appear in the bottom quartile of Nepal's private IPP generation performance data, alongside projects genuinely failing due to q-design-discharge optimism. This appearance is misleading. CARE Ratings Nepal's analysis confirms that the cause was not hydrology, not Q-design failure, and not a turbine defect. It was a grid evacuation bottleneck at the NEA New Khimti substation. The New Khimti substation — the single gateway connecting the Likhu basin to the national grid via the Khimti–Dhalkebar 220 kV backbone — was equipped with a single 100 MVA transformer when Likhu-2 commissioned. It had been sized to service Upper Tamakoshi (456 MW). As the Likhu cascade plants (combined ~213 MW) came online between 2021 and 2024, they saturated the node. When the substation cannot step up and push power down the 220 kV line, a run-of-river plant has one option: dump water. Likhu-2 effectively wasted 40% of viable contracted generation because the state transmission infrastructure was not ready for the private generation it had approved. See buildability. # The Recovery — Grid Fixed, Plant Proved In late 2023, NEA installed a new 200 MVA auto-transformer at New Khimti, raising total substation capacity to 300 MVA. The result was immediate: Fiscal Year | Contracted (GWh) | Actual (GWh) | % of Contracted | Cause | ---|---|---|---|---| FY 2023/24 | 242.37 | ~146 | 60% | NEA substation bottleneck (stranded generation) | FY 2024/25 | 242.37 | ~221 | 91% | Bottleneck resolved + favourable hydrology | Source: CARE Ratings Nepal (March 2026 issuer rating disclosure for GHAL). 91% of contracted energy in a fully operational year places Likhu-2 among the better-performing private IPPs in the sector — not an underperformer. The jump from 60% to 91% is not explained by improved hydrology (though that helped); it is explained by whether the state had built the transmission infrastructure to receive what the private plant was ready to generate. This has a direct implication for how the q-design-discharge performance table should read Likhu-2. The FY 2023/24 figure is not evidence of design-energy overestimation. It is evidence of transmission planning failure. # Financial Architecture The Likhu-2 SPV (GHAL) was originally budgeted at NPR 9,313 million. A capacity upgrade from 33.4 MW to 55 MW, combined with Interest During Construction, raised the final cost to NPR 10,968–11,246 million (~NPR 204 million/MW). Financing: Debt: NPR 8,534 million (~78% of capital) Equity: ~22% Debt consortium led by Machhapuchchhre Bank (MBL), with Mega Bank, Nepal SBI, Nepal Bangladesh Bank, Everest Bank, and Vibor Society Development Bank The financial metrics in FY 2024/25 (post-recovery): Metric | Value | ---|---| Overall gearing ratio | 3.60x | Total debt / Gross Cash Accruals | 19.51x (improved from 35.45x in FY 2023/24) | Interest coverage ratio | 1.66x | CARE Nepal rating (March 2026) | CARE-NP BBB- (Is) | A 1.66x interest coverage ratio is thin but serviceable — typical for a highly leveraged first-decade IPP when generation is near contracted levels. The main ongoing risk is exposure to Nepal's floating interest rate environment: with NPR 8.5 billion in variable-rate debt, base rate movements can quickly erode the 1.66x cushion. # The Take-and-Pay Exposure Approximately 25% of Likhu-2's contracted energy is on "take-and-pay" terms — NEA only purchases this tranche if the national grid requires it. During monsoon season, when all domestic RoR projects peak simultaneously and export channels to India are saturated, NEA actively curtails take-and-pay purchases. This structural revenue leakage is a persistent risk on top of the leverage ratio. Likhu-1 (the larger MV Dugar project upstream) has better terms: 80% take-or-pay, 20% take-and-pay. # The Likhu Cascade Likhu-2 is one of four projects in the Likhu cascade, all now fully operational: Project | MW | Developer | COD | Primary Equity | ---|---|---|---|---| Likhu-1 | 77.0 | Pan Himalaya Energy Ltd | Apr 2024 | MV Dugar Group + Mogha Energy (UAE) | Likhu-2 | 55.0 | Global Hydropower Associate Ltd | Jul 2023 | MV Dugar Group + Mogha Energy (UAE) | Likhu-4 | 52.4 | Green Ventures Ltd | Nov 2021 | Triveni Group + Bhilwara Energy (India) | Likhu Khola A | 29.04 | Numbur Himalaya Hydropower Ltd | Feb 2022 | MV Dugar Group + Mogha Energy (UAE) | Note: Butwal Power Company (BPC) has no equity stake in any cascade plant. BPC's subsidiary HCEL provided engineering consultancy only. The MV Dugar Group secured Foreign Direct Investment from Mogha Energy DMCC, an energy investment firm based in the UAE. This FDI model — a Nepali conglomerate pairing with foreign capital for a cluster of simultaneous projects — is a structural development in Nepal's IPP financing beyond the traditional domestic bank consortium. All four plants share the New Khimti evacuation corridor. Following the 2023 transformer upgrade, NEA secured export approvals from India's Central Electricity Authority (CEA) to wheel power from Likhu-4 and Likhu-2 across the Dhalkebar–Muzaffarpur 400 kV interconnector into the Indian day-ahead market — transforming the same corridor that caused stranded generation in 2023 into an export pathway by 2024/25. # Likhu-4 — A Different Story in the Same Cascade Likhu-4 (52.4 MW, Green Ventures Ltd) was originally designed as a 120 MW export-oriented project, intended to wheel power directly to India. A dispute over cross-border transmission wheeling charges caused GVL to abandon the export model entirely — redesigning and downscaling to 52.4 MW for the domestic grid. The project commissioned November 2021 but suffered a structural collapse of a desanding basin wall on the eve of production testing (May 2021), publicly blamed on the Indian civil contractor SSNR Projects. Green Ventures currently carries a CARE-NP BB rating, constrained by high capital costs and the legacy of its commissioning failures. See buildability. # Limitations & Controversies Grid evacuation bottleneck. Likhu-2 generated only ~60% of contracted energy in FY 2023/24 because the New Khimti substation transformer was undersized (100 MVA) for the cascade load. This is a state transmission planning failure, not a project failure — but the revenue loss fell entirely on the private developer. Take-and-pay exposure. ~25% of contracted energy is on take-and-pay terms, exposed to NEA curtailment during monsoon peaks when export channels are saturated. This structural revenue leakage persists even after the transformer upgrade. Thin interest coverage. A 1.66x interest coverage ratio is serviceable but vulnerable to Nepal's floating interest rate environment. With NPR 8.5 billion in variable-rate debt, base rate movements can quickly erode the cushion. Single-corridor dependency. All four Likhu cascade plants share the New Khimti → Khimti–Dhalkebar 220 kV evacuation route. A single substation or line failure returns all four plants to stranded-generation status. # See also buildability — transmission planning failure as a structural IPP risk q-design-discharge — why Likhu-2's 60% PLF in FY23/24 should not be read as design-energy failure ad-penalties — take-and-pay curtailment risk and the AD penalty interaction ppa-pricing — the wet/dry tariff structure and its effect on Likhu-2's revenue profile koshi-basin — the Likhu Khola drains to the Sun Koshi upper-tamakoshi — the 456 MW plant that shared the New Khimti bottleneck

pages.title: Likhu-4
headings: From Export Megaproject to Domestic Afterthought — A Regulatory Case Study
The Desanding Basin Collapse — Commissioning Catastrophe
Financial Position — Constrained by Legacy Costs
pages.excerpt: 52.4 MW · operating · on the Likhu Khola · in Ramechhap district. Originally designed as a 120 MW export-oriented project, completely redesigned and downscaled after a cross-border transmission dispute. Part of the Likhu Cascade (213 MW combined).
pages.body_text: Likhu-4 52.4 MW · operating · on the Likhu Khola · in Ramechhap district. Originally designed as a 120 MW export-oriented project, completely redesigned and downscaled after a cross-border transmission dispute. Part of the Likhu Cascade (213 MW combined). # Summary Likhu-4 is a 52.4 MW operating run-of-river hydropower project on the Likhu Khola in Ramechhap district. It was originally designed as a 120 MW export-oriented plant and was completely redesigned and downscaled after a cross-border transmission wheeling-charge dispute. The page tracks it as a regulatory case study and stranded-generation recovery example using the current CARE Nepal and JICA source set. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 52.4 MW | Status | Under construction | Registry licence | Generation | River | Likhu Khola (eastern koshi-basin) | District | Ramechhap | Province | Bagmati Pradesh | # Sources likhu-cascade-research-compilation jica-ipsdp-main-report-vol2 # Specifications (CARE Nepal / DoED data) Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Type | Run-of-river | COD | November 2021 | Developer | Green Ventures Ltd (GVL) | Primary equity | Triveni Group + Bhilwara Energy (India) | Original design | 120 MW export-oriented | Current design | 52.4 MW domestic grid | PPA | Standard NEA domestic PPA | CARE Nepal rating | CARE-NP BB | Contractor (civil) | SSNR Projects (India) | Evacuation | New Khimti substation → Khimti–Dhalkebar 220 kV | [!warning] Registry status correction. The Ministry of Energy registry and auto-generated spec table list Likhu-4 as "Under construction." The plant commissioned in November 2021. The narrative follows CARE Nepal credit rating data and DoED registries. # From Export Megaproject to Domestic Afterthought — A Regulatory Case Study Likhu-4 was originally conceived as a 120 MW export-oriented hydropower project, intended to wheel power directly to India across the Dhalkebar– Muzaffarpur cross-border interconnector. A dispute over cross-border transmission wheeling charges — the tariff India would charge for conveying Nepali-generated power across its grid to Indian buyers — caused Green Ventures Ltd (GVL) to abandon the export model entirely. The project was completely redesigned and downscaled to 52.4 MW to cater exclusively to the domestic grid via a standard PPA with NEA. This represents a 57% capacity reduction from original design — a regulatory-risk write-down that no developer voluntarily accepts unless the alternative (persisting with the export model) was financially non-viable. The Likhu-4 redesign is Nepal's clearest documented example of cross-border transmission policy directly determining project scale. The wheeling dispute with India did not kill the project — a 52.4 MW plant was still viable. But it killed two-thirds of it. Every other proposed export project in Nepal's pipeline (Upper Karnali, West Seti, Arun-3 free-power component, 28,500 MW target with 15,000 MW for export) faces the same wheeling charge risk, and Likhu-4 is the only completed project that has already absorbed it. See buildability and stranded-generation. # The Desanding Basin Collapse — Commissioning Catastrophe In May 2021, on the eve of production testing, a wall of Likhu-4's desanding basin suffered a catastrophic structural collapse. The developer publicly blamed the Indian civil contractor, SSNR Projects, alleging construction defects. A desanding basin failure at a RoR plant on a Himalayan sediment-loaded river is among the most consequential possible civil-engineering failures. The basin is the first line of defence protecting the headrace tunnel and turbines from abrasive sediment. A structural collapse on the eve of commissioning meant the plant could not operate safely — sediment-laden water entering the headrace would destroy the Francis turbine runners within weeks. The incident delayed full commissioning and required emergency repairs. The event remains one of Nepal's best-documented examples of how construction-phase quality failures at the contractor interface convert directly into revenue loss — and how the limited-recourse SPV structure concentrates that loss on equity while debt continues to capitalise interest. The plant eventually commissioned in November 2021, but the delayed revenue and repair costs pushed GVL's capital structure deeper into leverage territory. # Financial Position — Constrained by Legacy Costs Green Ventures currently carries a CARE-NP BB rating — two notches below investment grade and below both Likhu-2 (BBB-) and Likhu-1 (BB+). The rating is constrained by: 1. High capital costs — the redesign from 120 MW to 52.4 MW did not fully recapture sunk engineering and licensing expenditure from the export-design phase 2. Commissioning delay — the six-month delay from the desanding basin collapse meant six months of capitalized interest without revenue 3. Independent developer structure — unlike the Dugar-controlled plants (Likhu-1, Likhu-2, Likhu Khola A) which benefit from shared management and cross-SPV expertise, GVL operates as a standalone entity The BB rating, while below the cascade average, is not a default warning — it reflects the margin pressure of a project that absorbed extraordinary regulatory and construction-phase costs before generating a single kWh. Unlike the Dugar-controlled cascade plants, Likhu-4 has no UAE FDI component. The equity is held by Triveni Group (Nepal) and Bhilwara Energy (India) — making Likhu-4 the only Likhu cascade plant with Indian equity exposure. Indian EPC contractor failures (SSNR) combined with Indian policy disputes (wheeling charges) affecting an Indian-invested project is a concentration pattern that would concern any project finance credit committee. # Transmission — Same Corridor, Different Story Like the rest of the cascade, Likhu-4 evacuates through New Khimti. Following the late-2023 200 MVA transformer upgrade, Likhu-4 was among the first cascade plants to receive CEA export approval for Dhalkebar–Muzaffarpur wheeling into the Indian day-ahead market — a remarkable reversal for a project that abandoned export at the design stage. The transmission infrastructure that did not exist when the original 120 MW export model was conceived now exists, and Likhu-4 benefits from it at 52.4 MW. This is not a vindication of the Indian wheeling-charge regime. It is evidence that cross-border transmission policy evolves faster than a RoR hydro project can be redesigned and built. A project conceived for one regulatory environment commissions into a different one. Likhu-4 is the case study. # Limitations & Controversies The current page is strongest on regulatory-history and credit-rating context. It does not independently verify the desanding basin failure root cause, contractor liability adjudication, current month-by-month operating performance, or environmental/social compliance status beyond the existing source set. The redesign from 120 MW to 52.4 MW means some original-design data no longer reflects the built asset. # See also buildability — regulatory risk as a design-determining constraint stranded-generation — when the grid cannot receive what the plant generates q-design-discharge — Likhu-4's generation data in context koshi-basin — basin context for the Likhu Khola system khimti-dhalkebar-corridor — the 220 kV backbone the cascade depends on arun-3 — the India-developed export archetype Likhu-4's original design was modelled on

pages.excerpt: The Likhu Khola is a hydropower-rich tributary in the koshi-basin, straddling Solukhumbu and Ramechhap districts. The Likhu system has attracted significant IPP investment with multiple generation-licence projects across the upper and lower reaches.
pages.body_text: Likhu Cascade The Likhu Khola is a hydropower-rich tributary in the koshi-basin, straddling Solukhumbu and Ramechhap districts. The Likhu system has attracted significant IPP investment with multiple generation-licence projects across the upper and lower reaches. # Summary The Likhu Cascade is a 213 MW cluster of four run-of-river hydropower plants on the Likhu Khola in the Koshi basin, spanning Solukhumbu and Ramechhap districts. The page tracks the cascade as a single-corridor generation cluster with shared transmission infrastructure and mixed developer equity, using the current wiki source set. # Plants in the Cascade Plant | Capacity (MW) | Status | District | -------|--------------|--------|----------| likhu-1 | 77.0 | Under construction | Solukhumbu | likhu-2 | 55.0 | Under construction | Solukhumbu | likhu-khola-a | 29.04 | Operating | Solukhumbu | likhu-4 | 52.4 | Under construction | Ramechhap | lower-likhu | 28.1 | Under construction | Ramechhap | Nupche Likhu HEP | 57.5 | Survey | Ramechhap | Total | ~299 | | | [!note] Likhu-3 does not appear in the current MoE/DoED registry. The numbering (1, 2, 4) reflects the registry's actual naming — Likhu-3 may have been a planned designation that was never licensed, or the gap reflects the staggered licensing history of the corridor. # Corridor Context The upper Likhu projects (1, 2, Likhu Khola A) cluster in the Solukhumbu highlands, while Likhu-4, Lower Likhu, and Nupche Likhu sit further downstream in Ramechhap. The Likhu is a tributary of the Sun Koshi, and its projects share transmission corridors with the broader Khimti-Tamakoshi system via khimti-dhalkebar-corridor. # Sources likhu-cascade-research-compilation # Limitations & Controversies The current page is strongest on aggregate registry context and corridor-level narrative. It does not independently verify individual plant construction status, commissioning dates, current generation, or financing terms beyond the existing source set. Plant-level details should be checked against the respective entity pages and their source links before detailed use. The aggregate capacity figure includes projects at varying stages of development. # See also likhu-1 likhu-2 likhu-4 likhu-khola-a lower-likhu koshi-basin

pages.title: Likhu Khola 'A'
headings: The Finishing Line — First to Commission
Cascade Position — Smallest, but Structurally Identical
pages.excerpt: 29.04 MW · operating · on the Likhu Khola · in Solukhumbu district. The smallest plant in the Likhu Cascade (213.44 MW combined across 4 plants) and the first MV Dugar project to commission.
pages.body_text: Likhu Khola 'A' 29.04 MW · operating · on the Likhu Khola · in Solukhumbu district. The smallest plant in the Likhu Cascade (213.44 MW combined across 4 plants) and the first MV Dugar project to commission. # Summary Likhu Khola A is a 29.04 MW operating run-of-river hydropower project on the Likhu Khola in Solukhumbu district. It is the smallest plant in the Likhu Cascade and the first MV Dugar–Mogha Energy project to commission, in February 2022. The page tracks it as a cascade-financial benchmark with a two-tier PPA structure, using the current CARE Nepal credit-rating source set. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 51 MW | Status | Under construction | Registry licence | Generation | River | Likhu Khola (eastern koshi-basin) | District | Solukhumbu | Province | Province No 1 | # Sources likhu-cascade-research-compilation # Specifications (CARE Nepal / DoED data) Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Type | Run-of-river | COD | February 8, 2022 | Developer | Numbur Himalaya Hydropower Limited | Primary equity | MV Dugar Group + Mogha Energy DMCC (UAE, ~7% FDI) | Project cost | NPR 5,996 million (~NPR 206M/MW) | Debt / equity | 75:25 | PPA structure | 24.2 MW take-or-pay (135.68 GWh/yr), 4.84 MW take-and-pay | Financing consortium | Laxmi Bank (lead), Siddhartha Bank (co-lead), Century Commercial Bank, Citizens Bank, Bank of Kathmandu | CARE Nepal rating | CARE-NP BBB- (reaffirmed March 2025) | PBILDT margins | 82–91% | Evacuation | New Khimti substation → Khimti–Dhalkebar 220 kV | [!warning] Registry status correction. The Ministry of Energy registry and the auto-generated spec table list Likhu Khola A as "Under construction" at 51 MW. The plant commissioned on February 8, 2022 at a confirmed capacity of 29.04 MW. The narrative follows CARE Nepal credit rating data and developer operational disclosures. # The Finishing Line — First to Commission Likhu Khola A was the first MV Dugar project to reach the finish line, commissioning on February 8, 2022 — nearly 18 months before likhu-2 (July 2023) and over two years before likhu-1 (April 2024). For a conglomerate simultaneously developing three generation assets in the same river basin, getting the smallest project operational first was strategically essential: it established the developer's creditworthiness with lenders, demonstrated construction capability to the regulator, and generated early cash flow to support the larger builds. At NPR 5,996 million (~NPR 206M/MW), Likhu Khola A's capital cost sits in line with Nepal's post-2015 private IPP benchmark. The 75:25 debt-equity ratio is lower than the cascade's other Dugar-controlled plants (likhu-1 at 80:20, likhu-2 at 78:22), reflecting the conservative leverage typical of first-mover projects in an unproven basin. # The MV Dugar FDI Model Likhu Khola A shares the cascade's defining equity architecture: the MV Dugar Group (a Nepali conglomerate with interests in banking, insurance, automotive trading, and infrastructure) paired with Mogha Energy DMCC, a UAE-based investment firm. Mogha Energy holds a confirmed ~7% institutional promoter stake alongside Dugar family majority holdings. This FDI model — a domestic group clustering multiple projects under shared foreign capital through separate SPVs — is a departure from Nepal's traditional single-project domestic bank consortium structure. For the UAE investors, the cluster offers risk diversification: three projects (77 + 55 + 29 = 161 MW cumulative under Dugar control) share the same basin, corridor, and regulatory regime, but operate as legally distinct entities with independent PPAs and debt. Butwal Power Company (BPC) holds no equity in Likhu Khola A. BPC's involvement in the Likhu basin is exclusively technical — its subsidiary HCEL provided engineering consultancy and construction supervision, generating consulting revenue, not generation revenue. # PPA Structure — Partial Curtailment Exposure Likhu Khola A's PPA has a distinctive two-tier structure. Of the 29.04 MW installed capacity, only 24.2 MW (83.4%) is contracted on strict take-or-pay terms, yielding 135.68 GWh/year with no NEA curtailment risk. The remaining 4.84 MW (16.6%) was built targeting future uncontracted take-and-pay off-take, exposed to NEA dispatch discretion. This contrasts with likhu-1, where 80% is take-or-pay, and likhu-2, where 75% is take-or-pay. Likhu Khola A sits between the two on curtailment protection: better than Likhu-2's 25% exposure, below Likhu-1's 20%. # Financial Performance CARE Ratings Nepal reaffirmed the project's bank facilities at CARE-NP BBB- in March 2025, supported by: PBILDT margins averaging 82% to 91% — strong operating cash generation Improving debt coverage ratios as the project seasons past its commissioning ramp-up Revenue stability from the high take-or-pay share (83.4%) The BBB- rating places Likhu Khola A in the same CARE tier as likhu-2 (BBB- Is), above likhu-4 (BB). The rating reflects the project's conservative leverage structure and diversified lending consortium (5 banks), mitigated by the single-corridor transmission risk shared by the entire cascade. # Cascade Position — Smallest, but Structurally Identical At 29.04 MW, Likhu Khola A is dwarfed by likhu-1 (77 MW), likhu-2 (55 MW), and likhu-4 (52.4 MW) in capacity terms. But it shares the cascade's structural vulnerabilities: Hydrological interdependence: as an upstream plant in the Likhu system, its tailwater discharge affects downstream operators. Emergency shutdowns or desilting operations at Likhu Khola A alter inflow parameters for lower cascade plants — a cascade externality that no standalone PPA accounts for. Single corridor dependency: all four cascade plants evacuate through the New Khimti substation into the Khimti–Dhalkebar 220 kV line. The same 100 MVA transformer that bottlenecked likhu-2 at 60% PLF in FY 2023/24 constrained the entire cascade. The late-2023 upgrade to 300 MVA resolved the immediate crisis, but a single substation failure returns all four plants to stranded-generation status. See buildability and stranded-generation. # Limitations & Controversies The current page is strongest on credit-rating and PPA-structure context from CARE Nepal disclosures. It does not independently verify final design parameters, construction-phase quality records, current operating performance month-by-month, or environmental/social compliance status beyond the existing source set. Hydrological interdependence with downstream cascade plants is noted but not quantified. # See also likhu-1 — upstream 77 MW cascade leader with best PPA protection likhu-2 — downstream 55 MW plant, stranded generation case study likhu-4 — downstream 52.4 MW plant (non-Dugar developer) likhu-cascade — cascade overview and corridor context buildability — transmission planning failure as structural IPP risk stranded-generation — the grid evacuation bottleneck problem koshi-basin — basin context khimti-dhalkebar-corridor — the 220 kV backbone

pages.body_text: Lower Badigad Lower Badigad is a 380.3 MW JICA promising-storage candidate in the Gandaki basin. It is pinned in data-layer-storage-shortlist because it pairs large carryover storage with meaningful dry-season output, making it more relevant to system value than many larger wet-season-heavy projects. # Summary Lower Badigad is a 380.3 MW JICA promising-storage candidate in the Gandaki basin. It is pinned in the storage shortlist for its large carryover storage (995.9 MCM total, 505.5 MCM effective) and meaningful dry-season output (354.7 GWh, 26.0% dry share). The page tracks it as a planning-layer storage comparator using the current JICA/NEA source set. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 380.3 MW | Status | Survey / study | Category | jica promising storage | Basin | Gandaki (gandaki-basin) | Annual energy | 1366.0 GWh | Dry-season energy | 354.7 GWh | Dry share | 26.0% | Total storage | 995.9 MCM | Effective storage | 505.5 MCM | ## Storage Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Total storage | 995.9 MCM | Effective storage | 505.5 MCM | ## Output Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Annual design energy | 1366.0 GWh | Dry-season energy | 354.7 GWh | Dry-season share | 26.0 % | Type | Storage | # Sources jica-ipsdp-main-report-vol2 moewri-ipsdp-exec-summary-2025 # Why It Matters Lower Badigad is one of the stronger Gandaki storage candidates in the shortlist: 995.9 MCM total storage, 505.5 MCM effective storage, and 354.7 GWh of dry-season energy. Its dry share is lower than Nalsyau Gad or Dudhkoshi, but the reservoir scale is large enough that it remains important for seasonal regulation. Its strategic role is also geographic. The Gandaki basin is already a central hydropower corridor, and storage in that basin has a different grid value than remote far-western storage. Lower Badigad belongs in the wiki because it is a credible comparator to tanahu-hydropower, kali-gandaki-a, and other Gandaki assets. # Status And Timing Lower Badigad is a planning candidate from the JICA/NEA storage material, not an under-construction project. The IPSDP milestone ladder groups Lower Badigad STO in the 2031-2035 window. Treat that as a planning horizon rather than a confirmed construction-start date. The next evidence to watch is whether the project advances from storage-master-plan candidate to a named developer, updated feasibility package, environmental assessment, financing plan, and grid-connection commitment. # Map Interpretation The map marker is a river-aligned project reference. It is appropriate for comparing storage candidates and basin leverage, but not for property-level impact analysis. # Registry note JICA/NEA storage master plan volume 2 # Limitations & Controversies The current page is strongest on master-plan and shortlist context. It does not independently verify feasibility-study details, environmental and social assessment, financing plan, grid-connection commitment, or construction timeline beyond the existing source set. The IPSDP milestone window (2031–2035) is a planning horizon, not a confirmed construction-start date. Map markers are river-aligned references, not site-grade boundaries. # See also gandaki-basin storage-deficit firm-power tanahu-hydropower data-ipsdp-milestone-ladder-2022-2040 data-layer-storage-shortlist

pages.excerpt: Lower Jhimruk is a 142.5 MW JICA promising-storage candidate in the West Rapti basin. It is pinned in data-layer-storage-shortlist as a medium-basin storage option, with the important caveat that its layout conflicts with Naumure in the current design set.
pages.body_text: Lower Jhimruk Lower Jhimruk is a 142.5 MW JICA promising-storage candidate in the West Rapti basin. It is pinned in data-layer-storage-shortlist as a medium-basin storage option, with the important caveat that its layout conflicts with Naumure in the current design set. # Summary Lower Jhimruk is a 142.5 MW JICA promising-storage candidate in the West Rapti basin (Karnali basin). It contributes 94.4 GWh of dry-season energy with 386 MCM total storage and 211.6 MCM effective storage. The page tracks it as a medium-basin storage option using the current JICA/NEA source set, with the noted caveat that its layout conflicts with Naumure in the current design set. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 142.5 MW | Status | Survey / study | Category | jica promising storage | Basin | West Rapti (karnali-basin) | Annual energy | 454.7 GWh | Dry-season energy | 94.4 GWh | Dry share | 20.8% | Total storage | 386.0 MCM | Effective storage | 211.6 MCM | ## Storage Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Total storage | 386.0 MCM | Effective storage | 211.6 MCM | ## Output Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Annual design energy | 454.7 GWh | Dry-season energy | 94.4 GWh | Dry-season share | 20.8 % | Type | Storage | # Sources jica-ipsdp-main-report-vol2 # Why It Matters Lower Jhimruk contributes 94.4 GWh of dry-season energy, with 386 MCM total storage and 211.6 MCM effective storage. It is not a top-capacity project, but it belongs in the storage shortlist because it helps illustrate the range of medium-basin options. The caveat is central: the shortlist notes that Lower Jhimruk's layout conflicts with naumure-w-rapti in the current design. That means the project should not be counted naively alongside Naumure as if both could necessarily be built in the same configuration. # Status And Timing Lower Jhimruk is a planning candidate from the JICA/NEA storage material. The current wiki evidence set does not confirm construction start, financing, or a COD target. The next question is scheme selection: if Naumure advances, Lower Jhimruk may become less relevant or need redesign. If Naumure stalls, Lower Jhimruk remains a smaller West Rapti storage comparator. # Map Interpretation The marker uses an operating-project registry point near a mapped river reach as a reference. It is a planning-layer marker, not a final site boundary. # Registry note JICA/NEA storage master plan volume 2 # Limitations & Controversies The current page is strongest on master-plan and shortlist context. It does not independently verify feasibility-study details, environmental and social assessment, financing plan, grid-connection commitment, or construction timeline beyond the existing source set. The layout conflict with Naumure means the project should not be counted naively alongside it as if both could necessarily be built in the same configuration.
