pages.title: Lower Solu Hydropower Project
pages.excerpt: Lower Solu is an 82 MW run-of-river hydropower project under construction in the Solukhumbu district — part of the Dudh Koshi river system that includes the benchmark Sahas Urja (Solu Khola, 86 MW) project.
pages.body_text: Lower Solu Hydropower Project Lower Solu is an 82 MW run-of-river hydropower project under construction in the Solukhumbu district — part of the Dudh Koshi river system that includes the benchmark Sahas Urja (Solu Khola, 86 MW) project. # Summary Lower Solu is an 82 MW run-of-river hydropower project under construction on the Solu Khola in Solukhumbu district, part of the Dudh Koshi river system. It enters a corridor with an established capital-efficiency benchmark set by Sahas Urja's 86 MW Solu Khola project. The page tracks it as a build-cost-discipline case study using the current ICRA/Sahas Urja source set. # Solu Corridor The Solu Khola / Dudh Koshi river system in Solukhumbu has emerged as a significant eastern Nepal hydropower corridor. Sahas Urja's 86 MW Solu Khola project (commissioned March 2023) demonstrated that with disciplined capital deployment — achieving NPR 172–175 million/MW vs. industry averages exceeding NPR 200–250 million/MW — projects in this corridor can generate strong financial returns even under the standard NPR 4.80/8.40 PPA framework. Lower Solu, at a comparable 82 MW, enters a corridor with an established benchmark and transmission infrastructure shaped by its predecessor. # The Sahas Urja Benchmark The success of Sahas Urja creates both opportunity and pressure for Lower Solu: Opportunity: Transmission infrastructure exists, river hydrology data is available, and the financing community has a positive reference point in the same valley Pressure: Sahas Urja's NPR 172–175 million/MW build cost, 69% PLF, and NPR 900M+ annual profit set a high bar that investors will compare against # Build Cost Discipline The single most important variable determining Lower Solu's financial outcome is construction cost per MW. In the fixed-tariff regime where every MW-hour sells at the same regulated rate regardless of how much it cost to build, capital efficiency is the only lever for profitability. Sahas Urja proved that ~NPR 173M/MW is achievable in this corridor; projects that drift toward NPR 250M/MW or beyond will struggle to achieve positive equity returns. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 82 MW | Status | Under construction | Registry licence | Generation | River | Solu Khola | District | Solukhumbu | Province | Province No 1 | # See Also run-of-river-hydropower buildability sahas-urja-benchmark-icra-2026 # Limitations & Controversies The current page is strongest on corridor-benchmark and capital-efficiency context. It does not independently verify current construction progress, final cost per MW, commissioning date, financing closure, or environmental/social compliance status beyond the existing source set. The Sahas Urja benchmark creates comparative pressure, but Lower Solu's actual cost and performance will require project-level verification before detailed financial analysis. # Sources sahas-urja-benchmark-icra-2026

pages.excerpt: Madhya Bhotekoshi (Middle Bhotekoshi) is a 102 MW run-of-river hydropower project under construction on the Bhote Koshi River in Sindhupalchok district. It is one of the key capacity additions in the Bhote Koshi corridor, an area that has seen repeated geological setbacks includi
pages.body_text: Madhya Bhotekoshi Madhya Bhotekoshi (Middle Bhotekoshi) is a 102 MW run-of-river hydropower project under construction on the Bhote Koshi River in Sindhupalchok district. It is one of the key capacity additions in the Bhote Koshi corridor, an area that has seen repeated geological setbacks including landslides and glacial lake outburst floods. # Summary Madhya Bhotekoshi is a 102 MW run-of-river hydropower project under construction on the Bhote Koshi River in Sindhupalchok district. It is part of the Chilime Hydropower Company Limited expansion strategy and one of three Chilime-promoted projects forming a ~256 MW cluster in the Trishuli–Bhote Koshi system. The page tracks it as a geologically exposed corridor build using the current NEA and sector-analysis source set. # Chilime Group Strategy Madhya Bhotekoshi is part of the Chilime Hydropower Company Limited (CHCL) expansion strategy. After Chilime's own 22.1 MW plant established a highly profitable operational track record, CHCL used its internal accruals and brand equity to spin off downstream subsidiaries — Rasuwagadhi (111 MW), Sanjen (42.5 MW), and Madhya Bhotekoshi (102 MW) — effectively bypassing the terminal BOOT-model cliff where assets must be handed over to the state. This holding company model is the mechanism through which Nepal's most successful hydro entity perpetuates itself. # Bhote Koshi Corridor Risk The Bhote Koshi valley is one of Nepal's most geologically active river corridors. Projects in this stretch — including the original Bhote Koshi project, Upper Bhotekoshi (45 MW, operating), Madhya Bhotekoshi, and Rasuwagadhi — face elevated construction risk from landslides, flash floods, and seismic activity. Madhya Bhotekoshi's construction timeline and cost profile must be understood within this risk context. # Significance At 102 MW, Madhya Bhotekoshi represents a significant block of capacity in the under-construction pipeline. Along with Rasuwagadhi downstream and Sanjen in the adjacent valley, it forms a ~256 MW cluster of Chilime-promoted projects that will shape water allocation and transmission planning in the Trishuli-Bhote Koshi system. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 102 MW | Status | Under construction | Registry licence | Generation | River | Bhote koshi (eastern koshi-basin) | District | Sindhupalchok | Province | Bagmati Pradesh | # See Also run-of-river-hydropower buildability chilime sector-financial-analysis-triple-authority-2026 # Limitations & Controversies The current page is strongest on corporate-strategy and corridor-risk context. It does not independently verify current construction progress, final cost, commissioning date, financing closure, or geological event probability beyond the existing source set. The Bhote Koshi valley's landslide, flash-flood, and seismic risks are documented at the corridor level but not quantified for this specific project site. # Sources sector-financial-analysis-triple-authority-2026

pages.title: Madhya Marsyangdi
headings: The Marsyangdi Cascade — 170 MW in One Valley
The Contrast That Matters — Design vs Actual
Renewal Cycle — A Younger Plant with a Different Problem
pages.excerpt: Madhya Marsyangdi (Middle Marsyangdi) is a 70 MW operating hydropower project on the Marsyangdi River — one of Nepal's established generation assets with a multi-decade operational track record.
pages.body_text: Madhya Marsyangdi Madhya Marsyangdi (Middle Marsyangdi) is a 70 MW operating hydropower project on the Marsyangdi River — one of Nepal's established generation assets with a multi-decade operational track record. # Summary Madhya Marsyangdi is a 70 MW peaking run-of-river hydropower project operating on the Marsyangdi River in Lamjung district, Gandaki Province. Commissioned in December 2008, it is the middle anchor of the ~170 MW Marsyangdi cascade and recorded 107.6% of design generation in FY 2081/82. The page tracks it as an operating-plant performance benchmark using the current NEA annual report source set. # Marsyangdi Cascade Madhya Marsyangdi sits in the middle of one of Nepal's most productive hydropower corridors. The Marsyangdi River, a tributary of the Trishuli/Narayani system in the Gandaki basin, hosts a cascade of projects: Upper Marsyangdi A (50 MW), Madhya Marsyangdi (70 MW), and Marsyangdi Besi (50 MW, under construction). This ~170 MW cumulative capacity makes the Marsyangdi cascade a significant block of the national generation portfolio. # Operating History As an operating plant, Madhya Marsyangdi provides a different lens from the pre-COD and under-construction projects that dominate the pipeline: actual generation data, real maintenance costs, and historical PLF performance under the standard PPA framework. Operating projects reveal whether the financial models in IPO prospectuses materialize in practice — and at what cost. # Transmission The Marsyangdi valley's generation feeds into the national grid via the Marsyangdi corridor infrastructure, connecting to the east-west backbone. The Upper Marsyangdi 220 kV line provides the key evacuation route for this cascade. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 70 MW | Status | Operating | Registry licence | Operation | River | Marsyangdi (gandaki-basin) | District | Lamjung | Province | Gandaki Pradesh | # Specifications (NEA FY 2081/82) Middle Marsyangdi (MMHPS) is a 70 MW peaking run-of-river plant in Lamjung District, Gandaki Province — the middle anchor of the 170 MW Marsyangdi cascade. Commissioned in December 2008, it diverts flow from the Marsyangdi River originating in glacier-fed Tilicho Lake and can reserve flow for up to five hours of peaking, even during low discharge. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Type | Peaking run-of-river (PROR) | Units | Francis | Commissioning | December 2008 | Peaking capacity | 5 hours | Design generation | 398 GWh/yr | FY 2081/82 generation | 427.9 GWh | FY 2081/82 vs design | 107.6% | Year-over-year change | −3% | Cumulative lifetime generation | 7,091.1 GWh | District | Lamjung, Gandaki Province | In FY 2081/82, MMHPS completed overhaul of Unit 2, restored desander basins in-house, rebuilt spillway chute no. 1 with M60 concrete and steel lining, and installed a digital governor panel, 110V battery bank, and RTU for real-time Load Dispatch Centre communication. # The Marsyangdi Cascade — 170 MW in One Valley MMHPS sits between Upper Marsyangdi A (50 MW, operating, upstream) and Marsyangdi Besi (50 MW, under construction, downstream) — a cumulative 170 MW in the Marsyangdi valley of the Gandaki basin. This is one of Nepal's most concentrated generation corridors. The Marsyangdi River, a glacier-fed tributary of the Narayani system, provides more reliable base flow than the monsoon-dominated rain-fed tributaries where most private IPPs are located. The cascade's cumulative water use is increasingly significant as Marsyangdi Besi approaches commissioning. Environmental flow requirements and sediment management decisions at Upper Marsyangdi A directly affect MMHPS and the downstream plant. The Marsyangdi corridor connects to the national grid via the Upper Marsyangdi 220 kV transmission line, feeding the east-west backbone. # The Contrast That Matters — Design vs Actual MMHPS's 107.6% of design generation (427.9 GWh against 398 GWh) is the highest performance ratio in the NEA large-plant fleet. Compare: Plant | MW | Design (GWh) | FY 2081/82 (GWh) | % of Design | ---|---|---|---|---| Middle Marsyangdi | 70 | 398 | 427.9 | 107.6% | Kali Gandaki A | 144 | 842 | 863.5 | 102.5% | Marsyangdi | 69 | 462.5 | 451.8 | 97.0% | Chameliya | 30 | 184.2 | 142.4 | 77.3% | Upper Trishuli 3A | 60 | 489.8 | 356.0 | 72.7% | The divergence at the bottom of the table is q-design-discharge in action: the plants that underperform by 20–30% are the ones whose design hydrology assumptions were too aggressive. MMHPS's opposite result suggests the Tilicho-fed Marsyangdi basin has more reliable baseflow than the monsoonal rain-fed catchments where design overestimation is endemic — or that the 2008-era design hydrological study was appropriately conservative. This is the structural pattern the chilime page documents at 22 MW: conservative Q-design (Q65+) in a snow/glacier-fed basin produces actual generation above contracted energy. MMHPS demonstrates the same mechanism at 70 MW — and at three times the scale. See q-design-discharge for the full generation performance comparison across the RoR fleet. # Renewal Cycle — A Younger Plant with a Different Problem At 16 years post-commissioning, MMHPS is entering the phase where routine overhauls begin to graduate toward major rehabilitation. The FY 2081/82 work scope — Unit 2 overhaul, desander basin restoration, spillway chute rebuild with M60 concrete and epoxy coating — is heavier maintenance than the plant would have required in its first decade. The digital governor panel and RTU installation signals a shift from mechanical to digital control, the modernization trajectory that aging plants like kali-gandaki-a are now facing at greater cost and outage risk. MMHPS's relatively young age means this transition can be done incrementally rather than as an emergency rehab — but it also means it is a test case for what that incremental path looks like. Every NEA plant eventually follows it. # Sources nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 # Limitations & Controversies The current page is strongest on NEA annual-report and cascade-level context. It does not independently verify long-term maintenance cost trends, remaining useful life estimates, environmental flow compliance, or sediment-management records beyond the existing source set. FY 2081/82 generation data is a single-year snapshot; multi-year performance trends would require additional verification. The renewal-cycle discussion is forward-looking and not yet grounded in completed rehabilitation data. # See also gandaki-basin — the Marsyangdi feeds the Narayani / Gandaki system q-design-discharge — why MMHPS's 107.6% is a structural signal chilime — the same pattern at smaller scale (conservative Q + glacier-fed) marsyangdi — downstream PROR plant (69 MW, commissioned 1989) run-of-river-hydropower seasonal-mismatch — even 107.6% doesn't fix the monsoon-drought cycle

That makes it a moderate-size but system-relevant option in a basin where storage can support both seasonal power and broader water-management questions. The page matters because the storage shortlist is not just a list of mega-projects. Madi shows the middle tier of storage: not nationally transformative on its own, but potentially useful in a portfolio that needs multiple dry-season contributors. # Status And Timing Madi is a planning candidate from the JICA/NEA storage material. The IPSDP milestone ladder groups Madi Storage HEP in the 2026-2030 window, but the current wiki evidence set does not confirm physical construction. Next signals to watch are project sponsorship, feasibility refresh, environmental and social work, and whether it competes with or complements other West Rapti storage options such as naumure-w-rapti. # Map Interpretation The marker is a river anchor suitable for map storytelling and basin comparison. pages.title: Mahakali Basin
pages.excerpt: The Mahakali river forms Nepal's far-western border with India. It is a transboundary basin with far smaller current development than the three major eastern systems. The basin's significance is primarily geopolitical — it is the site of the pancheshwar multipurpose project and t
pages.body_text: Mahakali Basin # Summary The Mahakali river forms Nepal's far-western border with India. It is a transboundary basin with far smaller current development than the three major eastern systems. The basin's significance is primarily geopolitical — it is the site of the pancheshwar multipurpose project and the subject of the 1996 Mahakali Treaty. # Key Facts Fact | Value | ------|-------| Average discharge | ~600 m³/s | Monsoon share | ~73% | Lakes in basin (Nepal side) | 16 | # Hydropower Significance The Mahakali Treaty (1996) entitles Nepal to 50% of pancheshwar's output (6,480 MW total, or ~3,240 MW for Nepal). After 28+ years, Nepal has received zero megawatts from this treaty. See hydro-geopolitics. The Mahakali already supports irrigation via the Mahakali irrigation system on the Indian side. # Limitations & Controversies Zero megawatts after 28+ years. The Mahakali Treaty (1996) entitles Nepal to 50% of pancheshwar's output (~3,240 MW). After nearly three decades, Nepal has received zero megawatts. This is one of the most instructive cases of treaty promise without implementation in South Asia. Data scarcity. Average discharge (~600 m³/s), monsoon share (~73%), and lake count (16) are the only basin-scale figures in public sources. No detailed hydropower potential study, no sediment load data, and no climate projection specific to the Mahakali appear in the cited WECS basin plan. Geopolitical concentration. The basin's significance is almost entirely tied to the Nepal-India bilateral relationship. Unlike the Koshi, Gandaki, or Karnali basins — which host multiple projects and diverse financing — the Mahakali has one project (Pancheshwar) and one treaty. The basin cannot be analyzed independently of bilateral politics. No current operating large hydropower. Unlike the other three major basins, the Mahakali has no operating plant above a few megawatts. The basin is entirely prospective, with no operational data to ground planning assumptions. # Strategic Notes The basin is less about sheer resource volume and more about the diplomatic relationship with India. The failure of Pancheshwar to materialize is one of the strongest examples of how hydro-geopolitics shapes — and stalls — Nepal's energy future. # Map Assets Nepal Tributary Explorer Nepal River Geopolitics Explorer data-map-inventory

pages.title: Marsyangdi
headings: Why Marsyangdi Matters — The Aging Fleet Benchmark
pages.excerpt: Figure 6.3-16 River Longitudinal Profile of the Marsyangdi River
pages.body_text: Marsyangdi Figure 6.3-16 River Longitudinal Profile of the Marsyangdi River Unit No.1 overhauling works Monthly seasonal variation of last three fiscal years Wet vs Dry Season Generation of last three fiscal years Comparison: % of designed vs % of Target (FY 2081/82) Marsyangdi - Kathmandu 220 kV Transmission Line Construction of Shade at Phulbari Ghat, River bank protection at Gaidakot, Nawalpur Radial Gates 2 and 3 # Summary 69 MW · operating · on the Marsyangdi · in Gorkha district. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 69 MW | Status | Operating | Registry licence | Operation | River | Marsyangdi (gandaki-basin) | District | Gorkha | Province | Gandaki Pradesh | # Sources nea-transmission-annual-book-2077 nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 jica-ipsdp-main-report-vol2 # Specifications (NEA FY 2081/82) Marsyangdi is a peaking run-of-river plant — 4 hours of daily peaking capacity from 69 MW of installed generation across three Francis units. Commissioned in 1989, it has now operated for 36 years and accumulated over 15,000 GWh of lifetime generation. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Type | Peaking run-of-river (PROR) | Units | 3 × Francis | Commissioning | 1989 | Design generation | 462.5 GWh/yr | FY 2081/82 generation | 451.8 GWh | FY 2081/82 vs design | 97% | FY 2081/82 vs target | 97% | Year-over-year change | +1.28% | Cumulative lifetime generation | 15,046.929 GWh | District | Tanahun (not Gorkha — see correction note) | [!warning] Registry data correction. The Ministry of Energy registry and the auto-generated spec table list the district as Gorkha. The NEA's own FY 2024/25 report places Marsyangdi in Tanahun district, Gandaki Province. The map data reflects the registry. The narrative here follows the NEA source. This fiscal year, Marsyangdi completed overhaul of Unit No. 2 and maintained key infrastructure including radial gates, desander basin floating boom, and gantry crane wire rope. Repairs were also performed on the hook block, shaft seal, and sliding ring of Unit No. 3. # Why Marsyangdi Matters — The Aging Fleet Benchmark Marsyangdi is one of only a handful of NEA operating plants that actually hits its design numbers. At 97% of design generation (451.8 GWh against 462.5 GWh), it dramatically outperforms the median private IPP — where, as documented in q-design-discharge, zero of 100+ projects in a recent Urja Khabar audit exceeded 80% of contracted energy. This makes Marsyangdi a critical reference point. If a 36-year-old NEA plant with 1980s turbine technology can achieve 97% of its design energy, the design-energy gap at newer private IPPs cannot be explained by hydrology alone. Something else — Q-design optimism, build-quality shortcuts, commissioning-phase derating, or the PPA structure itself — is driving the performance divergence. See q-design-discharge and claim-mw-not-equal-value. The seasonal generation charts visible in the NEA FY 2024/25 report images above confirm the pattern: even a plant that achieves 97% annually still undergoes the classic RoR seasonal collapse — monsoon surplus tapering to a fraction of nameplate in January–February. Marsyangdi cannot escape seasonal-mismatch, regardless of its design-performance discipline. # Rehabilitation on the Horizon At 36 years old, Marsyangdi is the second-oldest large NEA plant still in regular service (after Trishuli, commissioned 1967). The Unit 2 overhaul completed this fiscal year is routine — but the plant approaches an age where major rehabilitation becomes a binary question: invest in full electromechanical replacement or accept progressive derating. The parallel is kali-gandaki-a (144 MW, commissioned 2002), where NEA floated a rehabilitation tender in 2024 to replace all three turbine runners after 22 years. Marsyangdi, at nearly double that age on the turbines, faces a larger decision. Every rehab of a fleet anchor plant introduces outage risk during dry season — precisely when the storage-deficit exposure peaks. The overhaul data from FY 2081/82 is an early signal: the maintenance scope is expanding. Radial gates, desander basin components, gantry crane wire rope, shaft seals — these are not routine wear items. They are the visible surface of an aging electromechanical fleet that NEA's capital budget will eventually need to confront at scale. # Limitations & Controversies Aging fleet anchor. At 36 years, Marsyangdi is the second-oldest large NEA plant still in regular service. The Unit 2 overhaul completed in FY 2081/82 is routine, but the plant approaches an age where full electromechanical replacement becomes a binary decision. Every rehab introduces outage risk during dry season — precisely when storage-deficit exposure peaks. Registry data error. The Ministry of Energy registry lists the district as Gorkha; the NEA FY 2024/25 report places Marsyangdi in Tanahun. The map data currently reflects the registry; this remains a reconciliation item. This kind of slug-location mismatch is a recurring data-quality issue across NEA's multi-source reporting. Non-replicable performance context. Marsyangdi's 97% of design energy is exceptional against the private IPP baseline, but it was built as an NEA plant in the 1980s with conservative Q-design, pre-climate-shift hydrology, and sovereign financing. The conditions that produced this performance are not replicable for modern private IPPs operating under the current PPA regime. Cannot escape seasonal mismatch. Even at 97% annual performance, Marsyangdi undergoes the classic RoR seasonal collapse — monsoon surplus tapering to a fraction of nameplate in January–February. The plant is a benchmark for design discipline, not a solution to seasonal-mismatch. # See also kali-gandaki-a — the next aging fleet anchor, now entering rehab q-design-discharge — why Marsyangdi's 97% is striking against the IPP baseline seasonal-mismatch — the structural problem even a well-run RoR cannot solve claim-mw-not-equal-value — nameplate vs delivered energy gandaki-basin — basin context; the Marsyangdi cascade feeds the Narayani run-of-river-hydropower

pages.title: MCA Central 400 kV Corridor (Lapsiphedi–Ratmate–Hetauda–Damauli–Butwal)
pages.excerpt: The second 400 kV spine Nepal is building — the Millennium Challenge Account (MCA-Nepal) compact's headline infrastructure, running from Lapsiphedi (Kathmandu Valley ring) through Ratmate, Hetauda, Damauli and terminating at New Butwal, where it feeds the gorakhpur-butwal-interco
pages.body_text: MCA Central 400 kV Corridor # Summary The second 400 kV spine Nepal is building — the Millennium Challenge Account (MCA-Nepal) compact's headline infrastructure, running from Lapsiphedi (Kathmandu Valley ring) through Ratmate, Hetauda, Damauli and terminating at New Butwal, where it feeds the gorakhpur-butwal-interconnection. When complete, this corridor ends the single-point-of-failure problem on the eastern backbone. # Key Facts Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Voltage | 400 kV | Status | Under construction (partial energisation 2025) | Route-length basis | 308.65 route-km | Circuit-length basis | 617.3 circuit-km | Owner | nea (construction by MCA-Nepal contractors) | Terminal substations | Lapsiphedi · Ratmate · Hetauda · Damauli · New Butwal | Financing | US MCC grant (~US$500M corridor share) + Government of Nepal | Target full commissioning | 2026–2027 | Corridor ID | | # Map Interpretation The connected transmission layer now uses a source-aware MCA atlas trace rather than the older RPGCL overview fragments. It is modeled as five project segments: Lapsiphedi-Ratmate, Ratmate-New Hetauda, Ratmate-New Damauli, New Damauli-New Butwal, and New Butwal-India border. Public decision: default-visible, high confidence. Validation shows 5 atlas-derived features, no inferred connectors, no endpoint gaps, and a -1.32% delta against the 308.65 route-km compact basis. # Significance Second 400 kV spine. Parallels hetauda-dhalkebar-inaruwa-backbone via an entirely different geographic axis (Kathmandu → Western Terai), providing real N-1 redundancy for the first time. Gateway to the second cross-border link. Terminates at New Butwal, the Nepal end of gorakhpur-butwal-interconnection. Evacuates the western IPP cluster. Picks up output from the Marsyangdi and Kali Gandaki basins that has historically been trapped behind legacy 132 kV — partially solving claim-transmission-immediate-blocker for the west. Symbolic role. First large US-funded infrastructure grant in Nepal; its progress is read as a proxy for Nepal's willingness to diversify foreign partners beyond India and China. # Limitations & Controversies Right-of-way disputes. Sections through Nuwakot and Kavre saw protracted community opposition over tower siting and compensation. Partial commissioning ≠ full rating. Early 2025 energisation covers the Ratmate–Hetauda link only; the full end-to-end 400 kV transfer capability awaits terminal substation completion at Damauli and New Butwal. Dependent on cross-border terminal. Full value is unlocked only when gorakhpur-butwal-interconnection also commissions. Atlas trace, not tower survey. The public geometry is route-grade for map and topology use, with sheet-level provenance, but it should not be read as a cadastral tower alignment. # See also hetauda-dhalkebar-inaruwa-backbone — the existing backbone it parallels gorakhpur-butwal-interconnection — the border link it feeds dana-kushma-butwal-corridor — the 220 kV it relieves claim-transmission-immediate-blocker

pages.title: Middle Tamor
headings: The Stranded Asset — Transmission Before Generation
pages.excerpt: 73 MW · under construction · on the Tamor River · in Taplejung district. A Sanima Group private IPP stranded pending completion of evacuation infrastructure in Nepal's easternmost Koshi basin development corridor.
pages.body_text: Middle Tamor 73 MW · under construction · on the Tamor River · in Taplejung district. A Sanima Group private IPP stranded pending completion of evacuation infrastructure in Nepal's easternmost Koshi basin development corridor. # Summary Middle Tamor is a 73 MW run-of-river hydropower project under construction on the Tamor River in Taplejung district, Koshi basin. It is a Sanima Group private IPP stranded pending completion of the Dhunge-Sanghu substation and Basantapur–Dhungesanghu 220 kV evacuation line. The page tracks it as a stranded-generation case study using the NEA licence and Urja Khabar/MoEWRI source set. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 54 MW | Status | Under construction | Registry licence | Generation | River | Tamor (eastern koshi-basin) | District | Taplejung | Province | Province No 1 | # Sources nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 urja-khabar-generation-audit # Specifications (NEA Licence / MoEWRI data) Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Developer | Sanima Middle Tamor Hydropower Ltd (Sanima Group; formerly Tamor Sanima Energy Pvt. Ltd.) | Capacity | 73 MW (73,000 kW — confirmed from NEA generation licence table and Urja Khabar MoEWRI data) | Status | Under construction — stranded pending Dhunge-Sanghu Substation completion | River | Tamor River, Taplejung district, Koshi basin (eastern Nepal) | Generation licence | 2073.09.26 (approx December 2016) | Loan | NPR 7.3 billion (per NEA licence table) | Evacuation | Basantapur–Dhungesanghu 220 kV line (127 towers, first circuit strung by April 2024) | Substation | Dhungesanghu substation commissioned July 6, 2025 | [!warning] Registry capacity discrepancy. The Ministry of Energy registry and the auto-generated spec table list Middle Tamor at 54 MW. Both the NEA generation licence table (73,000 kW) and the Urja Khabar/MoEWRI data confirm that the licensed and built capacity is 73 MW. The 54 MW figure likely reflects earlier survey-stage estimates. The narrative follows the NEA licence and MoEWRI confirmed data. # The Stranded Asset — Transmission Before Generation Middle Tamor is explicitly named in the Urja Khabar/MoEWRI report as one of 18 Nepali hydropower projects whose financial viability has been crippled by state-side transmission failures. The wording is stark: "Stranded pending the completion of the Dhunge-Sanghu Substation." The Basantapur–Dhungesanghu 220 kV transmission line was built specifically to evacuate Middle Tamor's 73 MW. Its 127 towers were erected across eastern Nepal's difficult terrain, and the first circuit was strung by April 2024. The Dhungesanghu substation was finally commissioned on July 6, 2025. But the project had already been waiting for years — generation capacity approved, financed, and built before the evacuation infrastructure that would make it useful. This is the classic Nepal hydropower timing failure that the buildability and stranded-generation pages document: private developers mobilise capital and construction on schedule, only to discover that the public-sector transmission backbone — promised in the same licensing window — is years behind. The financiers who underwrote NPR 7.3 billion in project debt did not underwrite the Nepal Electricity Authority's substation construction programme. # The Tamor Basin — Eastern Frontier The Tamor River drains the eastern flank of the Koshi basin, rising near the Kanchenjunga massif and flowing south through Taplejung district before joining the Sun Koshi to form the Sapta Koshi. Unlike the crowded Tamakoshi, Khimti, and Likhu corridors to the west — where multiple IPPs compete for the same transmission capacity — the Tamor basin is relatively undeveloped. Middle Tamor is one of the first large projects in the basin. Its 73 MW places it at a scale comparable to likhu-2 (55 MW) and likhu-1 (77 MW), but without the benefit of shared corridor infrastructure or the clustering advantages that the MV Dugar Group exploited in the Likhu Cascade. The Tamor's isolation cuts both ways: fewer competing offtakers on the line, but no neighbouring plants to share the political and financial burden of pushing transmission through. # Sanima Group — Portfolio Developer Sanima Middle Tamor Hydropower Ltd (formerly Tamor Sanima Energy Pvt. Ltd.) is the project SPV, backed by the Sanima Group — one of Nepal's largest private hydropower developers. Sanima's growing portfolio includes sanima-mai (22 MW), which has published Q40 design discharge data used in the q-design-discharge analysis. The group's strategy mirrors the cluster-development approach seen elsewhere in Nepali private hydro: establish a track record with a smaller project (Sanima Mai), then scale to larger capacity in a new basin (Middle Tamor). The corporate continuity — same developer, same financing relationships, same regulatory experience — reduces execution risk. But it does not solve the transmission problem. Sanima can build a power station; it cannot build a substation on land it does not own, using a budget it does not control. # The Transmission Problem The Basantapur–Dhungesanghu 220 kV line that will evacuate Middle Tamor's generation is a single-circuit corridor through eastern Nepal's steepest topography. 127 towers crossing landslide-prone terrain create single-point failure risks that the Likhu Cascade's khimti-dhalkebar-corridor also faces — but with less redundancy and no neighbouring plants to share the outage costs. For the full structural analysis of how transmission planning failures create systemic IPP risk, see buildability. For the growing inventory of projects that commissioned into a grid that could not take their power, see stranded-generation. # Limitations & Controversies The current page is strongest on licence and stranded-generation context from NEA and MoEWRI disclosures. It does not independently verify current construction progress, final cost, commissioning date, financing closure, or environmental/social compliance status beyond the existing source set. The 54 MW vs 73 MW registry discrepancy is noted but not resolved. Hydrological and transmission risk is documented at the corridor level but not quantified for this specific project site. # See also sanima-mai — 22 MW Sanima Group operating asset with Q40 data q-design-discharge — design discharge methodology and Sanima Mai data buildability — transmission planning failure as structural IPP risk stranded-generation — the grid evacuation bottleneck problem koshi-basin — basin context and eastern Nepal corridor geography

The largest single Phase I IPP plant by MWp. # Specifications Item | Value | ---|---| Capacity | 10.0 MWp | Location | Dhanusha District, Madhesh Province | Owner / Developer | Eco Power Development Company Pvt. Ltd. | Zone (solar-resource-geography-nepal) | B2 — Eastern Terai / Madhesh | Interconnection | Dhanusha 33 kV | Commissioning | ~2021 | PPA tariff | Phase I round (~NPR 8/kWh blended) | Site elevation | ~80 m | Expected annual generation | ~16 GWh/yr | Status | Operating | # Why it matters Mithila Solar's siting is the clearest Phase I validation of the grid-adjacent Terai siting archetype later encoded in the nea-960mw-solar-tender: Mithila / Janakpur is the heart of Nepal's densest 132 kV grid cluster (hetauda-dhalkebar-inaruwa-backbone). pages.title: Mugu Karnali Storage HEP
pages.excerpt: At a proposed 1,902 MW, Mugu Karnali would be the single largest generation asset Nepal has ever planned — by itself larger than the country's entire current operating hydropower fleet. Still at pre-feasibility stage under state-owned Vidhyut Utpadan Company (VUCL), open to publi
pages.body_text: Mugu Karnali Storage HEP At a proposed 1,902 MW, Mugu Karnali would be the single largest generation asset Nepal has ever planned — by itself larger than the country's entire current operating hydropower fleet. Still at pre-feasibility stage under state-owned Vidhyut Utpadan Company (VUCL), open to public–private partnership bidding, and attracting expressions of interest from India's Adani Group and Bangladesh's Chowdhury Group. Its schedule (construction from ~2030, commissioning ~2034) and transmission dependencies place it on a longer horizon than any of the other top-10 anchor projects. # Summary Mugu Karnali Storage HEP is a proposed 1,902 MW storage/pumped-storage hydropower project in the Karnali basin, at pre-feasibility stage under state-owned VUCL with PPP bidding underway. At 1,902 MW and ~5,883 GWh design annual energy, it would be Nepal's largest single generation asset. The page tracks it as a top-capacity planning candidate using the VUCL feasibility and bid-record source set. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 1,902 MW | Status | Pre-feasibility; PPP bidding underway | River | Karnali (karnali-basin) | District | Mugu (registry primary); Bajura referenced in early materials | Province | Karnali Pradesh | ## Engineering At 1,902 MW with 10 Francis units and ~285 m gross head, Mugu Karnali would be Nepal's largest generation asset — by itself larger than the country's entire current operating fleet. The storage / pumped-storage design makes it a grid-scale balancing asset: it can time-shift energy across daily and seasonal scales, the structural answer to seasonal-mismatch that Nepal has not yet built. All parameters are screening-level estimates subject to bankable feasibility revision. The pumped-storage component — the ability to pump water back into the reservoir during low-demand periods and release it during peaks — is what separates Mugu Karnali from a conventional storage dam. In a system with growing variable solar generation (see solar-hydro-complementarity), pumped storage converts daytime solar surplus into evening peak power. This is a value stream that did not exist when Kulekhani was designed in the 1970s. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Units | 10 × Francis | Gross head | ~285 m | Type | Storage / Pumped-storage | ## Output Design annual energy of ~5,883 GWh — the largest single-project energy contribution in Nepal's planning universe. For context: this is roughly 2.5x the annual generation of upper-tamakoshi (2,281 GWh) and approximately equal to Nepal's total current annual electricity consumption. The storage design means this energy can be concentrated in dry-season months and peak hours rather than spilling during monsoon when it is least valuable. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Annual design energy | 5,883 GWh | ## Governance Vidhyut Utpadan Company Limited (VUCL), a state-owned developer created to develop Karnali-basin projects, is seeking a 51% PPP partnership. The competitive dynamic is notable: Adani Group (India): Expressed interest — consistent with the India-developer pattern that runs through arun-3 (SJVN), upper-karnali (GMR), and west-seti (NHPC). Adani's interest signals that Indian conglomerates see Nepal's western Karnali as the next frontier after the eastern Koshi basin is fully allocated. Chowdhury Group (Bangladesh): Formal bid — the first time a Bangladeshi private group has bid for a large Nepali hydropower project. This is a direct consequence of Bangladesh's growing energy import strategy (see bangladesh-trade-route) and represents a structural expansion of the regional developer pool beyond the India-dominated pattern. The 51% PPP structure means whichever partner wins will have operational control of the project, including reservoir dispatch rules. This is geopolitically sensitive: control over 5,883 GWh of Karnali-basin dispatch affects downstream India's flood management and irrigation timing. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Developer | Vidhyut Utpadan Company Limited (VUCL) | Concession type | PPP (51% partnership sought) | Bidders | Adani Group (India), Chowdhury Group (Bangladesh) | ## Financial No public cost estimate exists at the current pre-feasibility stage. As a reference: dudhkoshi-storage (635 MW) has an estimated cost of ~USD 2.2 billion (~USD 3.5 million/MW). At comparable storage-project costs, Mugu Karnali at 1,902 MW could require USD 5–7 billion — roughly 2–3x the cost of budhigandaki (1,200 MW, ~USD 2.77 billion). The financing structure (sovereign, PPP, or mixed) will be determined by the partnership outcome. ## Schedule Targeted for construction from ~2030 with COD ~2034, Mugu Karnali sits outside the 5-year planning window most NEA decisions use. Every dry season until then must be managed without it. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Construction start | 2030 (target) | Commercial operation | 2034 (target) | # Top-Capacity Comparison Mugu Karnali belongs to a small class of projects that individually exceed Nepal's entire current operating fleet: Project | MW | Type | Status | Developer | ---------|-----|------|--------|-----------| Mugu Karnali | 1,902 | Storage / Pumped | Pre-feasibility | VUCL (PPP bid) | budhigandaki | 1,200 | Storage | Pre-construction | Budhigandaki Co. Ltd. | arun-3 | 900 | Peaking RoR | 74.6% complete | SJVN (India) | upper-karnali | 900 | RoR | Stalled (18 yrs) | GMR (India) | karnali-chisapani | 10,800 | Storage | Conceptual | None | pancheshwar | 6,480 | Storage | Stalled (30 yrs) | Bilateral (Nepal/India) | Mugu Karnali is distinguished from budhigandaki and the export projects by its pumped-storage capability — it is the only project in this class designed from the start as a grid-balancing asset, not just a generation source. # Significance Mugu Karnali changes the arithmetic of Nepal's planning rather than the arithmetic of the current grid. At 1,902 MW and ~5,883 GWh of design annual energy, it is the one pipeline project whose success or failure genuinely rewrites the national storage-deficit and firm-power picture — more than dudhkoshi-storage, budhigandaki or any combination of smaller reservoirs in the current pipeline. It is also the project that most clearly surfaces Nepal's post-India export opening. Adani's EOI reflects the India-developer pattern; Chowdhury Group's formal bid represents Bangladeshi developer interest — the first time a Bangladeshi private group has bid for a project of this scale in Nepal. Whichever way the 51% PPP lands, Mugu Karnali is where the question "who builds Nepal's biggest reservoirs?" stops being rhetorical. Because it is storage / pumped-storage, Mugu Karnali is also the project that would finally give Nepal the grid-scale balancing asset the run-of-river fleet needs. RoR over-generation in the monsoon and RoR under-generation in the dry season are the two faces of seasonal-mismatch; a 1,900 MW asset that can time-shift energy across days and partly across seasons is the structural answer the country has not yet built. The pumped-storage component adds a value dimension that pure storage lacks: the ability to absorb surplus generation (from solar during the day, from RoR during monsoon nights) and release it during peaks. In a future system with significant solar-hydro-complementarity, pumped storage is the enabling technology that makes solar viable at scale without destabilizing the grid. # Limitations & Controversies Horizon risk. Construction from ~2030 and COD ~2034 places Mugu Karnali outside the 5-year energy planning window most of NEA's current decisions use. Every dry season between now and 2034 has to be managed without it — by imports, by tanahu-hydropower and kulekhani-cascade augmentation, by demand response, or by accepting unserved energy. Transmission gap. A 1,902 MW generator at the head of the Karnali implies a new 400 kV (or higher) evacuation corridor through some of Nepal's most rugged terrain. That corridor is not in the current NEA transmission masterplan at scale. Without it, Mugu Karnali is stranded-generation by construction. The closest existing 400 kV infrastructure is the proposed Karnali corridor, which was sized for upper-karnali (900 MW) — Mugu Karnali would require an entirely new transmission spine from Mugu through the Karnali valley to the central grid. Feasibility depth. The project is at survey / pre-feasibility stage with a two-year DoED deadline (extensible to five). None of the capacity, head or energy figures above has yet been locked down by a bankable feasibility study. Expect all three to move — likely downward, as feasibility studies typically reduce screening-level estimates. Geopolitical visibility. Any bidder decision that confers control of 1,900 MW of upstream Karnali generation — and the reservoir operation rules that accompany it — will be read in Delhi and Dhaka. The downstream implications for Indian flood management and irrigation are material and not yet publicly modelled. An Adani win would be interpreted as India extending its downstream hydro-influence upstream; a Chowdhury win would signal a tri-nation energy architecture (Nepal–India–Bangladesh) that India's traditional bilateral framework does not easily accommodate. Competing Karnali priorities. The Karnali basin has multiple large projects competing for limited development and transmission bandwidth: upper-karnali (900 MW, stalled), phukot-karnali (426 MW, survey), nalsyau-gad (410 MW, survey), karnali-chisapani (10,800 MW, conceptual). Mugu Karnali must compete for developer attention, financing, and — critically — transmission capacity with projects at varying stages of readiness. # See also karnali-basin storage-deficit upper-karnali west-seti arun-3 hydro-geopolitics seasonal-mismatch stranded-generation solar-hydro-complementarity bangladesh-trade-route data-map-inventory # Sources mugu-karnali-feasibility-2025

headings: Why the zone is strategically interesting
1. It is the only Nepal zone where *winter* is the best solar month.
2. Off-grid solar + BESS at these sites has extraordinary kWh-value.

pages.body_text: Mustang / Trans-Himalayan High-Altitude Solar Zone Not a project, an entity classification of the geographic zone with Nepal's best solar resource. Covers the trans-Himalayan rain-shadow valleys of Mustang, Dolpa, upper Manang, upper Humla, Mugu (upper), and parts of Jumla — a band of high-elevation (2,500–4,500 m) valleys shielded from the monsoon by the Greater Himalaya. This zone has world-class GHI and DNI (5.8–6.5 kWh/m²/day, 6.0–6.8 kWh/m²/day respectively) with ~260–290 clear-sky days per year. It is also, for the foreseeable future, the hardest solar zone in Nepal to monetise because of grid distance, low local demand, and terrain-induced transmission costs. # Resource characteristics Parameter | Value | ---|---| Mean GHI | 5.8–6.5 kWh/m²/day | Mean DNI | 6.0–6.8 kWh/m²/day | Clear-sky days / year | 260–290 (among highest in Nepal) | Monsoon GHI penalty | 5–15% (rain-shadow intact) | Winter GHI (Dec–Feb) | 5.2–5.8 kWh/m²/day — highest in Nepal | Elevation | 2,500–4,500 m | Ambient temperature | Cool; module efficiency ~3–5% better than Terai | Zone (solar-resource-geography-nepal) | A | Comparative reference | Ladakh, Atacama, Tibetan Plateau | # Representative districts and sites District | Representative site | Elevation | GHI | Notes | ---|---|---:|---:|---| Mustang | Jomsom | 2,730 | ~6.0 | ESMAP pyranometer station | Mustang | Upper Mustang (Lo Manthang) | 3,850 | ~6.3 | Trekking-dependent demand | Dolpa | Dunai, Dho Tarap | 2,090–4,050 | 5.9–6.4 | Remote, low demand | Upper Manang | Manang village | 3,540 | ~6.1 | Seasonal demand | Upper Humla | Simikot area | 2,960 | ~6.0 | Grid-absent | Mugu (upper) | Gamgadhi area | 2,080–3,500 | 5.8–6.2 | Grid-absent | # Why the zone is strategically interesting Three genuine reasons, despite the grid-distance challenge: ## 1. It is the only Nepal zone where winter is the best solar month. Winter clear-sky days are more numerous than summer clear-sky days here (summer can have valley-mist + high-altitude storms; winter is cloudless). The complementarity argument in solar-hydro-complementarity is strongest here: Zone A in winter generates ~110% of its April peak, exactly when Nepal's hydro fleet is at its weakest. ## 2. Off-grid solar + BESS at these sites has extraordinary kWh-value. Incumbent energy source is mostly: (a) no electricity at all, (b) diesel generation at NPR 60–90/kWh, (c) firewood for heating and cooking. Displacing (b) makes Zone A solar the highest-value per-kWh energy investment in Nepal — 10–15× the utility-tariff-equivalent value. ## 3. It is the long-dated solar export corridor. The ratmate-rasuwagadhi-kerung-400kv line, if completed, opens a trans-Himalayan interconnection to Tibet. Zone A solar, transmitted northward, becomes relevant to China's western-grid imports. This is a 15–20 year story, not a near-term strategy, but Nepal's long-dated Zone A solar optionality is real and should be preserved through conservation-compatible land zoning. # Near-term constraints Grid distance: Nearest 132 kV substation is typically 100–200 km away. Terrain multiplies per-km transmission cost 3–5×. Local demand: Mustang's total population ~14,000; Dolpa's ~37,000. Grid-scale off-take is absent. Land tenure: Much of upper Mustang and Dolpa is inside Annapurna Conservation Area and Shey Phoksundo National Park. Utility-scale ground-mount is largely excluded. Access: Road connectivity seasonal; airlift-only sites in winter. Construction: Cold-climate installation window is April–October only. # What Zone A is for, realistically In order of near-term deployability: 1. Off-grid + BESS for remote institutional and community sites — the karnali-solar-energy-project template, extended to Mustang and Dolpa. 2. Diesel-displacement at trekking lodges and research stations — 5–50 kWp each, high unit economics. 3. Pilot research sites for high-altitude PV degradation / snow-load / bifacial performance — valuable to global solar R&D, underrated in Nepal. 4. Long-dated grid export optionality via trans-Himalayan interconnection. Utility-scale GW-class solar in Mustang is not a 2030 project. It is a 2040 project and the value is in preserving the land zoning and interconnection optionality now. # Related solar-resource-geography-nepal — zone framework data-nepal-solar-resource-zones — numerical tables karnali-solar-energy-project — template programme rooftop-minigrid-offgrid — track this zone lives in ratmate-rasuwagadhi-kerung-400kv — long-dated interconnection wb-esmap-solar-resource-assessment — the measurement source global-solar-atlas-nepal — the satellite cross-reference

pages.excerpt: Nalsyau Gad is a 410 MW storage candidate in the Karnali basin and the best dry-energy performer in the JICA promising-storage set used by this wiki. It is pinned in both data-layer-storage-shortlist and data-layer-priority-watchlist because it contributes the kind of dry-season
pages.body_text: Nalsyau Gad Nalsyau Gad is a 410 MW storage candidate in the Karnali basin and the best dry-energy performer in the JICA promising-storage set used by this wiki. It is pinned in both data-layer-storage-shortlist and data-layer-priority-watchlist because it contributes the kind of dry-season energy Nepal's run-of-river-heavy system is missing. # Summary Nalsyau Gad is a 410 MW JICA promising-storage candidate in the Karnali basin and the best dry-energy performer in the JICA shortlist used by this wiki, with 581.8 GWh dry-season energy (41.4% dry share). It is pinned in both the storage shortlist and priority watchlist. The page tracks it as a dry-season portfolio option using the JICA/NEA source set. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 410 MW | Status | Survey / study | Category | jica promising storage | Basin | Karnali (karnali-basin) | Annual energy | 1406.1 GWh | Dry-season energy | 581.8 GWh | Dry share | 41.4% | Total storage | 419.6 MCM | Effective storage | 296.3 MCM | ## Storage Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Total storage | 419.6 MCM | Effective storage | 296.3 MCM | ## Output Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Annual design energy | 1406.1 GWh | Dry-season energy | 581.8 GWh | Dry-season share | 41.4 % | Type | Storage | # Sources jica-ipsdp-main-report-vol2 moewri-ipsdp-exec-summary-2025 # Why It Matters Nalsyau Gad's value is not just its 410 MW nameplate. The JICA/NEA storage-screening figures give it 581.8 GWh of dry-season energy, equal to 41.4% of annual energy. That is the strongest dry-energy output in the promising-storage shortlist and one of the few project records that directly addresses the storage-deficit rather than only adding wet-season energy. ## Shortlist Context: How Nalsyau Gad Compares Among the JICA promising-storage candidates in the wiki, Nalsyau Gad occupies a unique position — highest dry-energy share by a significant margin: Project | MW | Annual (GWh) | Dry (GWh) | Dry Share | Effective Storage (MCM) | ---------|-----|-------------|-----------|-----------|--------------------------| Nalsyau Gad | 410 | 1,406.1 | 581.8 | 41.4% | 296.3 | Kokhajor-1 | 112 | 278.9 | 94.1 | 33.7% | 166.1 | Madi | 200 | 621.1 | 170.7 | 27.5% | 235.1 | Naumure (W. Rapti) | 245 | 1,157.5 | 309.9 | 26.8% | 580.0 | Lower Badigad | 380 | 1,366.0 | 354.7 | 26.0% | 505.5 | Chera-1 | 149 | 563.2 | 120.6 | 21.4% | 141.1 | Andhi Khola | 180 | 648.7 | 137.1 | 21.1% | 238.7 | Lower Jhimruk | 143 | 454.7 | 94.4 | 20.8% | 211.6 | Sun Koshi No.3 | 536 | 1,883.6 | 335.9 | 17.8% | 555.0 | What makes the 41.4% figure significant is that it approaches the dry-share range of seasonal-storage projects with much larger reservoirs. kulekhani-cascade achieves ~50% dry share with only 106 MW. budhigandaki projects 42% at 1,200 MW with 3,300 MCM of total storage. Nalsyau Gad is delivering comparable dry-energy concentration with less than one-tenth the reservoir volume of Budhigandaki and at a capacity point that is commercially viable for domestic financing. This is why it appears in the priority watchlist despite being survey-stage. A project can be strategically important before it is construction-ready if it changes the dry-season balance, especially in a system where kulekhani-cascade is still the only operating seasonal-storage anchor and tanahu-hydropower is the only large storage project in active construction. ## Reservoir Economics Nalsyau Gad's 296.3 MCM effective storage on 410 MW yields a storage-to-capacity ratio of 0.72 MCM/MW — lower than Naumure (2.37 MCM/MW) or Sun Koshi No.3 (1.04 MCM/MW), but the project achieves its high dry share through a different mechanism: favourable basin hydrology in the upper Karnali catchment rather than sheer reservoir volume. The Karnali basin receives reliable monsoon precipitation and has a less flashy dry-season recession than eastern basins like the Koshi, meaning a moderate storage volume can achieve proportionally more dry-season firming. This hydrological advantage is partly why the Karnali basin dominates the JICA shortlist: 6 of the 9 candidates (Nalsyau Gad, Lower Badigad, Naumure, Madi, Andhi Khola, Chera-1) are Karnali-basin projects. The basin's flow regime is intrinsically more storage-friendly. # Status And Timing Nalsyau Gad should be read as a planning / promising-storage candidate, not a confirmed near-term build. The IPSDP milestone ladder groups Nalsyau Gad STO in the 2031-2035 project window. That is a planning sequence, not a construction contract. Near-term milestones that would need to occur: Feasibility study update — the JICA IPSDP provides screening-level data; a bankable feasibility study is the next technical gate Developer assignment — currently no developer is designated (unlike Dudhkoshi/NEA or Tanahu/NEA). VUCL (Vidhyut Utpadan Company Limited) is the most likely candidate given its mandate for Karnali-basin storage (mugu-karnali-storage, phukot-karnali) Environmental and social screening — the Nalsyau Gad catchment requires baseline data on resettlement footprint, downstream water-use impacts, and biodiversity Financing structure — whether this follows the NEA/AIIB sovereign model (Dudhkoshi), the VUCL/PPP model (Mugu Karnali), or a new structure Transmission evacuation — routing from the upper Karnali catchment into the western hill grid and ultimately to the 400 kV backbone. See nepal-transmission-landscape-2025 # Transmission & Grid Integration Nalsyau Gad's location in the upper Karnali catchment presents a transmission challenge. The western Karnali region has limited 220 kV connectivity; the nearest 400 kV infrastructure is the proposed Karnali corridor. A 410 MW storage plant in this location would require: A dedicated 220 kV transmission line from the powerhouse to the nearest substation Integration with the planned Karnali basin transmission backbone (linked to upper-karnali and mugu-karnali-storage evacuation plans) Possibly a collector substation serving multiple Karnali storage projects (Nalsyau Gad, Lower Badigad, and Madi are all in the same general catchment) The transmission constraint is not a deal-breaker — 410 MW is within the range of standard 220 kV double-circuit capacity — but it adds a material cost component that the JICA screening-level cost estimates may not fully capture. Transmission costs for western hill storage are consistently higher per km than eastern corridor equivalents. # Geological & Site Character The Nalsyau Gad site is in the upper reaches of the Nalsyau Gad river — a Karnali tributary draining the southern flank of the Saipal Himal range in far-western Nepal. The JICA screening identifies the site as having suitable dam-axis topography for a storage reservoir with ~420 MCM total capacity, suggesting a relatively wide valley section upstream of a constriction — the classic storage-dam site geometry. Key geological considerations include: Himalayan foothill geology — sedimentary and metamorphic rock formations typical of the Lesser Himalayan zone, with potential for weak interbedded shales Seismic zone 4+ — within the active Himalayan deformation front Sediment load — the Nalsyau Gad drains steep terrain; sediment management in the reservoir design will be critical for maintaining active storage volume over the project life. See sediment-as-design-constraint GLOF exposure — lower than the Dudh Koshi or Arun basins, but the upper Karnali has glacially-fed tributaries that require assessment # Limitations & Controversies Survey-stage data only. The JICA IPSDP figures are screening-level, not bankable. A full feasibility study could shift capacity, energy, or storage numbers materially. No developer assigned. Unlike Dudhkoshi (NEA), Tanahu (NEA), or Mugu Karnali (VUCL), Nalsyau Gad has no institutional sponsor moving it forward. Transmission cost uncertainty. The western hill grid is less developed than the eastern and central corridors. Evacuation from a remote Karnali tributary adds cost. Competing Karnali priorities. The Karnali basin has multiple storage candidates vying for limited development bandwidth: Mugu Karnali (1,902 MW, pre-construction), Phukot Karnali (426 MW, survey), Upper Karnali (900 MW, stalled), Karnali Chisapani (10,800 MW, conceptual). Nalsyau Gad must compete for developer attention, financing, and transmission capacity with larger projects. Downstream water-use impacts. The Nalsyau Gad feeds the Karnali main stem; flow alteration could affect downstream ecosystems and, potentially, cross-border flows into India's Ghaghara system. See hydro-geopolitics. # Map Interpretation The map marker is a river-aligned project reference derived from the registry/project point. It is suitable for basin-level and corridor-level comparison, but it should not be treated as a final dam-axis coordinate. # Registry note JICA/NEA storage master plan volume 2 # See also karnali-basin storage-deficit firm-power data-ipsdp-milestone-ladder-2022-2040 data-layer-storage-shortlist data-layer-priority-watchlist mugu-karnali-storage — the largest Karnali storage project sediment-as-design-constraint nepal-transmission-landscape-2025 data-map-inventory

pages.title: Naumure (W. Rapti)
pages.excerpt: Naumure is a 245 MW JICA promising-storage candidate in the West Rapti basin. It is pinned in data-layer-storage-shortlist because its effective storage is unusually large for its installed capacity, giving it strong seasonal-regulation value in a water-deficit medium basin.
pages.body_text: Naumure (W. Rapti) Naumure is a 245 MW JICA promising-storage candidate in the West Rapti basin. It is pinned in data-layer-storage-shortlist because its effective storage is unusually large for its installed capacity, giving it strong seasonal-regulation value in a water-deficit medium basin. # Summary Naumure is a 245 MW JICA promising-storage candidate in the West Rapti basin (Karnali basin). It is pinned in the storage shortlist for its unusually large effective storage (580 MCM) relative to installed capacity, giving it strong seasonal-regulation value in a water-deficit medium basin. The page tracks it as a planning-layer storage comparator using the JICA/NEA source set. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 245 MW | Status | Survey / study | Category | jica promising storage | Basin | West Rapti (karnali-basin) | Annual energy | 1157.5 GWh | Dry-season energy | 309.9 GWh | Dry share | 26.8% | Total storage | 1021.0 MCM | Effective storage | 580.0 MCM | ## Storage Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Total storage | 1021.0 MCM | Effective storage | 580.0 MCM | ## Output Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Annual design energy | 1157.5 GWh | Dry-season energy | 309.9 GWh | Dry-season share | 26.8 % | Type | Storage | # Sources jica-ipsdp-main-report-vol2 moewri-ipsdp-exec-summary-2025 # Why It Matters Naumure is not the largest storage candidate by MW, but it is one of the most interesting by reservoir function: 1,021 MCM total storage, 580 MCM effective storage, and 309.9 GWh of dry-season energy. That combination makes it important to the wiki's argument that Nepal's deficit is about timing and controlled water, not only installed capacity. The project also matters because the West Rapti is not usually the headline basin in Nepal hydropower discussions. Including Naumure keeps the storage conversation from collapsing into only Karnali, Koshi, and Gandaki mega-projects. # Status And Timing Naumure should be read as a planning candidate. The IPSDP milestone ladder groups Naumure STO in the 2036-2040 window. There is no confirmed construction start in the current wiki evidence set. The key open questions are scheme selection, interaction with other West Rapti candidates, environmental and downstream water-use implications, financing, and whether the project becomes a power-only scheme or a broader multipurpose water-storage project. # Map Interpretation The map marker uses a named West Rapti / Rapti River anchor near Dang. It is a basin-level reference for map reading, not a final project-coordinate claim. # Registry note JICA/NEA storage master plan volume 2 # Limitations & Controversies The current page is strongest on master-plan and shortlist context. It does not independently verify feasibility-study details, environmental and social assessment, financing plan, grid-connection commitment, or construction timeline beyond the existing source set. The IPSDP milestone window (2036–2040) is a planning horizon, not a confirmed construction-start date. The layout conflict with Lower Jhimruk in the current design set means the project should not be counted naively alongside it. Map markers are basin-level references, not final site coordinates. # See also karnali-basin storage-deficit firm-power data-ipsdp-milestone-ladder-2022-2040 data-layer-storage-shortlist

A planned 132/33 kV substation project intended to improve supply reliability in Nawalpur and connect back into the Haripur 33/11 kV node through new 33 kV sub-transmission links. [!cite] nea-transmission-annual-book-2077 Book page 54 describes the Nawalpur substation as a 132/33 kV, 63 MVA node with additional 33 kV double-circuit line works to feed the local load area. # Why It Matters This is the kind of mid-voltage reinforcement asset that sits between the headline 220/400 kV corridors and the distribution-level service outcome. It adds detail to the broader story of nea trying to convert bulk power growth into local reliability improvements. # Limitations & Controversies The page is based on the FY 2019/20 NEA annual-book description and does not establish the current construction status, final equipment configuration, commissioning date, or measured reliability effect after completion. # See also nea nepal-transmission-landscape-2025 data-domestic-demand

pages.title: NEA 960 MW National Solar Tender
headings: Why this tender matters (beyond the MW)
1. It establishes the price floor for Nepal solar.
4. It is the test case for [[agrivoltaics-and-land]].
pages.excerpt: The single largest solar procurement event in Nepal's history. A national-scale competitive-bid tender launched 2024 for 960 MWp of utility-scale grid-tied solar PV across Nepal, awarded to 64 project selections from multiple IPPs. PPA signing and financial closure staged over FY
pages.body_text: NEA 960 MW National Solar Tender The single largest solar procurement event in Nepal's history. A national-scale competitive-bid tender launched 2024 for 960 MWp of utility-scale grid-tied solar PV across Nepal, awarded to 64 project selections from multiple IPPs. PPA signing and financial closure staged over FY 2025/26 and FY 2026/27; if ~70% of awards reach COD, Nepal's operating utility solar expands ~5× over the current fleet by FY 2028/29. The tender that represents the institutional bet that Nepal's solar scaling can be delivered through competitive IPP PPAs — not donor-funded NEA self-build, not off-grid AEPC programmes. # Key Facts Item | Value | ---|---| Total capacity tendered | 960 MWp | Number of projects selected | 63 | Typical project size | 5–25 MWp | Geographic distribution | Terai-dominant (Madhesh + Lumbini + Sudurpaschim + Koshi provinces) | Procurement model | Tariff-based competitive bidding | Tariff range (awarded) | NPR 4.99–5.55/kWh (gazette) ≈ $0.038–$0.042 | PPA tenor | 25 years, standard NEA PPA structure | Grid integration study | Cumulative Grid Impact Study completed FY 2024/25 under wb-grid-solar-ee-project TA line | Expected PPA closures | FY 2025/26–2026/27 | Expected first CODs | FY 2026/27 | Expected full portfolio COD | FY 2028/29 (if ~70% conversion rate) | # Tender structure by province (approximate) Province | MW in tender (approx.) | Notes | ---|---:|---| Madhesh (Bara, Parsa, Rautahat, Sarlahi, Dhanusha) | ~350–400 | Densest Terai grid; most bids received | Lumbini (Nawalparasi, Rupandehi, Kapilvastu, Banke) | ~200–250 | Hetauda-Bharatpur-Bardaghat corridor access | Sudurpaschim (Kailali, Kanchanpur) | ~80–120 | Far-west Terai | Koshi (Jhapa, Morang, Sunsari, Saptari) | ~150–200 | Eastern backbone | Bagmati (Makwanpur, Chitwan) | ~30–60 | Central, smaller allocations | Gandaki + Karnali (limited) | ~20–40 | Hydro co-location and resource-zone pockets | Total | ~960 | | The geographic weighting toward Terai provinces reflects the solar-resource-geography-nepal grid-adjacency priority — most awards sit within 10 km of existing 132 or 220 kV substations on the hetauda-dhalkebar-inaruwa-backbone and dana-kushma-butwal-corridor. # Why this tender matters (beyond the MW) Four reasons: ## 1. It establishes the price floor for Nepal solar. The awarded tariff range (4.99–5.55 NPR/kWh) is the first portfolio-scale solar price discovery in Nepal. Earlier rounds (Phase I at 8.40, Phase III at 6.40) were single-digit-count project awards; 960 MW with 64 project selections is the first price point that reflects actual competitive equilibrium. Future project evaluations should benchmark against this tariff, not against 2017 numbers. ## 2. It validates the market. Dozens of bidders winning awards implies a functional pipeline of developers, advisors, local EPC firms, and debt financiers. The Nepal solar market was single-digit-developer-deep before this tender; it is now broad enough to support multiple simultaneous project clusters. This matters more than the physical MW — a market of depth 1 cannot scale; a market with dozens of active sponsors can. ## 3. It stress-tests the institutional fit. The tender has four binding constraints: land acquisition (Terai agricultural politics), grid integration (penetration levels, forecast management), financial close (local-currency long-tenor debt), PPA discipline (NEA single-buyer liability). If the tender's 70%+ of awards reach COD on the FY 2026–28 schedule, the model works; if conversion falls below 50%, each of these four binding constraints becomes a programme-level fix. ## 4. It is the test case for agrivoltaics-and-land. The first awarded projects will surface which land-acquisition model works at scale. If pure-purchase / fee-simple conversion dominates and succeeds, agrivoltaics is merely an add-on. If land-acquisition delays kill > 30% of awards, agrivoltaic lease templates become a programme-level requirement for the next tender round. # Tariff context The tender tariff sits at the crossover point between solar and hydro (solar-lcoe-crossover): Benchmark | Price (NPR/kWh) | ---|---:| 960 MW tender awarded (weighted average) | ~5.43 | NEA small RoR hydro PPA (blended) | 6.20 | NEA PRoR hydro PPA (blended) | 6.80 | NEA time-weighted-value of solar | ~4.80 | NEA time-weighted-value of small RoR | ~7.00 | Each MW in this tender is already cheaper than equivalent small RoR hydro on a blended basis and substantially cheaper on a time-weighted basis. This is the tariff point that claim-solar-cheaper-than-small-hydro stands on. # Implementation risks and watch items Risk | Mitigation | Status | ---|---|---| Land-acquisition delays on fee-simple conversion | Lease templates, agrivoltaic structures | Not yet in tender docs | Grid-integration penetration issues | Completed Grid Impact Study + future BESS requirements | First pass complete | Local-currency long-tenor debt availability | Nepal Rastra Bank policy; donor blending | Partial; FX risk persists | PPA settlement delays from NEA | Escrow accounts; performance guarantees | Standard PPA mechanisms | Weather / monsoon COD delays | Schedule discipline, grid-extension coordination | Developer-by-developer | Tariff-crash political backlash | Transparent bidding + price disclosure | Tender ran transparently | # Related nea-solar — programme parent nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 — primary source solar-lcoe-crossover — the price story this tender anchors data-solar-fleet-inventory — the fleet this tender expands data-solar-hydro-lcoe — the numerical crossover agrivoltaics-and-land — the next-round institutional enhancement hybrid-siting-logic — the siting logic this tender operationalises claim-solar-cheaper-than-small-hydro, claim-solar-terai-only-short-cycle-build — the tracked claims this tender evidences

pages.title: NEA Solar Programme
headings: Major utility plants under the programme
1. Land acquisition is the new bottleneck
pages.excerpt: The utility-scale grid-tied solar programme operated by Nepal Electricity Authority. Sits inside NEA as a distinct programme line that has grown from a single 25 MWp NEA-EPC plant (Bidur/Trishuli, 2022) to a ~1.1 GWp pipeline as of FY 2024/25.
pages.body_text: NEA Solar Programme The utility-scale grid-tied solar programme operated by Nepal Electricity Authority. Sits inside NEA as a distinct programme line that has grown from a single 25 MWp NEA-EPC plant (Bidur/Trishuli, 2022) to a ~1.1 GWp pipeline as of FY 2024/25. # Programme evolution Phase | Years | Character | Key output | ---|---|---|---:| Pre-programme | 2010–2015 | Isolated small pilots | <1 MWp demonstration sites | Phase I — first IPP auctions | 2016–2018 | 5-developer competitive bid | 24 MWp awarded, 3 plants commissioned 2019–20 | Phase II — NEA self-build | 2019–2022 | WB Grid Solar & EE Project | 25 MWp Bidur/Trishuli commissioned 2022 | Phase III — IPP rounds | 2023–2024 | Competitive-bid IPP PPAs | 170 MWp PPAs signed (8 plants) | Phase IV — the 960 MW tender | 2024–2025 | National-scale IPP portfolio | 960 MWp awarded (64 project selections) (nea-960mw-solar-tender) | Phase V (emerging) | 2025– | Hybrid / floating / grid-impact | Khungri 50 MW hybrid, reservoir floating PV, ~585 MW additional study-stage | # Key Facts (FY 2024/25) Operating utility-scale solar: 141.74 MWp (all grid-tied; NEA-owned + IPP-owned combined) NEA-owned share: ~25 MWp (Bidur/Trishuli + smaller pilots) IPP-owned share: ~117 MWp (commissioned under Phase I / III) PPA-signed, pre-COD: 170 MWp (8 plants, FY 2024/25 signings) Tender-awarded, pre-PPA: 960 MWp (64 project selections from 2024/25 tender) Under grid-impact study, beyond 960 MW: ~585 MWp Annual PV generation (FY 2024/25): ~220 GWh (CF ~18%) # Tariff structure NEA's tariff-based competitive bidding framework for utility solar: Phase I (2016–18): NPR 7.30–8.40/kWh, single-round competitive Phase III (2023–24): NPR 5.94–6.50/kWh, competitive bidding with ceiling Phase IV (960 MW, 2024–25): NPR 4.99–5.55/kWh, national tender with province-balanced allocation See data-solar-hydro-lcoe for the full time-series and solar-lcoe-crossover for the cross-over narrative. # Programme organizational structure NEA's utility solar programme is scattered across several NEA directorates — a structural weakness: Generation Directorate — NEA-owned plant operation (Bidur/Trishuli) Project Management Directorate — tender design, PPA negotiation Transmission Directorate — grid-impact studies and interconnection Distribution Directorate — net-metering for rooftop Engineering Services Department / NEC — EPC supervision No single dedicated "solar cell" exists at senior-management level. The 960 MW tender exposed coordination friction across these five lines; a consolidated Renewable Energy Directorate is the obvious institutional fix. # Major utility plants under the programme Plant | Capacity (MWp) | Status | Owner | Notes | ---|---:|---|---|---| Bidur / Trishuli | 25.00 | Operating (2022) | NEA | bidur-trishuli-solar-25mwp | Butwal Solar | 8.50 | Operating (2020) | Ridi HP Development | butwal-solar-ridi-8-5mwp | Mithila Solar PV | 10.00 | Operating (2021) | Eco Power Development | mithila-solar-dhanusha-10mwp | Bishnu Priya Solar Farm | ~0.96 | Operating (2018) | Surya Power Company | bishnu-priya-nawalparasi | Khungri Solar Hybrid | 50 | Planned (2026) | NEA + IPP | khungri-solar-hybrid-50mw | Karnali Solar Energy Project | ~10 (pilot) | Planned/implementation | NEA / AEPC hybrid | karnali-solar-energy-project | 960 MW tender portfolio | 960 (64 project selections) | PPA in progress | Various IPPs | nea-960mw-solar-tender | Other small IPP plants (~17 plants) | ~90 (combined) | Operating | Various IPPs | From Phase I + III rounds | # Institutional challenges ## 1. Land acquisition is the new bottleneck Phase I–III plants were small enough (0.5–25 MWp) that land was project-specific. Phase IV (960 MW) triggers the land-at-scale question that agrivoltaics-and-land addresses. NEA does not have a land-programme office; this function needs to move to a new body or to AEPC. ## 2. Grid integration at 1+ GW solar The cumulative grid impact study NEA completed under Phase IV anticipates 4–6% instantaneous-penetration events by 2027 when 960 MW is partially commissioned. Forecast management, BESS requirements, and reactive-power compensation need to be designed in now. ## 3. PPA exposure balance NEA's PPA liability has grown to NPR 77.1B annual electricity purchase cost (see nea). Solar PPAs are adding ~NPR 6–8B/year to this. The single-buyer model (nepal-power-trade-schemes) plus fixed-price solar PPAs creates a structural interest-rate-sensitive liability that needs transparent treatment. ## 4. Talent depth NEA's solar engineering depth is thin; the Grid Solar & EE Project invested in training but the talent base for an additional 1 GW programme is a 3–5 year capacity-build, not a tender-cycle fix. # Related nea — the parent institution nea-960mw-solar-tender — the defining programme bidur-trishuli-solar-25mwp — the flagship wb-grid-solar-ee-project — the financing anchor for Phase II data-solar-fleet-inventory — the full portfolio solar-lcoe-crossover — the tariff trajectory hybrid-siting-logic — the direction Phase V should take
