pages.body_text: Water and Energy Commission Secretariat (WECS) # Summary WECS is Nepal's government planning body for water and energy, and its basin plans, hydropower-potential assessments, and energy balances are core sources for this wiki. Nepal's government planning body for water and energy. Produces the authoritative basin plans, potential assessments, and energy balances that form the data backbone of this research. # Key Publications wecs-river-basin-plan-2024 — Basin-level discharge, seasonal profiles, strategic planning wecs-hydropower-potential-2019 — Revised national hydropower potential (72,544 MW gross / 32,680 MW techno-economic) wecs-energy-synopsis-2024 — Full energy balance showing grid electricity as only 4.96% of final energy # Role in Sector WECS handles theoretical planning while nea handles operational execution. The Department of Electricity Development (DoED) manages licensing between them. This fragmented institutional structure is part of the governance weakness identified across the evidence base. # Limitations & Controversies This page is an institutional orientation page, not a full governance history of WECS; it does not independently assess mandate changes, staffing, budget authority, publication delays, or how WECS recommendations are implemented by operating agencies. # Related nepal-energy-profile — the system WECS plans for hydropower-potential-categories — WECS provides the definitive numbers

pages.title: West Seti Hydroelectric Project
pages.excerpt: Figure 6.3-2 River Longitudinal Profile of the West Seti River
pages.body_text: West Seti Hydroelectric Project Figure 6.3-2 River Longitudinal Profile of the West Seti River # Summary A long-stalled reservoir storage project in Sudurpashchim Province — the most prominent example of how Chinese withdrawal and project handoff have shaped Nepal's hydro-geopolitics. # Specifications Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Capacity | 750 MW | Status | Stalled — Chinese withdrawal 2018, NHPC takeover 2022, EIA hearings 2025 | River | Seti River (karnali-basin) | Districts | Bajhang / Baitadi / Doti / Dadeldhura | Province | Sudurpashchim | ## Engineering A 195 m concrete-faced rockfill dam (CFRD), 433 m long — the largest dam design in far-west Nepal. The project's political trajectory overshadows its engineering: conceived in the 1980s, awarded to China Three Gorges Corporation (2012), abandoned by CTG (2018), transferred to India's NHPC (2022). CTG's withdrawal was not purely technical — the commercial terms and geopolitical signaling (Indian sensitivity to Chinese infrastructure near the border) were likely decisive. See hydro-geopolitics. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Dam height | 195 m | Dam type | Concrete-face Rockfill | Dam length | 433 m | Type | Storage | ## Governance West Seti, alongside budhigandaki's history of Chinese-then-domestic pivots, represents a pattern: Chinese entities engage with Nepal's large storage projects but do not complete them. India then steps in — but progress remains slow. The net result is decades lost on projects that would directly address storage-deficit. Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Developer | NHPC Limited (India, since 2022) | Previous developer | China Three Gorges Corporation (2012–2018) | ## Schedule No construction timeline. NHPC is conducting EIA public hearings and updating the detailed project report as of late 2025. An associated project — SR-6 (450 MW) — has been proposed. Neither has a committed construction start. See buildability. # Limitations & Controversies Four decades of modality changes with zero construction. Conceived in the 1980s, held by SMEC for 17 years, awarded to CTG (2012), abandoned (2018), transferred to NHPC (2022), and still in EIA hearings as of late 2025. Each handoff resets the timeline. Chinese withdrawal pattern. CTG's 2018 withdrawal — citing geological issues, altitude, and resettlement — fits a broader pattern where Chinese entities engage Nepal's large storage projects but do not complete them. The net result is decades lost on storage that would directly address storage-deficit. No committed construction timeline. NHPC is updating the DPR and conducting EIA hearings, but no construction start has been announced. The associated SR-6 project (450 MW) is similarly undated. Geopolitical sensitivity. India's sensitivity to Chinese infrastructure near the border contributed to CTG's unfavorable operating environment. The NHPC takeover resolves the China problem but does not resolve the engineering, resettlement, or financing challenges. # Timeline of Stalling Year | Event | ------|-------| ~1980s | Project conceived | 2001–2011 | SMEC (Australia) held license; 17 years, limited progress | 2012 | Awarded to China Three Gorges Corporation (CTG) | 2018 (Sep) | CTG withdrew — cited geological issues, high altitude, resettlement difficulty. Rejected Nepal's proposal to reduce capacity from 750 to 620 MW | 2022 (Sep) | Transferred to India's NHPC Limited | 2025 (Oct) | Public hearings begun for Environmental Impact Assessment | # Current Status (as of late 2025) NHPC (India) is conducting EIA public hearings across affected areas Detailed project report is being updated An associated project — SR-6 (450 MW) — has been proposed below the confluence of Seti River and Budhiganga, in Doti/Achham districts, with a 207 m dam and potential 652 MW capacity No construction timeline announced # Why China Left CTG's withdrawal was not purely technical. The project illustrates the limits of Chinese hydropower engagement in Nepal: 1. Geological and altitude risk — genuine engineering concerns in far-west Nepal 2. Resettlement complexity — Nepal lacked a clear R&R framework 3. Commercial terms — Nepal proposed PPA payment in USD (unusual for Nepal), and CTG rejected a capacity reduction 4. Geopolitical signaling — India's sensitivity to Chinese infrastructure in border-adjacent areas created an unfavorable operating environment # Significance West Seti, alongside budhigandaki's history of Chinese-then-domestic pivots, represents a pattern: Chinese entities engage with Nepal's large storage projects but do not complete them. India then steps in (NHPC for West Seti, domestic for Budhigandaki) — but progress remains slow. The net result is decades lost on storage projects that would directly address storage-deficit. # Related hydro-geopolitics — the China-India triangulation storage-deficit — what West Seti would help solve budhigandaki — parallel trajectory of Chinese withdrawal, domestic/Indian pivot pancheshwar — another stalled storage mega-project, for different reasons # Sources jica-ipsdp-main-report-vol2

pages.body_text: Western Nepal 132 kV Backbone # Summary Western Nepal 132 kV Backbone is the operational 132 kV Terai-side grid chain represented in the map to show western grid reach beyond Butwal. The operational 132 kV Terai-side grid chain that carries the map west of Butwal: Butwal-Shivapur-Lamahi-Kohalpur, Kohalpur-Bhurigaun-Lamki, and Lamki-Pahalwanpur-Attariya-Mahendranagar. # Key Facts Parameter | Value | -----------|-------| Voltage | 132 kV | Status | Operational | Length basis | 404.89 route-km / 809.78 circuit-km | Source geometry | RPGCL 2021 official geospatial vector map | Status/length basis | NEA FY 2024/25 existing high-voltage line inventory | Corridor ID | | # Map Interpretation This corridor is now in the major transmission network because otherwise western Nepal looks emptier than it is. It is not a 400 kV export spine or a 220 kV bulk-transfer corridor; it is the operational 132 kV backbone that keeps Lumbini, Banke, Bardiya, Kailali, and Kanchanpur connected across the west. Current validation result: 3 features, 0 inferred connectors, 0 remaining endpoint gaps, and 418.149 km traced length against a 404.89 route-km basis. Public decision: default-visible, caveated. # Limitations & Controversies The route is source-backed but national-scale. It comes from RPGCL vector linework and NEA inventory control, not a tower-by-tower alignment sheet. It should be read as the western grid-reach backbone, with lighter visual weight than 220/400 kV lines. # See also data-layer-transmission-connected-traced-network chameliya-attariya-132 kohalpur-surkhet-dailekh-132 dana-kushma-butwal-corridor gorakhpur-butwal-interconnection

pages.excerpt: Availability Declaration (AD) penalties are financial deductions levied by NEA against hydropower producers when actual generation falls below the availability the producer declared in advance. The AD penalty mechanism is the primary financial instrument through which the nea-tri
pages.body_text: AD Penalties # Summary Availability Declaration (AD) penalties are financial deductions levied by NEA against hydropower producers when actual generation falls below the availability the producer declared in advance. The AD penalty mechanism is the primary financial instrument through which the nea-triple-authority conflict operates. # Simple Explanation AD penalties are the contractual fine a generator can face when it says it will produce one amount of electricity but delivers less. In Nepal, the problem is not only the fine itself. The same buyer that receives the power, controls dispatch, and pays invoices can also deduct the penalty, which makes the mechanism central to the IPP cash-flow and regulatory-conflict story. # The Penalty Mechanism The Availability Declaration system requires hydropower projects to declare their expected generation output in advance. When actual generation falls below the declared threshold, the project incurs a financial penalty deducted directly from its trade receivables owed by NEA. Verified penalty formula: Penalty = (0.8 × Contracted Energy − Actual Output) × Tariff The 0.8 threshold means a project must achieve at least 80% of its contracted energy output before penalties cease. Any shortfall below this threshold is penalized at the full per-unit tariff rate on the gap. Penalty destination: Penalties are deducted directly from the project's NEA trade receivables. They do not flow to an independent regulatory fund or system stability pool. NEA retains the deducted amount. [REQUIRES EXACT CITATION: statutory confirmation of destination mechanism — from PPA clause or ERC regulation] Revenue impact: The Independent Power Producers' Association, Nepal (IPPAN) and industry estimates suggest AD penalties can consume up to 16% of project revenue in severe cases. This figure is not a statutory ceiling — exhaustive search of IPPAN publications, ERC directives, ICRA/CARE rating rationales, and energy journalism archives confirms no legal cap or named project case study exists. The 16% figure is best understood as an aggregate empirical observation derived from the PPA penalty formula: Penalty = (0.80 × contracted energy − actual energy) × tariff. During severe dry seasons when a project generates well below 50% of contracted energy, the mathematical outcome of the formula approaches 16% of contracted energy value. The figure circulates as an IPPAN advocacy benchmark rather than a legally verified ceiling. The standard AD system requires generators to declare their available generation 30 days in advance for projects above 10 MW. The ERC formally acknowledged this burden for small projects, amending by-laws (ERC Bylaws 2076) to allow plants under 10 MW to declare availability one week in advance and exempting them from financial damages. See nea-triple-authority for the institutional framework. # The Barahi Hydropower Case Barahi Hydropower Public Limited is the best-documented case of the AD penalty mechanism overriding its own exemption clause. Barahi is a sub-10 MW run-of-river project. The Electricity Regulatory Commission (ERC) Bylaws 2076, Clause 8(2) and Schedule 5, explicitly exempt projects below 10 MW from AD penalties. Despite this exemption, NEA deducted penalty amounts for short supply from Barahi's invoices. Out of Rs 14.9 million in trade receivables, Barahi's management was forced to classify the deducted penalties as "receivable from NEA" in audited financial statements — publicly stating that NEA's actions contradict the prevailing ERC By-laws. Because NEA controls cash disbursement, the IPP carries the deducted penalty on its balance sheet while the ERC exemption exists on paper with no enforcement mechanism. The independent arbiter is absent. Project: Barahi Hydropower Public Limited Capacity: sub-10 MW (RoR) Regulatory protection: ERC Bylaws 2076, Clause 8(2), Schedule 5 Penalty deducted: part of Rs 14.9M in receivables Accounting treatment: "receivable from NEA" in audited financial statements Source: Barahi Hydropower audited financial statements [UNVERIFIED: exact fiscal year to be confirmed] The Barahi case is significant precisely because it documents the penalty mechanism overriding its own exemption clause. The project recorded the deduction as "receivable from NEA" — a forced loan to the off-taker with no resolution timeline on record. See barahi-hydropower. # The Structural Impossibility For run-of-river projects without storage, predicting output 30 days in advance in a Himalayan monsoon basin is not an engineering failure — it is an inherently unsolvable forecasting problem. RoR projects, lacking storage reservoirs, are at the absolute mercy of daily river hydrology. Holding RoR developers financially liable for standard deviation in monsoon hydrology via punitive AD penalties is fundamentally irrational from an engineering and grid-design perspective. The ERC acknowledged this by exempting projects under 10 MW from 30-day declarations and financial damages. The structural impossibility for larger projects remains unaddressed in regulatory or judicial rulings. [Under research — no primary regulatory or judicial source found yet.] # The Curtailment-Penalty Double-Bind — Confirmed The most consequential structural question about Nepal's AD penalty regime — whether any PPA version contains an exemption for shortfalls caused by NEA/NLDC curtailment orders — has now been confirmed by direct PPA text analysis. The answer is no. Article 10.2 of the standard PPA specifies the penalty formula: Compensation = [0.80 × min(Monthly Contract Energy, Availability Declaration) − (Actual Energy Delivered + Scheduled Outage Energy + Forced Outage Energy + Force Majeure Energy)] × Purchase Rate The formula counts only declared outages and force majeure as excusable causes. Curtailment by the off-taker is not listed. No PPA clause carves out NLDC dispatch orders from the penalty trigger. This is the double-bind in contractual form: the off-taker controls dispatch and enforces availability penalties, with no mechanism for the generator to claim relief when the two obligations conflict. International standard (IFC model PPAs) treats off-taker curtailment as a compensable "deemed generation" event — the IPP is paid as if it had generated, because the shortfall was caused by the buyer's decision, not the seller's failure. Nepal's PPA contains no such provision. Analysts have explicitly recommended adding deemed-generation protection in renegotiations, confirming its current absence. Source: Parajuli, S. (2023), "What does a RoR PPA contain?" — direct PPA text analysis. # The 10% Reserve Margin — Zero Compensation Article 10.1(Ka) of the standard PPA explicitly permits NEA/NLDC to withhold up to 10% of peak-period Contract Energy as a system reserve — with zero compensation to the IPP for that withheld energy. NEA can simultaneously: 1. Order an IPP to reduce output (curtailment) or withhold up to 10% as reserve 2. Apply a penalty for any shortfall below 80% of contracted energy 3. Face no compensation obligation for the generation it prevented The 10% reserve withholding, combined with the Article 10.2 penalty formula that excludes curtailment from excusable causes, means NEA can legally reduce a project's actual generation below the 80% penalty threshold through its own dispatch decisions — and then fine the project for the resulting shortfall. This makes the nea-triple-authority conflict not just an institutional design problem but a contractually encoded feature: the same entity controls both dispatch and penalty enforcement, and the PPA's penalty formula treats off-taker curtailment identically to generator failure. # Challenge Cases and Outcomes Beyond Barahi, no documented ERC arbitration rulings or court judgments on AD penalty disputes have been found in research passes to date. Any IPPAN legal challenges, ERC proceedings, or judicial outcomes concerning AD penalties should be documented here when located. [Under research.] # Common Misunderstandings AD penalties are not the same as ordinary project underperformance. The penalty is tied to declared and contracted energy, not simply to whether a plant is badly built. The 16% figure is not a verified legal cap. It is an advocacy/empirical benchmark derived from how the penalty formula behaves in severe shortfall cases. Curtailment relief is not currently documented in the standard PPA text reviewed here. The double-bind exists because off-taker curtailment is not carved out as an excusable cause in the analyzed formula. # Analytical links nea-triple-authority — the institutional framework this mechanism operates within barahi-hydropower — primary audited case study q-design-discharge — how design discharge sets the contracted energy threshold that triggers penalties hydro-insurance — the insurance market failure that strips working capital during penalty periods

pages.title: Agrivoltaics and Land
headings: What agrivoltaics is, in Nepal-specific terms
Why it is the politically survivable path
The policy moves this concept implies
pages.excerpt: Module costs have collapsed, grid costs are middling, LCOE is already below small hydro (solar-lcoe-crossover). The binding constraint on the next 5–10 GW of Nepal solar is neither technology nor money. It is land. Specifically, it is the politics of converting Terai agricultural
pages.body_text: Agrivoltaics and Land Module costs have collapsed, grid costs are middling, LCOE is already below small hydro (solar-lcoe-crossover). The binding constraint on the next 5–10 GW of Nepal solar is neither technology nor money. It is land. Specifically, it is the politics of converting Terai agricultural land into ground-mounted solar at the scale the grid can absorb. This page argues that agrivoltaics is not a "nice to have" framing for Nepal; it is the only politically survivable at-scale configuration for Terai utility solar, and explains why. # The land arithmetic Utility-scale ground-mount solar needs ~2.5 ha per MWp at typical Nepal spacing (row-to-row, tilt, O&M lanes). Building 5 GW on fee-simple purchased land requires ~12,500 ha — roughly 0.6% of Nepal's total cultivated area, but concentrated in a narrow belt: Terai agricultural land: ~1.4 million ha Within 10 km of a 132+ kV substation in Terai: ~220,000 ha Non-forest, non-protected, slope < 3%, within that belt: ~160,000 ha Of which, publicly-owned (sarkari) or non-permanently-cultivated: ~5,000–15,000 ha (estimates vary; no single cadastral register) So the fee-simple, non-agricultural, grid-adjacent land available for 5 GW of Terai solar is roughly the land needed for 2–6 GW. Nothing past that is buildable without either (a) buying agricultural land from smallholders, or (b) finding a way to share the land with agriculture. Option (a) is a political non-starter at that scale. Nepal's hydropower-era displacement politics (Upper Tamakoshi, Budhigandaki, Pancheshwar) has produced a sensitised Terai farming public, distrustful of large land conversions, with active civil society and elected representation. Fee-simple conversion of rice paddy to PV modules — at the ten-district Terai scale — produces a food-security / landlessness fight that a government elected with an agricultural base cannot win and should not try. Option (b) is agrivoltaics. # What agrivoltaics is, in Nepal-specific terms The generic agrivoltaic definition — dual-use of land for crop production and PV generation, through elevated or spaced modules — covers a range of configurations: Configuration | Module height | Crop compatibility | Yield interaction | Capex multiplier | ---|---|---|---|---:| Low-mount vegetable rotation | 0.8–1.2 m | Leafy greens, onion, garlic, turmeric, shade-tolerant veg | +5 to −10% crop yield under partial shade | 1.0–1.1× | High-canopy rice / wheat | 3.0–4.5 m | Rice, wheat, maize (partial-shade-tolerant varieties) | −10 to −25% crop yield; tractor access preserved | 1.35–1.55× | Animal-grazing (agri-PV) | 1.2–1.8 m with fencing | Goat / sheep grazing under; moderates heat | Forage gains; livestock welfare up | 1.05–1.15× | Tree / plantation (orchard-PV) | 2.5–4.0 m | Mango, litchi, guava, banana | Microclimate benefit; water saving | 1.2–1.4× | Pond-edge / irrigation canal | 1.5–3.0 m over canal | Fish / aquaculture below | Reduces evaporation from canals | 1.1–1.3× | Two of these configurations fit Nepal's Terai farming calendar especially well: Leafy greens + low-mount PV on the 6-month paddy-to-fallow rotation. Paddy in monsoon (when PV yield is lowest anyway), leafy greens Oct–May under the modules (when PV yield is highest and the crop benefits from shade in the pre-monsoon heat). Ideal match. High-canopy PV over rice + wheat double-crop. Higher capex but preserves the dominant Terai land-use pattern; yield penalty of 10–20% on rice is offset by a PV revenue-share of NPR 40,000–80,000 per ropani per year, a 4–10× uplift on smallholder cash income. The economics of this are not marginal. # Why it is the politically survivable path A solar project structured as: 25-year lease (not purchase) of 1–5 ha from each participating smallholder, with a right of return at lease-end. Revenue share of a defined percentage of PPA receipts, indexed to inflation. Preserved agricultural use under / between modules, with the farmer as the agricultural tenant. Shared community-scale services — rural electrification credit, pump irrigation at cost, cold-storage co-development. …has a fundamentally different political valence than "buy the land for a solar farm." It resembles a successful cooperative more than a land grab. It mirrors the structure that made India's Gujarat and Maharashtra agrivoltaic deployments land-lightly, while the pure-purchase models in Rajasthan and Karnataka have had recurring land-conflict problems. It is also the structure most compatible with Nepal's cooperative-heavy rural economy (aepc-renewable-framework) and with the farmers' cooperative (krishak sahakari) networks that already operate at the 10–500-household scale across Terai. # What this concept is not saying Not that every Terai solar site must be agrivoltaic. Government-owned sarkari parcels, degraded / alkali land, oxbow scrub, industrial-zone-adjacent land, and hydro-co-location sites (hybrid-siting-logic) remain the first choice where available — perhaps the first 1.5–2 GW. Not that agrivoltaics automatically solves all politics. It changes the coalition, but requires specific contract drafting (lease-not-sale, revenue-share, return rights) that Nepal does not yet have template law for. Not that it is capex-free. The ~1.3–1.5× capex multiplier on high-canopy configurations is real and must be priced into tariffs. At current module prices, the agrivoltaic LCOE is still well below hydro PPA (solar-lcoe-crossover). # The policy moves this concept implies If the argument holds, Nepal needs four things it does not yet have: 1. A lease-template law for 20–25 year solar leases on agricultural land, separating usufruct transfer from fee-simple conversion. Without this, every agrivoltaic site is negotiated one-off, which kills scaling. 2. An agrivoltaic tariff adder — NPR 0.30–0.50/kWh uplift for dual-use configurations, conditional on post-build crop verification. Creates the capex-offset incentive. 3. A recognised agricultural-technical standard for minimum module height, row spacing, and crop-light requirements — Nepal currently has none. 4. A VGF / green-finance channel for the incremental capex — the eib-rural-solar-phase2 and wb-grid-solar-ee-project are the most natural hosts, but neither currently prices an agrivoltaic multiplier. Without these four, Terai utility solar hits the land wall at roughly 2 GW and stalls. With them, the same physical resource becomes a 10–15 GW build-out path that takes nothing out of food production, and actively raises smallholder cash income. # Related solar-resource-geography-nepal — why Terai is the zone that matters here hybrid-siting-logic — the first ~2 GW without triggering the land fight solar-lcoe-crossover — why the capex multiplier is absorbable rooftop-minigrid-offgrid — the complementary non-ground-mount story nea-960mw-solar-tender — the first portfolio-scale test claim-solar-political-coalition-is-rural — the tracked claim this page operationalises

pages.title: Bay Of Bengal Terminal
pages.excerpt: This marker is the terminal reach of the generated route-to-ocean trace.
pages.body_text: Bay Of Bengal Terminal # Summary This marker is the terminal reach of the generated route-to-ocean trace. # Simple Explanation It is the map point that says: the Nepal-origin downstream route does not stop at the Indian plains. It continues through the lower delta system until it reaches the Bay of Bengal. # Why It Matters It gives the map a complete endpoint. Without it, the downstream river story visually stops in the plains or delta, even though the strategic route continues through the lower Padma-Meghna system to the sea. # How To Read The Marker Use it as the end of the strategic route trace, not as a detailed coastal or tidal model. # Caveat The terminal point comes from the HydroRIVERS route trace. It does not represent all distributaries, estuarine channels, or coastal sediment dynamics. # Common Misunderstandings It is not a coastal model. The point marks the route endpoint, not tides, ports, erosion, or delta morphology. It is not a claim that Nepal controls downstream outcomes. It only completes the visual trace from Himalayan basins to the sea. It is not a precise distributary selection. The lower delta contains many channels; this marker is a strategic route endpoint. # Related data-layer-nepal-origin-ocean-routes padma-meghna-delta lower-delta-bay-interface how-to-read-geopolitics-map

pages.title: Bihar Ganges Trunk Zone
pages.excerpt: This dependency zone marks the shared Ganges corridor where separate Nepal-linked routes become one downstream political geography.
pages.body_text: Bihar Ganges Trunk Zone # Summary This dependency zone marks the shared Ganges corridor where separate Nepal-linked routes become one downstream political geography. # Simple Explanation Several Nepal-origin river routes start as separate Himalayan basin stories. By the Bihar Ganges trunk, they have entered a shared lower-basin corridor, so the map shifts from individual tributaries to a common downstream zone. # Why It Matters The map needs this zone because users can otherwise over-focus on individual tributaries. By the Bihar Ganges trunk, Koshi, Gandaki, Karnali/Ghaghara, and Mahakali/Sharda routes are part of a broader lower-basin story. # How To Read The Zone Use it as the bridge between the upstream route merges and the ganges-padma-transition. It is where individual Nepal-linked routes become a shared downstream trunk. # Caveat The polygon is a broad context zone. It is not a model of flow shares, river operations, or local water allocation. # Common Misunderstandings The zone is not a hydrological allocation model. It does not estimate how much water comes from each Nepal-linked basin. It is not a legal or administrative boundary. It is a strategic map layer for reading downstream dependency. It does not collapse all tributaries into one story upstream. The merge matters downstream; basin-specific constraints still matter in Nepal. # Related kosi-ganges-merge gandak-ganges-merge ghaghara-ganges-merge ganges-padma-transition ganges-contribution

pages.title: Buildability
pages.excerpt: Buildability is the first-order filter on Nepal’s hydropower future: a project is not “good” because a desk study assigns a large MW number—it is good if the entire delivery package remains credible after geology, hydraulics, hazards, and grid realities are stressed.
pages.body_text: Buildability # Summary Buildability is the first-order filter on Nepal’s hydropower future: a project is not “good” because a desk study assigns a large MW number—it is good if the entire delivery package remains credible after geology, hydraulics, hazards, and grid realities are stressed. # Simple Explanation Buildability asks: can this project actually be built and operated, given Nepal's mountains, earthquakes, sediment, and thin construction market? A project that looks good on paper may fail because the tunnel collapses, the turbines wear out in months from silt, or the transmission line to evacuate the power never gets built. # What buildability actually tests A serious buildability review chains interdependent risks: Geology and underground works — tunneling and cavern stability under high cover, fault zones, and variable rock mass ratings. Sediment and abrasion — turbine technology, wear life, and maintenance cycles are not O&M trivia when concentrations swing orders of magnitude seasonally (see sediment-as-design-constraint). Hydraulic transients and flood/GLOF exposure — hazard tolerance and intake resilience. Evacuation — generation without stranded-generation-grade transmission is incomplete infrastructure. See the likhu-2: four private IPPs totaling 213 MW commissioned into a New Khimti substation sized for half their output, stranding ~40% of contracted generation in FY 2023/24 until a 200 MVA transformer upgrade restored the corridor. Execution realism — contractor capacity, local logistics winter, and financing covenants that survive delay. See chameliya-hydropower (11-year build, $7.5M/MW, headrace tunnel collapse) and upper-trishuli-3a (2024 flood destroyed gates and control room, 88-day outage at upper-tamakoshi). # Strategic implication The planning-relevant metric is therefore system value — incremental dependable energy, loss factors, curtailment risk, and delivered cost — rather than headline megawatts. That reframing connects naturally to storage-deficit (seasonal re-timing is worthless if the dam never reaches COD) and to basin-scale complexity in karnali-basin megaproject corridors. Megaprojects such as budhigandaki are instructive case files: the controversy is not only "how big," but whether the integrated package of reservoir, tunnels, communities, and finance can survive the decades-long path to operation. At the opposite scale, marsyangdi (69 MW, 36 years old) demonstrates that aging units approaching overhaul age carry a different buildability risk. khimti-i (60 MW, 1996) proves what an early-generation negotiated PPA can deliver, while likhu-4 (120→52 MW redesign after India wheeling dispute) shows buildability includes the regulatory environment the project commissions into. # Common Misunderstandings "Licensed = buildable" — many licensed projects stall for years due to financing, geology, or grid constraints. A license is a permit, not a construction guarantee. "Buildability is just engineering" — it includes social acceptance, financing, regulatory environment, and market access. "Big projects are inherently better" — megaprojects concentrate risk; a portfolio of smaller, buildable projects may deliver more system value. # Related sediment-as-design-constraint — the turbine-wear dimension stranded-generation — when buildable generation cannot be monetized storage-deficit — re-timing is worthless if the dam never reaches COD karnali-basin — basin-scale megaproject complexity budhigandaki — the largest buildability test case claim-governance-binding — institutional failures as binding constraint # Sources wecs-hydropower-potential-2019 adb-hydropower-growth-nepal wb-nepal-power-sector-reform-2022

pages.title: Consumption Trajectory Outlook
headings: The Consumption Story in One Sentence
Risk Factors — What Could Slow or Accelerate Growth
What the Data Cannot Yet Answer
pages.excerpt: What Nepal's electricity consumption growth trajectory implies for the country's energy strategy — the import-displacement opportunity, the growth risks, and the metric that determines whether the hydro build-out succeeds or fails on its own terms.
pages.body_text: Consumption Trajectory Outlook # Summary What Nepal's electricity consumption growth trajectory implies for the country's energy strategy — the import-displacement opportunity, the growth risks, and the metric that determines whether the hydro build-out succeeds or fails on its own terms. This page synthesizes data-domestic-demand, data-industrial-electricity-consumers, data-agricultural-energy-consumption, and data-consumption-geographic-distribution into a forward view. The companion supply-side analysis is twenty-year-strategy. # Simple Explanation Nepal is using much more electricity than it did a few years ago, but electricity is still a small share of total energy use. The concept asks whether new hydropower will be absorbed by domestic cooking, transport, industry, and agriculture, or whether weak domestic demand leaves Nepal dependent on low-value seasonal exports. # The Consumption Story in One Sentence Nepal's electricity consumption has grown ~55% in four years (from ~7,277 GWh to 11,288 GWh), but electricity is still only 7.23% of total final energy and 0.5% of households cook with it — meaning the growth runway is measured in decades, not years. # Current State — Electricity Consumption (FY 2024/25) Segment | GWh | Growth (4yr CAGR) | Electricity Penetration in Segment | ---------|------:|------:|------:| Residential | ~4,742 | ~10.8% | 5.0% of residential energy | Industrial | ~4,136 | ~10.1% | 11.6% of industrial energy (FY 2079/80) | Commercial | ~879 | ~14.5% | 9.9% of commercial energy (FY 2079/80) | Construction/Mining | ~591 | — | 55.5% of sector energy — already majority-electric | Agriculture | ~315 | — | 22.5% of agricultural energy | Transport | ~25 | — | 0.05% — essentially zero | Other (streetlight, irrigation, temp) | ~620 | ~17.8% | — | Total electricity | ~11,288 | ~11.6% | 7.23% of total final energy | \ Estimated from WECS sector share applied to FY 2024/25 total # The Consumption Growth Model Per-capita electricity consumption is 465 kWh/yr and growing ~10% annually. At this rate: Year | Per-capita (kWh) | Implied total (GWh) | Context | ------|------:|------:|---------| FY 2024/25 | 465 | 11,288 | Current | ~2029 | ~750 | ~18,000 | Nepal reaches current India per-capita | ~2034 | ~1,200 | ~28,800 | Reaches lower-middle-income norm | ~2040 | ~2,000 | ~48,000 | Reaches middle-income norm | This trajectory is not a forecast — it's a sense-check. At 10% annual demand growth, domestic consumption alone would absorb roughly the output of the planned hydro pipeline (see data-potential-pyramid) without needing massive export growth. But sustaining 10% demand growth requires the substitution pathway in energy-substitution-pathway to actually happen — cooking electrification, industrial fuel-switching, and EV uptake. # The Import Displacement Ledger The single most powerful number in the consumption profile is the gap between what Nepal currently imports (fossil fuels) and what it could displace with domestic electricity: Fuel | Total Consumption (TJ) | Import Cost (NPR Bill./yr, est.) | Displaceable by Electricity? | Electricity Equivalent (GWh) | ------|------:|------:|------:|------:| Diesel (all sectors) | 49,728 | ~120 | Yes — transport, ag pumps, gensets | ~13,800 | LPG (all sectors) | 23,677 | ~55 | Yes — induction cooking | ~6,600 | Petrol (all sectors) | 21,932 | ~75 | Partial — EV passenger vehicles | ~6,100 | Coal (industrial) | 34,016 | ~40 | Partial — electric kilns, hydrogen | ~9,400 | ATF / jet fuel | 6,191 | ~20 | No — aviation | — | Total displaceable | ~129,353 | ~290 | | ~35,900 GWh | [!finding] Total displacement opportunity is ~3× current electricity consumption If Nepal electrified all technically-displaceable fossil fuel consumption, it would need ~35,900 GWh of additional electricity — roughly triple the current 11,288 GWh. This is the domestic demand ceiling that the domestic-led-hydro-strategy is designed to capture. ## Displacement already underway EV passenger vehicles: >70% of new passenger vehicle imports in FY 2024/25 were EVs, driven by tax differentials Electric cooking: NEA FY 2024/25 report explicitly flags government policy to encourage electric cooking, transportation, and industry Industrial switching: diesel genset → grid connection is happening as reliability improves ## Displacement not yet started Brick kilns: ~1,500+ coal-burning kilns, essentially zero electric kilns deployed Freight transport: diesel trucks and buses, no material electrification Cement clinker: coal-fired, hydrogen co-firing still in concept stage (see green-hydrogen-nepal) LPG-to-induction cooking at scale: 0.5% household penetration, needs appliance cost reduction and reliability improvements # Risk Factors — What Could Slow or Accelerate Growth ## Upside risks (faster consumption growth) Factor | Mechanism | Magnitude | --------|-----------|-----------| LPG subsidy removal / rebalancing | Shift households from LPG to induction cooking | +50–75 PJ (~14,000–21,000 GWh) potential | Industrial policy for ferroalloys | Attract electro-intensive industry with cheap reliable power | +500–2,000 GWh per major plant | EV adoption beyond passenger vehicles | Electric buses, two-wheelers, three-wheelers | +500–1,500 GWh by 2030 | Data centres / ICT expansion | Nepal's competitive advantage — cheap green power + English-speaking workforce | +200–500 GWh | Cold chain build-out | Refrigerated transport and storage for agriculture | +500–1,000 GWh | ## Downside risks (slower consumption growth) Factor | Mechanism | Magnitude | --------|-----------|-----------| Manufacturing decline continues | Manufacturing already fell from 7.3% to 5.7% of GDP | −200–500 GWh vs trend | Grid reliability stalls | If outages persist, firms stay on diesel, households don't buy induction cookers | −300–800 GWh vs potential | Fuelwood inertia | Cultural preference + zero cash cost keeps biomass dominant in cooking | −100–200 PJ cooking load | Tariff distortion | If industrial tariffs don't reflect the true cost advantage over diesel, fuel-switching economics erode | −100–300 GWh | Migration / depopulation | Rural areas lose electricity consumers faster than urban gains | −100–200 GWh | # The Metric That Determines Success From energy-substitution-pathway: Biomass + fossil share of Nepal's final energy consumption. Today ~92.8%. A serious transition by 2040 should bring it below 70%, implying ~25–30 PJ of net displacement per year. Applied to 2025-2030 specifically, the intermediate targets are: Metric | Current (FY 2024/25) | 2030 Target | Status | --------|------:|------:|--------| Electricity share of final energy | 7.23% (FY 2079/80) | 12–15% | On track if 10% demand CAGR holds | Electric cooking penetration | 0.5% | 5–10% | Requires active policy push | EV share of new vehicle sales | >70% (passenger only) | >90% (all light vehicles) | Ahead on passenger, behind on freight | Industrial electricity share | 11.6% (FY 2079/80) | 18–22% | Requires grid reliability + industrial policy | Per-capita electricity | 465 kWh | 800–1,000 kWh | On track | Diesel displaced in agriculture | ~0 (currently rising) | 20–30% of ag diesel | Requires tubewell electrification programme | # The Export Surplus Question If domestic consumption grows at 10% CAGR and generation grows at roughly the same pace (the IPSDP pipeline implies ~12,000-15,000 MW installed by 2035), the net export profile depends on which grows faster: Scenario | Demand CAGR | Supply CAGR | 2030 Net Export (GWh) | Character | ----------|------:|------:|------:|-----------| Demand-led | 12% | 10% | ~500–1,500 | Imports still needed in winter | Balanced | 10% | 10% | ~2,000–3,500 | Monsoon exports, winter imports | Supply-led | 8% | 12% | ~5,000–7,000 | Large monsoon surplus, seasonal trade deepens | The current trajectory (~11.6% demand growth, ~10% supply growth) most closely resembles the "Demand-led" scenario — if it sustains. The key variable is whether the demand-side policies (cooking electrification, EV uptake, industrial switching) materialize at the same pace as the supply-side pipeline (22 projects commissioned in FY 2024/25 alone). The nightmare scenario is the "Supply-led" one: large monsoon surplus with weak domestic demand → exports at low spot prices while winter imports at high peak rates persist → the seasonal-arbitrage-trap institutionalizes. # What the Data Cannot Yet Answer 1. Hourly consumption by consumer category — we know the evening peak shape but not which sectors drive it (residential cooking + lighting probably dominates). Without this, the storage + demand-side management sizing is approximate. 2. Actual industrial sub-sector GWh — the estimates in data-industrial-electricity-consumers are indicative. NEA has this data but does not publish it. 3. Captive generation inventory — how much diesel generation capacity exists behind industrial meters, and how much is actually dispatched, is unmeasured. This is the hidden consumption layer. 4. Province-level sectoral splits — we have provincial totals but not the domestic/industrial/commercial breakdown within each province. 5. Price elasticity of demand — how sensitive is each consumer category to tariff changes? Essential for demand-side policy design but unresearched for Nepal. # Common Misunderstandings Fast electricity-demand growth does not mean the whole energy system is electrified. Electricity is still a small share of final energy consumption. Export surplus is not automatically a sign of success. It can reflect weak domestic absorption, especially if monsoon exports coexist with winter imports. Per-capita electricity growth is not the same as fuel substitution. The transition test is whether biomass, LPG, diesel, petrol, and coal are actually displaced. # Related data-domestic-demand — the core electricity demand data data-industrial-electricity-consumers — industrial sub-sector profile data-agricultural-energy-consumption — agricultural energy and diesel displacement data-consumption-geographic-distribution — where consumption is geographically data-final-energy-mix — the total-energy denominator energy-substitution-pathway — the strategic framework for displacement domestic-led-hydro-strategy — why domestic load matters more than exports twenty-year-strategy — the supply-side counterpart seasonal-arbitrage-trap — what happens if demand lags supply unresolved-questions — data gaps this page inherits

pages.title: Domestic-Led Hydro Strategy
headings: Why domestic demand is not a small story
The constraint is not "can Nepal export?" — it can
pages.excerpt: Domestic-led hydro strategy means planning Nepal's power system around its own load growth, reliability, and productivity — using exports to monetize surplus rather than defining the investment program around export markets. Hydropower remains central, but solar complementarity,
pages.body_text: Domestic-Led Hydro Strategy # Summary Domestic-led hydro strategy means planning Nepal's power system around its own load growth, reliability, and productivity — using exports to monetize surplus rather than defining the investment program around export markets. Hydropower remains central, but solar complementarity, BESS, and demand shaping now belong inside the strategy. # Simple Explanation Nepal could build dams mainly to sell electricity to India. A "domestic-led" strategy says: build dams (and solar) mainly to power Nepali homes, factories, and transport first. Sell any leftover electricity abroad. The sequencing matters because domestic demand creates jobs and tax revenue that exports alone do not. # Common Misunderstandings "Domestic-led means anti-export." It does not. Exports are valuable; the strategy says they should follow domestic need, not lead it. "Nepal lacks enough domestic demand." Per-capita electricity use is ~370–465 kWh/year — 5–7× below middle-income norms — indicating large headroom for efficient demand growth. "Domestic-led is only about hydro." The better operational phrase is domestic-led power strategy with a hydro backbone: solar, BESS, and demand shaping are integral. Domestic-led hydro means planning the power system around Nepal's own load growth, reliability, and productivity — using exports to monetize surplus, not to define the investment program. After the solar audit, the better operational phrase is domestic-led power strategy with a hydro backbone: hydropower remains central, but solar-hydro-complementarity, BESS, and demand shaping now belong inside the strategy rather than beside it. # The consensus across analytical lines Across multiple research threads in this project, the core strategic recommendation converges: Nepal should pursue domestic-led hydro with export support, not export-led hydro with domestic leftovers. The distinction is not anti-export; it is about sequencing and the objective function. Exports are valuable when they absorb genuine surplus at acceptable prices; they are costly when they institutionalize the seasonal-arbitrage-trap — cheap monsoon sales and expensive winter imports on the same national balance sheet. Recent trade and demand evidence frames the current failure plainly: "The system is getting better at monetizing surplus, but it still pays a winter scarcity tax, and it has not yet built enough domestic electrification depth to turn hydropower into broad-based wealth." # Why domestic demand is not a small story nepal-energy-profile makes clear that "low consumption" is better read as headroom than as lack of need. Per-capita electricity use is ~370–465 kWh/year — roughly 5–7x below a middle-income norm of 2,000–3,000 kWh/year. Electricity's share of final energy is small (7.23% in FY 2079/80, up from 4.96% the year before — see data-final-energy-mix) — so electrification of cooking, heat, mobility, and process heat is a multi-decade demand builder. The specific sinks to target, ranked by volume, are worked out in energy-substitution-pathway. The sectoral breakdown (FY 2020/21, NEA) reveals a critical structure (see data-domestic-demand): Residential: 43% of electricity sales (~3,138 GWh) Industrial: 39% of electricity sales (~2,816 GWh) — nearly as large despite being a tiny fraction of customer count Industry is already the second-biggest user and the highest-leverage expansion target The electric cooking gap is the most dramatic underdevelopment: fewer than ~1% of Nepal's households use electricity for cooking. Biomass and imported LPG dominate. This is not a preference story — it is a reliability and appliance-access story. Shifting even 20–30% of cooking loads to electricity would create large, distributed, flexible domestic demand that simultaneously absorbs monsoon surplus and cuts the LPG import bill. Industrialization, urbanization, and replacement of costly fossil inputs add concurrent load. Highest-value uses include displacing captive diesel, electrifying cooking and transport, and feeding manufacturing where reliability converts kWh into jobs and tax base. Order-of-magnitude estimates suggest ferroalloys and similar electro-intensive industry can yield 8–10x the domestic value of selling the same energy as a commodity export to India at spot-like realizations. # The constraint is not "can Nepal export?" — it can Nepal is improving its exchange-linked value capture: the IEX price spread flipped positive in 2023-24 (Nepal sold at ₹5.61/kWh, bought at ₹4.43/kWh). But the whole-system average was still negative (sold Rs 8.72/unit, bought Rs 9.17/unit) because structural winter imports at peak-hour rates wash out the monsoon gains. The hard constraint is "whether Nepal can build domestic demand and system efficiency fast enough that exports become a high-value optimization layer, not the primary story." # Exports as complement, not compass india-energy-relationship will remain decisive for corridors, approvals, and timing. bhutan-hydropower-model is often invoked as a managed export reference — useful less as a blueprint to copy than as a reminder that host-country load and fiscal design shaped outcomes. Nepal's geography and politics differ, but the lesson holds: contracts and domestic anchors matter as much as megawatts. # Links to supply-side innovation When surplus is structural in the monsoon, domestic absorption can be engineered — not only through wires but through electrolysis and ammonia. green-hydrogen-nepal is the most ambitious demand-creation path: it turns seasonal glut into chemical industry and food security inputs instead of low-priced spill. Solar adds a second supply-side innovation: it lets Nepal build dry-season daytime energy on a short cycle while reservoir hydro moves slowly through buildability and finance constraints. The domestic strategy should therefore treat nea-960mw-solar-tender as a bridge, not a distraction: solar buys time for storage hydro, and storage hydro makes solar useful after sunset. # Related data-domestic-demand — demand distribution data, cooking gap, load profile seasonal-arbitrage-trap — the cost of not building domestic demand stranded-generation — monsoon surplus that domestic load could absorb green-hydrogen-nepal — industrial-scale demand from surplus solar-in-the-master-narrative — how solar changes the strategy without replacing hydro claim-solar-terai-only-short-cycle-build — why solar is the short-cycle bridge twenty-year-strategy — how demand-building fits the phased strategy

The point is not that Nepal manages this region, but that river timing from Nepal-linked basins eventually passes into a densely used agricultural plain where floods, dry-season water, and settlement exposure matter. # Why It Matters The zone is included because the Ghaghara and Gandak routes connect Nepal-linked basin timing to dense agricultural and settlement geography. What this pathway implies for strategy
pages.excerpt: Energy substitution pathway names the specific question a hydro build-out must answer if it is to transform Nepal's energy system and not just its export ledger: which non-electric energy flows are being displaced, in what order, by what policy and infrastructure? Without this le
pages.body_text: Energy Substitution Pathway # Summary Energy substitution pathway names the specific question a hydro build-out must answer if it is to transform Nepal's energy system and not just its export ledger: which non-electric energy flows are being displaced, in what order, by what policy and infrastructure? Without this lens, "more hydro MW" and "more electricity consumption" can both rise while Nepal's overall energy system — dominated by fuelwood, coal, and imported petroleum — barely shifts. This is the strategic complement to domestic-led-hydro-strategy: where that page argues why domestic load matters more than exports, this one argues which specific loads to build. # Simple Explanation The substitution pathway is the bridge between electricity supply and actual energy transition. It asks which existing fuels Nepal stops burning when it adds clean electricity: fuelwood in kitchens, diesel in transport and pumps, LPG in cooking, or coal in industry. # Why the substitution frame exists The master-thesis treats hydropower as a conversion problem: turning hydrological advantage into firm, deliverable, financeable power. But even a perfectly converted fleet only creates kWh. Those kWh become welfare only when they displace something Nepal currently burns. From data-final-energy-mix, Nepal's FY 2079/80 final energy is: Biomass 68.7% (340 PJ) — overwhelmingly fuelwood in cooking Petroleum 19.4% (103 PJ) — diesel, petrol, LPG, ATF, all imported Electricity 7.23% (38.5 PJ) — 94% of it from hydro Coal 6.39% (34 PJ) — 99% of it burned in brick kilns and cement plants Other renewables (biogas, solar, µhydro, wind) 3.1% (16.5 PJ) Everything outside electricity is a candidate substitution target. Ranking them by physical magnitude yields a clear priority stack. # The three dominant sinks, ranked by volume ## Sink 1 — Fuelwood in residential cooking and heating (257 PJ) The single largest energy flow in Nepal. 48.3% of all final energy consumed. Affected population: essentially all of rural Nepal plus significant urban pockets. Substitute: electric induction cooking, heat-pump water heating, electric room heating in winter. Why it's hard: appliance cost, grid reliability (evening peak 18:30–19:25 is exactly cooking time), LPG subsidy currently undercuts electric cooking on marginal-cost terms. Why it's the biggest lever: displacing 20–30% of cooking load creates ~50–75 PJ of new electric demand — roughly doubling current electricity consumption. That is bigger than any plausible export contract. Connected wiki pages: data-domestic-demand (the Biomass + fossil share of Nepal's final energy consumption. Today that share is ~92.8% (68.7% biomass + 19.4% petroleum + 6.4% coal − small overlap). A serious transition by 2040 should bring that share below 70%, implying ~25–30 PJ of net biomass+fossil displacement per year. That in turn implies specific quantities of induction cookers deployed, kilns retrofitted, EVs sold, and industrial processes electrified — all measurable, all currently unmeasured at the system level. If Nepal builds 20,000 MW of hydro and the biomass+fossil share in 2040 is still 85%, the build-out has failed on its own terms. If Nepal builds only 10,000 MW but the share falls to 65%, the strategy has succeeded. # Common Misunderstandings More hydropower is not automatically substitution. New electricity must connect to a real end use that replaces biomass or fossil fuel. More domestic consumption is not automatically better. The quality of demand matters: displacing imported diesel or LPG has different value from adding low-value discretionary load. Exports and substitution are not interchangeable. A kWh exported earns revenue; a kWh used domestically can avoid imported-fuel spending and change the energy mix. # Related data-final-energy-mix — the underlying data domestic-led-hydro-strategy — the strategic envelope data-domestic-demand — sectoral electricity demand today green-hydrogen-nepal — the coal-displacement pathway twenty-year-strategy — phased implementation seasonal-arbitrage-trap — what happens if substitution is not built claim-mw-not-equal-value — the value-capture logic master-thesis — the overarching argument

pages.title: Environmental Flow Policy
pages.excerpt: The IPSDP executive summary treats environmental flow and protected-area restrictions as buildability constraints, not as side notes. In the SEA mitigation table on page 37, moewri-ipsdp-exec-summary-2025 says hydropower planning must evaluate and manage environmental flows and m
pages.body_text: Environmental Flow Policy # Summary The IPSDP executive summary treats environmental flow and protected-area restrictions as buildability constraints, not as side notes. In the SEA mitigation table on page 37, moewri-ipsdp-exec-summary-2025 says hydropower planning must evaluate and manage environmental flows and must respect statutory restrictions in protected areas. # Simple Explanation Environmental flow policy is the rule-of-thumb that a hydropower project cannot treat the whole river as available for diversion. Some flow must remain for downstream ecology, communities, legal requirements, and protected-area constraints. # What the IPSDP says directly Hydropower can alter downstream flow, habitat continuity, and river-wide flow patterns. Where adverse effects are expected, project planning should refer to the IFC Good Practice Handbook: Environmental Flows for Hydropower Projects (2018) and build an explicit E-flow management plan. For projects inside national parks, wildlife sanctuaries, hunting reserves, conservation areas, or buffer zones under Nepal's National Parks and Wildlife Conservation Act (2029/1973), prior permission is required. The same table says river modification and damming are not assumptions a developer can make inside protected areas; maintenance-flow and mitigation requirements remain in force. # Why this matters This is one of the clearest official signals in the current wiki that hydropower potential categories are not simply a matter of head and discharge. Protected-area law, river-ecology constraints, and mitigation hierarchy all cut directly into what is realistically developable. That makes this page a direct bridge between buildability, hydropower-potential-categories, and glof-risk: those concepts are all about why paper potential collapses when real-world constraints are applied. # Confidence boundary This page is limited to the policy and mitigation language stated in the IPSDP executive summary. It does not attempt to summarize Nepal's whole EIA or hydropower-permitting regime beyond what that table states. # Common Misunderstandings Environmental flow is not only an environmental side issue. It changes buildable energy, project design, and licensing risk. Protected-area restrictions are not captured by MW potential alone. A technically attractive site can still be constrained by law and mitigation requirements. This page is not a full legal guide. It summarizes the IPSDP signal, not the entire permitting regime. # Related buildability hydropower-potential-categories glof-risk moewri-ipsdp-exec-summary-2025

pages.title: Firm Power
headings: Installed MW ≠ what you can count on in February
Potential pyramids are not firm-power statements
pages.excerpt: Firm power is dependable, year-round, dispatchable electrical capability under credible drought and system stress assumptions—not a branding label for “big projects,” and not interchangeable with installed megawatts, annual energy (GWh), or even average seasonal output.
pages.body_text: Firm Power # Summary Firm power is dependable, year-round, dispatchable electrical capability under credible drought and system stress assumptions—not a branding label for “big projects,” and not interchangeable with installed megawatts, annual energy (GWh), or even average seasonal output. # Simple Explanation Firm power is the electricity you can actually count on when the grid is under the most stress — not the nameplate capacity printed on a turbine, and not the annual total generation. It is the amount of power that would still be available during the driest, darkest, most constrained weeks of the year. # Installed MW ≠ what you can count on in February A plant can be “online” while being strategically irrelevant for reliability if its energy is concentrated in monsoon weeks when the grid is already long—or if its output is volatile within-day in ways that the transmission system cannot absorb. Conversely, a smaller reservoir or import contract may contribute more firm value than a large RoR string, depending on commit rights, hydrology, and dispatch rules. The right planning question is therefore not “how many MW?” but how much electricity is deliverable when the alternative is rationing, diesel, or blackout—and at what cost. # Potential pyramids are not firm-power statements National “potential” figures sit at the top of a reduction chain from theoretical resource to what is financeable and buildable; see hydropower-potential-categories and the tabulated reductions in data-potential-pyramid. Those layers measure energy opportunity, not contract-grade dependability. Firm power is the bottom of the stack in strategic terms: it is what you underwrite, what you trade, and what industrialization plans should assume in dry weeks. # Examples A 100 MW RoR plant may generate near 100 MW in August but only 30–40 MW in January — its firm power contribution is closer to the January number for planning purposes. kulekhani-i (60 MW reservoir storage) can release stored water in dry weeks, making it one of Nepal's few sources of true firm power despite its small size. # Analytical payoff Keeping firm distinct from big clarifies why winter deficits can persist even as installed capacity rises, why export discussions hinge on commitment windows not annual averages, and why system adequacy is a seasonal adequacy problem first. # Common Misunderstandings "Installed capacity = dependable capacity" — nameplate MW is a hardware label, not a reliability guarantee. "Annual energy (GWh) proves adequacy" — a system can have high annual energy while still failing in scarcity hours. "Firm power = base load" — firm power can be peaking capacity; the concept is about dependability, not run duration. See ONTOLOGY.md disallowed alias. # Related seasonal-mismatch — the problem firm power addresses run-of-river-hydropower — why RoR delivers less firm power than nameplate suggests storage-deficit — the physical gap in seasonal firming claim-mw-not-equal-value — the canonical claim about conflation of MW, energy, and firm power data-potential-pyramid — the reduction chain from theoretical to dependable hydropower-potential-categories — the definitions that matter for planning # Sources wb-nepal-power-sector-reform-2022 nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 wecs-hydropower-potential-2019

pages.title: Nepal's Contribution to the Ganges
headings: Western basins as part of the same puzzle
pages.excerpt: Nepal occupies about 13% of the Ganges basin area yet contributes roughly 40–45% of mean annual flow and 70–80% of dry-season flow. This hydrological asymmetry — small footprint, large leverage on timing — is the physical basis for Nepal's upstream role in South Asian water secur
pages.body_text: Nepal's Contribution to the Ganges # Summary Nepal occupies about 13% of the Ganges basin area yet contributes roughly 40–45% of mean annual flow and 70–80% of dry-season flow. This hydrological asymmetry — small footprint, large leverage on timing — is the physical basis for Nepal's upstream role in South Asian water security. # Simple Explanation Nepal is a small country in a huge river basin. But the rivers that start in Nepal's Himalayas feed almost half the Ganges' water — and even more of its dry-season flow. This means what Nepal does with its rivers (dams, storage, diversions) affects hundreds of millions of people downstream, mostly in India and Bangladesh. # Common Misunderstandings "Nepal's contribution is proportional to its land area." It is not. Nepal's Himalayan geography concentrates precipitation and meltwater into a small area, producing outsized downstream contributions. "High contribution means Nepal has unlimited bargaining power." Contribution creates leverage, but leverage without institutional capacity and enforceable agreements does not translate into durable benefit. "The 40%/70% figures are exact and current." They are historical estimates from the 2005 National Water Plan that predate recent climate shifts; the directional conclusion is robust but the exact percentages should be treated cautiously. Nepal occupies only about 13% of the Ganges basin area, yet contributes roughly 40–45% of mean annual flow and on the order of 70–80% of dry-season flow measured at Farakka-style accounting points in strategic basin literature. This hydrological asymmetry—small footprint, large leverage on timing—is the physical basis for Nepal’s upstream role in South Asian water security. # Underused abundance Nepal's problem is not that the basin is empty. In National Water Plan framing, the country has roughly 225 BCM of annual water availability but uses only about 15 BCM for economic and social purposes. The strategic issue is therefore conversion: storage, delivery, irrigation timing, and coordinated releases — not raw annual scarcity. # What the asymmetry implies downstream Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, and—through the concatenated regime—Bangladesh are sensitive to Nepal-origin contributions for: Kharif and rabi irrigation scheduling (canal drafts depend on low-flow stability). Flood peaks shaped by transboundary storms and sediment pulses (see koshi-basin for the extreme case). Drought resilience when monsoon spatial correlation fails. Aggregated planning numbers in basin assessments commonly cite ~5–7 million hectares of irrigated agriculture and ~200–250 million people as significantly affected by Nepal-influenced flow regimes (definitions vary; treat as order-of-magnitude strategic scale, not a census). # Climate change raises the stakes If variability intensifies and low flows become less reliable while extreme events increase, the marginal value of upstream storage, forecasting, and coordinated releases rises. Nepal’s geography could translate into bargaining power—but only if institutional capacity converts hydrology into credible, enforceable cooperation. Today, the more common pattern is leverage without durable agreement: episodic crisis diplomacy rather than rules-based benefit sharing. # Geopolitics and national planning The strategic read is developed in parallel on hydro-geopolitics and india-energy-relationship: electrons and cubic meters are joint products in peoples’ minds even when markets separate them. Nepal’s National Water Plan discourse (see national-water-plan-nepal) is the domestic mirror—attempting to align IWRM, energy, and disaster risk under one national narrative. # Western basins as part of the same puzzle karnali-basin feeds the Ghaghara complex and therefore UP’s vast irrigated plains. Storage and diversion debates there are not “local” Nepali stories; they are subcontinental stories with Nepali headwaters at the center. # Analytical bottom line Nepal’s contribution to the Ganges is not proportional to its land share. That fact creates real upstream leverage—and also moral hazard if Nepal builds unilateral infrastructure that ignores downstream sensitivities. The research task is to map where cooperation creates surplus for both sides versus where zero-sum framing is unavoidable.

This marker helps readers understand why a Nepal-origin river trace eventually becomes a Bangladesh delta story. # Why It Matters For Nepal's upstream story, this is where the downstream frame shifts from northern India plains politics into Bangladesh delta dependence. It identifies a map-reading shift, not allocation rights. It is not a precise distributary model. The Padma-Meghna delta has complex local channels beyond this marker. It does not mean Nepal determines Bangladesh outcomes. pages.title: GLOF Risk
headings: Process: from lake instability to basin-scale impact
A concrete 2024 illustration: Thame / Dudh Koshi
Implications for hydropower design and siting
pages.excerpt: Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs) are rapid releases of water from moraine-dammed or ice-dammed lakes, capable of producing high-energy sediment slurries that exceed historical design flood bases. In Nepal, they are a first-order constraint on hydropower siting in trans-Himala
pages.body_text: GLOF Risk # Summary Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs) are rapid releases of water from moraine-dammed or ice-dammed lakes, capable of producing high-energy sediment slurries that exceed historical design flood bases. In Nepal, they are a first-order constraint on hydropower siting in trans-Himalayan basins. # Simple Explanation As glaciers retreat, they leave behind unstable lakes held back by loose rock and ice. When these dams break, the flood isn't just water — it's a fast-moving mix of water, rock, and mud that can travel hundreds of kilometers. For hydropower projects downstream, this means design assumptions based on historical river floods may be inadequate. # Common Misunderstandings "A GLOF is just a big flood." It is not. GLOFs can produce flow patterns and sediment loads that have no historical precedent at a given site. "GLOF risk is an environmental side issue." It is an infrastructure solvency issue — projects that ignore tail risks can fail non-market tests once those risks are priced honestly. "Only projects near glaciers are at risk." GLOF flow paths can extend hundreds of kilometers, affecting tributaries and mainstems far downstream. Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs) are rapid releases of water from moraine-dammed or ice-dammed lakes, often triggered by avalanches, seismicity, or hydrostatic/overpressure failure. In Nepal’s context, they are a first-order constraint on how confidently one can site run-of-river corridors, headworks, and storage in transboundary basins—because a GLOF is not a “flood” in the sense of a predictable monsoon stage; it can arrive as a high-energy sediment slurry with invented hydrographs that exceed historical design bases. # Process: from lake instability to basin-scale impact Glacier retreat creates and enlarges supraglacial and proglacial lakes, frequently impounded by unconsolidated moraines with weak spillway geometry. When the impoundment fails, the release can cascade: one lake drains into another valley reach, remobilizing sediment, eroding channels, and amplifying peak discharge far downstream. Flow paths can extend hundreds of kilometers, affecting tributaries and mainstems long after the originating valley. # A concrete 2024 illustration: Thame / Dudh Koshi The 2024 Thame Valley sequence—where a rock avalanche impacted Upper Ngole Cho, then contributed to failure dynamics affecting Lower Ngole Cho, producing on the order of a ~22 m head drop through a ~51 m breach width (figures as reported in rapid assessments)—generated a hyper-concentrated flow tracked >80 km down the Thame and Dudh Koshi systems, damaging settlements and hydropower works. The event is a textbook case for why stationary hydrology assumptions are inadequate: the initiating process was mass movement + lake chain, not a monsoon exceedance. # Implications for hydropower design and siting Planned RoR and storage projects along GLOF-prone corridors face three intertwined issues: 1. Hydraulic load cases that historically used gauge-based floods may understate tail scenarios driven by sudden moraine breaches and sediment bulking. 2. Sediment pulses from GLOFs connect hazard to turbine wear, intake burial, and channel avulsion—overlapping with sediment-as-design-constraint in basins like koshi-basin. 3. Insurance, financing, and EPC risk feed back into buildability: projects that look attractive on LCOE spreadsheets can fail non-market tests once tail risks are priced honestly. Storage concepts in high-hazard reaches—dudhkoshi-storage is a prominent example—must therefore integrate landscape stabilization, monitoring, and cascading-failure scenarios, not only energy-yield optimization. # Link to the glacio-hydrological arc The same deglaciation dynamics that define the peak-water window also produce unstable lakes. Mitigation (lowering, controlled drainage, early warning) competes for fiscal and institutional bandwidth with generation targets. Treating GLOFs as a side environmental issue is a category error: they are infrastructure solvency issues.

headings: Why fertilizer is the natural first anchor

pages.body_text: Green Hydrogen Nepal # Summary Green hydrogen in Nepal is best understood as a bridge technology between surplus monsoon electricity and hard-to-electrify domestic industry—not as a export commodity fantasy disconnected from grid physics. Electrolysis converts low-utilization wet-season kWh into storable molecules (hydrogen, then ammonia or other carriers), reshaping the economics of seasonal-arbitrage-trap by absorbing energy when the system is long and delivering products when the economy needs them. # Simple Explanation Green hydrogen turns electricity into a fuel or industrial input. For Nepal, the useful idea is not exporting hydrogen for its own sake; it is using wet-season surplus electricity to make domestic products such as fertilizer, industrial heat, or ammonia that are hard to electrify directly. # Why fertilizer is the natural first anchor Nepal imports essentially all chemical fertilizer; food security and farm productivity are therefore foreign-exchange and supply-chain dependent. A domestic ammonia pathway—hydrogen → Haber-Bosch → urea/ammonium products—ties directly to sovereignty and base-load demand. Order-of-magnitude sector sketches in national roadmaps suggest a modern fertilizer complex can present hundreds of megawatts of baseload-class demand (commonly cited ~500 MW in policy-grade scenarios—exact sizing is plant-design specific). That scale matters: it is large enough to change dispatch rather than decorate it. # Cement and other industrial offtake Cement decarbonization is another hydrogen sink: replacing fossil fuel combustion in clinker/pyroprocessing with hydrogen or hybrid fuels stacks up large annual H₂ demand in national modeling discourse (illustrative national figures on the order of ~228,000 tonnes H₂/year implying ~2 GW of electrolysis capacity are used in roadmap arithmetic—treat as planning magnitude, not a signed FEED package). The point for domestic-led-hydro-strategy is structural: these are domestic value chains that pay for reliability differently than spot export. # Policy trajectory The Green Hydrogen Policy (2024) signals official intent to coordinate standards, pilots, incentives, and safety. The typical staged narrative runs pilots 2025–2027 toward industrial scale by ~2035, with cost projections in policy documents clustering around ~$2.15/kg by mid-2030s under favorable renewable input cost paths—again, a directional planning anchor. # Relationship to curtailment and surplus If new RoR continues to outpace demand and storage, stranded-generation risk rises: energy with nowhere to go at non-trivial variable cost. Electrolysis is one of the few scalable sinks that can ride renewable variability if system integration (oxygen use, water treatment, grid connection, industrial symbiosis) is solved. Detailed citations and program structure belong in green-hydrogen-roadmap-nepal. # Common Misunderstandings Green hydrogen is not a substitute for basic grid planning. It can absorb surplus only if transmission, industrial siting, and offtake are designed together. Export hydrogen is not the core Nepal use case in this wiki. Domestic fertilizer, cement, and industrial substitution are the stronger near-term frames. Roadmap-scale numbers are planning magnitudes. They should not be read as financed projects, signed PPAs, or committed industrial plants.
