Why India And Bangladesh Marks Are Here
pages.excerpt: The geopolitics preset is not a Nepal-only map. It follows Nepal-linked rivers into the northern Indian plains, Bangladesh, and the Bay of Bengal because the political question is about downstream exposure, not just upstream origin.
pages.body_text: How To Read The Geopolitics Map # Summary The geopolitics preset is not a Nepal-only map. It follows Nepal-linked rivers into the northern Indian plains, Bangladesh, and the Bay of Bengal because the political question is about downstream exposure, not just upstream origin. # Simple Explanation Read the map as a route-and-exposure guide. It shows how rivers that begin in or pass through Nepal continue into downstream regions where timing, floods, sediment, dry-season flows, and future storage choices can become political. # Visual Grammar Read the layers in this order: Map mark | Meaning | ----------|---------| Nepal-linked basin polygons | Where Nepal sits inside the upstream basin geography. | Nepal rivers and downstream rivers | The main water routes from Nepal into the plains. | Ocean route | A strategic continuation through the Ganges/Padma/Meghna system to the Bay of Bengal. | Route notes | Merge, handoff, naming, and delta markers that explain the route. | Dependency zones | Broad downstream exposure areas for flood, dry-season, agricultural, population, sediment, and delta sensitivity. | Population anchors | City and delta points that help orient the human geography around the routes. | Flow regulation | Storage projects that could change timing, dry-season support, flood attenuation, sediment behavior, and cooperation risk. | # The Core Rule Do not read the downstream layers as water-control claims. They are exposure claims. The map does not say Nepal controls Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, or Bangladesh water security. It says Nepal-linked rivers pass through sensitive downstream geographies where timing, flood pulses, sediment, dry-season flow, and future storage decisions can matter politically. # How To Click Around Start with downstream-river-geopolitics. Then follow the route notes: 1. mahakali-sharda-handoff 2. ghaghara-ganges-merge 3. gandak-ganges-merge 4. kosi-ganges-merge 5. ganges-padma-transition 6. padma-meghna-delta 7. bay-of-bengal-terminal Then read the exposure zones: eastern-up-ghaghara-gandak-belt north-bihar-kosi-gandak-floodplain bihar-ganges-trunk-zone padma-meghna-delta-dependency lower-delta-bay-interface # Why India And Bangladesh Marks Are Here The downstream marks exist because Nepal's hydropower and storage choices are also timing choices. A run-of-river project mostly follows the hydrograph. A storage project can shift water across time, trap sediment, attenuate floods, or change the reliability of dry-season releases. That is why the map keeps data-layer-future-regulation-scenario visible with the downstream layers. The political value of storage is not just megawatts. It is the ability to regulate time. # Common Misunderstandings The map is not a claim of Nepalese control downstream. It shows exposure pathways, not authority. Dependency zones are not hydrological models. They are interpretive map layers for reading geography. Storage markers are not policy prescriptions. They show where timing regulation could matter if projects are built. # Related downstream-river-geopolitics ganges-contribution hydro-geopolitics data-layer-nepal-origin-ocean-routes data-layer-downstream-dependency-zones

pages.title: Hybrid Siting Logic
headings: Archetype 1 — Solar at existing hydropower sites ("hydro co-location")
pages.excerpt: Solar plants are not free-floating technology choices; they are three things co-located — a module field, a land parcel, and an interconnection. Cheap modules have collapsed the first; solar-lcoe-crossover. Land and interconnection are now the binding constraints on Nepal solar,
pages.body_text: Hybrid Siting Logic Solar plants are not free-floating technology choices; they are three things co-located — a module field, a land parcel, and an interconnection. Cheap modules have collapsed the first; solar-lcoe-crossover. Land and interconnection are now the binding constraints on Nepal solar, and the siting archetypes that minimise those two costs beat the ones that optimise GHI alone. This page frames the three siting archetypes — hydro co-location, substation-adjacent greenfield, floating PV on reservoirs — and argues that the first and third together will carry most of the political coalition for utility-scale solar in Nepal through 2035. # Archetype 1 — Solar at existing hydropower sites ("hydro co-location") The cheapest MW Nepal can build, in the specific sense that almost every non-module cost is already paid. What's already there at a typical operating hydropower site: An access road (often 3–15 km of graded mountain road, the single most expensive item in hill-country solar). An interconnecting substation (11/33 → 132/220 kV). Spare evacuation headroom, especially in dry season when the hydro plant runs at 30–40% of monsoon output and the transformer / line is underused. A skilled O&M crew, security, and a fenced site. Water for panel cleaning. Permitting precedent with NEA, local government, forest department, and the community. What the solar build adds: 1–10 MWp of PV modules (1–8 ha of dry / desilted terrain adjacent to the powerhouse or along the headrace road). A combiner box, inverters, and a tap into the existing step-up transformer. ~NPR 40–60 million per MWp installed (vs ~NPR 70–90 million for greenfield) — a 35–40% capex reduction from land, road, and interconnection savings. Why it is also operationally elegant: The interconnection loading pattern is anti-phased with the hydro plant. In the dry-season afternoon, the hydropower plant under-utilizes its evacuation; the solar PV fills the spare capacity of the same substation. In the monsoon-day overlap, dispatch holds hydro pondage through midday and releases it in the evening peak (see solar-hydro-complementarity). Net transformer capacity utilization goes up, not down. Candidate sites with published feasibility or public tender interest: kulekhani-cascade — reservoir + three cascade plants; ~10–20 MWp ground + ~15–30 MWp floating potential. kali-gandaki-a — 144 MW NEA flagship; dam-adjacent flats suited to 25–40 MWp ground PV. khimti-i — 60 MW IPP; headrace-adjacent terraces, 10–15 MWp candidate. marsyangdi / madhya-marsyangdi — cascade co-location, 20–40 MWp combined. tanahu-hydropower — storage reservoir under construction; co-location should be designed in before impoundment. The 50 MW solar project at Khungri village, designed to integrate into the Khungri substation adjacent to Madi Khola and Lungri Khola hydropower, is the first operational example of the archetype at scale in Nepal (NEA annual report FY 2024/25). # Archetype 2 — Substation-adjacent greenfield (Terai) The 960 MW NEA tender (nea-960mw-solar-tender) and the next 2–3 GW of utility-scale solar will overwhelmingly be this archetype: 10–50 MWp ground-mount, 1–8 km from an existing 132 or 220 kV substation, on the Terai plain. Why it works: Highest 132 kV grid density in the country (hetauda-dhalkebar-inaruwa-backbone, dana-kushma-butwal-corridor). Flat terrain (<3° slope), lowest construction cost in Nepal. Proximity to load centres and to Indian-grid interconnections for future export. Water for panel cleaning (Terai is canal-irrigated). Why it is politically fragile: Terai is Nepal's prime agricultural land; fee-simple conversion to solar triggers food-security objections (agrivoltaics-and-land). Land acquisition — even at 2–5 ha per site — collides with fragmented tenure, smallholder resistance, and the memory of hydropower-era displacement. Non-agricultural alienable land (government-owned sarkari parcels, dried-out oxbows, public waste) is scarce and over-subscribed. The design move that makes it durable: do not buy land. Lease for 25 years with a revenue-share clause, anchor on agrivoltaic configuration, and bundle rural-electrification / pump-irrigation offtake into the PPA. The 960 MW tender is experimenting with variants of this; the next decade of Terai solar depends on whether that politics stabilises. # Archetype 3 — Floating PV on reservoirs The highest-leverage single lever in Nepal's solar portfolio, by an uncomfortable margin. What floating PV buys that ground-mount does not: No land acquisition — the reservoir exists; deploying on ~5–20% of its surface takes nothing out of agricultural rotation. Cooler panel operating temperature — ~2–5% yield uplift from evaporative cooling. Reduced reservoir evaporation — 30–50% evaporation reduction on covered surface; in a country with storage-deficit and a dry-season water-tight operating regime, this is not a side benefit, it is a water-system benefit sold separately. Shared interconnection — dam powerhouse already carries the 11/33 kV step-up and the substation. Floating PV taps in at the tail. Anti-algae — covered water bodies see fewer blooms; Kulekhani in particular has had sedimentation / eutrophication concerns that floating PV partially mitigates. Candidate reservoirs: Reservoir | Surface (ha) | 10% coverage (ha) | Nameplate (MWp) | Status | ---|---:|---:|---:|---| kulekhani-cascade | ~220 | 22 | ~17 MWp | Operating; pilot-ready | tanahu-hydropower | ~700 | 70 | ~56 MWp | Under construction; design in now | budhigandaki | ~6,300 | 630 | ~500 MWp | Proposed; 10+ year horizon | dudhkoshi-storage | ~1,800 | 180 | ~144 MWp | Proposed | mugu-karnali-storage | ~9,000 | 900 | ~720 MWp | Proposed | uttarganga-storage | ~2,400 | 240 | ~192 MWp | Proposed | Even at conservative 5% coverage and discounting the long-dated projects, the near-term-buildable floating PV at Kulekhani + Tanahu is ~70–90 MWp — more than the entire operating utility-scale solar fleet as of FY 2024/25. The design move that matters most: require floating-PV integration in the tender documents for every new reservoir project, starting with Tanahu. Retrofitting is ~2× more expensive than designing it in. # The siting-cost stack, one table Archetype | Land cost | Grid cost | GHI (typical) | LCOE index (Terai greenfield = 100) | ---|---|---|---|---:| Hydro co-location | 0 (already owned) | 0 (spare headroom) | 4.5–5.5 | 60–70 | Substation-adjacent Terai | 15–25 | 5–10 | 4.8–5.3 | 100 | Floating PV | 0 | low | 4.5–5.5 | 75–85 | Trans-Himalayan (Mustang) | low | very high | 6.0–6.5 | 180–250 | Rooftop (Kathmandu Valley) | 0 (existing) | net-metering | 4.2–4.6 | 90–110 | Hill greenfield | 10–20 | 30–60 | 4.3–4.8 | 140–180 | Grid cost is the single widest column. In a country with stranded-generation as a current, real constraint, archetypes that spend zero new transmission (hydro co-location, floating PV, rooftop) are worth their ~5% higher module-side costs many times over. # The portfolio rule Over 2026–2035, roughly: ~60% of solar MW should be substation-adjacent Terai greenfield (Archetype 2), with ~70% of that as agrivoltaics. ~20% as hydro co-location (Archetype 1), increasingly standard in the next NEA tender batches. ~10% as floating PV on Kulekhani, Tanahu, and the earliest-operating reservoir sites (Archetype 3), scaling to more as reservoirs commission. ~10% as rooftop / distributed + off-grid mini-grids (see rooftop-minigrid-offgrid), which is a separate political track. This is the sort of portfolio a competent NEA + ERC could produce in a 10-year plan. Nothing in the 2024/25 annual report refutes it; the infrastructure for all four archetypes is under way. The missing piece is an explicit portfolio rule that treats the four archetypes as complements rather than competitors. # Related solar-hydro-complementarity — why these sites are valuable solar-resource-geography-nepal — which zones suit which archetype solar-lcoe-crossover — the price argument each archetype compounds agrivoltaics-and-land — the political condition for Archetype 2 rooftop-minigrid-offgrid — the fourth archetype, treated separately kulekhani-cascade, tanahu-hydropower, budhigandaki, dudhkoshi-storage — floating PV candidates nea-960mw-solar-tender — the first portfolio-scale test of Archetype 2

pages.title: Hydro-Geopolitics
headings: Downstream scale: why Nepal's choices ripple
India as decisive actor; China as absent partner
pages.excerpt: Hydro-geopolitics is the intersection of transboundary river geography, bilateral energy trade, and sovereignty questions that shapes Nepal's hydropower strategy and project siting. It treats Nepal's rivers as co-produced by geology, monsoon, ice, and downstream human systems — a
pages.body_text: Hydro-Geopolitics # Summary Hydro-geopolitics is the intersection of transboundary river geography, bilateral energy trade, and sovereignty questions that shapes Nepal's hydropower strategy and project siting. It treats Nepal's rivers as co-produced by geology, monsoon, ice, and downstream human systems — and therefore as objects of bargaining, not merely engineering inputs. # Simple Explanation Nepal's rivers don't stop at the border. What Nepal builds upstream affects irrigation, floods, and water supply for hundreds of millions of people downstream — mostly in India. This means every dam, reservoir, or power line is also a diplomatic negotiation. "Hydro-geopolitics" is the name for the fact that Nepal's electricity strategy cannot be separated from its relationship with its downstream neighbors. # Common Misunderstandings "Hydro-geopolitics means India is the enemy." It does not. The concept includes cooperation, market integration, and treaty negotiation — not just conflict. "Technical optimization is enough." Ignoring the geopolitical layer turns technically optimal projects into politically unrealizable ones. "Bhutan is a model Nepal can copy." Bhutan's export-led hydro works because of a specific patron relationship and fiscal design; Nepal's larger population and different downstream geometry make copy-paste misleading. Hydro-geopolitics is the lens that treats Nepal's rivers as co-produced by geology, monsoon, ice, and downstream human systems—and therefore as objects of bargaining, not merely as engineering inputs. Electricity is one slice of a larger portfolio that includes irrigation, flood management, navigation where relevant, ecosystem services, and disaster risk. Ignoring this layer turns technically "optimal" projects into politically unrealizable ones. # Downstream scale: why Nepal's choices ripple Nepal-origin rivers contribute a large share of Ganges annual discharge (commonly cited ~40–45%) and an even larger share of dry-season flow (~70–80% in Farakka-style accounting used in basin assessments). Those percentages imply hundreds of millions of people and many million hectares of irrigated command indirectly indexed to Nepal-influenced regimes. Illustrative orders of magnitude appear repeatedly in basin literature: Koshi irrigation on the order of 500–600 thousand hectares in Bihar; Gandak systems on the order of 1.5–2 million hectares across Bihar/UP; Karnali/Ghaghara complexes affecting roughly 2–3 million hectares in UP. The exact numbers shift with dataset and boundary definition; the strategic fact is extreme downstream dependence on upstream timing and quality of flows—developed analytically in ganges-contribution. # Treaties, asymmetry, and unfinished business Historical agreements (Koshi, Gandak, Mahakali) are often described as asymmetric in implementation experience: formal principles of equity and benefit sharing collide with as-built financing, maintenance, and interpretation disputes. pancheshwar remains the emblematic large joint project whose stall shows how sovereignty, resettlement, benefit splits, and India's internal federal politics can freeze decades of studies into zero concrete storage. # India as decisive actor; China as absent partner india-energy-relationship is decisive for cross-border trade, transmission corridors, grid codes, and perceptions of security. China's role in Nepal hydro has been receding, not growing: China Three Gorges withdrew from west-seti in 2018; China Gezhouba was blocked from budhigandaki on political grounds. No major Chinese-linked storage project is currently under active construction in Nepal. India, meanwhile, has expanded its presence: NHPC took over West Seti (2022), SJVN is building the 900 MW Arun-3, and India's Power Grid Corporation agreed in April 2025 to build high-capacity cross-border transmission. The triangulation is not symmetric: India can veto or complicate Chinese-backed projects through market access, transmission denial, and geopolitical pressure, while China has no equivalent lever over India-backed schemes. Nepal's ability to play one against the other is limited in practice — a finding that tempers the "strategic leverage" narrative. # Bhutan as comparator, not clone bhutan-hydropower-model illustrates how export-led hydro can work when fiscal rules, load management, and a patron relationship align. Nepal's larger population, internal political fragmentation, and different downstream co-riparian geometry mean copy-paste is misleading—but the comparison clarifies that governance is where opportunity is won or lost. # Basin anchors Transboundary technical narratives often anchor on koshi-basin as the hazard–sediment–irrigation nexus par excellence. Hydro-geopolitics is therefore not a "soft" add-on to power-sector economics; it is frequently the binding constraint on what can be built, financed, and operated.

Interaction with AD Penalties and Force Majeure
pages.excerpt: The insurance market for Nepal's hydropower sector — mandatory coverage requirements, premium escalation, claim settlement failures, and the systemic interaction with AD penalties and debt service obligations. The central connection is to nea-triple-authority: when physical damag
pages.body_text: Hydro Insurance # Summary The insurance market for Nepal's hydropower sector — mandatory coverage requirements, premium escalation, claim settlement failures, and the systemic interaction with AD penalties and debt service obligations. The central connection is to nea-triple-authority: when physical damage prevents generation, NEA may still apply AD penalties while the insurer delays settlement, draining the developer's working capital from both sides. # Simple Explanation Hydropower projects need insurance because floods, landslides, GLOFs, and equipment failures can stop generation. The concept matters because insurance is not just a safety net: rising premiums, delayed claims, and lender requirements can become a major financial stress for IPPs. # Premium Burden — Verified Project-Level Data Two verified data points establish the insurance premium burden on operational hydro projects: project | gross_revenue_npr | annual_premium_npr | premium_pct_revenue | fiscal_year | source | ---|---|---|---|---|---| Sanima Mai HPP | 764,000,000 | 13,770,000 | 1.80% | FY2023 | CARE Ratings Nepal + Sanima Reliance Life disclosures | Upper Tamakoshi | 8,678,000,000 | 99,000,000 | 1.14% | FY2080 | UTKHPL Annual Report | For infrastructure assets with 85%+ PBILDT margins, an insurance line consuming 1.8% of top-line revenue represents 10–12% of the entire operating cost envelope. Hydro project finance models assume minimal variable OPEX once construction is complete — insurance premium escalation directly compresses the DSCR headroom these models depend on. # Market Structure and the Premium Surge The premium surge originated from two simultaneous events: 1. Mandatory minimum premium policy introduced FY2078 BS by Beema Samiti (now Nepal Insurance Authority). This set statutory minimum premium floors across the hydro sector regardless of individual project risk profiles. 2. International reinsurer withdrawal from Nepal hydro risk portfolios post-2021, driven by accumulated flood, landslide, and GLOF loss experience. This removed the competitive pricing pressure that had previously kept domestic premiums manageable. Consequence: Nepal Re and Himalayan Re were ordered to raise paid-up capital from NPR 13 billion to NPR 20 billion to absorb the reinsurance gap. Source: Insurance Khabar (English edition). On the "800% surge" claim: This figure has no locatable primary source. IPPAN's documented public statements (Ekantipur/Kantipur, April 2025) cite "up to 500%" as the maximum increase. This figure should be used in preference to the 800% figure. [PARTIALLY VERIFIED: sourced to IPPAN lobbying statement, not independent actuarial calculation.] Data accessibility note: The IPPAN digital news archive (ippan.org.np/news/) was completely inaccessible during the research pass due to server timeout. Primary IPPAN documentation requires direct access to the IPPAN Secretariat in Kathmandu or retrieval of the specific Beema Samiti minimum tariff directive. This is flagged as a data transparency gap. # Market Concentration Shikhar Insurance Company Limited is the dominant non-life insurer in Nepal, collecting NPR 4.80 billion in premium in an 8-month period (FY2080/81 annual: NPR 5.25 billion). Source: Investopaper / Shikhar Insurance Annual Reports. The 14 non-life insurance companies in Nepal collectively collected over NPR 31.70 billion in premiums by the close of Falgun FY2082/83, reflecting a 13.11% year-over-year expansion. Source: Nepal Insurance Authority (NIA) via Insurance Khabar. The banking sector's requirement for comprehensive project insurance as a loan disbursement condition creates a captive market for domestic insurers. IPPs cannot self-insure or go uninsured without triggering lender covenant breaches — giving domestic insurers effective pricing power without competitive constraint. # Claim Settlement Delays The "90% claim settlement delays" claim circulating in industry discussions has not been numerically verified. No named project claim case — with documented damage, filing date, settlement date, and financial impact during the gap — has been found in research passes to date. The Nepal Insurance Authority (NIA) has recognized the systemic threat and proposed developmental roadmaps, but no market-making intervention has been implemented. [Under research — awaiting named claim cases and NIA settlement data.] # Interaction with AD Penalties and Force Majeure Whether the PPA contains force majeure or physical damage exemption from AD penalties during the insurance claim settlement period is unresolved. This is the mirror image of the ad-penalties curtailment double-bind: a damaged project unable to generate may simultaneously face AD penalty invoices from NEA while waiting for an insurance payout, draining working capital from both sides. [Under research — awaiting PPA clause text for force majeure and AD exemption language.] # Analytical links ad-penalties — the penalty mechanism that may compound insurance gaps nea-triple-authority — the institutional framework of NEA as off-taker and penalty administrator # Common Misunderstandings Insurance does not remove project risk. It can shift some losses, but premium cost, exclusions, and settlement delays still affect cash flow. A claim is not the same as cash in hand. Delayed settlement can matter as much as the covered amount. Hydro insurance is not separate from PPA risk. Physical damage can interact with AD penalties, debt service, and off-taker receivables.

pages.title: Hydropower Potential Categories
pages.excerpt: “Nepal has 83,000 MW” is a political slogan and a methodological landmine. Hydropower potential categories exist precisely because theoretical river power is not the same as financeable capacity, buildable projects, or firm winter electricity (see firm-power).
pages.body_text: Hydropower Potential Categories # Summary “Nepal has 83,000 MW” is a political slogan and a methodological landmine. Hydropower potential categories exist precisely because theoretical river power is not the same as financeable capacity, buildable projects, or firm winter electricity (see firm-power). # Simple Explanation Hydropower potential is a stack of increasingly strict filters. A river may have theoretical energy, but that does not mean a project can be engineered, financed, permitted, connected to the grid, or depended on in the dry season. # The reduction pyramid (conceptual chain) Think of a pyramid—quantified in data-potential-pyramid—where each step applies filters the previous step ignores: 1. Theoretical / gross potential — legacy national figures near ~83,000 MW appear in older discourse; WECS (2019) reframed theoretical potential around ~72,500 MW depending on methodological choices. 2. Technical potential — what is physically plausible with conventional technology; commonly discussed in the ~42,000–46,000 MW range in national studies (exact bounds depend on site database and assumptions). 3. Techno-economic potential — WECS (2019) reports 32,680 MW at this layer: sites that meet engineering and economic screening rules as modeled. 4. Economically viable (market window) — often discussed as ~25,000–35,000 MW under price and financing assumptions that move with interest rates, carbon policy, and India import terms. 5. Realistically developable by ~2040 — planning horizons frequently land around ~10,000–15,000 MW once execution risk, transmission, and social license are acknowledged. 6. Installed — roughly ~3,591 MW hydro installed (order-of-magnitude anchor for “today”). These categories are not interchangeable. Moving down the chain is not “being conservative”; it is changing the question. # Basin concentration A large share of gross potential concentrates in three major basins—koshi-basin, karnali-basin, and gandaki-basin—often cited on the order of ~94% of national potential. That concentration matters for cascade externalities, sediment, and geopolitical export corridors: “national potential” is geographically lumpy. # Why this matters for analysis Potential-category discipline prevents two common failures: inflating creditworthiness with theoretical MW, and confusing annual energy with dry-season dependability. Primary methodology and citations live under wecs-hydropower-potential-2019. # Common Misunderstandings Theoretical MW is not a build plan. It is the least filtered number in the chain. Technical potential is not the same as bankable potential. Financing, transmission, social license, and market value still apply. Installed MW is not firm winter power. Seasonal output and dispatchability determine how much capacity actually helps in dry months.

pages.title: IPO Hydropower Bailout
pages.excerpt: How Initial Public Offerings (IPOs) and rights share issuances in Nepal's hydropower sector are used to transfer project debt risk onto retail investors — and why the "Chilime success model" is not replicable.
pages.body_text: IPO Hydropower Bailout # Summary How Initial Public Offerings (IPOs) and rights share issuances in Nepal's hydropower sector are used to transfer project debt risk onto retail investors — and why the "Chilime success model" is not replicable. This page is under research. Verifiable data on IPO use-of-funds is blocked by SEBON's systemic use of non-machine-readable scanned PDFs for critical financial disclosures — frustrating automated accountability tracking. # Simple Explanation The concept describes a pattern where stressed hydropower companies raise money from public investors after project delays, weak generation, or debt pressure. The concern is that public equity can become a rescue channel for projects whose risks were not clearly priced or disclosed. # What is known Six hydro companies have issued IPOs and subsequent rights shares, documented in SEBON and NEPSE registries: Company | Capacity (MW) | IPO Year | IPO Amount (NPR Cr) | Rights Year | Rights Amount (NPR Cr) | Stated Use | ---|---|---|---|---|---|---| Rasuwagadhi | 111 | 2018 | 66 | — | — | Construction funding; delayed COD | Ankhu Khola Jalvidhyut | 8.4 | 2013 | 20 | 2024 | 120 (1:1.5) | Pay off bank loans | Peoples Power Ltd | 4.96 | 2022 | 31.6 | 2024 | 15.8 (1:0.5) | Repay commercial bank debt | Joshi Hydropower | 3 | 2018 | 24.1 | 2024 | 15.6 (1:0.65) | Prevent NPL status | Terhathum Power | 7.5 | 2021 | 12 | 2024 | 12 (1:1) | Blended debt restructuring | [UNVERIFIED: entries above compiled from media and secondary rating agency sources — SEBON prospectuses not independently audited.] NEPSE has suspended trading on multiple hydro companies: Upper Syange Hydropower (USHL) for insider trading and delayed disclosure of rights share bailout plans; Khani Khola Hydropower (KKHC) amid controversial Q4 reporting and promoter share dumping. # The Chilime contrast Chilime Hydropower's 2010 IPO occurred after seven years of profitable operations and distributed a 35% dividend within a year. Modern IPOs float pre-revenue, when the project is hemorrhaging cash from capitalized interest. See chilime for the pre-IPO profitability context and q-design-discharge for why Chilime's overperformance is not replicable. # The triple-authority blindspot Retail investors purchasing rights shares in distressed companies are not informed that the off-taker (NEA) can curtail the project and then penalize it for non-generation. IPO prospectuses project future revenue using the PPA tariff but do not model the scenario where a portion of that revenue is clawed back through AD penalties. See nea-triple-authority for the institutional framework and ad-penalties for the penalty mechanism. # What is missing The primary blocker is SEBON's non-machine-readable PDF filing system. Key questions that remain unresolvable without primary source access: What percentage of IPO/rights proceeds was actually used to retire promoter bridge loans vs bank debt vs new project investment? What risk disclosures about hydrological underperformance, PPA rate risk, and AD penalty exposure appear in hydro IPO prospectuses? What is the full list of NEPSE-listed hydro companies that issued rights shares within 3 years of IPO? What is NRB's specialized hydro loan book — the true extent of off-balance-sheet restructuring and informal forbearance? [Under research — awaiting SEBON prospectus data extraction or regulatory reform mandating machine-readable disclosures.] # Common Misunderstandings An IPO is not automatically a growth investment. In distressed hydro cases, proceeds or later rights shares may function as balance-sheet repair. The Chilime example is not automatically replicable. Chilime listed after profitable operations; many newer projects list before stable earnings. Retail participation does not prove risk transparency. Non-machine-readable filings and weak use-of-funds data limit independent scrutiny.

pages.title: Load Shedding Era
headings: The End of Shedding Was Not the End of the Problem
pages.excerpt: Nepal's electricity crisis of 2008–2018 is the historical backdrop against which every later development — the IPP boom, the trade transformation, the stranded generation problem, and the seasonal mismatch — must be read. The country did not drift into surplus from comfort. It br
pages.body_text: Load Shedding Era Nepal's electricity crisis of 2008–2018 is the historical backdrop against which every later development — the IPP boom, the trade transformation, the stranded generation problem, and the seasonal mismatch — must be read. The country did not drift into surplus from comfort. It broke out of a decade of forced power cuts that cost roughly a full year's GDP. # The Crisis in Numbers Metric | Value | Source | --------|-------|--------| Peak daily load shedding | 14–18 hours/day (2009–2016) | World Bank CGE model (timilsina-cge-load-shedding-2021) | Total GDP lost 2008–2016 | ~US$11 billion | Timilsina et al. 2021 | Annual GDP loss (average) | ~7% of GDP per year at peak | Timilsina et al. 2021 | Annual cost (worst) | US$1.6 billion/year | World Bank ESRF | Investment suppression | Annual investment 48% below potential | CGE model result | Scheduled load shedding ended | 2018 | wb-country-economic-memo-2025, nea-annual-report-fy2024-25 | The $11 billion cumulative GDP loss is roughly equivalent to Nepal's entire 2008 GDP. The era was not a footnote — it was a macroeconomic event comparable in scale to a major natural disaster, but spread across a decade. # What Ended It The end of scheduled load shedding was not a single policy decision. It was the confluence of three forces arriving together around 2018: 1. Improved NEA dispatch and load management — better scheduling, reduced technical losses, and more disciplined demand forecasting. 2. IPP commissioning wave — projects licensed during the 1990s and 2000s reached completion, adding hundreds of megawatts of new generation, most notably upper-tamakoshi (456 MW, commissioned 2021). 3. Indian import access — India's cross-border electricity trade guidelines (2016/2018) allowed Nepal to use Indian grid power as a dry-season backstop while domestic generation ramped. # The End of Shedding Was Not the End of the Problem Scheduled load shedding ended in 2018, but 76% of firms still reported regular power outages as late as 2022 (wb-country-economic-memo-2025). The shift was from chronic shortage to fragile seasonal surplus — a system that can export in the monsoon but still imports in the dry season, a system where generation curtailment replaces load shedding as the binding waste, and a system where the institutional architecture built for scarcity has not been reformed for surplus. That transition — from shortage-era survival to surplus-era structure — is the arc the rest of this wiki traces. # The Load-Shedding Legacy Today The crisis shapes Nepal's electricity system in ways that persist: IPP acceleration was a crisis response. The state could not build fast enough, so private developers were brought in. The regulatory architecture (PPA terms, single-buyer model, AD penalties) was designed for shortage-era discipline, not surplus-era efficiency. The industrial demand deficit traces to the shedding era. Nepal's industry still burns coal and biomass because the grid was historically unreliable (14 hours/day of outages). See data-industrial-electricity-consumers and energy-substitution-pathway. The "reliability premium" persists in political memory. Every policy conversation about export vs. domestic use, about storage vs. RoR, about solar vs. hydro, carries the implicit question: could this return us to 14-hour cuts? NEA's institutional culture was forged in the shedding era. The utility learned to control scarcity. It has not yet learned to manage surplus. See nea-triple-authority. # Related nepal-energy-profile — the post-crisis system snapshot upper-tamakoshi — the plant that broke the shedding era seasonal-mismatch — the structural pattern that persists beyond shedding stranded-generation — the surplus-era waste that replaced shortage-era cuts nea-triple-authority — the institutional architecture built in the shortage era data-industrial-electricity-consumers — the industrial demand suppressed by a decade of outages data-trade-time-series — the import-to-exporter transformation

pages.title: NEA Triple-Authority Conflict
headings: The incentive to favor NEA-owned generation
pages.excerpt: The NEA Triple-Authority Conflict describes how the Nepal Electricity Authority simultaneously holds three powers over private hydropower producers (IPPs) that, in a well-designed market, would be separated across independent institutions:
pages.body_text: NEA Triple-Authority Conflict # Summary The NEA Triple-Authority Conflict describes how the Nepal Electricity Authority simultaneously holds three powers over private hydropower producers (IPPs) that, in a well-designed market, would be separated across independent institutions: 1. Dispatcher — through the National Load Dispatch Centre (NLDC), NEA decides which plants run and which are curtailed. 2. Single Buyer — under the standard PPA framework, NEA is the sole off-taker. IPPs cannot sell to third parties, enter direct corporate PPAs, or export independently. 3. Penalty Administrator — NEA calculates, levies, and deducts Availability Declaration (AD) penalties from IPP receivables. The same entity controls the physical flow of electrons, the commercial flow of money, and the enforcement flow of penalties. No independent arbiter exists between these roles. # Simple Explanation NEA is not only a buyer of electricity. It also decides dispatch and can deduct penalties from project payments. The conflict arises because one institution can tell a private generator not to run, buy all of its power under the PPA system, and then enforce penalties when generation falls short. # The structural double-bind When NEA exercises role (1) to curtail a project — citing grid stability, N-1 transmission limits, or low domestic demand — the project's revenue stops. When NEA then exercises role (3), it can apply AD penalties for the generation shortfall that it itself ordered. Because role (2) guarantees no alternative market, the IPP cannot recoup the loss elsewhere. The standard PPA contains no explicit exemption clause protecting an IPP from AD penalties when the root cause of the generation shortfall was an NLDC/NEA curtailment instruction. Exhaustive reviews of legacy PPA templates have not found such a carve-out. This means NEA can legally order a project off-line and legally extract cash for it being off-line, in the same transaction. # The incentive to favor NEA-owned generation NEA generates approximately 34% of national power through its own plants and subsidiaries. When NLDC dispatches an NEA-subsidiary plant, NEA pays itself — no cash leaves the institution. When NLDC dispatches a private IPP, NEA must release budget funds. The structure gives NEA a built-in incentive to prioritize its own output, particularly during periods of surplus when curtailment decisions must be made. This structural favoritism has been independently verified in academic audit. The Fenner School of Environment and Society (Australian National University), Nepal State of Knowledge Report — Renewables and PSH, states: "The major complaint of the rising IPPs is that the playing field is not level, that NEA as generator, transmitter and distributor gives preferential terms to its own projects compared to IPPs; and indeed, this is seen in the case of the Chilime hydropower company that is owned by the NEA and its staff." Citation: Fenner School of Environment and Society, ANU, Nepal State of Knowledge Report — Renewables and PSH, p. 20. URL: https://fennerschool.anu.edu.au/files/Nepal%20State%20of%20Knowledge%20Report%20-%20Renewables%20%26%20PSH.pdf. No published merit order or dispatch protocol exists. NLDC's curtailment decisions affecting billions of rupees in annual revenue are made without public criteria. Neither the Auditor General nor any parliamentary committee has formally investigated dispatch discrimination. # Primary case study: Barahi Hydropower The Barahi Hydropower case provides the wiki's primary audited documentation of this double-bind in operation. NEA deducted AD penalties from a sub-10 MW project despite an explicit ERC statutory exemption (ERC Bylaws 2076, Clause 8(2)), and the project was forced to classify the deductions as "receivable from NEA" — a forced loan to the off-taker. See ad-penalties for full case detail and barahi-hydropower for the entity page. # The AD penalty formula The standard penalty formula documented in investment and tender materials is: Penalty = (0.8 × Contracted Energy − Electricity Output) × Electricity Tariff If a project's generation falls beneath 80% of its contracted energy (or declared availability, depending on the specific PPA tier), the developer pays a penalty effectively equal to the revenue of the undelivered power. These penalties are deducted directly from trade receivables owed by NEA — not remitted to an independent fund. Industry sources assert that AD penalties can consume up to 16% of project revenue. This figure is not a statutory ceiling — it is an IPPAN-circulated aggregate derived from the PPA penalty formula: Penalty = (0.80 × contracted − actual) × tariff. Exhaustive search of IPPAN, ERC, ICRA/CARE, and media sources confirms no legal cap or named project case study verifying a 16% ceiling exists. The figure represents the formula's mathematical outcome during severe dry-season shortfalls, not a codified statutory limit. The penalty impact is variable and project-specific. See ad-penalties. # The metrological impossibility The AD system requires generators to declare their available generation 30 days in advance. For a run-of-river project with no storage reservoir, predicting daily output in a Himalayan monsoon watershed 30 days ahead is not an engineering failure — it is an inherently unsolvable forecasting problem. The ERC formally acknowledged this for small projects, amending by-laws to allow plants under 10 MW to declare availability one week in advance and exempting them from financial damages. However, the Barahi case demonstrates that even explicit statutory exemption does not prevent NEA from deducting penalties when the institutional structure gives it unilateral power over cash disbursement. # Reform models A healthy market would separate the three functions: Independent system operator (ISO) — dispatch decisions separated from NEA's commercial interests. Multiple buyers or open access — IPPs able to sell to alternative off-takers (industrial consumers, export markets, trading companies). Neutral penalty authority — AD enforcement managed by the ERC or an independent entity, not the off-taker. The 2003 World Bank Nepal power sector review recommended "eliminating conflicts of interest" in NEA's structure. The draft 2025 Open Access policy envisions moving beyond the single-buyer model. No legislation implementing these reforms has been enacted. # Analytical links The Triple-Authority Conflict is the institutional mechanism underlying: stranded-generation — curtailment without compensation seasonal-arbitrage-trap — pricing structure that extracts value from IPPs ad-penalties — the penalty mechanics enforced through this conflict ppa-pricing — rate-setting by the same entity that enforces performance upper-tamakoshi — Nepal's largest plant: NEA as regulator set the tariff, NEA as shareholder (41%) saw equity diluted by IDC, NEA as off-taker buys at rates that can't service the debt. Three roles, one institution, zero resolution mechanism. khimti-i — the 1996 USD PPA that predates the triple-authority regime entirely chilime — NEA subsidiary with legacy billing architecture yielding 37% revenue advantage barahi-hydropower — primary audited case study of penalty enforcement sahas-urja — why the standard IPP rate succeeds only at exceptional scale, not as a replicable model chameliya-hydropower — state capital inefficiency absorbed off-balance sheet while private developers face rigid caps hydro-insurance — the insurance market failure that compounds the financial squeeze when NEA applies penalties during claim settlement gaps # Common Misunderstandings The conflict is structural, not just a claim of bad intent. The same institution holds roles that would normally be separated. Curtailment and AD penalties are linked. A generator can lose output because of dispatch decisions and still face penalty exposure if the contract does not carve out that cause. NEA ownership matters because dispatch has cash consequences. Dispatching an NEA plant and dispatching an IPP have different institutional cash-flow effects.

pages.title: Nepal Power Trade Schemes
headings: Generator-facing wholesale channels named in the IPSDP
Commercial modes layered on top of those channels
Why this matters to the wiki
pages.excerpt: In Section 2.4 of moewri-ipsdp-exec-summary-2025, the IPSDP does two different but related things. It names three generator-facing wholesale customer categories, and it separately describes the commercial modes those channels may use, including exchange-market sales and long-term
pages.body_text: Nepal Power Trade Schemes # Summary In Section 2.4 of moewri-ipsdp-exec-summary-2025, the IPSDP does two different but related things. It names three generator-facing wholesale customer categories, and it separately describes the commercial modes those channels may use, including exchange-market sales and long-term PPAs. # Simple Explanation Nepal power trade is not one single export mechanism. The IPSDP describes a mixed structure where power can move through NEA, trading companies, or direct overseas buyers, and those channels can use either long-term PPAs or more market-linked sales. # Generator-facing wholesale channels named in the IPSDP Channel | Buyer | How the PDF frames it | ---------|-------|------------------------| NEA default | nea | Conventional domestic trade. NEA buys power, serves the domestic market, and exports surplus itself. Lowest administrative burden for smaller projects. | Power-trading company | Nepal trading company such as NPTCL | A future channel in which trading companies intermediate between generators and markets. The PDF explicitly says sales may be either PPA-based or market-linked. | Direct overseas trade | DISCOs or large customers in India/Bangladesh | A generator deals directly with overseas buyers. The PDF ties this to larger projects, investor participation, and more complex transmission and contracting requirements. | # Commercial modes layered on top of those channels The executive summary then adds a second distinction that should not be collapsed into the buyer categories above: Long-term PPA mode: PPAs with NEA, with a trading company, or directly with foreign distribution companies / major customers. Market-linked mode: power sold through trading-company arrangements into exchange-style markets such as IEX, including the green-market discussion in the surrounding text. That is why the section reads as more than a simple "three-scheme" menu. The PDF clearly names three buyer categories, but it also makes room for multiple price-setting and dispatch arrangements inside them. # Why this matters to the wiki It clarifies that Nepal is not moving from one monolithic single-buyer system to one monolithic export system. The IPSDP is imagining a mixed commercial stack. It sharpens india-energy-relationship and bangladesh-trade-route by showing that cross-border trade is not just a transmission problem; it is also a buyer-structure and contract-structure problem. It explains why niettp and other interconnection corridors are enabling infrastructure rather than the whole trade model by themselves. # Confidence boundary This page sticks to what the executive summary says explicitly on pages 24-26. It does not claim that Nepal has already implemented this market structure. The document is a planning frame, not proof of execution. # Common Misunderstandings Trade schemes are not the same as transmission corridors. Lines enable trade, but buyer structure and contract mode determine how trade works. Direct overseas trade is not already normal practice. In this page it is an IPSDP planning category, not proof of implementation. Market-linked sales and long-term PPAs are different commercial modes. They should not be collapsed into one generic export bucket. # Related india-energy-relationship bangladesh-trade-route niettp seasonal-arbitrage-trap

pages.title: Peak Water
headings: Mechanism: more melt before less water
Why it matters for hydropower planning
The Karnali decomposition: what "glacier-fed" actually means
pages.excerpt: Peak water (in the glacio-hydrological sense used across Hindu Kush-Himalaya work) is the period when a glacierized catchment reaches maximum annual meltwater yield before long-term decline sets in. It is not "peak" in the oil-depletion sense of a single day; it is a multi-decade
pages.body_text: Peak Water # Summary Peak water (in the glacio-hydrological sense used across Hindu Kush-Himalaya work) is the period when a glacierized catchment reaches maximum annual meltwater yield before long-term decline sets in. It is not "peak" in the oil-depletion sense of a single day; it is a multi-decade phase where retreat temporarily increases exposed ice area and melt efficiency, then yields to shrinking ice volume and lower dry-season baseflows. # Simple Explanation As glaciers shrink, they can temporarily release more meltwater before the stored ice is depleted. For hydropower planning, that means some basins may look strong for a few decades while the long-term dry-season buffer is actually weakening. # Mechanism: more melt before less water As glaciers retreat, many basins first see higher annual melt — more energy at the surface, longer melt seasons, reconfiguration of flow paths — before entering a regime where ice storage is depleted and late-century flows fall, especially in the low-flow months that hydropower and irrigation care about most. For most Nepal river basins, literature and regional assessments commonly place peak water between ~2040 and 2070, with uncertainty driven by emissions pathway, debris cover, and sub-grid hypsometry. # Why it matters for hydropower planning Nepal's dominant fleet is sensitive to intra-annual and inter-annual hydrographs; see seasonal-mismatch. Peak water defines a planning window: roughly 20-40 years during which glacial contribution is near its maximum for many catchments — not a stable eternity, but a phase where high-head, glacier-fed rivers can look deceptively "strong" in mean annual flow statistics. The climate-rational engineering strategy is dual: 1. Build and finance during peak water where projects clear benefit, consent, and hazard screens — because energy and water yields for glacier-dependent schemes are comparatively favorable. 2. Design for post-peak decline — reservoir operating rules, sediment management, environmental flows, and downstream expectations must assume a worsening dry-season regime, not a stationary 20th-century hydrograph. Basin-specific discharge framing lives in koshi-basin and karnali-basin pages; cryosphere evidence synthesis is anchored on icimod-hkh-glacier-change. # Hazards ride the same trend Retreat does not only alter means; it reconfigures risk. Lake formation, moraine instability, and cascading processes connect peak-water-era construction to glof-risk: the same decades that maximize certain yields also maximize some tail-risk exposures unless design assumptions are updated. Glacial lake area has been expanding at ~0.83%/year since 1987 — a slow accumulation of potential energy with episodic catastrophic release. # Orders of magnitude for urgency Quantitative markers from recent Himalayan climate reviews and ICIMOD: Indicator | Value | Confidence | -----------|-------|------------| Nepal temperature rise rate | 0.02–0.16 °C/year (recent decades) | Moderate — regional variation wide | HKH glacier mass balance | −0.3 to −0.8 m water-equivalent/year | Moderate — peer-reviewed | Glacial lake area expansion | ~0.83%/year since 1987 | Moderate — satellite-derived | Nepal glacier area (1980s -> 2010) | 5,168.3 -> 3,902.4 km² (−24.5%) | Moderate — inventory comparison | Snow/ice cover decline (Nepal) | ~40% documented | Medium — boundary definition varies | Long-run volume loss (high emissions) | ~65% by 2100 across HKH | Low precision — model range is wide | HKH glacier area loss 1990-2020 | ~12% | Moderate — ICIMOD aggregates | The policy point is not precision to the third decimal: it is that Nepal's hydropower golden window is time-bounded and should be used to build durable domestic value, not only nameplate MW. # The Karnali decomposition: what "glacier-fed" actually means A peer-reviewed high-resolution hydrological decomposition of the Karnali basin breaks long-term discharge into contributions: Rainfall runoff: ~40% Baseflow (groundwater): ~35% Snowmelt: ~24% (peaks pre-monsoon, buffers late dry season) Glacier ice melt: ~0.8% of annual volume This is the corrective to the "glacier-fed = reliable" assumption. Glacier ice melt is a tiny share of annual Karnali flow — snowmelt and baseflow are the real dry-season buffers. As warming shifts more precipitation from snow to rain at high elevations and depletes snowpack, the dry-season buffer degrades even before glacier volume is substantially reduced. The near-term risk is loss of snowmelt buffer, not yet major glacier volume loss — the timing of this risk is earlier than most public narratives acknowledge. # Climate change and seasonal amplification Recent climate synthesis points to this directional consensus: Monsoon precipitation: likely to intensify (heavier events, more flood risk), while total annual rainfall shows mixed regional trends Snowpack: declining as warming shifts precipitation from snow to rain at progressively higher elevations Net seasonal effect: wetter wet seasons, drier dry seasons — amplifying seasonal-mismatch over time Hydropower implication: more extreme flood risk in monsoon (structural and safety design), more acute lean-season deficit (reliability design) — both costs rise simultaneously The seasonal-mismatch that already defines Nepal's energy problem today will structurally worsen over the planning horizon. Storage becomes more valuable, not less, as climate instability increases. # Common Misunderstandings Peak water is not one peak day or one flood. It is a multi-decade hydrological phase. Glacier-fed does not mean permanently reliable. Snowmelt, baseflow, and seasonal precipitation matter more than glacier ice volume in many annual-flow budgets. Higher near-term melt does not remove long-term risk. The same warming that can raise meltwater for a period also depletes the storage that supports future dry-season flows.

pages.title: PPA Pricing
headings: NEA Internal Generation Cost vs Commercial PPA Rates
NEA Subsidiary vs Private IPP Differential Analysis
The billing architecture is the mechanism, not the rate
pages.excerpt: Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) pricing in Nepal is set project-by-project through bilateral negotiation between developers and NEA, without a publicly disclosed cost-reflective formula (prior to the 2026 ERC Directive). Rates are differentiated by season (wet/dry) and project typ
pages.body_text: PPA Pricing # Summary Power Purchase Agreement (PPA) pricing in Nepal is set project-by-project through bilateral negotiation between developers and NEA, without a publicly disclosed cost-reflective formula (prior to the 2026 ERC Directive). Rates are differentiated by season (wet/dry) and project type, with significant structural divergence between NEA subsidiaries and private IPPs. # Simple Explanation When a private company builds a hydropower plant in Nepal, NEA signs a contract to buy the electricity at a fixed rate. That rate is different in the wet season (when rivers are full) and the dry season (when they're low). But the rate isn't set by a public formula — it's negotiated bilaterally. And NEA's own subsidiary companies often get better terms than private developers, creating a two-tier market. # Common Misunderstandings "PPA rates are market prices." They are regulated, negotiated tariffs — not set by competitive auction or spot market dynamics. "All projects get the same rate." NEA subsidiaries (like Chilime) use different billing architectures that produce structurally higher blended rates than private IPPs. "Lower PPA rates are always better for consumers." Rates below cost of capital deter investment, lengthen project timelines, and can increase system risk. How Power Purchase Agreement rates are set for hydropower projects in Nepal — and whether rate-setting follows an economic formula or a discretionary process. The central institutional framework is nea-triple-authority: the same entity that sets PPA rates (NEA as single buyer) is also the penalty enforcer and dispatcher. # PPA Rate Comparison Table Nepal's Power Purchase Agreement rates are set project-by-project through bilateral negotiation between the developer and NEA, without a publicly disclosed cost-reflective formula prior to 2026. The table below compiles verified PPA rates from primary sources. Rates marked with escalation notes reflect the initial contracted rate; actual current rates will be higher for projects within their escalation window. project | capacity_mw | ppa_wet_npr_kwh | ppa_dry_npr_kwh | ppa_blended_npr_kwh | entity_type | ppa_year | escalation | source | confidence | ---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| Chilime Hydropower | 22.1 | 4.08 (Excess) | 8.17 (Regular) | 7.57 (derived FY2078/79) | NEA_subsidiary | 1997 | No escalation clause found in legacy contract | Chilime Annual Report FY2078/79 | VERIFIED | Sanima Mai — Mai HPP | 22.0 | 4.80 (promo, expired mid-Apr 2022) → 5.08 (current) | 8.40 → 8.89 (current) | — | private_IPP | 2010 | 3% × 5 years promotional, then standard escalation | CARE Ratings Nepal Apr 2025 | VERIFIED | Sanima Mai — Mai Cascade | 7.0 | 5.52 | 9.66 | — | private_IPP | 2013 | 3% annual | CARE Ratings Nepal | VERIFIED | Rasuwagadhi | 111.0 | 4.80 | 8.40 | — | NEA_subsidiary | 2011 | 3% × 8 years | ShareSansar / NEA Annual Report | VERIFIED | Upper Trishuli 3A | 60.0 | N/A (internal transfer pricing) | N/A | N/A | NEA_owned | N/A | N/A | NEA Annual Report 2021/22 | VERIFIED | Nyadi Hydropower | 30.0 | 4.80 | 8.40 | — | private_IPP | 2015 | 3% × 8 years | CARE Ratings Nepal Oct 2024 | VERIFIED | Sahas Urja (Solu Khola) | 86.0 | 4.80 | 8.40 | ~5.1 (implied from 520 GWh design and NPR 2.648B revenue) | private_IPP | 2015 | 3% × 8 years, retained via on-time COD | ICRA Nepal A.996 and B.119 | VERIFIED | Upper Tamakoshi | 456.0 | 3.63 | 6.96 | — | NEA_subsidiary | ~2012 | — | UKHLL Annual Report | VERIFIED | Upper Chameliya (Api Power) | 40.0 | 4.00–4.80 | 7.00–8.40 | — | private_IPP | ~2020 | 3% annual | CARE/ICRA Nepal rating rationales | PARTIALLY VERIFIED | NOTE 1 — Trishuli 3A and Chameliya classification: Upper Trishuli 3A (60 MW) and Chameliya Hydropower (30 MW) are directly NEA-owned generation assets, not independent corporate entities. They use internal transfer pricing based on cost of generation rather than commercial PPAs. Trishuli 3A is frequently confused with Trishuli Jal Vidhyut Company Limited (37 MW, the 3B cascade), which IS a subsidiary entity with a standard commercial PPA at NPR 4.80/8.40. Similarly, Chameliya (NEA-owned, 30 MW, Darchula) is frequently confused with Upper Chameliya (Api Power, 40 MW, private IPP), which DOES have a commercial PPA. Prior research cycles carried an erroneous NPR 8.85/5.40 rate for Chameliya — this figure is a data hallucination derived from misattributed retail consumer tariffs in the NEA Annual Report FY2016/17. Chameliya has no commercial PPA. Source: NEA Generation Directorate Report 2080/2081 (16th Issue, 2024). See chameliya-hydropower. NOTE 2 — Sanima Mai promotional tariff expiry: The Mai HPP (22 MW) initially operated under a government promotional tariff of NPR 4.80 wet / 8.40 dry. This expired mid-April 2022 after 7 years from COD. The current active rate of NPR 5.08/8.89 reflects accumulated escalations post-expiry. The promotional tariff mechanism — and its expiry — is itself a structural feature of Nepal's PPA framework, not an anomaly. NOTE 3 — Sahas Urja reframing: Sahas Urja operates on the identical base rate as Nyadi and Rasuwagadhi (NPR 4.80/8.40). Its superior financial performance (NPR 902M net profit on NPR 2.648B revenue, FY2023/24) is entirely attributable to cost efficiency (NPR 172–175M/MW build cost vs industry average NPR 200–300M/MW) and scale (86 MW generating large absolute dry-season cash flows despite a ~19% dry energy mix). Sahas Urja does not demonstrate that the standard IPP PPA rate is viable — it demonstrates that the rate is only viable at exceptional scale and cost discipline unavailable to most developers. See sahas-urja. NOTE 4 — Upper Chameliya seasonal modality: Unlike the standard 8-month wet / 4-month dry split, Api Power's Upper Chameliya PPA uses a 6-month wet / 6-month dry modality, with the dry-season rate mathematically double the wet-season rate. This significantly bolsters the blended tariff average and enhances cash flow for commercial debt service. Source: CARE Ratings Nepal. [PARTIALLY VERIFIED: exact base rate is a range rather than single confirmed figure — CARE/ICRA rationales give wet ~NPR 4.00–4.80, dry ~NPR 7.00–8.40.] -- # NEA Internal Generation Cost vs Commercial PPA Rates Directly NEA-owned generation assets do not operate under commercial PPAs. They use internal transfer pricing based on operational cost, royalty, and allocated depreciation — accounting figures that bear no relation to the full capital cost of the asset. These internal generation costs are structurally incomparable to commercial PPA rates and should not appear in rate comparison tables alongside IPP or subsidiary PPAs. The table below shows FY2080/81 internal generation costs for five major NEA-owned assets: NEA Direct Asset | Capacity (MW) | FY2080/81 Generation (MWh) | Total Cost (Million NPR) | Generation Cost (NPR/Unit) | ---|---|---|---|---| Kaligandaki 'A' | 144 | 841,596 | 1,805.87 | 2.15 | Middle Marsyangdi | 70 | 441,127 | 1,684.58 | 3.82 | Upper Trishuli 3A | 60 | 427,055 | 538.62 | 1.26 | Chameliya | 30 | 133,968 | 406.66 | 3.04 | Trishuli | 24 | 117,042 | 316.41 | 2.70 | Source: NEA Generation Directorate Report 2080/2081 (16th Issue, 2024). Why these figures cannot be compared to commercial PPA rates: NEA internal generation costs reflect post-subsidy accounting where sovereign capital failures are absorbed off-balance sheet. The state utility tolerates catastrophic inefficiency in its own construction — Chameliya cost $7.5M/MW vs the global benchmark of $1.5–2.5M/MW — without letting those financial failures reflect in the energy pricing metric. Simultaneously, the NEA enforces rigid PPA caps on private developers who must fully amortize commercial debt at double-digit interest rates. A private IPP that suffered Chameliya's $226M cost overrun on a 30 MW asset would be insolvent at any standard PPA rate. The NEA's own asset registers that same energy at NPR 3.04/kWh. This asymmetry is the quantitative core of the nea-triple-authority governance problem. See chameliya-hydropower. The tariff regime's evolution is best understood through two bookend cases. khimti-i (60 MW, 1996 PPA) — Nepal's first large private IPP — negotiated a USD-denominated tariff (US$0.052–0.059/kWh) with US CPI escalation and no seasonal split, before the NPR 4.80/8.40 standard existed. It generated 103% of contracted energy over 25 years. upper-tamakoshi (456 MW, ~2012 PPA) — Nepal's largest plant — was built at NPR 87–89.4 billion with an effective 88:12 debt-to-equity ratio at commissioning (capitalized interest from an 11-year construction period). At NPR 3.63/6.96/kWh, even 90% of contracted generation cannot cover interest expense. Khimti's PPA was arguably too generous; Upper Tamakoshi's is demonstrably unserviceable. The gap between them is the arc of Nepal's PPA evolution: from attracting first-mover capital at premium terms to imposing rates that cannot sustain the projects they license. # Rate-Setting Mechanism and Regulatory History The Electricity Regulatory Commission (ERC) now vests with rate-setting authority. The "Directive on Electricity Purchase and Sale of Reservoir-Based Power Plants, 2026" (issued 11 February 2026 / Magh 2082 BS) transitions large projects (>100 MW) to a transparent cost-plus determination model — factoring in loan interest, depreciation, foreign exchange risks, and hedging costs. Sub-100 MW reservoir projects are capped at NPR 14.80/kWh (winter) and NPR 8.45/kWh (monsoon). Legacy contracts like Chilime's 1997 PPA remain grandfathered into the system, perpetually skewing the competitive balance. # Royalty and Taxation Schedule Royalties: Electricity Act, 2049 (1992), Section 11 — NPR 100/kW capacity royalty + 2% of average tariff as energy royalty for first 15 years; NPR 1,000/kW capacity royalty + 10% of tariff from year 16 onward. Corporate income tax: 20% rate with 100% rebate for first 10 years of operation and 50% rebate in years 11–15 (Income Tax Act provisions). Free-power provisions (typically 10–22% of generation to the government) are negotiated project-by-project in concession PPAs rather than codified in statute. At end of license (30–35 years), the plant transfers to the state. # NEA Subsidiary vs Private IPP Differential Analysis The PPA rate comparison table reveals a structural divergence in how NEA treats its own subsidiaries versus private IPPs. This differential is not executed through a published discriminatory rate card — the Electricity Act theoretically mandates uniform treatment — but through bespoke contract structuring that allows subsidiaries to bypass seasonal pricing constraints. ## The mathematical proof Take the two clearest comparable cases: NEA subsidiary — Chilime Hydropower (22.1 MW): Chilime's 1997 PPA discards the wet/dry seasonal constraint entirely. Instead, it uses a "Regular" and "Excess" quota system. In FY2078/79, Chilime generated 156.06 GWh — and 85.4% of it (133.24 GWh) was billed at the premium NPR 8.17/kWh Regular rate year-round, regardless of season. Only 22.82 GWh was classified as Excess at NPR 4.08/kWh. Total revenue: NPR 1.18 billion. Blended rate: NPR 7.57/kWh. Private IPP baseline (Nyadi/Sahas Urja model): A standard private RoR IPP is locked into NPR 4.80/kWh (wet) and NPR 8.40/kWh (dry). Assuming an optimized 20% dry energy yield — generous for most Nepalese rivers — the blended rate is: (0.20 × 8.40) + (0.80 × 4.80) = NPR 5.52/kWh. The differential: NPR 2.05/kWh = 37.1% revenue advantage per unit for the NEA subsidiary. For a 50 MW comparable private IPP generating 200 GWh/year, this represents approximately NPR 410 million in foregone annual revenue relative to an identically-sized project that received the Chilime billing architecture. ## The billing architecture is the mechanism, not the rate Chilime's per-unit rates (8.17/4.08) are not dramatically higher than the private IPP cap (8.40/4.80). The advantage comes from classification escape: Chilime's PPA categorizes output by "Regular" vs "Excess" rather than by season, allowing the vast majority of its generation to bill at the premium rate continuously. A private IPP cannot reclassify its monsoon output this way — the season determines the rate. ## Independent academic verification The Fenner School of Environment and Society (Australian National University), Nepal State of Knowledge Report — Renewables and PSH, independently documents this dynamic: "The major complaint of the rising IPPs is that the playing field is not level, that NEA as generator, transmitter and distributor gives preferential terms to its own projects compared to IPPs; and indeed, this is seen in the case of the Chilime hydropower company that is owned by the NEA and its staff." Citation: Fenner School of Environment and Society, ANU, Nepal State of Knowledge Report — Renewables and PSH, p. 20. URL: https://fennerschool.anu.edu.au/files/Nepal%20State%20of%20Knowledge%20Report%20-%20Renewables%20%26%20PSH.pdf. ## Legacy contract grandfathering Chilime's 1997 PPA remains fully active and has not been downgraded to match contemporary IPP standards. The ERC now vests with rate-setting authority and the 2026 Directive on reservoir-based PPAs transitions large projects to cost-plus determination, but legacy contracts like Chilime's are grandfathered — perpetually skewing the market's competitive balance. See chilime for the full PPA billing architecture and nea-triple-authority for the institutional framework. # Analytical links nea-triple-authority — the institutional conflict that pervades PPA rate-setting, dispatch, and enforcement chilime — the primary documented case of subsidiary PPA rate advantage sahas-urja — why the standard IPP rate only works at exceptional scale q-design-discharge — how design discharge determines contracted energy (the denominator of all PPA economics) ad-penalties — the penalty mechanism that compounds the PPA rate disadvantage
